stages.label: Absent
stages.desc: Nothing of the kind exists, and a dated source says so.

stages.label: Preparing
stages.desc: Announced, drafted, piloted: an intention with an instrument or a pilot behind it.

stages.label: Establishing
stages.desc: In service, but limited in scope, coverage or use.

stages.label: Operating
stages.desc: In service at scale: funded, regulated, used, maintained.

stages.label: Leading
stages.desc: Embedded: interoperable, measured, sustained; at or beyond the continental norm.

grey.label: Unplaced
grey.desc: Not staged: evidence found that meets no rung.

blank.label: No evidence
blank.desc: Not staged: nothing found states any fact the ladder tests.

topics.name: Public debate and participation in policymaking

indicators.label: Sustainable domestic financing of digital transformation
Sufficient energy and water for data centres
Robustness of government hardware and software
Local capacity to maintain, manage and develop government systems
Use of digital id in other systems
National maintenance of id and credentials systems
Interoperability of birth registration and digital id
Digitalisation of rural health clinics: HMIS
Digitalisation of rural health clinics: EMR
Use of AI in government administration
Use of AI in sectoral management information systems
Development of national / regional AI systems
Think tanks and academic departments contributing to DT policy
National strategy for development of statistics

gov.legislate--access-to-information-leg.label: Access to information legislation

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no access to information law and no draft of one. A right of access written in the constitution alone is not a law.

A bill or draft exists: published, validated, out for consultation, before cabinet or parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated. A law that is only announced, planned or called for does not count.
An access to information law is in force, however old: an act, ordinance or decree with the force of law that gives a right to ask public bodies for information.
The law has been put to work: a decree, regulation or order made under it, or its information commission or commissioner set up, or an existing body it names taking up the oversight.

The law has been applied in the past three years: a decision, order or penalty by the oversight body or a court, published figures of requests or complaints, or a rule made under the law. Training, an awareness campaign or an oversight body merely existing does not reach this stage.

gov.legislate--access-to-information-leg.norm: The African Commission's 2019 Declaration of Principles sets out a right of access to information, a duty to publish and an independent oversight body set up by law. Its 2013 Model Law on Access to Information is the template.

dpi.registry--address-register.label: Address register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says there is no national addressing system.
A national addressing policy is adopted, or street naming, numbering or digital addressing is under way in some cities.
An address register or digital addressing system is in service.
The addressing system covers the whole country, rural areas included.
The post, emergency services, utilities or other registers use the address system.

dpi.registry--address-register.norm: The Universal Postal Union's Addressing the World asks every country for a national addressing policy, an address for everyone and an address register other systems can use.

data.statistics--statistics-from-adminis.label: Statistics from administrative data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no official statistics are drawn from administrative records and no work towards them is under way.

Work is under way to draw statistics from administrative records: a register assessed, staff trained, a data-sharing agreement signed or a pilot, in the past three years. A plan only announced does not count.
Statistics derived from at least one administrative data source have been published in the past three years.
Statistics derived from at least one administrative data source have been published at least twice in the last three years.
Statistics derived from at least three administrative data sources have been published at least twice in the last three years.

data.statistics--statistics-from-adminis.norm: The African Charter on Statistics and SHaSA 2 ask each country to draw its official statistics from administrative records as well as censuses and surveys, civil registration first among them.

data.satellite--agricultural-use-of-sate.label: Agricultural use of satellite data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no farming service or institution uses satellite or remote-sensing data.
A ministry, agency or research institute used satellite or remote-sensing data in a farming study or pilot, or is preparing a service that will.
A government crop-monitoring, drought or locust early-warning, or land-use service using satellite data is in service, for part of the country or for one purpose.
Such a service publishes bulletins, maps or forecasts on a schedule.
A number of farmers, extension workers or districts receiving advice, alerts or insurance based on the service's satellite data is on record.

data.satellite--agricultural-use-of-sate.norm: The African Space Strategy asks that space-derived products be used for decision-making; the AU Digital Agriculture Strategy asks for remote sensing in monitoring and forecasting.

tech.ai--control-of-ai-abuse.label: Control of AI abuse

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no authority, rule or mechanism addresses harms from AI.
A bill, draft regulation or draft guideline addressing a harm from AI is published, or a draft provides for an authority over AI.
A law, decree, regulation or binding directive in force addresses a harm from AI, such as deepfakes, automated decisions or AI in elections.
A body is designated by law or decree with a mandate over AI harms or AI systems.
A dated enforcement, audit, takedown, penalty or redress decision about a harm from AI is on record.

tech.ai--control-of-ai-abuse.norm: The Continental AI Strategy asks for risk-based regulation, an independent oversight body with enforcement and redress, technical safety standards and a part in regional oversight.

tech.ai--use-of-ai-in-government-adminis.label: Use of AI in government administration

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no AI system is in use in public administration.
A government body has tendered, piloted or is testing an AI system for its own work or its services.
A government body uses an AI system in service, such as a chatbot for a public service or AI processing documents.
AI systems are in service in two or more government bodies, or one government-wide AI platform serves several.
The government has issued rules for its own use or purchase of AI, or published a register of its AI systems.

tech.ai--use-of-ai-in-government-adminis.norm: The Continental AI Strategy asks for AI adopted in the public sector under a governance framework, with innovation-friendly procurement and use cases shared and reported.

gov.legislate--ai-legislation-regulation.label: AI legislation / regulations

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no law or regulation on AI and no draft of one.
A bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI exists: published, out for consultation, or before cabinet or parliament. A law that is only announced or planned does not count.

A law, decree or regulation in force names AI and sets a rule for it, in one sector or for one use: AI in higher education, AI-generated content in the media or in elections. A strategy, ethics guidelines or a data protection law's general rule on automated decisions does not count.
A law on AI itself is in force and applies across sectors.
That law has been applied in the past three years: a regulation or order has been made under it, or the body it names has registered, licensed, decided or penalised.

gov.legislate--ai-legislation-regulation.norm: The African Union's Continental AI Strategy (2024) asks states to review and amend existing laws and put an enabling framework in place, with independent institutions to oversee it. It sets no date and requires no AI act.

tech.ai--use-of-ai-in-sectoral-managemen.label: Use of AI in sectoral management information systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no public sector's system uses AI.
An AI tool for a public health, education, agriculture, tax, customs or other sector's system is piloted, tested or being built.
An AI tool is in service in a public sector's system and producing outputs, such as diagnoses, risk scores, forecasts or notices.
AI tools are in service in the public systems of two or more sectors.
Measured results of a sectoral AI system in service are reported, such as cases detected, revenue recovered or accuracy.

tech.ai--use-of-ai-in-sectoral-managemen.norm: The Continental AI Strategy asks for AI adopted in the core sectors, with national centres of excellence or datasets supporting it and outcomes reported.

gov.policy--ai-strategy.label: AI strategy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national AI strategy and none is being written.

A national AI strategy, policy or roadmap is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has run out with no successor adopted. A task force appointed to write it counts. AI named as a priority in a digital strategy does not.
A national AI strategy is adopted and still running: approved by cabinet, or launched or issued by the head of state, the minister or the agency responsible. No body is yet named to carry it out.
The government has named a body to carry out the strategy: a council, office, agency, committee or ministry unit set up or named for it.

Public money has gone into carrying out the strategy in the past three years: a dated source names money allocated to it, or an action in it started with its funding named. How good the strategy is, is not judged.

gov.policy--ai-strategy.norm: The African Union's Continental AI Strategy (2024) says member states must develop national AI strategies, with strategies and governance structures due in its first phase, to 2026.

tech.ai--development-of-national-regiona.label: Development of national / regional AI systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no AI model, dataset or AI computing is developed or hosted in the country.
A national AI model, dataset or AI computing facility is being built, piloted, or planned with a named builder, funder or site.
An AI model built in the country is released, a dataset made for AI is published, or AI computing is in service.
A facility with GPUs or other AI accelerators is in service in the country.
National AI computing, models or datasets are open to researchers, startups or other countries, with users named or counted.

tech.ai--development-of-national-regiona.norm: The Continental AI Strategy asks that a country can manage its own data and AI, Local First: sovereign or regional computing, open national datasets and talent, taking part in continental AI infrastructure.

dpi.id--authentication.label: Authentication

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no digital authentication service exists; credentials are checked by eye.
A state-accepted authentication, e-signature or PKI service is authorised, contracted or piloted.
A state-accepted authentication service is in use for one purpose: a certification authority operating, or an online check of the ID for one system.
State-accepted authentication is used across services or channels: licensed trust service providers, a verification service used by several bodies, mobile ID.
People prove who they are online with a state-accepted mobile ID app, digital ID wallet or signed digital credentials in service.

dpi.id--authentication.norm: The African Union's interoperability framework and the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol ask for authentication and e-signature services in layers, up to remote authentication recognised across borders.

dpi.id--interoperability-of-birth-regist.label: Interoperability of birth registration and digital id
dpi.id--interoperability-of-birth-regist.short_label: Interoperability of birth registration and digital id

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the civil register and the ID system do not exchange records.
A link between the civil register and the ID system is planned, contracted or piloted, or one body is made responsible for both.
Records pass one way or for one event, such as births feeding the ID system, or one body holds both registers.
Births enrol people in the ID system and deaths retire their ID numbers.
A source from the past three years gives a figure for records exchanged, numbers retired on death or records reconciled.

dpi.id--interoperability-of-birth-regist.norm: The African Union's interoperability framework and the African ministers responsible for civil registration ask that civil registration, vital statistics and the ID system work as one, each event updating the others.

gov.policy--broadband-strategy.label: Broadband strategy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national broadband plan and none is being written.
A national broadband plan is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has ended with no successor adopted.

A national broadband plan is adopted by the government or the minister and its period has not ended. It may be part of a larger digital strategy or development plan that states broadband targets. No money tied to it is on record in the past three years.
Money has been committed to the plan in the past three years: a budget line, a universal service fund allocation or a financed programme that the source ties to the plan.
The plan is funded, and the government has published figures against the plan's own targets in the past three years. Whether the targets are met is not judged.

gov.policy--broadband-strategy.norm: The Broadband Commission's first target is a funded national broadband plan in every country by 2025. The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy sets the 2030 outcome: universal access at 6 Mb/s or more, at no more than one US cent a megabyte.

dpi.pay--b2b-and-b2g-functionality.label: B2B and B2G functionality

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says public procurement runs on paper.
An e-procurement system is procured, being built or piloted.
Government tenders are published or bid online through a system in service.
E-procurement runs from tender to award or payment, or is required of all public bodies.
A source from the past three years gives a figure for e-procurement: tenders, value or share of purchasing through it.

dpi.pay--b2b-and-b2g-functionality.norm: The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol asks states to enable electronic transactions, electronic invoicing and interoperable payments between businesses and with government.

dpi.registry--business-register.label: Business register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says business registration is on paper and held locally.
A digital business register is procured, its records are being digitised, or a one-stop registration counter has opened.
Online business registration is in service.
Registration gives a firm one number shared with the tax authority or social security.
The register holds the beneficial owners of every company in the country, and a firm's number is shared with tax or social security.

dpi.registry--business-register.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for an electronic business register, and the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol for the identity of firms to be recognised across borders.

data.statistics--censuses-and-surveys.label: Censuses and surveys

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no population census has been counted in ten years and none is being prepared.
A census is being prepared: mapping, a pilot, funding or a date set in the past three years. A census only promised does not count.
A population census has been counted in the past ten years, with no results out yet.
Preliminary or final results of that census have been published.
The census's results are out and a national household survey (DHS, MICS, living standards or labour force) has published results in the past three years.

data.statistics--censuses-and-surveys.norm: The African Charter on Statistics and SHaSA 2 ask each country to produce its core statistics from censuses and surveys; the UN's 2030 round asks for a population and housing census at least once every ten years.

dpi.pay--governance-role-of-central-bank.label: Governance role of central bank

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the central bank has no mandate over payment systems or e-money.
The central bank's payments mandate or e-money rules are being drafted, or it oversees payments by circular only.
The central bank licenses or authorises mobile money, e-money or payment service providers.
The central bank runs or oversees a national payment switch or interoperability arrangement in service.
The country is live on PAPSS: its banks or payment providers send and receive payments through it. Joining PAPSS, or a regional payment system, does not count.

dpi.pay--governance-role-of-central-bank.norm: The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol's annex on digital payments asks central banks to oversee payment systems, make them interoperate at home and across borders, and join the continent's Pan-African Payment and Settlement System.

dpi.registry--civil-register.label: Civil register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says civil registration is on paper with no digital register.
A digital civil registration system is procured, piloted or rolled out to some offices.
Births are registered in a digital system in service nationally.
Deaths are registered in the digital system, in service.
A source from the past three years puts the share of births registered in the digital system at 90% or more.

dpi.registry--civil-register.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy and the Africa Programme on Accelerated Improvement of CRVS ask for digital civil registration; the SDG target is every birth and 80% of deaths registered.

capacity.literacy--digital-literacy-civi.label: Digital literacy (civil service)

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says civil servants receive no digital-skills training.
A government body has launched, piloted or is preparing a digital-skills programme for civil servants, or held digital-skills courses for officials.
A government digital-skills programme, academy or learning platform for civil servants is in service and has trained a stated number of public servants.
The programme is open to or required of civil servants in all ministries, or has trained staff across most of government.
The share of the civil service that has completed digital-skills training is published, or the number trained beside the civil-service headcount.

capacity.literacy--digital-literacy-civi.norm: The AU Charter on the Principles of Public Service and Administration asks for systematic capacity development of public servants; the Digital Transformation Strategy asks for digital and data skills in state institutions.

gov.policy--data-storage-cloud-strategy.label: Data storage / cloud strategy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the government has no hosting or cloud policy and none is being written.

A government hosting or cloud policy is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has ended with no successor adopted. A data centre or government cloud with no policy behind it does not count.

A policy on where the state's data is hosted, or on how public bodies may use cloud, is adopted and in force. It may be a cloud-first policy, a circular, a hosting standard or part of a larger strategy or law. Where public bodies must host is not yet named.
The government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre in service that the policy tells them to use, or a published list of approved providers.
Public bodies have moved onto the named hosting in the past three years: a dated source names or counts the ministries or agencies that have. How good the policy is, is not judged.

gov.policy--data-storage-cloud-strategy.norm: The African Union's Data Policy Framework asks each state to set rules for hosting its own data, by category, and to build national or regional cloud capacity. Its Digital Transformation Strategy sets a target for hosting the continent's content on the continent.

dpi.pay--consumer-protection.label: Consumer protection

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services.
Consumer-protection rules for digital financial services are being drafted.
Consumer-protection or conduct rules covering digital financial services or digital lending are in force.
A financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit takes complaints about digital financial services.
A source from the past three years reports a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services under these rules.

dpi.pay--consumer-protection.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for consumer protection in digital financial services across disclosure, responsible lending, data privacy and dispute resolution.

infra.capacity--robustness-of-government.label: Robustness of government hardware and software

ladder.text: A source from 2023 or later says the government's finances are not run on a computer system.
A source from 2023 or later says the government budgets, accounts and pays through a computer system.
Tax collection and the civil-service payroll also run on computer systems, by sources from 2023 or later.
One of the three core systems went live on a new or upgraded system in the last three years.
The government has published an enterprise architecture or an inventory of its systems.

infra.capacity--robustness-of-government.norm: The African Charter on the Values and Principles of Public Service, Art. 8, asks that modern technologies support public service delivery; the Digital Transformation Strategy asks for mission-critical systems hosted to a standard.

dpi.pay--cross-border-functionality.label: Cross-border functionality

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no regulated cross-border digital payment channel exists.
A cross-border digital payment corridor is piloted or licensed, or rules for it are being drafted.
Cross-border mobile money or digital remittances through a named corridor are in service.
The country takes part in PAPSS or a regional payment system in service.
A source from the past three years gives a figure for cross-border digital payments through the country's corridors: volume, value or cost.

dpi.pay--cross-border-functionality.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy and the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System aim at a single African payments area, with cross-border mobile money regulated and costs brought down.

dpi.mis--customs.label: Customs

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says customs declarations are processed on paper.
A customs management system is procured, being installed, piloted at some posts or upgraded.
Customs declarations are lodged and processed in an automated system at the main port, airport or border posts.
A trade single window is in service, joining customs and other border agencies.

The customs system exchanges declaration or transit data electronically through a system open to every country of its regional economic community, such as ECOWAS's SIGMAT or the EAC single customs territory, even where not every member yet reciprocates.

dpi.mis--customs.norm: The AfCFTA Protocol on Trade in Goods asks for customs automation, a single window connecting border agencies and electronic exchange with trading partners.

infra.cybersec--national-cybersecurity-r.label: National cybersecurity readiness

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no cybersecurity strategy and no national cyber body or response team.
The country has adopted a national cybersecurity strategy, or created a national cyber agency or response team by law, decree or order.
The national body has handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.
The country has designated its critical information infrastructure, or bound the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.
The national body publishes a count of incidents it handled, for a quarter or more ending within the past two years.

infra.cybersec--national-cybersecurity-r.norm: The Malabo Convention, chapter III, asks each party for a national cybersecurity policy and strategy (Art. 24) and a body that governs cybersecurity (Art. 27). It sets no test of whether the body works.

gov.legislate--cybersecurity-legislation.label: Cybersecurity legislation

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no cybercrime or cybersecurity law and no bill for one.
A cybercrime or cybersecurity bill is drafted, before parliament or passed. No law is known to be in force.
A cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force, as an act of its own or as part of a penal or digital code. No use of it is on record in the past three years.
The law has been used in the past three years: a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty from the body it sets up. Who it was used against is not judged.
The law is used, and a count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under it is published for a period ending within the past two years.

gov.legislate--cybersecurity-legislation.norm: The Malabo Convention commits each party to legal measures against cybercrime: Article 25 on legislation and Articles 29 to 31 on the offences. It sets no test of whether a law is used.

infra.energy--sufficient-energy-and-wate.label: Sufficient energy and water for data centres
infra.energy--sufficient-energy-and-wate.short_label: Power and water for data centres

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says a data centre was stopped, delayed or rationed for want of power or water, or runs on diesel as its main supply.
A data centre in service has a secured power supply: two grid feeds, its own substation or line, or its own power plant.
Power is set aside for data centres: a signed supply contract, a plant built for them, or a tariff or zone in force.
A data centre in service states a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.6 or less, from the past three years.
A data centre in service publishes its water use, or states that its cooling uses no water, from the past three years.

infra.energy--sufficient-energy-and-wate.norm: The Smart Africa Data Center and Cloud Blueprint asks that data centres run on dual grid feeds with backup generation and report their power usage effectiveness.

infra.store--local-data-centre-capacity-.label: Local data centre capacity (all providers)
infra.store--local-data-centre-capacity-.short_label: Data centres for hire in service

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no data centre in the country rents space or computing to others.
A data centre in the country rents space, power or computing to other organisations.
One such data centre is Tier III or above.
Two or more such data centres are Tier III or above.
A global cloud provider sells its services from a cloud region in the country.

infra.store--local-data-centre-capacity-.norm: The Smart Africa Data Center and Cloud Blueprint asks every country for data centres built to recognised tiers, so that content and data can be hosted in Africa.

dpi.exchange--national-data-exchange-sys.label: National data exchange system

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says government systems have no data exchange platform between them.
A government data exchange platform is procured, being built or piloted between a few systems. A framework or law with no platform does not count.
The platform is in service, carrying data between two or more public bodies' systems.
Ten or more institutions, systems or services are connected to the platform, counted by a source from the past three years.
A source from the past three years gives a figure for the exchanges or transactions through the platform.

dpi.exchange--national-data-exchange-sys.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy and its interoperability framework ask for a secure exchange layer through which government systems reuse each other's data and registers.

gov.policy--data-governance-policy.label: Data governance policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national data policy and none is being written.

A national data policy, strategy or framework is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has run out with no successor. A draft validated at a workshop is still a draft. A tender to hire the writer, or a stated intention, does not count.

The government has adopted the policy and it has not run out: approved by cabinet, or launched or issued by the head of state, the minister or the agency responsible. A policy on sharing or managing data across the whole government counts; a data protection law or an open data policy does not. No body is yet named to carry it out.

A body is named to carry out the policy: a council, office, agency, committee, chief data officer or ministry unit set up or named for it. The ministry that wrote the policy being responsible for it in general does not count.

A rule or standard the policy called for has been issued in the past three years: a law, regulation, standard or guideline, such as one on classifying data or on sharing it between public bodies. How good the policy is, and whether it follows the African Union's framework, is not judged.

gov.policy--data-governance-policy.norm: The African Union's Data Policy Framework (2022) asks each member state to write a national data policy, put it into its own rules and institutions, and monitor it.

gov.policy--data-localisation-policies.label: Data localisation policies

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no rule that data must be kept in the country and none is being written.

A rule that data, or a named kind of data, must be stored or processed in the country is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one was repealed with no successor. A minister's stated intention with no drafting begun does not count, and nor does a data centre.

A rule is in force: a law, decree, regulation or regulator's directive that data, or a named kind of data, must be kept in the country. A rule on one kind of data counts; a condition on sending data abroad does not. No body is yet named to enforce it.
A body is named to enforce the rule: a regulator, agency or ministry unit that checks compliance or grants exemptions. A regulator that issued the rule for the bodies it licenses counts.

The rule has been applied in the past three years: a dated source names an organisation ordered to bring data into the country, penalised or exempted under it, or counts those that have moved data to comply. How wide the rule is, and whether the country should have one, is not judged.

gov.policy--data-localisation-policies.norm: The African Union's Data Policy Framework (2022) asks states to keep only certain kinds of data in the country. The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol (2024) says a state shall not require computing facilities to be in its territory, with exceptions for public policy.

gov.protect--data-protection-authority.label: Data protection authority

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no data protection authority, and no law in force names one.
A law names a data protection authority. No source says its head or members have been appointed.
The authority's head or members are appointed, or an existing body given the job is doing it. No ruling against a named organisation is on record in the past three years.
The authority has ruled against a named organisation in the past three years: a decision, fine or order. A court's judgment does not count.
The authority publishes a count of its decisions, fines or complaints settled, for a period of a quarter or more ending within the past two years.

gov.protect--data-protection-authority.norm: The Malabo Convention, Articles 11 and 12, commits each party to an independent authority with stated duties and powers. The African Union's Data Policy Framework asks for authorities that are "independent, funded, and effective".

gov.legislate--data-protection-legislati.label: Data protection legislation

ladder.text: A dated source states that the country has no general data protection law, and none is on record as enacted or in preparation.
A data protection law is announced, being drafted, before parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated.
A data protection law is enacted or in force, whether it stands alone or is part of a larger law. No decision under it is on record in the past three years.

The law is in force and has been applied: a dated sanction, order, decision or court judgment on a controller within the past three years. Without a constituted supervisory authority the stage is capped at 3.
The law has regulations in force under it, and a count of decisions, sanctions or complaints settled is published for a period ending within the past two years.

gov.legislate--data-protection-legislati.norm: The African Union's Malabo Convention: Article 8(1) commits each party to a legal framework for personal data, Article 13 sets the principles and Articles 16 to 19 the rights. It sets no test of whether a law is applied.

gov.protect--national-data-protection-re.label: National data protection readiness

ladder.text: No data protection law is in force: there is none, or it is still a bill or has not yet commenced.
A data protection law is in force. The country has not ratified the Malabo Convention and no authority is appointed.
A law is in force, and the country has ratified the Malabo Convention or appointed an authority. Nothing in the past three years shows the authority at work.
The law is being implemented: in the past three years an appointed authority has registered organisations, taken breach reports, issued guidance or inspected.
The authority is acting: in the past three years it has ruled against a named organisation, or it publishes a count of its rulings. A court's judgment does not count.

gov.protect--national-data-protection-re.norm: The African Union's Data Policy Framework (2022) asks each member state for a data protection law, an independent authority and working practice, and to ratify the Malabo Convention. It sets no measure of them.

gov.regional--cross-border-data-transfer.label: Cross-border data transfers

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no rule on sending personal data abroad and none is being written.

A rule on sending personal data, or a named kind of data, out of the country is being written: a bill or a published draft that sets a condition for it. A law passed but not reported in effect counts here. A stated intention with no drafting begun does not.

A rule is in force: a law, regulation or directive that lets data leave only on a condition, such as the receiving country's protection judged good enough, the authority's permission, the person's consent or a contract. A data protection law alone does not count, and nor does a rule that data must stay in the country.

The authority has published the means of complying: a list of countries data may go to, model contract terms, a procedure for applying for permission, or guidance on transfers. A procedure in the rule's own text, or guidance on the whole law, does not count.

The rule has been applied in the past three years: a dated source names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad, or gives a count of permissions. How strict the rule is, is not judged.

gov.regional--cross-border-data-transfer.norm: The Malabo Convention, Article 14, bars sending personal data outside the African Union unless the receiving country protects it adequately. The Data Policy Framework (2022) and the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol (2024) ask states to let data cross borders under stated safeguards.

include.divides--bridging-of-digital-div.label: Bridging of digital divides

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no programme brings internet access to rural areas.
The government or its universal service fund has launched, funded or is preparing a programme to bring internet access to rural or underserved areas.
A rural connectivity programme has connected a stated number of rural sites, towers, localities or people.
The share of people using the internet in rural areas and in urban areas is published, from a household survey or the statistics office.
Rural internet use is 80 per cent or more of the urban rate, from a household survey.

include.divides--bridging-of-digital-div.norm: The Digital Transformation Strategy asks for universal, equitable and affordable access for all people wherever they live; the ITU's 2030 targets ask for universal internet use.

gov.legislate--legislation-covering-digi.label: Legislation covering digital id

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national identity law and no bill for one.
A bill for a national identity law is drafted, before parliament or passed and not yet promulgated, or the identity system runs on a decree or order with no law behind it.

A national identity law is in force: a law, ordinance or decree-law that sets up the identity number, the register of persons or the identity card, however old. A data protection law, or a civil registration law that sets up no identity number or card, does not count.

The law in force provides for a digital identity: a biometric register, an identity number unique to each person, or an identity that can be checked electronically. A law for a paper card only does not reach this stage.

Rules have been made under that law in the past three years: a regulation or decree applying it, or a rule that banks, phone companies or public bodies must check identity against the system. Cards issued, people enrolled and changes to fees do not count.

gov.legislate--legislation-covering-digi.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy targets digital legal identity for 99.9% of people by 2030, and its Interoperability Framework for Digital ID asks for a harmonised legal framework. The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol, Article 14, commits each party to digital identity systems.

capacity.literacy--digital-literacy-gene.label: Digital literacy (general population)

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no programme teaches the public digital skills.
The government, alone or with partners, has launched, piloted or is preparing a programme to teach digital skills to the public.
A national digital-skills programme for the public is in service and has trained a stated number of people.
A measured share of adults or of the population with basic digital skills is published, from a survey.
A measured share of half or more of adults with basic digital skills is published.

capacity.literacy--digital-literacy-gene.norm: The Digital Transformation Strategy asks for 300 million Africans a year trained in e-skills; Agenda 2063's second ten-year plan asks for 80 per cent of primary completers digitally proficient by 2033.

geopol.sovereignty--digital-sovereignty.label: Digital sovereignty

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no policy or law governs where state data is held or who may process it.
The government adopted, published or announced a strategy, plan or draft rule to keep government data or systems under national control.
A law, decree or policy in force classifies government data or requires named categories of data to be held in the country.
Government data or a core system is hosted in a government or nationally owned data centre or cloud in the country.
A government contract or agreement with a foreign provider or partner includes terms on data jurisdiction, portability, exit or handing over source code.

geopol.sovereignty--digital-sovereignty.norm: The AU Data Policy Framework asks for localisation of certain categories of data only, with portability so that no one is locked into a single provider; the Digital Transformation Strategy asks for 30 per cent of content hosted in Africa by 2030.

gov.policy--digital-transformation-strat.label: Digital transformation strategy

ladder.text: A dated source states that the country has no national digital strategy, and none is on record as adopted, launched or in preparation.
A national digital strategy is announced, being drafted, or validated and awaiting adoption. Or one is adopted and its text is not public. Or its period has ended and a successor is in preparation.

A national digital strategy is adopted, its text is public, and its period has not ended. A text the government has published, and no source calls a draft, counts as adopted. A strategy with no stated period stops here.

The strategy has a delivery plan with dated actions or costs, and the government has published results against its own targets within the past three years. Without a mandated body and a domestic budget line the stage is capped at 3.
The delivery plan is costed, and results against the strategy's targets are published on every pillar within the past two years.

gov.policy--digital-transformation-strat.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy for Africa 2020-2030 asks states to "develop and implement national and sectorial digital strategies".

include.access--inclusion-of-persons-wit.label: Inclusion of persons with disabilities

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no law or policy addresses access to information or digital services for persons with disabilities.
A government body has drafted, launched or is preparing a law, policy, standard or programme to make information or digital services accessible to persons with disabilities.
A law, regulation, policy or standard in force requires public information, websites or digital services to be accessible to persons with disabilities.
A government body delivered accessible digital services, assistive technology or devices to persons with disabilities, or made public websites or broadcasts accessible.
The results of an audit or survey of how accessible public websites or digital services are to persons with disabilities are published.

include.access--inclusion-of-persons-wit.norm: The AU Disability Protocol asks for public information in accessible formats and technologies and for affordable devices; the UN CRPD asks the same of states.

finance.budget--sustainable-domestic-fin.label: Sustainable domestic financing of digital transformation
finance.budget--sustainable-domestic-fin.short_label: The state's own money for digital programmes

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the state budget gives no money to digital programmes, or that they are paid for wholly by donors and lenders.
In the past three years the state budget gave money to a digital ministry, a digital agency or a named digital programme. A line paid wholly by a loan or grant does not count.
That money was higher in the latest budget than in the one before, in the country's own currency and not adjusted for inflation. Lower or the same holds a country at stage 2, whatever else it has.

In the past three years a fund, levy or tax assigned by law to digital programmes was created, collected money or paid for a project, or the government put state money to a digital programme it had said the country must pay for itself. A fund abolished, or held only in an old law, does not count.
A budget execution report, settlement law, audited accounts or the fund's own account gives what was actually spent, for a year from 2024.

finance.budget--sustainable-domestic-fin.norm: Agenda 2063, Goal 20, asks that Africa finance its own development. The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy proposes a digital sovereignty fund and calls for universal service funds to be put to use. Neither sets a share of the budget for digital programmes.

gov.legislate--e-commerce-legislation.label: E-commerce legislation

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no law on electronic transactions or e-commerce and no draft of one.
A bill or draft exists: published, out for consultation, before cabinet or parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated. A law that is only announced or planned does not count.

A law is in force that gives electronic contracts, records or signatures legal effect, or sets rules for selling online, however old. A law on electronic signatures alone counts, as does the part of a digital code or consumer protection law that does this job.
A decree, regulation or order has been made under the law: on electronic signatures, on those who certify them, or on those who sell online.

The law has been applied in the past three years: a provider of electronic signatures accredited or licensed under it, online sellers registered or licensed, or an order or penalty made. A government office using electronic signatures does not reach this stage.

gov.legislate--e-commerce-legislation.norm: The Malabo Convention, Chapter I, sets rules for electronic commerce, contracts and advertising. The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol commits each party to a legal framework for electronic transactions (Article 16) and to protecting those who buy online (Article 27).

dpi.exchange--interoperability-of-educat.label: Interoperability of education systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country's education systems exchange no data.
A link between two education systems is contracted, being built or piloted.
Two education systems exchange data in use: the EMIS with the examinations body, teacher payroll or learner registration.
Learners carry a unique identifier used by two or more education systems.
Learner records are linked to the national ID, civil registration, health or social protection.

dpi.exchange--interoperability-of-educat.norm: The African Union's Digital Education Strategy asks for an individual, identifier-based education management information system linked to the national ID and other sectors.

dpi.mis--education.label: Education

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says there is no education management information system.
The education ministry procured, piloted or is building an education management information system.
The ministry collected or published an annual school census or education statistics through its education information system.
The system holds individual learner records with a unique learner number, in service for schools across the country.
Learner records are linked to the national ID or birth registration number, or exchange data with another government system.

dpi.mis--education.norm: The AU Digital Education Strategy asks for education management information systems to move from aggregate school returns to records for each learner, teacher and school.

dpi.govtech--e-government-services.label: e-government services

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no government service is available online.
The government launched a services portal or app, or piloted a service that can be applied for or paid online.
Ten or more government services can be completed online.
One national portal or app carries services of several ministries, with sign-in by the national ID or one shared account.
A number of users, applications or transactions through the national portal is published.

dpi.govtech--e-government-services.norm: The Digital Transformation Strategy asks for a single digital gateway carrying government services to citizens, businesses and government; the AU Public Service Charter asks for modern technologies in service delivery.

dpi.registry--electoral-register.label: Electoral register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the voters' roll is compiled by hand for each poll.
A digital or biometric voter register is procured or piloted.
A digital or biometric voter register is in service.
The roll was published or open to voters to check, online, by text message or at centres.
The voters' roll is drawn from or checked against the national ID, population or civil register.

dpi.registry--electoral-register.norm: The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance and the AU's election observation guidelines ask for an accurate voters' roll, open to public inspection and kept up to date.

include.access--citizen-participation-in.label: Citizen participation in policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says laws and policies are adopted with no public consultation and no way for citizens to take part.
A ministry, parliament or regulator posted a named draft law, policy or regulation online for public comment, or ran an online consultation or survey on one.
A government consultation portal, e-petition system or online platform for comments on drafts is in service and open to the public for more than one draft.
The government published the comments it received in an online consultation, a report of one, or its answer to them.
A consultation was held online because a law, decree or published procedure requires drafts to be put online for public comment.

include.access--citizen-participation-in.norm: The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance asks for citizen participation in the development process; the UN E-Participation Index measures it online.

infra.connect--internet-exchange-points.label: Internet exchange points

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no internet exchange point operates in the country.
An exchange point is in service: networks hand each other traffic there directly, whoever runs it.
A global content network such as Google, Meta, Akamai, Netflix or Cloudflare has a cache at the exchange or peers there.
The exchange's traffic is shown growing: figures at two dates a year or more apart, the later higher and from the past three years.
The exchange reaches beyond one city: a second exchange or point of presence in another city, or operators from other countries peering there.

infra.connect--internet-exchange-points.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy and its African Internet Exchange System ask every country for an exchange point that keeps local traffic local and links to the region.

include.access--citizen-feedback-portals.label: Citizen feedback portals

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says people have no digital channel to complain about or comment on public services.
A government body has launched, piloted or is preparing a web portal, app or messaging service through which people report problems with or complain about public services.
A digital complaints or feedback channel is in service and a number of complaints, reports or cases it has received or handled is on record.
A national channel takes complaints about the services of most ministries or of local governments, or routes them to the bodies responsible across government.
The share of complaints resolved, response times, or a report of the cases and what was done about them is published.

include.access--citizen-feedback-portals.norm: The AU Charter on Decentralisation asks that ICT be used so residents can give feedback to their representatives; the UN E-Participation Index ranks e-information, e-consultation and e-decision-making.

infra.connect--national-fibre-backbone.label: National fibre backbone

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national fibre backbone, and nothing later says one is being built.
In the past three years a national fibre backbone has been put under contract or works have begun. A plan, a study, a tender or money promised does not count.
Backbone fibre is in service between the capital and at least one other region, whoever owns it: the state, a utility or an operator.
A source states that the backbone reaches every province or region.
The backbone reaches every province or region, and other operators buy capacity on it, or it runs on open-access or wholesale terms.

infra.connect--national-fibre-backbone.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy and its Programme for Infrastructure Development in Africa ask each state to build a national backbone that reaches every region and to share it among operators.

dpi.pay--g2p-functionality.label: G2P functionality

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says government payments to people are made in cash.
A government programme is piloting or has contracted digital payment to people.
A government social transfer, salary or pension is paid digitally, in service.
Two or more of social transfers, civil service salaries and pensions are paid digitally.
A source from the past three years says government payments to people are checked against the national ID or a social registry.

dpi.pay--g2p-functionality.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks governments to digitise government-to-person payments.

include.access--gender-equity.label: Gender equity

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2023 or later, puts the gender gap in internet use above 30 per cent.
The gender gap in internet use is 30 per cent or less, in the latest figure for 2023 or later, from ITU's series or a national household survey.
The gender gap in internet use is 20 per cent or less.
The gender gap in internet use is 10 per cent or less.
The gender gap in internet use is 2 per cent or less: parity.

include.access--gender-equity.norm: The Maputo Protocol asks for women's access to and control of information technologies on equal terms; the Digital Transformation Strategy asks for digital skills for women and girls.

infra.energy--grid-reliability.label: Grid reliability

ladder.text: The latest count, for 2023 or later, is more than ten power outages a month.

The power goes off ten times a month or fewer, in the latest count for 2023 or later: the regulator's or utility's interruption frequency divided by 12 where one is published, otherwise the outages firms report in the World Bank's Enterprise Surveys.
Five times a month or fewer.
Twice a month or fewer.
Once a month or less. A count of grid collapses, hours of load shedding or how long outages last is never used at any stage.

infra.energy--grid-reliability.norm: The African Union's single electricity market and Continental Power System Master Plan ask for secure, reliable and affordable electricity across the continent. They set no outage figure.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.label: Digitalisation of rural health clinics: HMIS

ladder.text: A dated source states that routine health reporting is not entered digitally at any level of the health system.

A digital reporting system is used by hospitals only or in some districts, or a national rollout is contracted or being prepared: staff trained, equipment delivered or an agreement signed. Primary clinics do not use it, beyond pilot sites.
A national system takes the clinics' reports, which are keyed in at district level from the clinics' paper forms. A minority of primary clinics enter their own reports, or no figure is published.
More than half of primary clinics enter their own reports at the facility, on a published share or count of primary clinics alone; a share of all health facilities does not settle it.
At least 90 per cent of primary clinics enter their own reports at the facility, on a figure published within the past two years. Reporting completeness is published as well.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.norm: Africa CDC's Digital Transformation Strategy (2023) and PHC Digitalisation Framework (2025–26): 100,000 facilities connected by 2030 and 90 per cent digitally enabled primary care by 2035.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.label: Digitalisation of rural health clinics: EMR

ladder.text: A dated source states that patient records are kept on paper at every level of the health system.

Electronic patient records are in use in some hospitals or pilot facilities, or a national system is procured or being prepared: staff trained, equipment delivered or an agreement signed. Primary clinics do not use them, beyond pilot sites.

Electronic patient records are in use in most hospitals, or in primary clinics in some districts, but each record stays in the facility that made it. A minority of primary clinics use them, or no figure is published.
More than half of primary clinics keep electronic patient records, entered at the point of care. Each record is held under a unique patient identifier and can be retrieved at another facility.
At least 90 per cent of primary clinics keep such shared records, on a figure published within the past two years. A record can be retrieved anywhere in the public network.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.norm: Africa CDC's Digital Transformation Strategy (2023) and PHC Digitalisation Framework (2025–26): 100,000 facilities connected by 2030 and 90 per cent digitally enabled primary care by 2035.

dpi.exchange--interoperability-of-health.label: Interoperability of health systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country's health systems do not exchange data.
An exchange between health systems is contracted, being built or piloted, or a health information exchange is being set up.
Two or more health systems exchange data in routine use, such as the HMIS with patient records, a laboratory or supply-chain system.
Three or more health systems exchange data, or a national health information exchange is in service.
Patient records are linked across systems through the national ID or a national unique health identifier.

dpi.exchange--interoperability-of-health.norm: Africa CDC's health information exchange guidelines and Smart Africa's digital health blueprint ask for a national exchange policy, common standards and identifiers, then exchanges in service across the health system.

dpi.mis--health.label: Health

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says health reporting is on paper and there is no national health information system.
The health ministry procured, piloted or is rolling out a health management information system, or one is in use in some districts.
A national health management information system is in service, with facilities or districts across the country reporting through it.
The system is linked to, or exchanges data with, disease surveillance, the medicines supply chain, or a patient or immunisation register.
The reporting completeness or timeliness of the national system is published.

dpi.mis--health.norm: The Africa CDC Digital Transformation Strategy asks for national digital health systems strengthened to its Health Information Exchange Guidelines, with integrated surveillance.

capacity.training--graduates-entering-dt.label: Graduates entering DT ecosystem

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2023 or later, puts employment in information and communication below 0.3 per cent of all employment.
Information and communication employs 0.3 per cent or more of all workers, in the latest figure for 2023 or later, from ILOSTAT's series.
Information and communication employs 0.6 per cent or more of all workers.
Information and communication employs 1 per cent or more of all workers.
Information and communication employs 1 per cent or more of all workers, and youth unemployment is 14 per cent or less on the national labour force survey.

capacity.training--graduates-entering-dt.norm: Agenda 2063's second ten-year plan asks for 40 per cent of graduates in STEM and youth unemployment down to 14 per cent by 2033; the Continental TVET Strategy asks for wider technical training.

tech.industry--national-capacity-in-dt-r.label: National capacity in DT-related production

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2023 or later, puts ICT service exports below 0.05 per cent of GDP.
ICT service exports are 0.05 per cent of GDP or more in the latest figure, for 2023 or later, from the World Bank's series.
ICT service exports are 0.2 per cent of GDP or more.
ICT service exports are 0.5 per cent of GDP or more.
ICT service exports are 0.5 per cent of GDP or more, and a plant assembling or making phones, computers or other ICT equipment is in production in the country.

tech.industry--national-capacity-in-dt-r.norm: The Digital Transformation Strategy's digital industry pillar asks for ICT assembling and manufacturing plants and growing ICT exports; STISA-2034 asks for technology-based production.

gov.policy--ict-strategy.label: ICT strategy

ladder.text: A dated source states that the country has no ICT or telecommunications sector policy, none is on record as adopted or in preparation, and no national digital strategy is held.
A sector policy is announced, being drafted, or validated and awaiting adoption. Or one is adopted and its text is not public. Or its period has ended and a successor sector policy is in preparation.
A sector policy is adopted, its text is public, and its period has not ended. A policy with no stated period stops here. A national digital strategy is assessed on its own row and does not count.

The policy has a delivery plan with dated actions or costs, and the government has published results against the policy's own targets within the past three years. Without a mandated body and a domestic budget line the stage is capped at 3.
The delivery plan is costed, and results against the policy's targets are published on every objective within the past two years.

gov.policy--ict-strategy.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy for Africa 2020-2030 asks states for "national and sectorial digital strategies". It names the subject and sets no measure.

dpi.id--registration-of-entire-populatio.label: Registration of entire population

ladder.text: A source from the past three years counts fewer than a third of the population holding a national ID.
A source from the past three years counts a third of the population or more holding a national ID.
A source from the past three years counts two-thirds of the population or more holding a national ID.
A source from the past three years counts 99.9% of the population or more holding a national ID.
A source from the past three years puts birth registration at all births and death registration at 80% or more.

dpi.id--registration-of-entire-populatio.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy sets a target of 99.9% of people in Africa holding a digital legal identity by 2030, from birth.

dpi.id--digital-id-from-birth.label: Digital id from birth

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says a birth creates no identity record: registration and ID are separate, or registration is on paper only.
A law or programme provides for a unique ID number at birth, or it is piloted in some districts or facilities.
Children receive a unique ID number when their birth is registered, in at least part of the country.
Every birth registered in the country receives the number, the birth record creating the identity record.
Birth registration reaches all births, each given the number, and death registration 80% or more.

dpi.id--digital-id-from-birth.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for a digital legal identity for every person from birth, through civil registration; the SDG target is all births and 80% of deaths registered.

dpi.id--national-maintenance-of-id-and-c.label: National maintenance of id and credentials systems
dpi.id--national-maintenance-of-id-and-c.short_label: National maintenance of id and credentials systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says a foreign supplier builds, hosts and runs the national ID system, with no national capacity.
National operation of the ID system is a stated goal, or a transfer of skills is announced, while a supplier still runs it.
The national authority operates the ID system day to day, even on a platform built abroad.
The authority's own staff or a national company maintain and upgrade the ID system, or the foreign contract has ended.
The ID system in service runs on code the state owns: built in-house, on open source such as MOSIP, or with the code handed over.

dpi.id--national-maintenance-of-id-and-c.norm: The African Union's interoperability framework asks that countries own and operate their identity systems on open standards, with no vendor lock-in and sustainable finance.

dpi.id--use-by-other-systems.label: Use by other systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says public registers do not use the national ID number.
A public register's adoption of the national ID number is planned or piloted.
A public register uses the national ID number: the electoral roll drawn from it, the tax register, payroll or a social registry.
Three or more of the electoral, tax, social protection, civil service payroll and business registers use the number.
A source from the past three years gives a figure from checking a register against the ID: ghost workers removed, duplicates found.

dpi.id--use-by-other-systems.norm: The African Union's interoperability framework and Data Policy Framework ask that the national ID be the single source of truth for identity across public registers.

dpi.id--robustness-of-system.label: Robustness of system

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says there is no national ID system, or only a paper one with no unique number.
A national ID system is procured, being built or piloted, or is ready and waiting on its law.
The national ID system is in service, issuing each person a unique number or credential.
The system checks fingerprints, face or iris to stop one person enrolling twice.
A source from the past three years reports a security certification, a published audit or a level of assurance set for the system.

dpi.id--robustness-of-system.norm: The African Union's interoperability framework asks that a national ID system have technical integrity: unique identities, defined levels of assurance and security baselines that others can trust.

dpi.exchange--use-of-digital-id-in-other.label: Use of digital id in other systems
dpi.exchange--use-of-digital-id-in-other.short_label: Use of digital ID in other systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no other system checks people against the national ID.
Another system's use of the national ID is contracted, being built or piloted: a SIM-registration link, a bank's KYC check, a social programme's enrolment.
A service in use checks people against the national ID: SIM registration, a bank's or mobile money provider's KYC, a social programme, health insurance.
Services in two or more sectors check people against the national ID, shown by sources from the past three years.
A source from the past three years gives a figure for verifications made against the ID, or counts the services relying on it.

dpi.exchange--use-of-digital-id-in-other.norm: The African Union's interoperability framework and the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol ask that a national digital ID be the credential other public and private services rely on, recognised across borders.

infra.connect--international-internet-ba.label: International internet bandwidth
infra.connect--international-internet-ba.short_label: Fibre routes to the rest of the world

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no international fibre route: satellite or microwave only.
One fibre route carries the country's internet traffic abroad: a submarine cable landing in the country, or a fibre link through a neighbour.
Two or more international fibre routes are in service, though they share one landing station or one neighbour.
Two of the routes share no landing station: cables at different stations, a cable and a land link, or for a country without a coast, links through two neighbours.
Two independent routes, and other operators buy capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or it runs on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

infra.connect--international-internet-ba.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks every member state for at least two international connections, and for operators to share infrastructure.

gov.standards--adoption-of-international.label: Adoption of international standards
gov.standards--adoption-of-international.short_label: International standards for information technology and data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country belongs to no international standards organisation.

The country's standards body is a member of ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, or of IEC, its counterpart for electrical technology. Full, correspondent and subscriber members all count. Membership of the African or a regional standards organisation does not.

The country has adopted an international standard on information technology or data as a national standard: a named ISO, IEC or ITU standard on information technology, information security, software or data. A count of adopted standards that names none, a draft, and a standard in another field do not count.

Public bodies must meet a named international standard: a law, decree, regulation, directive or circular names an international standard on information technology or data and requires ministries, agencies or government systems to meet it. A rule for one sector, a text modelled on a standard, and a system built to one do not count.

The country has taken part in writing international standards on information technology in the past three years: a dated source names the standards body or a public body as a participating member, chair or secretariat of an ISO or IEC committee on information technology or data. An observer seat does not count.

gov.standards--adoption-of-international.norm: The AfCFTA annex on technical barriers to trade, Article 6(2), commits its parties to adopt or adapt international standards, and the African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for rules in line with international norms. Neither names the standards.

infra.connect--internet-usage.label: Internet usage

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2024 or later, shows fewer than a quarter of the population using the internet.

At least a quarter of the population uses the internet: 25 per cent or more in the latest figure, for 2024 or later. A national survey, census or government figure for a share of people is used where one is held, otherwise the International Telecommunication Union's estimate.
At least half use it: 50 per cent or more.
At least four in five use it: 80 per cent or more.
Nearly everyone uses it: 95 per cent or more. Counts of subscriptions, regulators' and operators' user counts, and figures for adults only, are never used at any stage.

infra.connect--internet-usage.norm: The African Union's Agenda 2063 plan asks that broadband reach 80 per cent of the population by 2033. The International Telecommunication Union's 2030 target is that everyone aged 15 and over uses the internet.

gov.policy--data-interoperability-framew.label: Data interoperability framework / roadmap

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the government has no interoperability framework and none is being written.

A framework, standard or regulation for how government systems exchange data is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has ended with no successor adopted. An exchange platform with no framework behind it does not count, and nor does interoperability named only as an aim.

A framework for how government systems exchange data is adopted and published. It may be an interoperability framework, a standard, a decree or part of a larger law. No instrument yet makes it compulsory and names who enforces it.
Public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

Public bodies are following the framework in the past three years: a dated source names or counts the ministries, agencies or systems that exchange data under it or are certified as meeting it. How good the framework is, is not judged.

gov.policy--data-interoperability-framew.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for an interoperability framework with implementing acts. Its Data Policy Framework asks for open data standards, and its interoperability framework for open standards with no dependence on one supplier.

gov.legislate--legislation-enabling-data.label: Legislation enabling data interoperability

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no law or decree on public bodies sharing data with each other and no draft of one.

A bill, draft decree or draft regulation on public bodies sharing data is published, before parliament or cabinet, or passed and not yet in force. An executive order that legislation is to replace stops here.

A law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force, however old. An interoperability framework counts where it is issued as a decree or regulation. A law for one sector, or a data protection law, does not count.

The law in force requires public bodies to share: to exchange data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds. A law that only allows sharing does not reach this stage.
The law has been applied in the past three years: a regulation, decree or order has been made under it, or public bodies are named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

gov.legislate--legislation-enabling-data.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for an interoperability framework with implementing acts, and the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol, Article 19, for mutual recognition of electronic authentication. No African Union instrument requires a data sharing law.

gov.standards--national-interoperability.label: National interoperability standards

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the government has no technical standards for its systems to exchange data and none are being written.

Standards are being written: a named set of technical standards for government systems to exchange data is being drafted or is out for consultation. An unapproved edition counts here. A mandate or a stated intention to write standards does not.

Standards are published: the government, the agency responsible or the standards body has issued the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols its systems must use. An interoperability framework counts only where a source says it sets technical standards. Standards for one sector or one function do not count.

Public bodies are required to use the standards: a law, decree, regulation or circular makes them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy. A text that says of itself that it is compulsory does not count.

A system has been checked against the standards in the past three years: a dated source names a public body, system or product tested, audited or certified against them, or gives a count. How good the standards are is not judged.

gov.standards--national-interoperability.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for technical standards, built on open standards, for checking identity in dealings between government, business and citizens. Its interoperability framework names international ones.

infra.capacity--local-capacity-to-mainta.label: Local capacity to maintain, manage and develop government systems

ladder.text: A source from 2023 or later says a government body relies on outside suppliers or outside help to run its systems.
A source from 2023 or later says government's own staff run or maintain one of its systems.
A government agency or state company builds, hosts or runs systems for the rest of government, by a source from 2023 or later.
A system built by government staff, not a contractor, went live in the last three years.
Three or more of the government's systems are run, maintained and changed by its own staff, with no contractor doing the work, by a source from the past three years.

infra.capacity--local-capacity-to-mainta.norm: The African Charter on the Values and Principles of Public Service, Art. 21, asks for systematic capacity development across the public service; the Digital Transformation Strategy asks for skills built in state institutions.

dpi.mis--justice.label: Justice

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says court proceedings and records are on paper with no case management system.
A case management or e-justice system is procured, piloted in some courts or being built.
A case management system is in service in some courts or one tier.
Lawyers or litigants can file cases or documents with the courts online.
Court decisions are published online or the public can look up a case's status online.

dpi.mis--justice.norm: The African Commission's Fair Trial Principles ask for systems recording proceedings and storing court information, with public access to decisions.

dpi.mis--land.label: Land

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says land transactions, valuation and planning are run on paper.
A land information or land administration system is procured, piloted in some regions or being built.
Transfers, registrations or mortgages are processed in a land information system in service, in some areas at least.
The system joins land records with the cadastre's survey maps or with property valuation.
Land or property tax, stamp duty or rates are assessed or paid through, or from, the land system.

dpi.mis--land.norm: The AU Framework and Guidelines on Land Policy asks for a computerised land information system through which rights are registered and tracked across the administration's functions.

dpi.registry--land-register.label: Land register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says land rights are recorded on paper or not recorded.
Titles are being digitised or a digital cadastre or land information system is under way in some areas.
A digital title register, cadastre or land information system is in service for part of the country.
The digital land register is in service nationally or in all land offices.
Land searches, title applications or transfers can be made online.

dpi.registry--land-register.norm: The AU Framework and Guidelines on Land Policy asks for land rights, customary tenure included, to be registered and tracked in a computerised land information system with public access.

digital.localgov--ict-infrastructure-for.label: ICT infrastructure for local government

ladder.text: A dated source states that local government offices have no connection of their own. Staff working on their own phones or modems does not change this.
