A programme to connect local government offices is being prepared or piloted: equipment handed over, a contract signed or pilot offices connected. Or only the capital city or the regions above are connected.

Some local government offices outside the capital are connected, past any pilot, or work in a national system. They are a minority, or no share of local governments is published. A share equipped or covered by a programme, however high, places here.
More than half of local governments have a connection provided to the office by the state or the authority. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.

At least 90 per cent of local governments are connected and work in national systems over the connection, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural local governments.

digital.localgov--ict-infrastructure-for.norm: The African Union's decentralisation charter (2014), Article 16(2): local governments "shall be provided with the required human, financial and technological resources", and ICT "shall be made accessible and effectively used".

digital.localgov--digitalisation-of-loca.label: Digitalisation of local government records

ladder.text: A dated source states that local governments keep their revenue records on paper, with no system in use.
A system is being prepared or piloted, or a one-off survey has built a register with no system to keep it. Or only the capital city or the regions above record digitally.

Some local governments outside the capital record payments in a system, past any pilot. They are a minority, or no share is published. Electronic receipts with no register of payers place here, and so does a share given a system or trained on it, however high.
More than half of local governments keep a digital register of their payers, with each bill and payment against it. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of local governments keep that register in a national or shared system, on a figure published within the past two years.

digital.localgov--digitalisation-of-loca.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks states to "establish electronic government registers or digitalise existing ones" and to let organisations "reuse core registers". Its decentralisation charter, Article 16, covers local government's technology.

data.satellite--meteorological-use-of-sa.label: Meteorological use of satellite data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the national weather service receives no satellite data.
The national meteorological service has a satellite receiving station or data stream installed, contracted or being upgraded.
The national meteorological service uses satellite data in its forecasts or nowcasting.
The national meteorological service issues early warnings or impact-based forecasts that draw on satellite data.
The national meteorological service holds ISO 9001 certification for its services.

data.satellite--meteorological-use-of-sa.norm: The Integrated African Strategy on Meteorology asks for sustained access to geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites, WMO's observing standards and ISO 9001 certification for every national weather service.

infra.connect--mobile-affordability.label: Mobile affordability
infra.connect--mobile-affordability.short_label: The price of mobile data against income

ladder.text: The newest figure, for 2024 or later, puts 5 GB of mobile data for a month above 10 per cent of average monthly income.

5 GB of mobile data for a month costs 10 per cent of average monthly income or less, on the newest figure for 2024 or later. Any dated, documented figure counts: a stated share of income, or a stated price set against World Bank income per person.
It costs 5 per cent or less.
It costs 2 per cent or less, the international target.
It costs 1 per cent or less. Promotional, daily and weekly bundles, plans sold with voice, and price floors are never used at any stage.

infra.connect--mobile-affordability.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks that access cost no more than one US cent a megabyte by 2030. The Broadband Commission's target, carried by the International Telecommunication Union, is entry-level broadband under 2 per cent of monthly income per person.

infra.connect--mobile-penetration.label: Mobile penetration
infra.connect--mobile-penetration.short_label: People who own a mobile phone

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2024 or later, shows fewer than half of people aged 10 and over owning a mobile phone.

At least half of people aged 10 and over own a mobile phone: 50 per cent or more in the latest figure, for 2024 or later. A national survey or census is used where one is held, otherwise the International Telecommunication Union's estimate.
At least two in three own one: 65 per cent or more.
At least four in five own one: 80 per cent or more.
Nearly everyone owns one: 95 per cent or more. Counts of SIM cards and subscribers, and figures for adults only, are never used at any stage.

infra.connect--mobile-penetration.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks that every person be digitally empowered by 2030, with a device costing no more than USD 100. The International Telecommunication Union's 2030 target is that everyone aged 15 and over owns a mobile phone.

infra.store--local-data-centre-capacity-.label: Local data centre capacity (national providers)
infra.store--local-data-centre-capacity-.short_label: Nationally owned data centres for hire

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no data centre for hire in the country is nationally owned.
A data centre owned by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned in the country rents space, power or computing to others.
One such nationally owned data centre is Tier III or above.
Two or more nationally owned data centres for hire are Tier III or above.
Two at Tier III or above, and the government's own systems or data are hosted in a nationally owned data centre in the country.

infra.store--local-data-centre-capacity-.norm: The African Union's Data Policy Framework asks that national providers hold data centre capacity and that the state's sensitive data be hosted under national jurisdiction.

finance.new--mobilisation-of-non-state-f.label: Mobilisation of non-state finance

ladder.text: A source from 2024 or later says no private money has gone into the country's digital businesses, or that investors have withdrawn.

From 2024 on, a named amount was lent to, invested in, guaranteed for or granted to a private digital business, fund or partnership in the country, or a company said what it was investing there itself. Money to the state, and memoranda and plans, do not count.
Such amounts were signed or started in two different years from 2024. Two in one year hold a country at stage 2, whatever else it has.

From 2024 on, a named amount came from a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of the country itself, or was raised by a bond or share issue on the country's own market. The state's own funds do not count.

From 2024 on, the government signed a public-private partnership, concession or joint venture in which the private partner puts a named amount into a public digital project, or private investors paid into a state fund.

finance.new--mobilisation-of-non-state-f.norm: Agenda 2063, Goal 20, asks that Africa's capital markets carry a growing share of its development. The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy calls for private investment in digital infrastructure, and Smart Africa set an ambition of USD 300 billion. None sets a country figure.

infra.store--off-site-backup-capacity.label: Off-site backup capacity

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says government systems have no off-site backup or disaster-recovery site.
A ministry, agency or the central bank keeps its systems or data at a backup site in service, 200 km or more from its main site or abroad.
A backup site 200 km or more away serves the government's shared systems: the national data centre or government cloud.
A recovery plan or a failover test from the past three years is on record for that backup site.
The government's main data centre and its backup site are both Tier III or above.

infra.store--off-site-backup-capacity.norm: The Smart Africa Data Center and Cloud Blueprint asks that e-government run on a Tier-classified primary site with a secondary site for disaster recovery.

gov.policy--open-data-policy.label: Open data policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no open data policy and none is being written.

An open data policy, strategy, decree or law is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has run out with no successor. A draft validated at a workshop is still a draft. A portal with no policy behind it, or a commitment in an open government action plan, does not count.

The government has adopted the policy and it has not run out: approved by cabinet, or launched or issued by the head of state, the minister or the agency responsible. The open data part of a wider data policy counts where a source says it sets the rule; an access to information law does not. No government portal is yet reported running under it.
A government open data portal is running under the policy. A statistics office's data portal, or one a donor or development bank runs for the country, does not count.

Public bodies have published data under the policy in the past three years: a source names a ministry or agency that has released data, or counts the datasets or the bodies publishing. How good the policy is, and how open the licence, is not judged.

gov.policy--open-data-policy.norm: The African Commission's 2019 Declaration of Principles, Principle 29, asks public bodies to publish information of public interest without being asked, including by digital means. The African Union's Data Policy Framework (2022) asks states to open government data.

data.open--use-of-open-data.label: Use of open data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no public body publishes data for anyone to download.
A public body publishes data online for anyone to download, on a portal or its own site, in the past three years. A dashboard with nothing to download, or a portal only planned, does not count.
That data is published under an open licence or terms that let anyone reuse it, such as Creative Commons or the Licence Ouverte.
Two or more public bodies publish data that way, named or counted by a source from the past three years.
Four or more public bodies publish data that way, named or counted by a source from the past two years.

data.open--use-of-open-data.norm: The African Union's Data Policy Framework (2022) and the Africa Data Consensus (2015) ask governments to open the data they hold for anyone to use, and to see it used.

gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.label: Open discussion of government policy
gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.short_label: Freedom to discuss policy online and in the press
gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.topic: Public debate and participation in policymaking

ladder.text: In the past twelve months the government, a regulator or the security forces cut the internet or blocked a social media service, messaging service or news site, anywhere in the country; or a source from the past three years says no independent newspaper, broadcaster or news site is allowed to work.
In the past three years a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and no cut is on record in the past twelve months.

A source says the country went the past twelve months with no one arrested, charged or jailed, and no outlet suspended or closed, for what was said or published. One such arrest or closure in the twelve months holds a country at stage 2.
In the past three years parliament repealed, or a court of the country struck down, an offence of criminal defamation, false news, sedition or insulting the head of state.
In the past three years a law, a ruling of the country's own court that a cut was unlawful, or an undertaking given in court barred the government from cutting the internet.

gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.norm: The African Commission's 2019 Declaration of Principles asks states not to disrupt access to the internet (Principle 38) and to repeal sedition, insult and false-news crimes (Principle 22). The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance commits its parties to freedom of the press.

gov.legislate--digital-payments-legislat.label: Digital payments legislation

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no payments law or e-money rules and no draft of either.
A payments bill or draft e-money rules are published, before parliament or passed and not yet in force, or mobile money runs on a central bank's letter with no rules behind it.

A payments law or central bank rules on e-money or payment services are in force, however old. A regional central bank's regulation counts for each member it binds. A law on crypto or virtual assets does not count.
Companies that are not banks can be licensed under the law or rules in force to offer payments or issue e-money: a source says so, or names one licensed.

A rule requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch. A switch that providers may join by choice, or a rule that binds banks only, does not reach this stage.

gov.legislate--digital-payments-legislat.norm: The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol, Article 15, and its Annex on Cross-Border Digital Payments commit each party to interoperable payment systems. The Malabo Convention, Article 7, commits each to state-approved electronic payment methods.

dpi.pay--population-uptake.label: Population uptake

ladder.text: A survey from the past three years puts adults with a bank or mobile money account below 26%.
A survey from the past three years puts adults with an account at 26% or more.
A survey from the past three years puts adults with an account at 53% or more.
A survey from the past three years puts adults with an account at 79% or more.
A survey from the past three years puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

dpi.pay--population-uptake.norm: The World Bank's Global Findex 2025 puts account ownership at 79% of adults worldwide; the frame takes that as the target.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.label: Digitalisation of rural police stations

ladder.text: A dated source states that police stations record reports and cases on paper only. A fingerprint database, a crime statistics return or an online reporting portal does not change this.

A system for stations to record reports or cases is being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot stations using it. Or one runs at headquarters or in the capital only.

Reports or cases are entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital; they are a minority, or no share of stations is published. A share of stations equipped or connected, however high, places here.
More than half of stations enter reports or cases digitally at the station when they are taken, into the national system. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of stations do so, for both the first report and the case file, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural stations.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.norm: Corpus's own: no African Union instrument on local police stations was found. The AFRIPOL Statute of 2017 connects national police agencies and says nothing below the national level.

capacity.research--think-tanks-and-acade.label: Think tanks and academic departments contributing to DT policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no local institution researches digital policy.
A local institution has held a research workshop, opened a chair, centre or project on digital policy, or joined a research network on it.
A local think tank, university centre or department has published research on digital policy, such as a report, study or index.
A local institution submitted evidence to a consultation, was commissioned by government for a study, or sits on an advisory body, on a digital policy, law or strategy.
A local research institution holds a standing advisory role in digital policy, or a national research agenda on digital transformation is adopted.

capacity.research--think-tanks-and-acade.norm: STISA-2034 and Agenda 2063's second ten-year plan ask for research systems funded toward 1 per cent of GDP and contributing to policy; neither counts think tanks.

dpi.registry--population-register.label: Population register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no population register exists.
A population register is being built, procured or provided for in a new law.
A population register, or a national ID register serving as one, is in service.
Births or deaths registered are entered in the population register.
Other registers or services take people's records from the population register.

dpi.registry--population-register.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy puts an electronic population register first among the base registers, continuously updated from civil registration.

gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.label: Non-governmental contribution to national policy
gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.short_label: Consultation on digital law and policy
gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.topic: Public debate and participation in policymaking

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says a named digital law or policy was made without consulting people outside government, or that they were refused a part in it, and none says they were asked.

In the past three years the government, parliament or a regulator asked people outside government for their views on a named digital law or policy: a draft put out for comment, or a hearing, workshop or meeting they took part in. A national internet governance forum, a consultation on something that is not digital, and a workshop of officials, donors and consultants do not count.
In the past three years it published what it was told: a report of the consultation, the comments received, or its written answer to them.

In the past three years a consultation on a digital law or policy was held because a law, decree or published procedure required it. The rule alone, with no consultation held under it, does not count.
In the past three years a standing body with members from outside government gave its view on a named digital law or policy. A body that has only been set up or has only met does not count.

gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.norm: The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance commits its parties to dialogue between government, civil society and the private sector. The Malabo Convention, Article 24, asks each party to draw up its cybersecurity policy with stakeholders. Neither says how.

gov.standards--national-quality-standard.label: National quality standards
gov.standards--national-quality-standard.short_label: National standards for information technology and data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national standards body.
A national standards body exists: a body set up by a law or decree to write or adopt national standards. One announced and not yet created does not count.

The body has issued a national standard on information technology or data: a named standard on information technology, information security, software or data, issued or adopted as a national standard. A national quality policy, telecoms quality-of-service rules and quality management standards do not count.

An organisation can be certified against such a standard in the country: the standards body, or a certifier accredited in the country, offers certification against it or has certified an organisation. A certificate from a certifier abroad does not count.

A public body has been certified in the past three years: a dated source names a ministry, agency or state-owned body certified against such a standard by the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country. How good the standards are is not judged.

gov.standards--national-quality-standard.norm: The Abuja Treaty, Article 67, commits member states to a common policy on standardisation and quality assurance, and the Pan-African Quality Infrastructure is the continent's platform. Neither says what standards for information technology or data should be.

include.access--inclusion-of-refugees-an.label: Inclusion of refugees and IDPs

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says refugees or internally displaced people are not registered, hold no documents, are barred from SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID, or that their registration is suspended.
The government or UNHCR planned, began or resumed registering or documenting refugees or internally displaced people, or piloted a digital service for them.
Refugees or internally displaced people have been registered and issued identity documents, with a number stated.
Refugees or internally displaced people may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID, by law or in practice.
The number or share of refugees or displaced people with a registered SIM, a mobile money or bank account, or a national digital ID is published.

include.access--inclusion-of-refugees-an.norm: The Kampala Convention asks for registers and documents for internally displaced people; the Global Digital Compact and UNHCR ask for their digital inclusion.

gov.regional--shared-regional-infrastruc.label: Shared regional infrastructure
gov.regional--shared-regional-infrastruc.short_label: Digital links and facilities shared with other African countries

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no digital link with a neighbour, or stands outside the shared links of its region, and none is on record.

In the past three years the country has agreed to build or join a link or facility shared with another African country: a cross-border fibre link, a sea cable joining two African countries, a shared exchange point, data centre or satellite. Talks, a study or a bid to host do not count.
Building has started in the past three years: a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid. A tender opened or money promised does not count.
A shared link or facility is in service: lit, commissioned or opened to traffic. A ceremony for the start of works, or a test, does not count.

It is reported carrying another country's traffic in the past three years: published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, a named user from the other country, or a fault that cut the other country's service.

gov.regional--shared-regional-infrastruc.norm: The African Union's Programme for Infrastructure Development in Africa and its Digital Transformation Strategy ask states to join their networks across borders, give landlocked countries a route to the sea cables and share exchange points and data centres.

gov.regional--regional-legal-harmonisati.label: Regional legal harmonisation
gov.regional--regional-legal-harmonisati.short_label: Regional digital law taken into national law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has not signed, and no other shared African legal text on a digital matter is on record for it.

The country has signed an African legal text on a digital matter, such as the African Union's cyber security and data protection convention, or is bound by a named act or regulation of its regional community. It has not ratified.
The country has ratified or acceded to such a text, by a law or decree approving it or by depositing the instrument. A cabinet approval, a bill or a promise to ratify does not count.
A national law, decree or regulation has been passed or amended to give effect to a shared text. A draft, a consultation or a study does not count.

The shared law is reported applied across a border in the past three years: a licence or signature recognised, a request between authorities answered, a ruling, or the regional body's finding that the country complies.

gov.regional--regional-legal-harmonisati.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy for Africa asks member states to ratify the Malabo Convention and to bring their digital laws into line through the Union and its regional communities.

gov.regional--regional-policy-collaborat.label: Regional policy collaboration

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country is suspended from, has left or stands outside the African bodies that make digital policy, and no agreement is on record.

The country belongs to an African body that makes digital policy, or takes part in its meetings, and nothing more is on record. Membership of the African Union or a regional community alone does not count.

In the past three years the country has signed a digital agreement or declaration with another African government or African body, hosted or chaired a meeting of such a body, or won a seat or office in one. Talks, visits and meetings attended do not count.

Something the country agreed has been put into effect: roaming charges cut with a neighbour, a joint body set up and meeting, a regional guideline adopted as a national rule, or a shared service opened.

What was put into effect is reported in use in the past three years: published figures of its use, a decision of the joint body, or a review of what the agreement delivered. A launch, a renewal or projects agreed do not reach this stage.

gov.regional--regional-policy-collaborat.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy for Africa asks member states to coordinate their digital policies through the Union and its regional communities. Its policy and regulation initiative, PRIDA, is the working track.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-r.label: Digitalisation of rural registry offices

ladder.text: A dated source states that local civil registration offices register births and deaths on paper only. Scanning or keying old registers does not change this.
A system for local offices to register births digitally is being prepared or piloted, or one runs at the national office or in the capital only.

Births are entered digitally when they are registered, past any pilot, in some local offices; they are a minority, or no share of offices is published. A share of offices equipped or connected, however high, places here.
More than half of local offices enter births digitally at the office when they are registered, into the national register. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of local offices do so, for deaths as well as births, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural offices.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-r.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy: legal identity for 99.9 per cent of people by 2030. SDG 17.19.2(b): registration of 100 per cent of births and 80 per cent of deaths.

dpi.pay--p2p-p2g-and-p2b-functionality.label: P2P, P2G and P2B functionality

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no mobile money or retail digital payment service is licensed.
A mobile money or e-money service is licensed or piloted, with none yet in service.
A mobile money or e-money service is in service.
Payments between different mobile money providers, or between wallets and banks, are in service.
A national switch connects mobile money wallets and bank accounts, in service.

dpi.pay--p2p-p2g-and-p2b-functionality.norm: The African Union's Digital Transformation Strategy asks for interoperable e-money and digital financial services, with low-cost channels and agents reaching underserved areas.

dpi.pay--revenue-collection.label: Revenue collection

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says taxes, duties or fees are paid in cash or on paper only.
Electronic payment of a tax or fee is piloted or contracted, or e-filing is announced.
Electronic payment is in service for some taxes or fees.
Electronic filing and payment are in service for the main taxes and for customs duties.
A source from the past three years gives a figure for revenue paid electronically: a share or an amount.

dpi.pay--revenue-collection.norm: The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol asks states to accept electronic payment and electronic documents for trade and dues.

infra.energy--rural-electrification.label: Rural electrification

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2023 or later, puts rural access to electricity below 27 per cent.
27 per cent or more of rural people have electricity, in the latest figure for 2023 or later, from the World Bank's series.
53 per cent or more of rural people have electricity.
80 per cent or more of rural people have electricity: the Agenda 2063 figure.
95 per cent or more of rural people have electricity: universal access.

infra.energy--rural-electrification.norm: The African Union's Agenda 2063 first ten-year plan asks for 80% of households to have electricity; Mission 300 aims to connect 300 million Africans by 2030.

infra.connect--satellite-broadband-licen.label: Satellite broadband licensing and availability

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no satellite broadband provider is licensed, or that its sale or use is banned.
The regulator or ministry has licensed a provider to sell internet over satellite in the country.
Households or businesses can buy satellite broadband from a licensed provider.
Services on two different satellite networks are on sale, such as Starlink and a OneWeb or Konnect service.
The regulator publishes the number of satellite broadband subscribers, from the past three years.

infra.connect--satellite-broadband-licen.norm: The African Telecommunications Union's Recommendation 005-0 asks every country to license satellite broadband simply, so that users can buy it from more than one provider.

capacity.training--dt-related-training-i.label: DT-related training in secondary education

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2023 or later, puts secondary schools with internet for teaching below 17 per cent.
17 per cent or more of secondary schools have internet for teaching, in the latest figure for 2023 or later, from UNESCO's SDG 4.a.1 series.
33 per cent or more of secondary schools have internet for teaching.
50 per cent or more of secondary schools have internet for teaching.
50 per cent or more of secondary schools have internet for teaching, and digital literacy or computing is a compulsory subject in the national secondary curriculum.

capacity.training--dt-related-training-i.norm: The AU Digital Education Strategy asks for half of institutions connected by 2027 and a digital literacy and coding framework for all students.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.label: Digitalisation of rural primary schools

ladder.text: A dated source states that primary schools keep their learners' records on paper only. An annual school census, however it is collected and whatever it is called, does not change this.
An EMIS for primary schools is being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot schools using it. Or one runs in secondary schools only.

An EMIS is past its pilot and in live use in some primary schools, which enter attendance or results during the year; they are a minority, or no figure is published. Or schools past the pilot fill a national learner register once a year.
More than half of primary schools enter attendance or results for each learner during the school year, at the school. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of primary schools do so, with attendance entered daily, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural schools.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.norm: The African Union's Digital Education Strategy (2022): a move from aggregate annual school statistics (EMIS 1.0) to individual-level data on unique identifiers (EMIS 2.0) in at least half of member states by 2027.

dpi.exchange--interoperability-of-social.label: Interoperability of social protection systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says social protection programmes keep separate lists with no exchange between them or with other systems.
A link from a registry or programme to the national ID, a payment provider or another programme is contracted, being built or piloted.
A social registry or programme system exchanges data with the national ID, a payment provider or another programme in use.
Two or more programmes draw their beneficiaries from a shared social registry.
The registry is linked to the national ID and to civil registration, health, education or tax.

dpi.exchange--interoperability-of-social.norm: The African Union's Protocol on Social Protection asks for a social protection information system that works with the ID, civil registration, payments and other sectors, so benefits follow the person.

dpi.mis--social-protection.label: Social protection

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says social programmes are administered on paper.
A management information system for a social programme is procured, piloted or being built.
A social programme's beneficiaries are enrolled and managed in an information system in service.
The programme's system sends payments to beneficiaries through banks or mobile money.
One information system serves two or more social programmes, or contributory and non-contributory schemes together.

dpi.mis--social-protection.norm: The African Union's Protocol on Social Protection asks for an integrated social protection information system across schemes, with disaggregated data published.

dpi.registry--social-protection-register.label: Social protection register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no social registry exists and programmes hold their own lists.
A social registry is procured, piloted or being populated in some districts.
A social registry is in service.
Two or more social programmes choose who receives support from the social registry.
The social registry is linked to or checked against the national ID.

dpi.registry--social-protection-register.norm: The African Union's Protocol on Social Protection asks states for a social registry and integrated beneficiary registry, interoperable with civil registration and payments.

tech.innovate--tech-startup-ecosystem.label: Tech startup ecosystem

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no startup law, strategy or public support for startups exists.
A startup bill is drafted or tabled, or a startup strategy is being written or in consultation.
A startup act is passed or a startup strategy adopted.
Startups are labelled or registered under the act or strategy, or its tax or other measures are applied to them.
A public or public-backed fund set up under the act or strategy has financed startups, with investments named or counted.

tech.innovate--tech-startup-ecosystem.norm: The Digital Transformation Strategy and the AU Startup Model Law Framework ask for a national startup law and strategy across seven areas, an innovation fund and angel networks.

gov.legislate--statistics-legislation.label: Statistics legislation

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no statistics law and no draft of one.

A bill or draft exists: published, validated, out for consultation, before cabinet or parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated. A law that is only announced or planned does not count. A statistics office set up by an ordinary decree, with no statistics law behind it, stops here.
A statistics law is in force, however old: an act, ordinance or decree with the force of law that governs official statistics or sets up the national statistics office.
A decree, regulation or order has been made under the law: on the statistics office, the statistics council or board, the approval of surveys or the confidentiality of data.

The law has been applied in the past three years: its council or board appointed or meeting, a standard, release calendar or survey approval issued under it, a rule made under it, or a penalty. A census or survey carried out, a strategy or a budget does not reach this stage.

gov.legislate--statistics-legislation.norm: The African Charter on Statistics (2009) obliges its parties to bring national law into line with its principles: professional independence, confidentiality and coordination.

data.statistics--national-strategy-for-d.label: National strategy for development of statistics

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no current statistics strategy and none in preparation.
A national statistics strategy is being designed, drafted, validated or put to cabinet, or one adopted in the past three years has run out. A strategy only promised does not count.
An adopted strategy is current: its stated period covers today. One with no stated period counts for five years.
Progress on the current strategy has been reviewed in the past three years: an annual review, a progress report or a meeting of its steering body.
A mid-term or final evaluation of the current strategy, or the final evaluation of the one it replaced, has been completed in the past three years.

data.statistics--national-strategy-for-d.norm: The African Charter on Statistics and the Strategy for the Harmonisation of Statistics in Africa (SHaSA 2) ask each country to design, carry out and evaluate a national strategy for the development of statistics.

capacity.training--dt-related-university.label: DT-related university facilities and qualifications

ladder.text: The latest figure, for 2023 or later, puts STEM graduates below 13 per cent of tertiary graduates.
STEM graduates are 13 per cent or more of tertiary graduates, in the latest figure for 2023 or later, from UNESCO's series.
STEM graduates are 27 per cent or more of tertiary graduates.
STEM graduates are 40 per cent or more of tertiary graduates.
STEM graduates are 40 per cent or more of tertiary graduates, and a national research and education network is in service connecting the public universities.

capacity.training--dt-related-university.norm: The AU Digital Education Strategy asks for a national research and education network in every country by 2027; Agenda 2063's second ten-year plan asks for 40 per cent of graduates in STEM by 2033.

dpi.mis--tax.label: Tax

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says tax returns are filed and taxes paid on paper.
An integrated tax administration or e-filing system is procured, piloted or being built.
Taxpayers can file returns online for at least one core tax.
Taxes can be paid online, by bank transfer or by mobile money, through the tax authority's system.
Online filing is mandatory for some taxpayers, or half or more of returns are filed online.

dpi.mis--tax.norm: TADAT asks for electronic filing and payment of all core taxes, filing mandatory for designated taxpayers, with immediate confirmation.

dpi.registry--tax-register.label: Tax register

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says taxpayers are registered on paper or not registered.
A computerised taxpayer register or new taxpayer number is being built, migrated or rolled out.
Taxpayer numbers are issued from a computerised register in service, online or at offices.
The taxpayer number is issued at business registration or used by customs, one number for both.
The taxpayer number is the national ID number or is checked against the national ID.

dpi.registry--tax-register.norm: The TADAT framework asks for every taxpayer to hold one unique identifier in one central database, shared with other registers.

tech.innovate--technology-hubs.label: Technology hubs

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says no technology hub, incubator or park operates in the country.
A technology hub, incubator or park is being built, or one is open with no programme on record.
A hub or incubator in service runs an incubation or acceleration programme with a cohort of startups.
Hubs with programmes are in service in two or more cities.
A science or technology park is in service with companies or startups as tenants.

tech.innovate--technology-hubs.norm: The Digital Transformation Strategy asks for a technology park and incubation hub in each region, and local innovation centres.

AGO.short: Angola's 2002 law on access to administrative documents is in force; no source found reports rules made under it and an oversight body.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. Angola's law is Law no. 11/02 of 16 August 2002, the Law on Access to Administrative Documents. It gives a right to ask public bodies for the documents they hold and has stood since 2002, which makes it one of the oldest laws of its kind on the continent.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 11/02 of 2002. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Angola.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

BDI.short: Burundi's Senate adopted an access to public information bill on 29 September 2026; no source found says whether it has been promulgated.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi has a bill and no law. The Council of Ministers adopted the draft law on access to public information on 10 June 2026, with the ministry describing a legal vacuum on the subject. The bill was on the programme of the National Assembly's session opened on 3 August 2026, and the Senate adopted it unanimously on 29 September 2026. Its promulgation is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill the Senate adopted on 29 September 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

BEN.short: Benin's 2015 code gives limited access rights with no request procedure; a new law was in draft in December 2022; no source found reports oversight.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Benin's access provisions sit in Loi n° 2015-07, the Code de l'information et de la communication of 2015. The World Bank's December 2022 open data readiness assessment calls them extremely limited, with articles 84 and 90 restricting access rights, no request procedure, no designated contact point and no annual report on requests. The same assessment says the BAI presidential reform office was drafting a new access to information law, with no adoption timetable.

Law put to work and applied. The same assessment says the HAAC, the body named under Loi n° 2015-07, the Code de l'information et de la communication of 2015, does not appear to have undertaken any initiative to promote access to information. Civil society organisations found the right little known and little used, and their test letters to administrations were generally ignored.

Not found. Nothing found says an access to information law is in force, or that any rule or oversight body exists under one.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso's 2015 access law is in force and existing bodies oversaw it in 2023; no source found reports decisions on requests.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. Burkina Faso's law is Law no. 051-2015/CNT on the right of access to public information and administrative documents, which the government named to UNESCO as its legal guarantee for 2023. The Centre national de presse Norbert Zongo's digital rights report, published in February 2025, records no change to the law and says it has fallen into oblivion. The report names no repeal and no replacement, so the law stands.

Law put to work and applied. Existing bodies have taken up the law's oversight. The government told UNESCO that the national data protection commission, the national human rights commission, a ministry and the Conseil Supérieur de la Communication oversee it, and that in 2023 they published an annual report, gave guidance and training to officials, raised awareness and kept statistics on requests and appeals. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by those bodies, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

Not found. No source found dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, or published figures of requests or appeals, in the last three years.

BWA.short: Botswana's Access to Information Act of 2024 is made and starts on a date set by notice; no source reports that date and any rules.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. Botswana's law is the Access to Information Act, Act 16 of 2024, dated 26 July 2024, which creates a general right of access to information held by public authorities and starts on a date to be set by notice. The President's State of the Nation Address in November 2025 counted the Act among the laws Parliament had passed. The date it starts is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, the Access to Information Act of 2024. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Botswana.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

CAF.short: Nothing found says whether Central African Republic has an access to information law or a draft of one, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found names an access to information law or a draft of one, or says there is none.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire's 2013 access law is in force, and its commission recorded 45 referrals in 2024.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Côte d'Ivoire's law is Law no. 2013-867 of 23 December 2013 on access to information of public interest. The president of the commission that oversees it describes it as guaranteeing every citizen the right of access to public information.

Law put to work and applied. The law's oversight body is in place and at work. The Commission d'Accès à l'Information d'intérêt public et aux Documents Publics, the CAIDP, was created in 2013. In 2024 the CAIDP recorded 45 referrals, 12 of them from journalists, and a body that breaks the law can be fined up to FCFA 360,000. Its president presented a programme named ACCESS CAIDP on 25 July 2025, and in September 2026 the commission began a national register of public documents with about 200 information officers.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

CMR.short: Cameroon's draft law on access to public information was validated by a workshop in November 2025; it has not reached parliament.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. Cameroon has a draft and no law. A draft law on the right of access to and use of public information and on the digital transformation of the administration was published on 22 May 2023. A national workshop at Ebolowa on 3 to 14 November 2025 gave the draft its technical validation, and the project behind it lists the text among those examined there.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the draft validated at Ebolowa in November 2025. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

COD.short: DR Congo's National Assembly took up an access to information bill in March 2026; it is still a bill.
COD.summary:
Law in force. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has a bill and no law. On 27 March 2026 the National Assembly declared receivable a private member's bill on access to information and transparency of public life and sent it to a joint committee with ten days to report. The right of access written in the constitution has no law behind it until the bill passes.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill declared receivable on 27 March 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

COG.short: Congo has no access to information law and no draft, by a UNESCO assessment of 2025.
COG.summary:
Law in force. The Republic of the Congo has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's assessment of the country's internet development, dated 2025, recommends that the government draft and adopt a freedom of information law, and lists a commission on access to public information among the bodies still to be set up. The assessment names no bill in preparation.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's 2025 assessment. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. A bill published, put out for consultation or sent to cabinet or parliament would be the first step, and a law in force the second.

Not found. Nothing further: every question is answered.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2022 law on access to administrative documents is in force; no source found reports rules made under it and an oversight body.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. Cabo Verde's law is Law no. 10/X/2022 on access to and reuse of administrative documents, approved on 8 April 2022, promulgated on 9 May 2022 and published on 16 May 2022. It gives everyone a right to consult and copy administrative documents and to be told what they contain.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 10/X/2022. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Cape Verde.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

DJI.short: Djibouti's Council of Ministers approved a draft Digital Code with a right of access to information in 2023; no source found says whether it passed.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. The Council of Ministers, chaired by the head of state, examined and approved a draft law on the Digital Code in June 2023. Book VII of the draft provides a general right of access to administrative documents and public information, with rules on how it is exercised. The report was published on 1 June 2023, and the draft is titled Projet de loi portant Code du Numérique. Its owner is the Ministère délégué chargé de l'Économie numérique et de l'Innovation.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the same Council of Ministers report, which concerns a draft only: the Code du Numérique, examined and approved by the Council of Ministers under the head of state in June 2023. Nothing found shows a rule made, an oversight body set up or a request decided under an access law.

Not found. Nothing found says the draft was passed, or that any access law is in force or applied.

DZA.short: Nothing found says whether Algeria has an access to information law or a draft of one, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: Not found. Nothing found names an access to information law or a draft of one, or says there is none.

EGY.short: A freedom of information bill signed by 60 members was submitted to Egypt's parliament in August 2026; no law is in force.
EGY.summary:
Law in force. Egypt has a bill and no law. A freedom of information bill backed by the Journalists Syndicate was submitted to the House of Representatives on 9 August 2026 with the signatures of 60 members; it would create an Authority for the Protection of Freedom of Information. Its explanatory memorandum says the right in Article 68 of the constitution has had no law for years.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill submitted on 9 August 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

ERI.short: Eritrea has no freedom of information law and no draft, by a UNESCO statement of January 2026.
ERI.summary:
Law in force. Eritrea has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's contribution to the country's Universal Periodic Review, published in January 2026, states that no freedom of information law has been adopted and recommends that the government introduce one. The contribution names no bill in preparation.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's contribution of January 2026. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. ETH.short: Ethiopia has had a mass media and access to information proclamation since 2008; no source found reports its Ombudsman oversight is reported ineffective, and application.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. Proclamation No. 590/2008 on Freedom of the Mass Media and Access to Information, dated 4 December 2008 and proclaimed under Article 55(1) of the Constitution, is published by the Ministry of Justice and affirms in its preamble individuals' right to access information held by public bodies and a duty on public officials to facilitate it. A June 2023 study lists it among Ethiopia's laws, and a draft Access to Information Proclamation prepared by a media law working group had not been passed as of March 2023.

Law put to work and applied. The same study says the Ethiopian Institution of the Ombudsman was designated the organ responsible for implementing freedom of information. The study is dated 1 June 2023. It reports studies finding the Ombudsman ineffective for lack of resources to evaluate public bodies, and it gives no date for that finding.

Not found. Nothing found names rules made under the proclamation, says its oversight body is set up as such, or shows requests or decisions under it.

GAB.short: Gabon has no access to information law and no draft, by a UNESCO statement of December 2025.
GAB.summary:
Law in force. Gabon has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's contribution to the country's Universal Periodic Review, published in December 2025, states that Gabon has no access to information law and encourages it to adopt one. The contribution names no bill in preparation, in cabinet or before parliament.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's contribution of December 2025. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. A bill published, put out for consultation or sent to cabinet or parliament would be the first step, and a law in force the second.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2019 Right to Information Act is in force, and its commission fined 254 public institutions in August 2026 for missed reports.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Ghana's law is the Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989). It puts the constitutional right to information to work and sets the procedure for asking public institutions for what they hold.

Law put to work and applied. The Right to Information Commission, with a board and chairman, oversees and enforces the Act, and the 2026 budget votes it GHS 20,413,271. On 5 August 2026 the Commission imposed penalties of GHS 20,000 each on 254 public institutions that had not filed their 2025 annual reports under the Act. A newspaper count puts the practice lower: 21 institutions failed to release information in 24 requests made between January 2025 and July 2026. The penalties are for missed reports; a published decision on a single request is not recorded.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

GIN.short: Guinea's 2020 law on access to public information is in force; no source found says whether its commission has been appointed.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. Guinea's law is Law no. 2020/0027/AN on the right of access to public information, signed in Conakry on 19 December 2020, in effect from its promulgation. The law provides for an autonomous commission on access to public information; its members being appointed is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 2020/0027/AN. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Guinea.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2021 Access to Information Act is in force and its Information Commission is at work; no source found reports decisions on requests.
GMB.summary:
Law in force. The Gambia's law is the Access to Information Act, 2021, cited as Act No. 10 of 2021 in the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2025. The Gambia Press Union said in August 2026 that it had been in force for more than a year, and the Immigration Department reaffirmed its commitment to it in October 2026.

Law put to work and applied. The Act's oversight body is set up. The Information Commission, with a deputy chairperson, was implementing the Act in September 2026. The Press Union sits on technical committees with it, a United Nations agency tendered in August 2026 for a communication strategy for the Commission, and the 2025 data protection Act defines the Commission as established under the Access to Information Act.

Not found. No source found dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, published figures of requests, or a rule made under the law, in the last three years.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau's draft access to information law was validated in April 2024 and awaits the Ministry of Justice; no law is in force.
GNB.summary:
Law in force. Guinea-Bissau has a draft and no law. A drafting commission met on 17 to 23 April 2024 and all those taking part validated the draft law on access to information, by UNESCO's account. The next step it gives is submission to the Ministry of Justice for adoption. No law is in force.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the draft validated in April 2024. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.
