GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea's Senate passed a transparency and access to public information bill in May 2026; no source found reports promulgation.
GNQ.summary:
Law in force. Equatorial Guinea has a bill passed by parliament and not shown as promulgated. The Prime Minister presented the bill for a Code of Transparency, Access to Public Information and Good Governance in Public Finance Management to the Chamber of Deputies on 5 February 2026. The Senate approved it unanimously on 8 May 2026, which leaves promulgation by the Head of State.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill the Senate approved on 8 May 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2016 Access to Information Act is in force, with regulations made under it in 2023; no source found reports decisions on requests.
KEN.summary:
Law in force. Kenya's law is the Access to Information Act, 2016. It gives effect to Article 35 of the Constitution, and the press describes it as the guarantee of the right to information. It has stood since 2016 with no repeal recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The Access to Information Regulations of 2023, made under the Act, define proactive disclosure and set what public bodies must publish. Regulations made in the last three years are counted as the law applied. A forum in September 2026 assessed how public institutions carry the Act out. A decision or penalty on a request, and published figures of requests, are not recorded. A separate bill of 2026 on classified information is noted and does not change the Act's standing.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

LBR.short: Liberia's 2010 Freedom of Information Act is in force and its commission ran a compliance campaign in 2026; no source found reports decisions on requests.
LBR.summary:
Law in force. Liberia's law is the Freedom of Information Act of 2010. The Press Union of Liberia cited it in August 2026 as law a government agency's staff confidentiality agreement must fit. The Act gives a right to ask public bodies for information and has stood since 2010.

Law put to work and applied. The Act's oversight body is set up. The Independent Information Commission, with an executive director and directors for outreach and compliance, ran a compliance campaign across public bodies from 11 August to 2 September 2026. A campaign is not a decision on a request. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded. In October 2026 the Press Union said the Commission, the statutory body that enforces the Act, had publicly opposed the Civil Service Agency's new confidentiality policy.

Not found. No source found dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, published figures of requests, or a rule made under the law, in the last three years.

LBY.short: Libya's cabinet issued a draft bill in 2022 that would let citizens request information from public bodies; no law is in force.
LBY.summary:
Law in force. Libya has a draft and no law. A Council of Ministers draft bill on the national information system, issued on 8 October 2022 over the Prime Minister's signature, would give every citizen a right to request information from the information units of public bodies. Its passage is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the draft bill of October 2022. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

LSO.short: Lesotho's Access and Receipt of Information Bill of 2000 had not been passed by 2021; no law is in force.
LSO.summary:
Law in force. Lesotho has an old bill and no law. An assessment of September 2021 says the country has no real freedom of information law, and that the Access and Receipt of Information Bill of 2000, drafted by the Law Reform Commission, has not been passed by Parliament. Nothing later on the bill is recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the Access and Receipt of Information Bill of 2000. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2018 law on the right of access to information is in force and its commission is at work; no source found reports its decisions.
MAR.summary:
Law in force. Morocco's law is Law no. 31-13 on the right of access to information, promulgated on 22 February 2018 and published on 3 May 2018, in force one year after publication. The Ministry of Justice says requests and complaints are filed and handled under it.

Law put to work and applied. The law's oversight body is set up. The Commission on the Right of Access to Information, led by its president, signed a partnership agreement with the Minister of Justice on 31 March 2026, and it runs the national portal through which requests are made. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

Not found. No source found dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, published figures of requests, or a rule made under the law, in the last three years.

MDG.short: Madagascar's access to public information bill has been before the National Assembly since 2026 and was left off its August session; no law exists.
MDG.summary:
Law in force. Madagascar has a bill and no law. A decree of the Prime Minister presented bill no. 017/2025 on access to information of a public nature, in 88 articles, after the Council of Ministers deliberated it on 3 December 2025. Deputies debated it in committee from 8 May 2026, and it was left off the agenda of the extraordinary session opened on 25 August 2026.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, bill no. 017/2025. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

MLI.short: Mali has no single access to information law; a 2026 study finds the right spread across several laws, one of 1998.
MLI.summary:
Law in force. Mali has no single access to information law. A study published in April 2026 finds the legal framework for the right spread across several laws, among them Law no. 98-012 on relations between the administration and its users, and calls for a specific law. The existing laws are counted here for the part that gives the right; the study names no draft of a single law.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, the laws the 2026 study describes. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Mali.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

MOZ.short: Mozambique's 2014 Right to Information Law is in force; public bodies received 60,433 requests in 2024, the Ombudsman reported.
MOZ.summary:
Law in force. Mozambique's law is Law no. 34/2014 of 31 December 2014, the Right to Information Law, passed by the Assembly of the Republic to set how the right to information is exercised. It applies to the bodies of the State and to the public administration. The Ombudsman's annual report to the Assembly, reported in November 2025, says the law is being carried out.

Law put to work and applied. The law is applied and its use is counted. The Ombudsman's annual report says public bodies received 60,433 requests for information in 2024, of which 57,998 were granted, 1,589 refused and 846 still pending, so about 95 per cent of requests that year were granted. The Ombudsman, who monitors the law, reports these figures to the Assembly of the Republic in an annual report.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

MRT.short: Mauritania's government bill on access to public information has been under discussion since April 2026; it has not reached parliament.
MRT.summary:
Law in force. Mauritania has a bill and no law. Reporters Without Borders reported on 23 June 2026 that a bill drafted by the government on access to and use of public information had been under discussion since April 2026 and had yet to go through parliament. No law is in force.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the government bill under discussion since April 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

MUS.short: Mauritius had no access to information law as of February 2026, only promises of one; no bill is known.
MUS.summary:
Law in force. A Defi Media blog of 14 February 2026 says successive Mauritian political parties have promised Freedom of Information and failed to deliver. It says Senior Counsel Rama Valayden urges the government to introduce it, and names no law or bill; his 2022 draft is a constitutional amendment to section 12, put forward by Senior Counsel Valayden himself. The blog is headed with his call for action on Freedom of Information and the proposed constitutional change.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the same February 2026 blog, which describes a promise not yet delivered by any of the successive political parties, and the 2022 draft it mentions amends section 12 of the constitution. Nothing found shows a rule made, an oversight body set up or a request decided under an access law.

Not found. Nothing found shows an access to information bill or draft law before the government or parliament.

MWI.short: Malawi's Access to Information Act has run since 2020; its oversight body reported over 36,000 requests handled in the year to March 2025.
MWI.summary:
Law in force. Malawi's law is the Access to Information Act, 2016, assented to on 10 February 2017 and published in the Gazette on 16 February 2017. It became operational on 30 September 2020, and it gives a right to information held by public bodies and by the private bodies it names.

Law put to work and applied. The Malawi Human Rights Commission, which the Act makes its oversight body, presented a report on carrying the Act out on 10 October 2025. The report says that from April 2024 to March 2025 information holders handled over 36,000 requests and rejected 11. The Commission has also used the Act on a private company: it issued a notice to Mota-Engil to assess whether the company could comply, a step that reached the High Court on 6 March 2026.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

NAM.short: Namibia's 2022 Access to Information Act has regulations of December 2024 for choosing its commissioner; no source found says whether the Act has started.
NAM.summary:
Law in force. Namibia's law is the Access to Information Act, 2022 (Act No. 8 of 2022), published in the Government Gazette on 28 December 2022. It gives a right of access to information held by public and private bodies and starts on a date the Minister sets; that date is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. Regulations made under the Act were gazetted on 9 December 2024, setting the terms of the selection committee and the process for appointing the Information Commissioner. Regulations made in the last three years are counted as the law applied. The appointment of a commissioner, a decision on a request and published figures of requests are not recorded, so what is held shows the Act being prepared for use and not yet used.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

NER.short: Niger's 2011 ordinance on access to public information is in force and was cited by a minister in 2025; no source reports rules under it.
NER.summary:
Law in force. Niger's law is Ordinance no. 2011-22 of 23 February 2011 on the charter of access to public information and administrative documents, an ordinance with the force of law that gives any person a right to ask public bodies for information. The Minister of Communication cited it on 22 October 2025 as standing.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Ordinance no. 2011-22. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Niger.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

NGA.short: Nigeria's 2011 Freedom of Information Act is in force and the Federal High Court ordered disclosure under it in 2025 and 2026.
NGA.summary:
Law in force. Nigeria's law is the Freedom of Information Act, 2011, assented to on 28 May 2011, which gives any person a right to request information held by public institutions. The Federal High Court treats it as taking precedence over the Petroleum Industry Act where the two conflict.

Law put to work and applied. The courts enforce the Act. On 13 October 2025 the Federal High Court in Abuja held the national oil company a public institution under the Act and ordered it to supply information requested on a $3 billion loan. On 24 February 2026 the Federal High Court in Lagos ruled that the Nigeria Shippers Council had breached the Act over a journalist's request of 2020, and ordered disclosure or reasons. The Act has no information commission; rules made under it are not recorded.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

RWA.short: Rwanda's 2013 law on access to information is in force; no source found reports rules made under it and an oversight body.
RWA.summary:
Law in force. Rwanda's law is Law no. 04/2013 of 8 February 2013 relating to access to information, published on 11 March 2013. It is the country's access to information law and has stood since 2013, with no repeal or replacement recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 04/2013. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Rwanda.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

SDN.short: Sudan's Right to Access Information Law of 2015 is on the books; nothing since 2016 says how it stands or is used.
SDN.summary:
Law in force. Sudan's law is the Right to Access Information Law of 2015, ratified by the National Assembly on 27 January 2015 and signed by the President on 22 February 2015, in effect from signing. The National Information Center listed it in 2016 among the laws governing the sector.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, the Right to Access Information Law of 2015. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Sudan.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

SEN.short: Senegal's access to information law was promulgated in September 2025 and provides for a commission; no source found says whether its members are appointed.
SEN.summary:
Law in force. Senegal's law is Law no. 2025-15 on access to information, adopted by the National Assembly on 26 August 2025, promulgated on 4 September 2025 and published on 25 September 2025. It is the first law to set how the right of access is exercised. ARTICLE 19 and AFIC say it guarantees a right to ask public bodies for information, and Reporters Without Borders says it covers public institutions and certain private bodies performing a public service. An October 2026 public note to the Prime Minister says law no. 2025-15 of 4 September 2025 gives citizens, legal residents and legal persons a right of access to information held by public bodies, with a reply due in eight clear days, extendable to fifteen, and an appeal to the national access to information commission.

Law put to work and applied. ARTICLE 19 and AFIC say the law sets up an independent body to oversee it. The Open Government Partnership's review of May 2026 reports that Senegal created the Commission nationale d'accès à l'information under the law, and that the law carries sanctions for bodies that do not comply.

Not found. No source found says the commission has been appointed or is at work, or names rules made under the law.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's 2013 access act is in force; its commission fined two bodies in 2024 and 2025, and a replacement bill reached Cabinet in 2026.
SLE.summary:
Law in force. Sierra Leone's law is the Right to Access Information Act, 2013, signed by the President on 31 October 2013. A replacement is being written: a Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill was validated on 7 November 2025, and Cabinet approved repealing the 2013 Act and enacting the new one, announced on 21 April 2026.

Law put to work and applied. The Act's oversight body is long set up and has fined public bodies. The Right to Access Information Commission presented its sixth annual report to the Minister of Information and Civic Education on 17 November 2025. In September 2024 it fined the Corporate Affairs Commission NLe80,000 for missing the 15-working-day deadline on a request of 18 June 2024, acting under the Act and the Right to Access Information Regulations 2022. On 13 October 2025 it ordered Freetown City Council to release requested documents within seven days and fined it Le 70,000.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

SOM.short: Somalia's cabinet approved an access to information bill in 2024; in September 2025 it still awaited the Lower House.
SOM.summary:
Law in force. Somalia has a bill and no law. The Council of Ministers approved the Official Information Bill in March 2024 and sent it to the House of the People. A Ministry of Information official said on 28 September 2025 that the Cabinet had passed the access to information law and that it awaited presentation to the Lower House.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill awaiting the Lower House. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not found. No source found says an access to information law is in force.

SSD.short: South Sudan has an Access to Information Commission with a budget line; the law is not named in what is held, nor any decision.
SSD.summary:
Law in force. South Sudan's access to information law is not itself named in what is recorded; its commission is. The Minister of Information's paper of 6 September 2023 lists the Information Commission among six bodies under the ministry, and a commission set up shows a law in force behind it.

Law put to work and applied. The oversight body exists and is funded through the budget. The budget performance report for 2024/25 lists the Access for Information Commission among the agencies with an allocation. On 4 September 2025 the Ministry of Information said it had estimated a budget for the Commission's operations and described it as facing operating challenges. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

Not found. No source found dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, published figures of requests, or a rule made under the law, in the last three years.

STP.short: Sao Tome and Principe had a draft access law before the National Assembly in 2018, still not adopted in 2021; no source reports later status.
STP.summary:
Law in force. Civil society organisations (CIP-STP, FONG-STP, PDHEG and Wêbeto) submitted a draft Lei de Acesso aos Documentos e Informações Administrativas to the President of the National Assembly in 2018. It was written by a national consultant under the Pro PALOP project. In November 2021 those organisations were still calling for the draft to be adopted, and STP Digital reported on 1 December 2021 that it was not yet adopted. UNESCO's contribution to the 51st Universal Periodic Review, of 2026, states that there is no legislation on freedom of information and recommends introducing an access to information law.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the same STP Digital report, which concerns a draft only: the calls made during the Quinzena da Cidadania, 15 to 30 November 2021. Nothing found shows a rule made, an oversight body set up or a request decided under an access law.

Not found. Nothing found says the draft was adopted since 2021, or that any access law is in force or applied.

SWZ.short: Nothing found says whether Eswatini has an access to information law or a draft of one, so no stage is set.
SWZ.summary: Not found. Nothing found names an access to information law or a draft of one, or says there is none.

SYC.short: Seychelles' 2018 Access to Information Act is in force, and its commission found public bodies in breach and ordered disclosure in 2024.
SYC.summary:
Law in force. Seychelles' law is the Access to Information Act, enacted on 20 July 2018. The Information Commission was created under it, and the Commission proposed amendments to the Act in a paper of November 2025.

Law put to work and applied. The Act's oversight body is set up and rules on appeals. The Information Commission was created under the Act and was later named the data protection authority as well. It found the Planning Authority non-compliant with sections 11 and 17 of the Act and ordered full access to the requested files within five days, in a notice of May 2024, and found the Agriculture Department in breach of sections 11(1), 12 and 21, closing that case on 15 November 2024. Its paper of November 2025 says information holders have ignored its orders, the Act giving no clear way to enforce them.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

TCD.short: Chad had no freedom of information law in January 2023; nothing newer is held, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not found. No law or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has none.

TGO.short: Togo's 2016 law on access to public information is in force with an implementing decree of 2017; nothing done under it since is known.
TGO.summary:
Law in force. Togo's law is Law no. 2016-006 of 30 March 2016 on freedom of access to public information and documentation, adopted by the National Assembly on 10 March 2016. It guarantees citizens a right of access to information held by public bodies and has stood since 2016, with no repeal or replacement recorded.

Law put to work and applied. Rules have been made under the law. Decree no. 2017-104/PR of 10 August 2017 applies it, naming the public bodies it covers and the officials responsible. The decree is older than three years and nothing later is recorded. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

Not found. No source found dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, published figures of requests, or a rule made under the law, in the last three years.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2016 access law is in force; its oversight body received 7,347 appeals in 2023 but lacked a president by late 2025.
TUN.summary:
Law in force. Tunisia's law is Organic Law no. 22 of 2016 on the right of access to information, promulgated on 24 March 2016. It gives every person a right to ask public bodies for information and took effect one year after publication.

Law put to work and applied. The law's oversight body is set up and has handled appeals, but has since stalled. The government's 2024 return to UNESCO says a national information commission oversees the law, and reports 7,347 appeals received in 2023 and 6,375 requests received in 2021. The government told a deputy, as reported on 30 November 2025, that the access to information body, nine members elected by Parliament for six years, has been working without its president and deputy, which has blocked legally valid meetings.

Not found. No decision of the oversight body since 2023 is recorded.

TZA.short: Tanzania's 2016 Access to Information Act has been in force since July 2017; no source found reports rules made under it.
TZA.summary:
Law in force. Tanzania's law is the Access to Information Act, 2016, assented to on 23 September 2016, gazetted on 30 September 2016 and commenced on 1 July 2017. It gives every person a right of access to information held by public bodies.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, the Access to Information Act of 2016. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Tanzania.

Not found. No source found names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

UGA.short: Uganda's 2005 Access to Information Act is in force, and courts ruled on requests and on the Act itself in 2025 and 2026.
UGA.summary:
Law in force. Uganda's law is the Access to Information Act, 2005, assented to on 7 July 2005, which gives every citizen a right of access to the records of public bodies. The Constitutional Court ruled on it on 4 December 2025, holding its exemption for court records before a case ends unconstitutional.

Law put to work and applied. The courts decide requests under the Act. On 7 August 2026 the High Court allowed the national examinations board's appeal against a magistrate's order, made on a complaint under the Act, that had compelled release of a candidate's examination script. The judgment applies the Act's section 4 right of access. The Act has no information commission; rules made under it are not recorded.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

ZAF.short: The Information Regulator enforced the 2000 access law in May 2026, ordering a mining firm to disclose records; no source found reports request volumes.
ZAF.summary:
Law in force. South Africa's law is the Promotion of Access to Information Act, 2000, the law under which the Information Regulator acts on complaints about refused requests. It was amended on 17 April 2025, and a public service data governance directive of 2 April 2025 says it facilitates implementation of the Act. A parliamentary committee approved the publication of proposed amended court rules under it in September 2026, which would repeal the existing rules.

Law put to work and applied. The Information Regulator, established on 1 December 2016, monitors and enforces the Act alongside the data protection law, and Pansy Tlakula chairs it. On 22 May 2026 it issued an enforcement notice under the Act directing the mining company Sibanye-Stillwater to give a complainant access to compliance reports, after a complaint lodged in September 2023. The Regulator briefed the press on its enforcement of the Act on 31 August 2026.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

ZMB.short: Zambia's 2023 Access to Information Act came into force in June 2025, with regulations and oversight guidelines issued the same year.
ZMB.summary:
Law in force. Zambia's law is the Access to Information Act, 2023 (Act No. 24 of 2023), assented to on 22 December 2023. It came into force on 25 June 2025, when the minister signed a commencement order.

Law put to work and applied. Rules followed within months. The Minister of Information and Media made the Access to Information (General) Regulations, 2025, setting request forms, fees and procedures, signed on 20 August 2025. The Human Rights Commission, which the Act names as its oversight body, issued guidelines under it on 5 December 2025. Court rules under the Act were still being finalised in July 2026. Rules made in the last three years are counted as the law applied; a decision on a request is not recorded.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's 2020 Freedom of Information Act is in force, and its oversight commission issued release orders, reported in 2024; no source found says how many.
ZWE.summary:
Law in force. Zimbabwe's law is the Freedom of Information Act, 2020, published and commenced on 1 July 2020. It gives a right to ask public bodies for information and repealed the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act. MISA Zimbabwe's chairperson says Zimbabweans are increasingly using the Act to claim their right to information.

Law put to work and applied. Rules have been made under the Act and its oversight body issues orders. A joint submission to the United Nations of July 2026 says the Act was put to work through the Freedom of Information (General) Regulations, 2021, and recommends that the Act be fully carried out. MISA Zimbabwe's 2024 annual report says the Zimbabwe Media Commission has issued release orders to public institutions that must provide information requested under the Act.

Not found. No count or date of the Commission's release orders has been found.

AGO.short: Nothing found since 2023 names a national addressing system, so no stage is set.
AGO.summary: Not found. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether an addressing system is under way or in service.

BDI.short: Nothing found since 2023 names a national addressing system, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether an addressing system is under way or in service.

BEN.short: An addressing system was under way in 2026; none in service is on record.
BEN.summary:
Addresses in service. The Ministry of Cadre de Vie says a 21 May 2026 meeting of ANAT, EDENMAP and others agreed a shared vision and guidelines to continue implementing a national strategy to standardise street and door addressing across the territory. The Council of Ministers on 22 April 2026 authorised a mission with a specialist firm to start a digital, geolocated, participatory addressing system first in Abomey-Calavi, Cotonou, Ouidah, Porto-Novo, Sèmè-Podji and Parakou, under a national addressing strategy.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the addressing system covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Used by services. No source found since October 2023 says other services use the address system. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says: is an address register or digital addressing system in service.

BFA.short: Digital address platforms served Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso in 2023; no source found reports national coverage.
BFA.summary:
Addresses in service. A pilot of the urban information project, financed by the European Union with about EUR 1 million, addressed more than 93,000 doors and 16,000 streets in three arrondissements of Ouagadougou and in Bobo-Dioulasso, and built two digital address platforms for the two cities, Easy Geo and Webmapping grand Ouaga data, presented to officials and the security services on 24 October 2023. On 2 April 2025 the commune of Ouagadougou extended street naming and door numbering to arrondissements 5 and 12, more than 2,277 streets and 43,000 doors, after arrondissements 1 and 2, with European Union support.

Nationwide. Addressing reaches two cities. The 2023 pilot covered three arrondissements of Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso, and Ouagadougou has since been adding arrondissements one pair at a time.

Used by services. No service has been found as using the addresses. The nearest held fact: the two cities' digital address platforms were built under the 2023 pilot.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the addressing system covers the whole country; the digital address platforms held serve Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso.

BWA.short: An addressing system was under way in 2024; none in service is on record.
BWA.summary:
Addresses in service. The journal article says Botswana adopted LAPCAS but village-level addressing remains unresolved, and the authors built a prototype location addressing system for Tlokweng using Python, GeoPandas and Django. It is the only fact held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined. This is a first pass, which read at most twenty stories a country; the nightly deep dive reads further and may move the stage either way.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the addressing system covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Used by services. No source found since October 2023 says other services use the address system. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

The chatbot was built for the ministry by the consultants UChat Africa.

Several bodies. Only the education ministry is held with AI in service. The National Budget Automation System, described as AI-driven, held its second piloting workshop in September 2026. The budget system is still being piloted and is not reported in service.

The ministry for telecommunications and information technology lists a proposed law on artificial intelligence on its public consultation portal, which in August 2026 recorded 18 contributions from companies, 18 from specialists and five from the public. A review published in December 2025 describes the draft as a comprehensive framework for developing, supplying and using AI, built on levels of risk and reaching providers outside the country.

General AI law and the law applied. No law on AI is in force. The draft under consultation would apply to AI across sectors and not to one sector or one use. It has not been sent to the Council of Ministers or the National Assembly in any source dated to September 2026.

BDI.summary:

It names no bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI, and no rule for one sector or one use that names AI is recorded for the country. The review gives the personal data protection law of 10 March 2026 as the main hard law bearing on AI; it is a data protection law, not a law on AI.

General AI law and the law applied. With no dedicated AI law in June 2026, Burundi has no general AI law to apply, and no body holds powers under one. The data protection law of March 2026 is the nearest instrument in force, and it applies to personal data across sectors rather than to AI.

BEN.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Benin has no binding rule on AI. The Forum on Information and Democracy and ALCRER stated in April 2025 that, outside the national AI and big-data strategy 2023-2027, there is no specific and sufficiently binding regulation on developing, deploying or using AI systems in Benin. Their statement names no bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI. Levellers said in June 2026 that Benin has no dedicated AI law, bill or statute, and that AI is governed indirectly through the Digital Code's book on personal data.

General AI law and the law applied. With no specific binding regulation on AI outside the strategy as of April 2025, Benin has no general AI law to apply. The national AI and big-data strategy for 2023 to 2027 is a strategy, not a law, and no rule for one sector or one use that names AI is recorded for the country.

COD.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. A law-faculty dean writing on droitnumerique.cd published an article on 23 August 2024 about AI policy and automated decision-making in the DR Congo. In the dean's account, soft law and not hard law is what governs AI in the DR Congo.

General AI law and the law applied. No general AI law is described in the same 23 August 2024 article on droitnumerique.cd. The dean places the country's rules on AI in soft law, which still largely prevails, and names neither a hard law on AI nor a draft of one. The article is the dean's account of how the DR Congo governs AI and automated decision-making, and it describes soft law as the instrument in use.

COG.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. On 8 April 2026 the Congolese National Assembly adopted a bill on the orientation and development of scientific research. The bill introduces an ethical framework for AI and institutes a national committee to oversee responsible AI use. The report of the adoption, published by the Congolese news agency ACI, does not say the bill is in force. The bill is a law on scientific research, and AI is one of the matters it regulates.

General AI law and the law applied. The only measure held is the research bill, adopted by the National Assembly on 8 April 2026. Its AI provisions, the ethical framework and the national committee on responsible AI use, sit within a bill on scientific research. They cover AI within scientific research and not across sectors. No other law, decree or regulation on AI has been found for the Republic of the Congo.

COM.short: A media code in force since February 2026 requires AI-generated content to be labelled; there is no law on AI itself.
COM.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. The Code of Information and Communication, adopted by Law 25-021/AU of 26 December 2025 and promulgated by decree on 2 February 2026, requires any content generated or heavily modified by AI to be labelled as such, under its article 231. The media regulator, the Conseil national de la presse et de l'audiovisuel, can impose penalties of up to 1,000,000 Comorian francs. Al-watwan reported on 2 October 2026 the UNESCO finding that the Comoros has legislation with several provisions on artificial intelligence in the media.

General AI law and the law applied. The rule in force covers one use, AI-generated content in the media, and sits in a code that governs the press and broadcasting. The same UNESCO assessment, reported by Al-watwan on 2 October 2026, finds no AI-specific legal instrument and a framework that is mainly sectoral rather than cross-sector.

DJI.short: A national newspaper said in August 2026 that no law in Djibouti addresses AI; no draft is named.
DJI.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Djibouti has no law on AI. La Nation, reporting the country's AI readiness assessment in August 2026, said that no law specifically addresses artificial intelligence to date. It describes the Digital Code as a framework for data protection only. The article names no bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI, and no ministry asked to write one.

General AI law and the law applied. With no law that addresses AI in August 2026, there is no general AI law to apply. The article reports the readiness assessment carried out with UNESCO's support, and sets the missing law beside it as part of where the country stands on AI. The Digital Code it names is the nearest rule the country has, and it covers personal data and not AI.

DZA.short: Deputies registered a bill to regulate AI in parliament in 2024; no rule on AI is known in force.
DZA.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Algeria has a bill and no rule in force. The secretary general of the National People's Assembly told an inter-parliamentary meeting in October 2024 that a bill by a group of deputies to regulate the development and use of AI had recently been registered and would be examined by the Assembly's bureau. Digital Policy Alert's digest of April 2025 states that the country has not yet adopted laws or regulations specifically governing the development and use of AI, and no rule for one sector or one use that names AI is recorded for the country.

General AI law and the law applied. With no law or regulation specifically governing AI in April 2025, Algeria has no general AI law to apply. The rules the digest describes on personal data, the hosting of cloud services on Algerian territory and online content are general ones that do not name AI, and no body has been given powers under an AI law.

EGY.short: A 2024 financial regulator decree on robo-advisors is in force; a general AI law is still a draft in 2026.
EGY.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. FRA Board Decree No. 57 of 2024 regulates robo-advisors for investment and is AI-specific. It requires client suitability assessments and gives clients a right to discontinue automated transactions. A 2026 Legal 500 guide by a law firm also says the Government is preparing a draft AI law with the House of Representatives' Communications and IT Committee, and elsewhere calls it the draft currently before Parliament. MP Amira Saber submitted a 24-article bill on governing AI applications to the House in June 2024, and in October 2025 the House ICT committee chair said the ministry's comprehensive draft would go to the House in January 2026.

General AI law and the law applied. The same 2026 Legal 500 guide states that no binding AI-specific statute is in force in Egypt. The one binding AI-specific measure it names is the 2024 decree of the Financial Regulatory Authority board on robo-advisors for investment, which reaches that sector and no other. The decree dates from 2024 and the draft law from the guide's 2026 imprint.

Not found. No source found says a law on AI itself, applying across sectors, is in force.

ERI.short: A review of June 2026 says Eritrea has no AI law and no AI-specific legislation; no draft is named.
ERI.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Eritrea has no law on AI. A legal-status page last reviewed on 8 June 2026 states that Eritrea has no dedicated AI law and no AI-specific legislation, and that AI is not governed by any specific national framework. It names no bill, draft decree or draft regulation, and no ministry or body asked to prepare one.

General AI law and the law applied. With no AI-specific legislation in June 2026, there is no general AI law in force and nothing to apply. The same page says no national framework of any kind governs AI in the country, so no regulator holds a duty to oversee it. No rule for one sector or one use that names AI is recorded either.

ETH.short: A draft AI law was tabled by 2026; no binding rule on AI is known in force.
ETH.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Ethiopia has a draft and no rule in force. Writing in The Conversation in June 2026, two scholars say Ethiopia has tabled a draft AI law that follows the EU's risk-based approach and bans unacceptable-risk AI systems. UNESCO's readiness assessment profile of the same month says the country's legal framework is not AI-specific and that it has no binding legislation on the public procurement of AI systems, on algorithmic transparency or on liability for harm caused by AI.

General AI law and the law applied. With a legal framework that is not AI-specific in June 2026, Ethiopia has no general AI law to apply. The tabled draft is not yet law, and no rule for one sector or one use that names AI is recorded for the country.

Not found. No source found says the draft has been passed, or that a rule on AI is in force.

GAB.short: An ordinance of April 2026 governs AI-generated content and bans deepfakes; there is no law on AI itself.
GAB.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Gabon has a binding rule on one use of AI. A report of August 2026 cites an ordinance of April 2026 governing AI-generated content, which among other things prohibits deepfakes. The report gives no number for the ordinance and quotes none of its articles. It sets the ordinance beside a national technical committee on AI and a national AI agenda for 2026 to 2036.

General AI law and the law applied. The ordinance of April 2026 covers content generated by AI and not AI across sectors. Gabon has no law on AI itself in any source dated to September 2026, and no bill or draft of one is named. No prosecution, order or penalty under the ordinance is on record, and the body that enforces it is not named.

Not found. No source found says a law on AI itself, applying across sectors, is in force.

GHA.short: A draft information technology bill of 2026 would regulate AI among other technologies; no rule on AI is in force.
GHA.summary:

A report of 26 May 2026 says the proposed National Information Technology Authority bill, written to replace the 2008 law on the authority, includes regulation of emerging technologies such as AI and blockchain. It is one of 15 digital bills the government put out together, and the report records a consultant's objection to the speed of the consultation.

General AI law and the law applied. No law on AI is in force. The draft bill treats AI as one of several emerging technologies an information technology regulator would oversee, and is not a law on AI itself. No source dated to September 2026 says it has gone to cabinet or to parliament, and none names a separate AI bill.

The same official, speaking on 14 October 2025 at the opening of the diagnostic workshop, said Guinea has not adopted an AI-specific law, unlike other countries of the sub-region. The statement covers the whole legislative and regulatory framework on AI, and no law on AI of any scope is named. The statement is the ministry official's own account of the legal position on AI.

It is the one source found that says in terms that no draft exists as well as no law.

General AI law and the law applied. With no legislation on AI in force or proposed in June 2026, there is no general AI law to apply. KEN.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Kenya has a bill before parliament and no rule in force. The Artificial Intelligence Bill was introduced in the Senate on 19 February 2026. A memorandum sent to the Senate in May 2026 describes the bill as creating an AI Commissioner's office, an advisory committee and a classification of high-risk systems, with transparency duties and standards for the public sector. It was still a bill in September 2026, and in October 2026 the Senate ICT Committee recommended that the Senate not proceed with it.

General AI law and the law applied. No law on AI is in force: a university centre wrote in September 2026 that Kenya has no AI laws and that most regulation touching AI falls under the Data Protection Act. The Senate bill would apply across sectors. An earlier Robotics and Artificial Intelligence Society Bill of 2023, which proposed licensing, was not passed.

It says the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications, the telecoms regulator and the National Security Agency have yet to set AI-specific frameworks, and it names no bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI.

General AI law and the law applied. With no guardrails on AI in place in March 2026, Liberia has no general AI law to apply, and no body has been given powers under one. The memorandum asks for legislation; it does not say one is being drafted.

Binding rule on AI in force. Morocco has a binding rule on one use of AI. An interview published in July 2026 says the revised electoral law for the 2026 legislative elections makes it a crime to use AI and digital means to alter the truth or to harm the private lives of individuals and candidates. The government's draft organic law 53.25, laid before the House of Representatives in October 2025, set two to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 dirhams. The broadcasting regulator's decision 50-26 binds licensed radio and television not to broadcast misleading AI-generated or AI-altered election content; it does not reach online platforms. In June 2026 the digital transition minister said her ministry was preparing a digital administration bill with provisions specific to AI.

General AI law and the law applied. The rule covers elections and not AI across sectors. A private member's bill on regulating the use of AI, of 17 articles, was received by the bureau of the House of Representatives in January 2025; no source dated to September 2026 says it has been debated or passed.

Binding rule on AI in force. Mauritius has binding rules on AI in two sectors. The Higher Education (Use of Artificial Intelligence) Regulations 2026, Government Notice 39 of 2026, were made by the minister under the Higher Education Act 2017 and came into operation on 31 March 2026. They oblige higher education institutions to adopt policies on AI and require the use of AI tools to be disclosed. The Financial Services Commission's Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services Rules of 2021 apply to licensees offering investment and portfolio management through AI-enabled algorithms.

General AI law and the law applied. The higher education regulations and the Financial Services Commission's rules each reach one sector. Mauritius has no law on AI itself applying across sectors in any source dated to September 2026, and no bill or draft of one is named. Its AI strategy and its guidelines on the development and use of AI are not binding. No decision or penalty under the regulations is on record.

MWI.short: In 2025 Malawi had passed no dedicated AI law; an AI bill is announced but no draft is known.

No rule for one sector or one use that names AI is recorded for the country, and no published bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI has been found.

NAM.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Namibia has no law on AI. The minister for information and communication technology said at a meeting on 3 August 2026 that the government has put a national AI strategy before legislation, so no AI legislation has yet been introduced; a second report of the meeting says the same. A year earlier, at the launch of the country's AI readiness assessment, the absence of a formal regulatory framework for AI was named as a standing problem. In October 2026 a commentator wrote of the absence of explicit, standalone national AI laws, leaving parastatals bound only by governance and privacy law.

General AI law and the law applied. With no AI legislation introduced by August 2026, there is no general AI law to apply and no draft of one is named. The readiness assessment recommended a national framework for governing AI, and the strategy the minister described is the step the government has chosen to take first.

NGA.short: A 2025 data protection directive sets duties for anyone deploying AI; several AI bills are before parliament and none has passed.
NGA.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Nigeria has a binding rule that names AI, inside its data protection rules. The data protection commission's General Application and Implementation Directive of 2025 requires an organisation deploying AI to document its parameters, assess unequal outcomes and test the system, under article 43, and to stop using AI systems that pose undue risks to human rights, under article 44. In October 2026 the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics described the proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill as covering sovereignty, investment and risk management.

General AI law and the law applied. No law on AI itself is in force. Four AI bills passed second reading in the House of Representatives on 3 December 2024, and a proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill with a licensing regime and an AI council was under debate in November 2025. In January 2026 the government was preparing to regulate AI through the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, with yearly impact assessments for high-risk systems.

RWA.short: A review of September 2026 says Rwanda has no AI act and relies on its 2023 AI policy; no draft is named.

Binding rule on AI in force. Rwanda has no law on AI. A university centre wrote in September 2026 that there is no AI Act in Rwanda, and that the country's framework for AI rests on the National AI Policy of April 2023, with the laws on personal data and privacy as supplementary support. It names no bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI.

General AI law and the law applied. With no AI Act in September 2026, there is no general AI law to apply. The policy of 2023 that carries the field is a statement of the government's aims and binds no one; the data protection and privacy laws beside it apply to AI only as they apply to any processing of personal data. No rule for one sector that names AI is recorded.

SDN.short: The Council of Ministers discussed a draft data and AI law in August 2026; no rule on AI is in force.
SDN.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. Sudan has a draft and no rule in force. On 6 August 2026 the Council of Ministers discussed a draft Data and Artificial Intelligence Law put forward by the ministry for digital transformation, and directed that it be studied further before going for approval to the interim parliament, a joint sitting of the Sovereignty Council and the Council of Ministers.

General AI law and the law applied. No law on AI is in force. Five days later the undersecretary of the justice ministry said the ministry was preparing, with the digital transformation ministry, three draft laws for 2026, one of them the law regulating data and AI. The draft joins AI to data in one law across sectors; nothing on its content is recorded.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation that sets a rule for AI is in force.

SEN.short: A July 2024 diagnostic found no AI-specific legal text in Senegal; no source found says whether a draft has appeared since.
SEN.summary:
Binding rule on AI in force. An IPAR diagnostic published in July 2024 covers the policy, legal and ethical framework on AI in four West African countries, Senegal among them. It says there is as yet no legal text specific to AI at continental, regional or national level.

General AI law and the law applied. The same July 2024 IPAR diagnostic adds that, of the four West African countries it covers, only Benin has a framework suited to regulating AI. It names no such framework for Senegal, and it finds no legal text specific to AI at national level. The diagnostic names no law, decree or regulation on AI in force in Senegal, and none for the West African region or for the continent as a whole.
