MWI.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2025; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
MWI.summary:
Licensing providers. The Reserve Bank of Malawi licenses payment service providers. On 30 September 2026 it granted the local fintech PayChangu Limited payment service provider licence PSP-003/26 for payment aggregation, letting it bring mobile money, card payments and bank transfers onto one platform for businesses. The Reserve Bank issued the licence under the Payment Systems Act, 2016, and the company's chief operating officer credited it with making room for local firms. In October 2023 it granted Flutterwave an International Money Transfer Operator licence.

Overseeing a switch. The Reserve Bank of Malawi and the Bank of Zambia supervise the COMESA Digital Retail Payments Platform linking the two countries. The Reserve Bank of Malawi rolled out the National Switch in 2015, linking banks, mobile money platforms and ATMs into one network (2015, before the three-year window). Malawi's 2025 ID4Africa deck says National Switch Limited, which connects all banks and mobile money operators for instant payments, is supervised by the Reserve Bank of Malawi.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: the Reserve Bank of Malawi supervises Malawi's participation in the COMESA cross-border payments platform.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

NAM.short: The central bank ran or oversaw a national payment switch in 2026; no source found reports a regional link.
NAM.summary:
Licensing providers. Bank of Namibia Deputy Governor Leonie Dunn said licensing and supervisory responsibilities for payments are being transferred to the central bank under a new Payments Association framework. The Bank of Namibia issued the PSD-1 determination under section 45 of the Payment System Management Act 2023, setting the licensing and authorisation of payment service providers, including electronic money issuers, effective on Gazette publication on 6 January 2026.

Overseeing a switch. The Bank of Namibia said its instant payments solution became operational in June 2026, with live transactions first processed between its Currency Management and Banking Operations Department and Bank Windhoek, Nampost and Letshego Bank Namibia.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found says Namibian banks or providers send and receive payments through PAPSS. The Bank of Namibia's directive of March 2025 orders providers to move low-value transfers within the Common Monetary Area from SADC-RTGS to the TCIB scheme by April 2027.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

NER.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2026; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
NER.summary:
Licensing providers. The BCEAO's list of payment institutions licensed under Instruction n°001-01-2024 shows one in Niger, iFUTUR, licensed 6 May 2025. Bénin Web TV reports, from the BCEAO list, that Niger has one licensed payment institution at 31 August 2026. Airtel Money Niger SA is authorised by the BCEAO as an electronic money issuer under Décision n° 194-07-2022, per ActuNiger (2022, before the three-year window).

Overseeing a switch. BCEAO says it set up the PI-SPI instant-payment interoperability platform, allowing account-to-account transfers between different types of accounts across the UMOA, of which Niger is a member. BCEAO runs PI-SPI, the instant payment platform for UEMOA members including Niger, launched 30 September 2025 with 175 connected participants a year later. The BCEAO's list updated to 30 September 2026 authorises 13 participants in Niger to open PI-SPI services to the public: eleven banks, Airtel Money Niger and i-FUTUR.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: Niger is a UEMOA member in the BCEAO's PI-SPI regional instant payment system, in service. BCEAO says it set up the regional payment systems STAR-UMOA, SICA-UMOA and SAGETIL-UMOA for the Union. Niger is a UEMOA member state on the regional PI-SPI platform that BCEAO runs, with its institutions required to connect by 30 June 2026.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

NGA.short: The central bank took part in a regional or continental payment system in 2026.
NGA.summary:
Licensing providers. TechCabal reports that under Central Bank of Nigeria licensing requirements, mobile money and payment service bank licences must be held by an entity with the relevant telco licence, and that a CBN directive required Airtel Money to transfer its 25% SmartCash stake back to Airtel Networks. BusinessDay says TeamApt is a Central Bank of Nigeria-licensed switching and processing company.

Overseeing a switch. No source found since October 2023 says the central bank runs or oversees a national switch. The nearest held fact: PAPSS CEO Mike Ogbalu said Nigeria was the first chair of the PAPSS Governing Council, made up of central bank governors, and continues to lead its rollout.

Live on PAPSS. PAPSS CEO Mike Ogbalu said Nigeria was the first chair of the PAPSS Governing Council, made up of central bank governors, and continues to lead its rollout. Remita's consumer app, launched 22 September 2026 in Lagos, supports instant transfers from Nigerian bank accounts to other African countries through PAPSS, per Remita's managing director. Nairametrics reported in May 2025 that 22 Nigerian commercial banks were fully onboarded on PAPSS, after the Central Bank of Nigeria told all banks to adopt it and start sending payments.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

RWA.short: The central bank ran or oversaw a national payment switch in 2026; no source found reports a regional link.
RWA.summary:
Licensing providers. The National Bank of Rwanda said in March 2026 that its passporting agreement with the Central Bank of Kenya covers payment service providers licensed by their home central bank, so a provider licensed in one country can offer its services in the other. The two central banks signed the agreement that month, at a ceremony where the National Bank's speech was given.

Overseeing a switch. The National Bank of Rwanda says it monitors the eKash payment and transfer system, launched nationally on 14 July 2026, and works with providers to fix disruptions. Taarifa reports that interoperability runs through the National Bank of Rwanda's eKash platform, rolled out months before July 2026.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found says Rwandan banks or providers send and receive payments through PAPSS or a regional payment system. The nearest held fact is the national launch of eKash in July 2026, a domestic system.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country takes part in PAPSS or a regional payment system.

SDN.short: The central bank licensed payment providers in 2026 and supervised the national switch linking all banks; no source found reports live payments through PAPSS.
SDN.summary:
Licensing providers. The Central Bank of Sudan licenses electronic payment service providers. It revoked Al-Asjad's licence after review by a technical and legal committee. Licences depend on meeting its published standards, and any integration needs its written approval. Bede Sudan launched its BBAN wallet after the central bank approved it, Sudan Horizon reports.

Overseeing a switch. In October 2026 the head of EBS said it runs Sudan's national payments infrastructure under the central bank's supervision. That includes the national switch, which connects all Sudanese banks, and settlement with the central bank.

Live on PAPSS. No source since October 2023 says Sudan's banks send or receive payments through PAPSS. The nearest fact is the national switch EBS runs, which links banks inside the country.

Not found. No source since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

SEN.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2026; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
SEN.summary:
Licensing providers. BCEAO counted 31 licensed payment institutions in the UMOA at end of February 2026, 11 of them in Senegal, under its 23 January 2024 instruction on payment services. BCEAO lists 11 authorised electronic money initiatives in Senegal at 30 September 2024: three licensed e-money issuers and eight banks issuing through partners. Wave holds an e-money issuer licence granted by the BCEAO in Senegal.

Overseeing a switch. BCEAO launched PI-SPI, the regional interoperable instant payment platform, on 30 September 2025, running 24/7; 80 participants were connected at 24 June 2026. Financial Afrik says BCEAO operates the PI-SPI instant-payment system, with 19 Senegal institutions authorised on its list, the most in the Union.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: the BCEAO's PI-SPI instant payment platform counts 175 authorised participants across the eight WAEMU countries, with Senegal holding the most at 43, and Wave was authorised to open its services in Senegal on the list updated 30 September 2026. Financial Afrik says 19 Senegal institutions are authorised by BCEAO to offer PI-SPI, the WAEMU regional real-time payment system.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

SLE.short: The central bank took part in a regional or continental payment system in 2025.
SLE.summary:
Licensing providers. No source found says the central bank's role over payments is under way or in service. The nearest held fact: PAPSS lists eight Sierra Leonean banks (UBA, SLCB, Access, Bloom, Rokel, GTBank, Vista, FBNBank) as live, update May 2025. A later answer places the country above that step.

Overseeing a switch. The Bank of Sierra Leone's representative cited the central bank's launch of the National Switch among its inclusion efforts. The Bank of Sierra Leone launched a national payment switch in April 2023 and on 13 February 2025 a national instant payment switch linking seven banks and two mobile money operators, with full integration due by 1 April 2025. In January 2026 the head of the Bank's National Switch Department said it runs the Salon Payment Switch, which now includes every commercial bank, and an instant payment system.

Live on PAPSS. PAPSS lists eight Sierra Leonean banks (UBA, SLCB, Access, Bloom, Rokel, GTBank, Vista, FBNBank) as live, update May 2025.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

SOM.summary:
Licensing providers. Guleid Osman writes that the Central Bank of Somalia licenses and supervises financial institutions, has introduced mobile-money regulation, and its website reports fifteen licensed commercial banks and six mobile-money service providers. The House of the People passed the National Payment System Bill 154-2, empowering the Central Bank of Somalia to license, supervise and oversee payment systems and digital money platforms; it goes to the Senate.

Overseeing a switch. Guleid Osman writes that the Central Bank of Somalia has launched the National Payment System, the Somali Payment Switch and the Somali Instant Payment System (SIPS), which the Bank states supports real-time transfers among banks, mobile wallets and points of sale.

Live on PAPSS. The Central Bank of Somalia joined PAPSS in March 2026, but no Somali bank is reported live on it. No source found since October 2023 says the country takes part in PAPSS or a regional payment system in service.

Licensing providers. The Central Bank of Eswatini says it oversees the safety and soundness of national payment systems and lists five licensed payment service providers: MTN Fintech, E-Mali, Instacash, Shoprite mobile Money Services and DeltaPay. The Deputy Governor said in March 2025 that the Central Bank of Eswatini has licensed and regulated mobile money operators since 2011.

Overseeing a switch. The Central Bank of Eswatini says the Eswatini Payment Switch fast payments platform is fully active, connecting banks and mobile money providers in real time, 24/7. The Central Bank of Eswatini's Fast Payments system enables transactions across different account types and wallets, and the central bank describes the Eswatini Payment Switch as its payments infrastructure.

SYC.short: The central bank oversees interoperable interbank payment systems by 2025; no source found says whether the country is live on PAPSS.
SYC.summary:
Licensing providers. The Central Bank of Seychelles gave Fusepay final approval as a licensed payment service provider in November 2025, and Fusepay now runs a business-to-business payments platform under that licence, with the central bank's approval.

Overseeing a switch. Governor Caroline Abel said in July 2025 that banks interoperate fully on the country's most used payment systems, the Seychelles Electronic Funds Transfer and electronic cheque clearing, under the Act that governs the operation and oversight of national payment systems. She was opening meetings of the payment system committees of the SADC central bank governors.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found says Seychelles takes part in PAPSS. The governor said cross-border payments are processed through the central bank on the SADC-RTGS platform, with volumes too small to bring in the commercial banks.

Not found. No source found says Seychelles banks or providers send and receive payments through PAPSS.

TCD.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2023; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
TCD.summary:
Licensing providers. Chad's payment-institution licences are granted by the Central African Banking Commission (Cobac) under the CEMAC regulation of 21 December 2018; Airtel Money (2023), Konoom (2025) and Moov Money Tchad (2026) hold one. AfricaNenda says the regional central bank BEAC, whose rules apply to the six CEMAC states including Chad, regulates payment market structures including technical approvals and authorisations of payment solutions.

Overseeing a switch. AfricaNenda says BEAC owns 99.2% of GIMACPAY, is its overseer and settlement agent, and the switch serves payment providers in Chad.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: Chad's mobile money providers are interoperable via GIMACPAY in the CEMAC zone, per Tchadinfos. Chad is one of six CEMAC states covered by GIMAC's interoperable QR Code standard, validated by the UMAC ministerial committee in April 2026 and launched on 29 July 2026 over GIMACPAY, in service since 2021.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

TGO.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2026; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
TGO.summary:
Licensing providers. Mixx holds an e-money institution licence (agrement) from the BCEAO. The BCEAO widened market access in Togo by licensing new fintech players, per Togo First. TechCabal reports the BCEAO granted Togolese fintech Semoa its Level 3 payment institution accreditation on 29 January 2026, the first of its kind for a Togolese company. TechCabal says INTOUCH Togo obtained its BCEAO electronic money institution licence in June 2025.

Overseeing a switch. LeFaso.net reports that the BCEAO, which sets the connection deadlines for banks, e-money and payment institutions and microfinance, launched the PI-SPI interoperable instant payment platform on 30 September 2025, with 80 institutions connected by 24 June 2026. Togo First says BCEAO's PI-SPI instant-payment platform, launched in September 2025, lets Togo's six BCEAO-authorised institutions transfer funds instantly 24 hours a day.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: LeFaso.net reports that PI-SPI is a BCEAO instant payment platform across the UEMOA, in service since 30 September 2025. Mixx Togo joined the BCEAO's PI-SPI platform, and Ecobank, Orabank and Bank of Africa in Togo are connected to it. Togo is part of the rollout of the interoperable instant payment platform PI-SPI, though adoption remains very gradual, per Togo First.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

TUN.short: The central bank oversaw the national interbank clearing system in 2026; no source found says whether Tunisian payments run on a continental payment system.
TUN.summary:
Licensing providers. The Central Bank of Tunisia published Circular 2026-10 on 2026-09-25 governing payment institutions, repealing Circular 2018-16 and tightening its oversight of their agents and governance, per African Manager. The Fintech Times says Konnect describes itself as a payment facilitator certified by the Central Bank of Tunisia. Ooredoo Fintech received approval from the Central Bank of Tunisia to launch its digital wallet walletii by Ooredoo. La Presse says the Central Bank of Tunisia's licensing commission granted OFT Tunisie definitive authorisation as a resident payment institution, and that 16 payment service providers are licensed in Tunisia.

Overseeing a switch. The BCT states it manages and supervises the SGMT RTGS (in service since November 2006) and performs surveillance of the SIBTEL clearing system.

Live on PAPSS. The Banque Centrale de Tunisie's note 2024-77 says the central bank has belonged to PAPSS since 6 February 2024, and banks and the postal office on Elyssa RTGS need its non-objection attestation to join directly. La Presse reported in August 2025 that only two Tunisian commercial banks had subscribed to PAPSS.

Not found. No source found reports Tunisian payments running on PAPSS.

TZA.short: The central bank ran or oversaw a national payment switch in 2025; no source found reports a regional link.
TZA.summary:
Licensing providers. The finance minister told the National Assembly that as of March 2026, 113 service providers were licensed to operate payment system services, with the Bank of Tanzania licensing new players. 2 facts are held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

Overseeing a switch. The Bank of Tanzania capped the maximum cost of single transactions in the Tanzania Automated Clearing House and the instant payment system at 2,000/- in 2024 and 2025, with a focus on the Tanzania Instant Payment System (TIPS). A March 2025 Co-Develop release says the Bank of Tanzania launched the Tanzania Instant Payment System (TIPS) in 2019, linking banks and mobile money providers, with over 45 institutions taking part.

Live on PAPSS. No source found since October 2023 says the country takes part in PAPSS or a regional payment system. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country takes part in PAPSS or a regional payment system.

UGA.short: Nothing found since 2023 says what the central bank does over payments, so no stage is set.
UGA.summary: Not found. Nothing found since October 2023 says what the central bank does over payments: whether it licenses providers, oversees a national switch or is live on PAPSS.

ZAF.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2025; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
ZAF.summary:
Licensing providers. The South African Reserve Bank's National Payment System Department says it regulates payment systems, third-party payment providers and e-money providers, with access to the payment system by designation or authorisation under the National Payment System Act 78 of 1998 and its directives. ASAPP says it has engaged the SARB on its Banks Act Exemption and Authorisation Framework, covering future authorisation of payment activities for regulated fintech payment providers. The Reserve Bank published a draft framework for authorising non-bank payment and e-money providers in May 2026, with the final framework due by the end of November 2026.

Overseeing a switch. TechCentral reports the South African Reserve Bank took a 50% interest in PayInc, operator of PayShap, in late 2025, and the 2026 budget speech named PayInc the shared digital payments infrastructure supporting interoperability across providers.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: the Reserve Bank's governor said on 20 October 2026 that qualifying regional payments are carried on the SADC real-time gross settlement system and that those under R100,000 are to move to TCIB by the end of April 2027. In 2022 the Reserve Bank designated the SADC Real Time Gross Settlement System (SADC-RTGS) as a settlement system.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

ZMB.short: The central bank oversaw a national payment switch in 2024; live participation in PAPSS is not on record.
ZMB.summary:
Licensing providers. The Bank of Zambia issued fourteen designation certificates to payment service providers in 2024 (seven payment aggregators, six electronic money issuers, one money transfer operator) and revoked four. 3 facts are held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

Overseeing a switch. The Bank of Zambia says it oversees the national payment systems, including the National Financial Switch, which processed K131.9 billion and 140,496,750 transactions in 2024 with 34 participants live.

Live on PAPSS. Nothing found shows the country live on PAPSS. What is held is a regional payment system, which does not count: Zambian commercial banks process payments through the SADC Real Time Gross Settlement System (ZAR13.4 billion paid and ZAR13.9 billion received in 2024).

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the country is live on PAPSS.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe processed payments through a continental payment system in 2026; no source found says whether the central bank licenses providers.
ZWE.summary:
Licensing providers. The Herald reports that the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe oversees mobile money by directive. A 2021 directive enforced one line, one wallet for each customer, and the Monetary Policy Statement of February 2026 directed mobile money operators to verify their customers by 30 June 2026. The Reserve Bank sets these rules for the operators directly, through its own directives and policy statements.

Overseeing a switch. The nearest held fact is the Reserve Bank's oversight of mobile money operators by directive, including its order of February 2026 that every operator verify its customers by 30 June 2026.

Live on PAPSS. Afreximbank says Zimbabwe is processing $5.8 million a month through PAPSS, the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, as reported in October 2026. The same source says most banks in Southern Africa have joined the system, which places Zimbabwe among the countries whose payments run on it. The Financial Gazette reported on 9 October 2026 that CBZ Bank had gone live on PAPSS.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the Reserve Bank licenses payment providers or oversees a national switch.

Angola's presentation to the registrars' meeting says amendments to the civil registry and identity card laws led to operations merging the two systems, with a multifunctional database under the Ministry of Justice built on the existing Sistema do Registo Civil. Novo Jornal reports that identification and civil registration posts in Luanda and nearly all the country were without their system for months, which the Justice Ministry blamed on telecom breakdowns, showing a computerised registry in use at posts.

BDI.summary:

The Directorate General for territorial administration says civil registration is digitised in pilot communes, and UNICEF says thirteen communes already have a biometric registration system, per RTNB. The Ministry of the Interior presented a digital platform for managing civil registration, with infrastructure nearly complete and a decree governing its use awaited, per We Are Tech Africa. ID Tech reported in August 2026 that 13 municipalities have biometric civil registration systems, with vital events registered electronically in pilot municipalities.

Deaths digital. No source found since October 2023 says deaths are registered in the digital system. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

BEN.short: Births and deaths are registered digitally in the national civil status file, said in 2026; no source found reports the share of births registered.
BEN.summary:
Births digital. ANIP says secure birth certificates are now issued from data in the RNPP and the national civil-status file, per a note signed 5 May 2026. ANIP's director general says the single-window birth declaration and registration is in a pilot in ten health facilities, with health agents now using new internet-connected terminals for declarations and registration feeding the national register of natural persons (RNPP), with generalisation to all facilities planned. Law 2020-34 of 6 January 2021 dematerialised civil status and abolished paper civil registers, so every birth is registered in the RNPP, which counts as the civil-status declaration, per ANIP (2021, before the three-year window). ANIP says the 2021 law removed paper registers and created a national civil status file, with the old paper registers fully digitised.

Deaths digital. ANIP says a death declared by a health worker or a village or neighbourhood chief sets the person's status to deceased in the identification system and is registered automatically in the national civil status file.

Births at 90%. No source found since October 2023 puts birth registration at 90% or more. The nearest held fact: ANIP gives nearly 94% for births declared on time, which counts declarations, not registrations.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 puts birth registration at 90% or more.

The Minister of Territorial Administration said 30 communes of Burkina Faso now hold fully digitised civil-status registers, reported by the Primature. AMADE Mondiale lists deployment of a digital birth registration platform and health-registry interoperability among completed activities of its 2025-2028 project in Kaya, Tenkodogo and Koupela.

Deaths digital. The same session covered real-time entry of deaths, alongside births and marriages, on VENEEM at central and secondary registration offices, per the Agence d'Information du Burkina.

The state IT agency NITDA signed the National Cloud Computing Guideline, a technical guideline and an assurance framework earlier that month. The new policy targets US$750 million in private cloud and data-centre investment. A May 2026 release from the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority says the National Cloud Policy 2025 requires sensitive government and financial data to be hosted in the country.

Named hosting and moves. Part II of the policy designates the state-owned Galaxy Backbone the primary digital infrastructure provider for government, aggregating its cloud demand and operating shared government platforms, with only certified providers listed on the National Digital Marketplace. Galaxy Backbone will aggregate government cloud demand from registered providers and negotiate framework agreements, with buying through a National Digital Marketplace on which NITDA registers providers. A 24-month roadmap plans the migration of priority ministries in months six to twelve. NITDA's director-general said in August 2026 that the Cloud First policy remains in force.

RWA.short: Rwanda has required critical government systems to be hosted in the National Data Center since 2012; no source found says which bodies have moved recently.

They include a rule on hosting critical government data and systems, and state no end date and no replacement.

Named hosting and moves. Article 17 of the instructions requires all government IT systems and applications that process, store or provide critical government data to be hosted in the National Data Center, website, email and shared applications included. Article 18 requires institutions that keep data centres of their own to arrange disaster recovery from the National Data Center. The instructions name the centre as the one place for critical systems, and both articles have stood since 2012.

SEN.summary:

Commissioning the Diamniadio National Datacenter in June 2021, President Macky Sall instructed the government to migrate all state data and platforms to it and to repatriate national data hosted outside the country. State-owned businesses such as the electricity company Senelec are to move their data too, he said. A later account says Senegal then required all servers to be housed within its borders.

Named hosting and moves. The instruction names one place: the Diamniadio National Datacenter, built with Huawei on a Chinese loan at a cost given as $18.2 million. It is managed by the state IT agency ADIE, and all government data and applications are to be migrated to it and hosted there. The 2021 report gave its hosting capacity as 500 square metres and said its first phase would open in about six months.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2024 Cloud First circular sets hosting tiers and a list of labelled providers was published in 2026; no source found says which bodies have moved.
TUN.summary:
Policy adopted. A ministerial order of 13 September 2023 requires public bodies' software, platforms and infrastructure to be hosted in-house or with cloud providers according to four tiers, any other arrangement needing the cybersecurity agency's approval. Circulaire n° 16 of 22 July 2024, from the Head of Government to ministers, governors and heads of public bodies, generalises cloud adoption under the "TN Government Cloud First Policy". A circular of 2 September 2026 tightens the hosting requirements.

Named hosting and moves. The 2024 circular sends sensitive internal systems to a private cloud or to national or sectoral government cloud centres, shared government systems to government cloud centres, and public e-services to the body's private cloud, government cloud centres or providers holding the N-Cloud label. The cybersecurity agency published its list of labelled providers on 17 September 2026, with six N-Cloud entries. Two providers received the G-Cloud label in July 2024; the agency's November 2025 register listed seven N-Cloud providers and no G-Cloud label.

TZA.short: Tanzania approved hosting standards for public institutions in February 2026; the approved hosting environments are not named.
TZA.summary:
Policy adopted. The e-Government Authority's Data Center Standards and Guidelines for Public Institutions, version 2.0, was approved by its board chairperson on 18 February 2026. It is issued under section 49 of the e-Government Act No. 10 of 2019, which requires the authority to issue technical standards on storing and processing electronic data.

Named hosting and moves. The standard rests on section 25 of the Act, which requires a public institution to host its systems in a government-approved hosting environment. The authority says it wrote the standard to guide public institutions in deciding where to host government ICT applications, and to stop them setting up new data centres. It will also serve as the minimum requirements for judging whether an existing data centre can be an approved hosting environment.

Not found. No source found says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

UGA.short: Cloud-first guidelines from October 2018 require ministries and agencies to host classified information in the government data centre; no source found says how many have moved.
UGA.summary:
Policy adopted. NITA-U issued the National Guidelines on Cloud Computing for Government, Ministries, Departments and Agencies in October 2018, requiring all ministries, departments, agencies and local governments to adhere to Cloud First for IT-enabled services. The document gives no end date. It is version CPG1 of the guidelines and applies to the government bodies it lists.

Named hosting and moves. The same guidelines require those bodies to host information assets classed Official, Secret and Top Secret in the Government Cloud, the National Data Center run by NITA-U. They must also use it when procuring new ICT, and migrate existing classified services to it at contract expiry or refresh. NITA-U can approve offshore exceptions. The Government Cloud serves ministries, departments, agencies and local governments. NITA-U's 2023 statistical abstract lists the National Data Centre as serving 95 government entities in FY2022/23.

ZAF.short: South Africa gazetted its National Policy on Data and Cloud in May 2024; no government cloud or list of providers is named.
ZAF.summary:
Policy adopted. The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies published the National Policy on Data and Cloud as Notice 2533 of 2024 in Government Gazette 50741 on 31 May 2024. It covers national and provincial government and organs of state. It was published under section 3(1) of the Electronic Communications Act, 2005, and the department listed the drafting of a Data and Cloud Strategy among its work in October 2024. National Treasury replied on 10 September 2024 that it had considered the policy's implications and planned to convert its 2016 integrated financial management system licences to cloud-based.

Named hosting and moves. The policy says government data shall be stored in unified, cloud-enabled data centres in designated locations, names the State Information Technology Agency as the authority to source data infrastructure and cloud services for government, and makes cloud the first option for new ICT procurement. A law firm's reading of June 2024 is that it requires government data-centre infrastructure to be in the country and still needs implementing with the agency and departments. In June 2025 National Treasury told Parliament it had begun talks with Oracle on moving its financial system from its own premises to a cloud platform, in line with the government's cloud computing policy.

Not found. No source found says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

ZMB.short: A 2023 regulation requires public bodies to store personal data in Zambia; no source found says which hosting they must use.
ZMB.summary:
Policy adopted. Statutory Instrument No. 43 of 2023, the Electronic Government (General) Regulations, gazetted on 6 October 2023 under the Electronic Government Act 2021, requires every public body to store the personal data it processes on infrastructure domiciled in Zambia, under regulation 8 of the regulations, which cite the Act as their authority. Storage abroad needs authorisation from the Electronic Government Division and the Data Protection Commissioner.

Named hosting and moves. The regulations require all public bodies to integrate their services with the Government Service Bus, run by the Electronic Government Division, and refer to the Government Wide Area Network for e-government services where applicable. They set the rule for where personal data is stored, not which hosting to use. Authorisation for storage abroad rests with two bodies, the Electronic Government Division and the Data Protection Commissioner.

Not found. No source found says the government has named where public bodies must host, whether a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

ZWE.summary:
Policy adopted. Zimbabwe has a government cloud policy announced but not yet adopted. At the first workshop of government ICT directors in May 2026, the ICT minister, Tatenda Mavetera, set out a Zimbabwe Government Cloud as a companion policy to a cloud-first and mobile-first direction, to end the practice of ministries buying their own servers and to consolidate the state's infrastructure. The same address outlined a legislative agenda to back the directives. No adopted policy, circular or regulation has been found.

Named hosting and moves. Nothing found names a government cloud or data centre in service that public bodies are told to use, or a list of approved providers. The nearest held fact is the minister's announcement of the Zimbabwe Government Cloud, which is described as the intended shared platform for ministries; the report does not say whether it is running or whether any ministry has moved onto it.

AGO.summary:

Banco Nacional de Angola Aviso 7/17 sets transparency, information and contract rules for payment service users and requires providers to follow financial consumer protection rules (2017, before the three-year window). Aviso 12/2016 sets rules for marketing financial products and services, payment-service providers' included, under the bank's conduct supervision (2016, before the three-year window).

Complaints handled. The Banco Nacional de Angola's report on complaints in the financial system counted 16,548 complaints in the first quarter of 2024, mobile banking at non-bank institutions among them. Its ranking for the second quarter of 2025 recorded 10,707 complaints across the financial system.

Enforcement reported. The bank's ranking put Afrimoney, a mobile money platform, at 1,138 complaints in the second quarter of 2025, up 180% on the first quarter, with Unitelmoney at 935 and Paypay at 453. In the first quarter of 2024 Afrimoney drew 8,453 complaints about mobile banking, Unitel Money 532 and PayPay 110.

Complaints handled. The Observatoire de la qualité des services financiers (OQSF-BF), created by decree in December 2022, offers financial mediation in disputes between users and providers, electronic money issuers among them, and the UEMOA Banking Commission can be seized when a complaint is not settled. In 2025 the observatory was merged with two other bodies into the national financial-inclusion agency, ANPFI, whose staff stressed its dispute-settlement role in July 2026. In October 2026 the OQSF-BF, housed in ANPFI, said it mediates free of charge in disputes with banks, microfinance institutions, insurers and e-money issuers, and had handled more than 220 cases since 2022.

Enforcement reported. Citing the BCEAO, the OQSF-BF's December 2024 study says electronic money issuers in Burkina Faso recorded 4,200 complaints in 2022 and resolved 85% of them within the deadline.

Complaints handled. An assessment of the second National Financial Inclusion Strategy, reported by The Reporter in October 2026, says the strategy set up a dedicated financial consumer protection directorate that handles complaints. The same auditors cautioned that consumer safety mechanisms remain ill-equipped for digital fraud, scams and social-engineering risks, given weaknesses in the law on liability for electronic transactions.

UNCDF's November 2023 diagnostic said a new regulation on digital financial consumer protection, revising the one in force since 2011, was expected.

GHA.short: The central bank shut down over 400 illegal online lenders in 2025 and reports complaints against payment service providers.
GHA.summary:
Rules in force. The Bank of Ghana says the Directive for Digital Credit Service Providers in Ghana (September 2025) is in force and that 20 named mobile loan apps operate in contravention of it. Its Second Deputy Governor said the directive requires digital credit providers to be licensed, disclose all loan terms and follow consumer protection rules. The Governor says the Bank's pricing requirements apply to issuers' agent and merchant networks, and licensing requires applicants to disclose fees and commissions.

Complaints handled. The Bank of Ghana's Complaints Management Office received 695 complaints in 2023, 23 of them against payment systems and service providers, and resolved 66% of the total. A mobile money user dissatisfied with the provider's handling of a complaint can take it to the Bank of Ghana.

Enforcement reported. In October 2025 the Bank of Ghana, with EOCO and the Cyber Security Authority, said it had uncovered and shut down more than 400 illegal online lending operators. Its 2023 complaints report counts 23 complaints against payment systems and service providers, with digital-fraud complaints up 48% on 2022.

In August 2026 the lawyer Fodé Mourana Soumah described the standards as giving clients of microfinance institutions, e-money services and postal financial services the right to know the conditions of a service before they commit.

NGA.summary:

TechCabal reports that in April 2026 Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission subjected airtime lending services such as MTN's to new licensing and consumer-protection requirements. On 21 January 2026 the FCCPC began enforcement, withdrawing conditional approval from digital lenders that missed the compliance deadline and removing them from its register.

The regulations give every financial consumer the right to complain to the Competent Authority (the Central Bank of Seychelles or the Financial Services Authority) against a provider's decision, which must investigate and determine within 30 business days; providers must run their own complaint units and answer within 21 business days. The Central Bank of Seychelles received 50 complaints directly in 2025 from customers of banks and payment service providers unsatisfied with the providers' response.

Its financial consumer protection department takes unresolved complaints about banks, microfinance institutions and mobile money providers through a digital screening system, and received over 1,500 complaints in 2024.

Tax. No source found from 2023 or later says the tax authority's system is in use; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

GAB.short: Finance, tax and payroll systems in use, one renewed in 2026; no published map of government systems is known.
GAB.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. A seminar at Oyem from 4 to 11 March 2026 trained credit officers from the five departments of Woleu-Ntem on the expenditure module of the State's new digital public-finance management application, whose rollout began in 2026 with expenditure.

Tax. SIGFIP, launched 15 January 2026, centralises the state's tax, customs and non-tax revenue collection and payments in a single database with a single payment interface (Ecofin Agency).

Payroll. The Fichier unique de référence, in operation for about twenty years, is the application the public service ministry currently uses to manage state human resources and feeds the Solde payroll, though it has coding malfunctions that leave regularised situations invisible to payroll (L'Union, 27 August 2026; meeting of 25 August 2026).

Renewal. SIGFIP went live on 15 January 2026, moving Gabon from fragmented systems to one integrated platform (Ecofin Agency).

A map of the systems. No source found says the government has published an enterprise architecture or an inventory of its systems; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Not found. No source found says the government has published an enterprise architecture or an inventory of its systems.

GHA.short: Finance, tax and payroll run on computer systems by 2026; none is known to have been renewed since 2023.
GHA.summary:

Tax. The GRA Domestic Tax Revenue commissioner said ITAS is being deployed as a single platform replacing the separate legacy system, and that some ITAS capabilities are already operational while others roll out progressively (reported 2026-09-23; no event date given).

Payroll. The Controller and Accountant-General's Department, in a statement dated 24 August 2026, referred to the government payroll system on which employees' NIA numbers are captured and said salaries of employees lacking valid NIA details would be suspended from 15 September 2026. The payroll system was linked to the national identity database in January 2024.

Renewal. No source found says the financial, tax or payroll system went live on a new or upgraded system since October 2023; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

GMB.short: The government budgets and pays through a computer system by 2026; the tax system is run largely by hand.
GMB.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. The Accountant General's Department stated that IFMIS is operational, that Kanifing Municipal Council's IFMIS cashbooks and ledger were updated to August 2026, and that larger ministries, departments and agencies operate with it. The World Bank project record (approved 2016-09-27, US$5m, closed) describes expanding the existing IFMIS to additional ministries, departments and agencies and interfacing it with revenue and treasury systems.

Tax. The GRA Commissioner General said the current domestic tax administration system is largely manual and that the new ITAS, ahead of rollout, is to replace it.

Payroll. No source found from 2023 or later says the civil-service payroll runs on a computer system; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Renewal. No source found says the financial, tax or payroll system went live on a new or upgraded system since October 2023; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

A map of the systems. A validation and sign-off workshop supported by the ITU formally endorsed The Gambia's National Enterprise Architecture under GovStack.

Not found. A source found says the tax system is run largely by hand.

GNB.summary:

Tax. Nothing found from 2023 or later describes the tax system. The nearest held fact is the IMF's figure that the wage bill fell from 84% of tax revenue in 2020 to 50% in 2024.

Payroll. The IMF says Guinea-Bissau launched a blockchain platform for the public payroll in May 2024, under its Extended Credit Facility programme. It was being extended to other ministries and, the IMF said, could cover all 26,600 civil servants and 8,100 pensioners by November 2024.

Renewal. The IMF's project lead says the new payroll ledger went live in May 2024, after four years of work with the Fund and Ernst & Young.

A map of the systems. Nothing found says the government has published an inventory of its systems. The nearest held fact is a World Bank procurement plan for a national government cloud.

Techweez reported in June 2024 that IFMIS had been updated and procuring entities still use its e-Procurement module.

Tax. The Star column reports Kenyans filed annual returns and VAT returns on the KRA iTax portal in June and August 2026, with intermittent delays and errors but filing continuing, and VAT filing moved onto iTax from an offline template.

Payroll. The Treasury Cabinet Secretary said in 2024 that the Unified Human Resource system, which brings together public-service HR and payroll data, had been rolled out and linked to the revenue authority's iTax since July 2023. Nothing found since then describes the payroll.

The ministry states it is taking measures to integrate IFMIS with LITAS, SIGTAS, ASYCUDA, the transitory accounts and the General Revenue Account, treating IFMIS as an existing system. The World Bank project P165000 (US$23.5m, approved 2019-07-16, closed 2024-10-31) supports expansion and upgrade of Liberia's IFMIS.

Tax. The finance ministry, revenue authority and central bank state that the Tax Administration System records revenue and that LITAS is being expanded across regional tax offices, with an audit of 2018-2024 finding variances between its records and bank deposits. The revenue authority's IT project coordinator said in August 2025 that filing, assessments, payments and collections run on LITAS.

Payroll. No source found from 2023 or later says the civil-service payroll runs on a computer system; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

LBY.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. Nothing found from 2023 or later describes a financial management system in use. The finance minister said in 2025 that new systems for financial management information, electronic payments and revenue collection are part of the government's strategy, and the ministry held talks on a government financial management system in October 2025.

Tax. The Libyan Tax Authority announced the official start of work on the Unified Tax System in December 2025, under a decision of that year.

Payroll. The finance minister said August 2025 public-sector salaries were processed on the new unified treasury account system, after basic data for about 41% of state employees had been uploaded.

Renewal. Nothing found says the new treasury account system or the tax system replaced an older one. The nearest held fact is the minister's statement that the treasury account is part of a wider digital transformation strategy.

A map of the systems. Nothing found says the government has published an inventory of its systems. The nearest held fact is the African Development Bank's notice for an IFMIS project.

Not found. No source found from 2023 or later describes the financial management system itself in use. Nothing found says a core system replaced an older one or that the government has published a map of its systems.

LSO.summary:

The World Bank said in December 2023 that the IFMIS, upgraded in 2019, had its budget and treasury modules active, though network problems often made it unavailable.

Tax. Revenue Services Lesotho's guide of February 2025 describes its e-Taxation platform, on which taxpayers register, file and amend company, individual, VAT and PAYE returns and pay by mobile money or bank.

Payroll. The World Bank appraisal document states a Human Resource Management Information System is in place and its payroll module is in use, with most other modules little used (document published 2023-12-22, used as the date).

At its twentieth anniversary in November 2024 the ministry said e-SISTAFE has 11 modules, all working except internal audit, with transactions reaching the Single Treasury Account in real time.

The Central Information Systems Division states it handles monthly payroll processing for every Ministry and Department, on a revamped payroll system with an e-payroll module for Finance Officers. The CISD page lists the e-Payroll system as launched in October 2020 and revamped in September 2023.

Renewal. The CISD page lists a revamped e-Payroll System in September 2023.

The Central Informatics Bureau's progress update on the Digital Government Transformation Strategy marks as implemented the recommendation to publish a catalogue of information systems and services, saying a list of operational systems by ministry and department is available on the CIB website.

MWI.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. The Accountant General said in May 2024 that the SAP-based IFMIS, rolled out to all ministries, departments and agencies a year earlier, was fully operational and producing reports including annual financial statements; its contract management and revenue modules did not yet cover every agency. The World Bank said in 2024 that most agencies still transacted outside it in real time.

Tax. No source found from 2023 or later says the tax authority's system is in use; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Payroll. The Accountant General told a parliamentary committee in February 2024 that the government payroll runs on the human resource management information system and is being moved to the IFMIS human capital module. Councils process salary payments through the central government IFMIS.

Renewal. No source found says the financial, tax or payroll system went live on a new or upgraded system since October 2023; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

NGA.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. The audit directive of 28 August 2026 names GIFMIS, the Treasury Single Account and Sub-TSA as government platforms whose interfaces with IPPIS are to be examined.

Tax. No source found from 2023 or later says the tax authority's system is in use; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Payroll. President Tinubu directed on 28 August 2026 a forensic audit of the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System, reviewing reported ghost workers and payroll fraud on the running system. The Accountant General's office said in October 2025 that IPPIS remains the federal government's central payroll platform; federal tertiary institutions' salaries moved to GIFMIS in late 2024, with delays reported.

Renewal. The IPPIS HR modules went live on 27 July 2026 on the locally developed SoftSuite platform, a migration from foreign software. The office said one of IPPIS's payroll platforms moved to SoftSuite in 2024, with the rest being consolidated onto it in October 2025.

A map of the systems. NITDA took over the Nigeria Government Enterprise Architecture infrastructure from KOICA at a handover in Abuja, reported 27 March 2026, with the NGEA described as now operational.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

RWA.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. MINECOFIN says Rwanda's IFMIS supports government budgeting, expenditure control, payments, accounting and financial reporting across public institutions.

Tax. No source found from 2023 or later says the tax authority's system is in use; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Payroll. No source found from 2023 or later says the civil-service payroll runs on a computer system; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Renewal. MINECOFIN says it completed a major technological upgrade of the IFMIS, replacing legacy components that had reached end of support with new enterprise technologies.

SEN.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. The nearest held fact is the tax directorate's notice that its new platform replaces the old one, which does not name the Treasury's systems.

Tax. Since 1 September 2026 the DGID's platform, which it calls SENTAX, has been mandatory for every declaration and payment by large-enterprise taxpayers, with paper returns no longer accepted, and it opened to the CME1, CME2 and CPR taxpayer groups from 1 October 2026. Taxpayers file and pay online, send and consult tax documents, and track their requests on it.

Payroll. The nearest held fact is the same notice, which covers tax and not the civil-service payroll.

Renewal. The directorate's communiqué of 27 August 2026 says SENTAX now replaces the ETAX application for online declaration and payment by large taxpayers, and its SENTAX page dates the change to 1 September 2026.

A map of the systems. The nearest held fact is the SENTAX page, which describes one platform and not a map of government systems.

SLE.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. World Bank terms of reference of 2025 say the finance ministry has launched IFMIS among its core public finance systems. They say these systems run standalone. In October 2025 the Principal Deputy Financial Secretary said the government had invested over USD 300 million in standalone systems including IFMIS. He said they had advanced several operations but run in isolation.

Tax. The Revenue Authority's Commissioner General said taxpayers can now file and pay electronically through ITAS. The 2025 terms of reference list ITAS among the core systems already running. The Deputy Financial Secretary named the tax system among those running in isolation in October 2025.

Payroll. No source found from 2023 or later says the civil-service payroll runs on a computer system. The nearest held fact: the 2025 list of core public finance systems.

Renewal. No source found says a finance, tax or payroll system went live on a new or upgraded system since October 2023. The nearest held fact: IFMIS among the core systems already launched.

A map of the systems. No source found says the government has published an enterprise architecture or a systems inventory. The nearest held fact: the World Bank's 2025 list of the core systems.

The FY2025 annual report states digital signatures were introduced in SFMIS to re-engineer payment processes and its budget preparation module was enhanced for use in the 2027 budget. The finance ministry signed a contract in September 2026 to extend SFMIS to four federal member states, moving them off the BISAN platform.

Tax. The Electronic Tax Administration System (ETAS) and other digital platforms improved automation and streamlined revenue collection in 2025, with total domestic revenue of USD 404.3 million.

Payroll. The Office of the Accountant General's letter of 29 August 2026 refers to the existing government payroll system, to be linked to NIRA's national ID system from a pilot on 1 October 2026.

SWZ.short: The government's financial system was restored in October 2026 after an outage; no source found reports tax and payroll systems.
SWZ.summary:
Budget, accounts and payments. The Ministry of ICT acknowledged on 23 September 2026 outages of government platforms including the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS), and lenders could not reach IFMIS from about 29 September. On 23 October 2026 the ministry said IFMIS was among 13 government services restored, working with the Royal Science and Technology Park, while the government website was still being restored. In November 2025 every ministry began entering its budget directly into the new IFMIS, which replaces a 1992 mainframe.

Tax. Nothing found describes the tax system. The nearest held fact is the ministry's list of 13 restored services, which names no tax system.

Payroll. Nothing found describes the civil-service payroll. The nearest held fact is the October 2026 report that civil servants' loans stalled while IFMIS was out of reach.

Renewal. Nothing found says a core system went live on a new or upgraded platform. The nearest held fact is IFMIS's restoration on 23 October 2026.

The finance ministry launched SIGFiP at Bardai in January 2025, completing its installation across the country.

Tax. The director general of taxes states E-TAX has been operational since 2021 in the public finance circuit, alongside SIGFIP (Tchadinfos, 5 May 2026). The article names e-tax as a tax platform with which SIGFIP interoperates, in the present tense (published 2026-01-24; no event date given).

A strategy or a national body. Law 13/2026, in force from 29 September 2026, makes INTIC the National Cybersecurity Authority. The law sets up the national CSIRT, nCSIRT.MZ, inside the ICT regulator. The 2021-2025 Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy was approved by Resolution 69/2021. A 2026-2030 strategy was out for consultation in October 2026.

Responding to incidents. The Prosecutor-General said the national CSIRT logged 182,031 incidents in 2024. On 28 September 2025 nCSIRT.mz issued a public alert on fake social media profiles of senior officials.

Critical infrastructure. Law 13/2026 requires critical information infrastructure operators to register with the authority. They must notify the national CSIRT of significant incidents, with fines for failing to. Reporting became mandatory when the law took effect.

Published figures. INTIC's chairman said the national CSIRT detected 5,654 ransomware infection attempts from January to July 2026.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

MRT.summary:

The National Cybersecurity Strategy 2022-2025, which includes a planned national CERT/CSIRT, is still being implemented. Ecofin says a April 2024 decree created the National Agency for Cybersecurity and Electronic Certification to protect national cyberspace, and a government presentation of November 2024 dates the agency to 23 April 2024 and gives it the task of setting up CERT Mauritanie.

Responding to incidents. No source found says the national body handled an incident or issued a public alert since October 2023, so no response to an attack is on record; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Critical infrastructure. No source found says the country designated its critical information infrastructure or required the operators of its critical systems to report incidents to the national body; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Published figures. No source found says the national body published a count of the incidents it handled for a quarter or more ending in the last two years; the stage rests on the source that sets it.

Not found. No source found says the national body handled an incident or issued a public alert since October 2023.

The National Cybersecurity Committee is set up under section 3 of the Cybersecurity and Cybercrime Act 2021. The National Audit Office found the committee not yet working at the end of 2025.

Responding to incidents. On 22 October 2026 CERT-MU rated the PHP2Shell flaws critical in a security bulletin. On the committee's advice the government took about 70% of its sites offline.

Critical infrastructure. Regulations gazetted in June 2026 let the National Cybersecurity Committee designate critical information infrastructure. No source found says any system has yet been designated.

Published figures. Figures from CERT-MU and ICT Authority data show reported security incidents rising from 5,221 in 2024 to 6,073 in 2025. CERT-MU's MAUCORS+ platform logged 47 phishing cases in 2025.

NAM-CSIRT is stated to be housed at the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia (CRAN) and to have issued an advisory.

NAM-CSIRT confirmed unauthorised activity on the Ministry of Defence and Veterans Affairs network, attributed it to RansomHouse and said it is coordinating investigation, remediation and post-incident review.

(Reported by The Namibian, 2026-09-20.). NAM-CSIRT states 1,701,883 cyber-attack events and 2,231,970 reported vulnerabilities for January to December 2025.

NgCERT, published on the NCC CSIRT site, issued advisory ngCERT-2026-050005 on 2026-09-24: a critical-rated advisory on WhatsApp vulnerabilities CVE-2026-23866 and CVE-2026-23863.
