AGO.short: Angola's new cybersecurity law and Law 7/17 of 2017 are in force as of October 2026; no use of either is known.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. A UNITA deputy, quoted by Novo Jornal on 23 January 2026, says Law 7/17 of 16 February, on the protection of computer networks and systems, is part of the current legal order and that the new bill would repeal it. The Council of Ministers considered the Cybersecurity Bill on 27 October 2025 for sending to the National Assembly. The Assembly approved it in general terms on 23 January 2026, with 105 votes for and 75 UNITA abstentions, and adopted the cybersecurity law on 12 August 2026, with MPLA votes carrying it. Angola's minister said the Cybersecurity Law has entered into force, as SADC reported on 16 October 2026.

Use of the law. The law adopted on 12 August 2026 sets fines of 7 to 4,000 national minimum wages, by gravity, according to ANGOP. The National Assembly's specialised committees approved the proposed law before the final vote, as Telecompaper reported on 10 August 2026. PTI reports that the final vote of 12 August 2026 was taken globally, with 104 in favour.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BDI.short: A 2022 cybercrime law is in force and was cited as applied in 2026; no use against anyone is known.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi's cybercrime law is Law No. 1/10 of 16 March 2022 on the prevention and repression of cybercrime. At a workshop in Bujumbura in February 2026, a government delegate cited it as adopted and in application. A speaker at the same workshop said the president signed it in 2022. The law is named in the article as the country's cybercrime law, and the Malabo Convention was the standard against which the workshop measured it.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is the same February 2026 workshop in Bujumbura, where experts and participants discussed the law's enforcement and its gaps against the Malabo Convention. The government delegate presented the law at that workshop as being in application. The article gives that discussion and the 2022 date of signature, and the law is the Burundian text on cybercrime prevention and repression adopted in March 2022.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BEN.short: The 2018 Code du numérique is in force; in 2025 about 1,500 online-fraud suspects were arrested.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, the Code du numérique, was adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President. Its Livre VI defines illegal access to and penetration of an information system. The code carries the date 20 April 2018, and its Livre VI treats unauthorised entry into computer systems as an offence, in two forms: illegal access and penetration.

Use of the law. Benin's Centre national d'investigations numériques reported over 6,500 digital-offence complaints in 2025, against about 4,000 the year before, and about 1,500 arrests of online-fraud suspects. During INTERPOL's Operation Sentinel, from 27 October to 27 November 2025, Benin took down 43 malicious domains and shut 4,318 extortion and scam accounts, leading to 106 arrests. The complaints figure covers the whole of 2025, and the arrests figure covers suspects in online fraud.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

BFA.short: A 2024 information-security law is in force; the cybercrime brigade made arrests in 2025. No yearly count of cases is published.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. The Council of Ministers of 30 July 2026 adopted decrees applying law n°014-2024/ALT of 9 July 2024 on the security of information systems. One identifies and categorises critical-infrastructure bodies, and the other sets periodic security audits and auditor accreditation. The law itself, headed Loi n°014-2024/ALT of 9 July 2024, sets rules to control and protect information systems and govern the actors in them, with licensing and fines.

Use of the law. Burkina Faso's cybercrime brigade, the BCLCC, arrested two people in August 2025 over a TikTok video. It referred them to the Ouaga II prosecutor for offences committed through ICT, under articles 375-2, 375-3 and 524-4 of the Penal Code. During Opération Cyber-Balayage, from 27 to 31 October 2025, the brigade arrested 22 people for online fraud, identity theft, sextortion and privacy offences. Eleven of them were referred to the judicial authorities.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

BWA.short: A 2025 cybersecurity act awaits commencement and the 2018 cybercrime act stays in force until then; no use of either is known.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. The Cybersecurity Act, 2025 (Act No. 21 of 2025) was assented to on 5 November 2025 and gazetted on 11 November 2025. Its commencement is on a date the Minister appoints by Order, and it repeals and replaces the Cybercrime and Computer Related Crimes Act 2018. In March 2026 the communications minister said the Act was expected to come into force in April. Parliament had passed the Cybersecurity Bill, 2025 on 14 August 2025 under a certificate of urgency presented by the Minister of Communications and Innovation, after a public consultation on the draft Bill held on 20 June 2025.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is that the ICT minister said, as ITWeb reported in May 2026, that the Act was passed in November 2025 and establishes a National Cybersecurity Authority. Botswana Daily News reported on 25 February 2026 that the Act, signed into law the year before, sets up that Authority.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

CAF.short: A cybercrime law, Loi 24.002 of February 2024, is in force; a 2026 opinion piece says police and prosecutors use it. No case is known.
CAF.summary:
Law in force. The official laws index of the telecoms regulator ARCEP lists Loi 24.002 of 21 February 2024 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime among the country's laws. Africa Top Success reported that the National Assembly voted the cybersecurity and anti-cybercrime bill by acclamation on 25 January 2024, with promulgation by the President expected within days. The bill sets prison terms of 6 to 10 years and fines of 5 to 10 million CFA francs. In March 2023 terms of reference for a consultant described a draft law on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime that needed improving, and asked the consultant to draft amendments and implementing texts.

Use of the law. An opinion piece published on 18 August 2026 refers to the government's cybercrime law as wielded by the prosecutor's office and police. It dates from 2026, more than two years after the Assembly vote of January 2024.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

CIV.short: A 2024 cybersecurity ordinance is in force; the cybercrime platform handled 12,100 files in 2024, with the law used not named.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Ordinance No. 2024-950, a cybersecurity text, is in force, and on 16 June 2025 the Senate unanimously adopted the bill ratifying it. The same bill updates the 2017 ordinance on electronic exchanges. The source describes the measure as a cybersecurity bill and reports no dissent in the vote. The 2013 law on the fight against cybercrime, no. 2013-451 of 19 June 2013, was amended by law no. 2023-593 of 7 June 2023.

Use of the law. The national information-security agency's report for 2024, presented on 22 May 2025, says its cybercrime platform received and handled 12,100 files in 2024, up from 8,132 the year before. The largest groups were 2,822 files on attacks on human dignity and 2,326 on online fraud, and the files also covered fraudulent access to information systems. The agency put the financial loss at about 7 billion CFA francs, down from more than 9 billion a year earlier. The report as relayed does not name the law the files were handled under.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided that names the law they were brought under, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

CMR.short: A cybercrime law from December 2010 is in force and was reviewed at a June 2026 workshop; no use against anyone is known.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on cybercrime is treated as the existing law in a June 2026 Le Jour report on a workshop in Yaounde on 8 and 9 June that reviewed its articles. A Nkafu brief of 4 September 2026 says the legal framework is anchored in a 2010 cybersecurity law and 2012 decrees, and calls for the 2010 law to be revised. A July 2025 African Law & Business article lists the law among the complementary laws that make the data protection Act enforceable, and an August 2024 CENADI workshop heard it listed among the local texts that frame data protection.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is a workshop reported by Le Jour on 16 June 2026. Held on 8 and 9 June 2026 in Yaounde, the workshop reviewed articles of law no. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on cybercrime.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

COD.short: A digital code has been in force since 2023, and in August 2026 police were told to enforce it; no case is known.
COD.summary:
Law in force. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has the Code du numérique, promulgated in 2023. The news agency ACP states that the Code du numérique makes non-consensual sharing of intimate content, privacy breaches and cyberharassment criminal offences in the country. On 17 August 2026 the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation treated the Digital Code as in force, as the news agency ACP reported that same day.

Use of the law. On 17 August 2026 the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation told judicial police officers to take up offences under the Digital Code on their own initiative. This is an instruction to the officers who bring cases, issued in the Code's fourth year, and it covers the offences the Code creates. ACP also reports that the offences the Code du numérique names include cyberharassment and privacy breaches.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

COG.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime laws of 2020 are in force; no arrest or case under them is known.
COG.summary:
Law in force. The Republic of the Congo has two laws of 5 June 2020, loi n° 26-2020 relative à la cybersécurité and loi n° 27-2020 portant lutte contre la cybercriminalité. The Journal officiel of 18 June 2026 prints a decree of 6 May 2026 that cites both as in force. The Journal officiel of 9 April 2026 prints decrees of 29 December 2025 that cite both the same way. The World Bank diagnostic of December 2020 says Loi 26-2020 governs the national legal framework for information-system and network security.

Use of the law. In its 2025 assessment, UNESCO states that application of the cybersecurity and cybercrime laws still has to be strengthened and calls for implementing texts for the cybercrime law. The same report cites no arrest, prosecution, conviction or case count under either law. The World Bank diagnostic adds that operationalising the bodies the cybersecurity law defines remained to be done in 2020.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

COM.short: Cybercrime offences are in the Penal Code in force since 2021; a separate cybersecurity law was only a draft; no use is known.
COM.summary:
Law in force. The Comoros has cybercrime offences in its Penal Code. According to the national digital agency ANADEN, the President promulgated by decree on 16 February 2021 the new Penal Code, loi n°20-38/AU of 29 December 2020, whose articles 449 to 505 set out cybercrime offences, online intellectual property infringement and service-provider liability. The same ANADEN publication of 4 March 2021 lists a specific cybersecurity law as drafted but not yet adopted, to follow the Penal Code.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is the promulgation itself. ANADEN states that the President promulgated the Penal Code by decree on 16 February 2021, with its cybercrime offences in articles 449 to 505. The same source gives the Penal Code as the first step, with a specific cybersecurity law and a digital code to follow. It records no case brought under these articles.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

CPV.short: A 2021 cybersecurity decree-law is in force; no case under it is known.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. Cabo Verde has Decreto-lei n.º 9/2021, its regime jurídico de cibersegurança, together with Decreto-Regulamentar n.º 1/2021, which creates the national CSIRT. The 2026 State Budget law cites them as in place. The 2024 annual plan and budget of NOSi states that both decrees exist, and gives no further date for them. Both documents name the cybersecurity regime as a text that is already part of the country's rules.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is that the national CSIRT the regulating decree creates is named in official documents. The 2026 State Budget law cites Decreto-lei n.º 9/2021 and its regulating decree as in place, and the NOSi plan for 2024 lists them among existing texts. Neither document records any case brought under the law, and neither gives a date for any use of it by the authorities of Cabo Verde.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

DJI.short: A digital code with a cybercrime book passed parliament in 2025 but is only a bill so far; no use of it is known.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. Djibouti's National Assembly passed the Digital Code on 30 June 2025, covering cybersecurity and cybercrime and punishable online offences. The legislative section was still to be promulgated by the President and published in the Journal Officiel. TechAfrica News reported on 2 July 2025 that the Code has eight books and nearly 800 articles, and that Book VI deals with Cybersecurity and Cybercrime. It is Djibouti's first Digital Code and was passed in plenary.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is in the text itself: Jones Day reports, in a note of 1 July 2025, that the Digital Code makes online offences punishable. The Assembly adopted it on 30 June 2025, and the same report says its legislative section awaited promulgation by the President, then publication in the Journal Officiel. That adoption was reported within days: TechAfrica News carried it on 2 July 2025 under a headline saying Djibouti enacts the Code.

Not found. No source found says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force. Nothing is held on any arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under such a law.

DZA.short: A 2009 law on offences linked to information technology is treated as in force by a 2020 decree; no use of it is known.
DZA.summary:
Law in force. Algeria's Law 09-04 of 5 August 2009 sets rules on preventing and fighting offences linked to information and communication technologies. Presidential decree 20-05 of 20 January 2020 lists it among the laws the decree rests on. In March 2026 the director general of the information systems security agency, ASSI, announced a draft cybersecurity bill. It would make security measures mandatory for institutions.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is the state's own reliance on the text, not a case brought under it. Presidential decree 20-05 of 20 January 2020 cites Law 09-04 of 5 August 2009 among the laws it rests on, which shows the executive treating the law as current in 2020. The law's French title is the Loi n° 09-04 du 5 août 2009 portant règles particulières relatives à la prévention et à la lutte contre les infractions liées aux technologies de l'information et de la communication.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law has been reported in the last three years.

EGY.short: A 2018 information technology crimes law is in force and courts convicted content creators under it in 2025; no count of cases is known.
EGY.summary:
Law in force. Egypt's Law 175 of 2018 on combating information technology crimes is treated as the current law in a bill an MP put forward on 22 April 2026, which would tighten its provisions. A separate bill from an MP, referred to committees by the House speaker, also amends Law 175, which its sponsor calls the current law, with penalties too weak.

Use of the law. In November 2025 Egyptian courts convicted a series of TikTok content creators under Article 25 of Law 175 of 2018, with sentences from six-month suspended terms to two years and fines of EGP 100,000 each. People of Internet calls the law Egypt's principal cybercrime statute. Two bills reported on 22 April 2026, one from an MP to tighten its provisions and another its sponsor says answers penalties that are too weak, take it as the current text.

Not found. No published count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law has been found.

ERI.short: Eritrea's Penal Code, read in 2020, covers computer offences in place of a cybercrime act; no use of it is known.
ERI.summary:
Law in force. Eritrea has no separate cybercrime act. The Council of Europe cybercrime office's legal profile, in its version of 5 May 2020, maps the Penal Code to the Budapest Convention's offence articles as the domestic equivalent. Article 374 covers unauthorized use of a computer, including access, interception, and data and system interference. Article 298 covers violation of privacy. The same profile lists Eritrea as not a signatory to the Budapest Convention.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the scope of the provisions themselves. The 2020 legal profile places unauthorized computer use and interference with data and systems under Article 374 of the Penal Code, and violation of privacy under Article 298, as the offences that stand in for a cybercrime act.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

ETH.short: A 2016 computer crime law is in force; a court convicted a YouTube host under it in 2024. No yearly count of cases is published.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. Ethiopia's cybercrime law is Computer Crime Proclamation No. 958/2016, which the Federal High Court applied in a conviction in November 2024. A 2024 law journal article treats it as the current cybercrime law and describes a 2019 draft proclamation as a further reform. The Federal Negarit Gazette carries Critical Infrastructure Cyber Security Protection Proclamation No. 1426/2026, signed on 21 July 2026. Its article 28 brings it into force one year after publication, in July 2027. INSA's Director General said it sets 18 obligations for owners of 12 critical sectors.

Use of the law. In November 2024 the Federal High Court found Meskerem Abera guilty on two counts under Proclamation No. 958/2016. The case concerned two YouTube programmes of Ethio Neqat, which she founded, and her lawyer told BBC Amharic that sentencing was set for 11 November 2024. Birr Metrics reported in December 2025 that Yohanis Daniel faced an added charge under the computer-crime law. He had recorded and live-streamed an August 2024 flight incident on TikTok.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

GAB.short: A cybersecurity and cybercrime law, numbered 027/2023, was in force in 2025; no use of it against anyone is known.
GAB.summary:
Law in force. Gabonreview, in an article published on 1 June 2025, presents law no. 027/2023 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime as a national law. It is the law with which ANINF's SecBOM, the Security Bill of Material, must comply. The article treats the law as the standing national framework for cybersecurity in Gabon, and names ANINF as the agency whose tool is held to it. ANINF is described there as reinforcing national cybersecurity through the SecBOM, a tool on which the article reports. A law ratifying the ordinance on social networks, promulgated by decree 0436/PR of 5 October 2026, punishes using another person's identifying details to deceive users and take their confidential data with five years' imprisonment and a fine of FCFA 5 to 20 million.

Use of the law. The nearest fact held is the same article of 1 June 2025, which links the law to ANINF's SecBOM: the tool must comply with law no. 027/2023. That is a compliance requirement placed on an agency tool, stated in a news article, and it is the only application of the law described in the source.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

GHA.short: A cybersecurity law is in force; in 2026 the authority fined a state registry and a private firm under it.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Digital Policy Alert states that Ghana's 2020 Cybersecurity Act establishes measures for critical information infrastructure protection, cybercrime prevention and incident response, and that Ghana implemented the Act. It names the Cyber Security Authority as the body created under the Act. In August 2026 the Cyber Security Authority sanctioned bodies under Section 92 of the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), which the article treats as the law in force. An October 2026 op-ed describes the Act as the framework for protecting critical information infrastructure and prosecuting cybercrimes.

Use of the law. In an article published on 13 August 2026, the Cyber Security Authority fined the Office of the Registrar of Companies GH¢240,000, being 10,000 penalty units for each of two instances of non-compliance under Section 92(2) of Act 1038. It also fined Purpleline Solutions Limited GH¢120,000 for providing cybersecurity services without a licence. Both were fined as bodies, one a state office and one a private company.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

GIN.short: A cybersecurity law is in force; in 2025 the media regulator said it will be used against web media. No case is known.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. Guinea has had a law on cybersecurity and personal data protection since 2016, mainly aimed at cybercrime, according to the director of ANSSI's alert centre. The ministry's secretary-general, Nouhan Traore, said in October 2025 that Guinea has put the law in place. On 13 August 2026 ANSSI held a consultation workshop on draft texts on cybersecurity and cybercrime. The drafts were prepared with SOCSLAWYERS to update the 2016 framework.

Use of the law. The nearest fact held is the same statement of 26 July 2025. In it the regulator's president said the cybersecurity law will be applied to web media that break the rules, and that the penalty is prison for any person who breaks them, whoever that person is.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law has been reported in the last three years.

GMB.short: A 2009 act with cybercrime offences is in force and a cybercrime bill was still pending in 2026; no use of either is known.
GMB.summary:
Law in force. The Information and Communications Act, 2009 (No. 2 of 2009) entered into force on 29 May 2009. Its Part III of Chapter III, "Computer Misuse and Cyber Crime", creates offences such as unauthorised access to computer data. Parliament introduced a proposed Cybercrime Bill in March 2024, and the Oxford Institute of Technology and Justice states that, as at June 2026, it has not been enacted. In May 2026 the Gambia Press Union cited the Cybercrime Bill as pending legislation with broad surveillance powers, heavy fines and prison terms.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the penalty the Act's offences carry: unauthorised access to computer data is punishable by a fine of 200,000 dalasis or up to five years' imprisonment, or both. Separately, The Gambia signed the African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection on 2 December 2022, a continental treaty covering both subjects.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years.

GNB.short: No source found names a cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not found. Nothing names a cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill for Guinea-Bissau, or says there is none.

GNQ.short: Ley 7/2024 is in force; in September 2026 the vice-president's lawyers filed four complaints under it, which await the court. No charge is known.
GNQ.summary:
Law in force. The Government stated on 1 July 2026 that Ley 7/2024 of 23 December 2024, regulating social networks, computer crimes and cybercrime, is fully in force. In September 2026 a law firm treated it as applicable law, grounding complaints on its articles 2, 50 and 60.

Use of the law. On 16 September 2026, lawyers acting for vice-president Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue lodged four criminal complaints under Ley 7/2024 at Juzgado de Instruccion Numero I de Malabo. They name Maria Luzmila Ondo, Mocache Massoko of Diario Rombe, Jose Carlos Ndong and Maria Teresa Siemfum. The complaints rest on the law's articles 2, 50 and 60, and the case is at an initial stage, awaiting the court. The complainant is the vice-president himself. The law's own title covers social networks, computer crimes and cybercrime together.

Not found. No arrest, charge by a prosecutor or court decision under the law has been found, and no count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under it.

KEN.short: The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act is in force; a journalist was charged under it in 2026. No yearly count of cases is published.
KEN.summary:
Law in force. The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act of 2018 stands. In March 2026 the Court of Appeal struck down sections 22 and 23, its false-publication offences, and upheld the rest, including the investigative powers. The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act, 2025 amended it from 4 November 2025. On 3 September 2026 Kenya launched an official guide to investigating and prosecuting 76 listed cyber offences under the Act.

Use of the law. CPJ reports that journalist Peter Mwita was charged in a Mombasa court under the Act in February 2026, over a WhatsApp message, and pleaded not guilty. CPJ lists other bloggers and journalists arrested under it. The Daily Nation says dozens of young social media users have faced arrest and prosecution under the Act, more of them after the June 2024 protests. They include the teacher Albert Ojwang, arrested over a post, who died in custody in June 2025.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

LBR.short: Cybercrime law in force since 2026; used in September 2026 to arrest a commentator over images of the Vice President.
LBR.summary:
Law in force. Liberia's Cybercrime Act of 2025 was signed into law by President Boakai in 2026, and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications has published the approved Act. One report says the Act requires regulations within six to twelve months, and another says the country has entered the enforcement phase. The Act is being operationalized by the Liberia Telecommunications Authority and the Ministry of Justice, and ten civil society organisations plan to engage lawmakers on amendments. President Boakai approved the Cybercrime Act on 3 July 2026, after the House passed it in 2023 and the Senate in November 2025.

Use of the law. In September 2026 police arrested the commentator Jerry Nyantee Wrato over AI-generated images of the Vice President, then charging him and forwarding him to court. The Inspector General's letter of 21 September resolved to prosecute him under sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Act, covering misuse of devices, cyberstalking, incitement and harmful data messages. A court ordered him released on habeas corpus on 22 September. The arrest was presented as the Act's first major public test.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

LBY.short: A parliamentary committee was preparing a cybersecurity bill in July 2026; a cybercrime draft went to experts in 2025. No law in force is known.
LBY.summary:
Law in force. Libya has bills, not an enacted law. On 15 July 2026 a temporary House of Representatives committee, created by Speaker's decision 115 of 2025, met National Security Council officials in Benghazi to work on preparing a comprehensive cybersecurity bill. A near-finalized draft law on cybercrime and digital evidence was presented for expert feedback at the Informatics Governance Forum workshop in 2025, with earlier drafts dating from 2008, 2009 and 2015.

Use of the law. The nearest held facts concern bills, not a law in operation. The 15 July 2026 committee meeting in Benghazi was work on preparing the cybersecurity bill. The draft on cybercrime and digital evidence was at the stage of expert feedback in 2025, and no enacted text is described in either source.

Not found. No source found says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

LSO.short: Cybercrime and cybersecurity bills were still awaiting Parliament in September 2026; no law in force is known, and no use of one.
LSO.summary:
Law in force. Lesotho's nearest held fact is a pair of bills. Cabinet split the 2024 bill into a Cybercrime Bill 2026 and a Cybersecurity Bill 2026, and the Department of Information reports a second stakeholder consultation on the Cybersecurity Bill 2026 after a draft circulated in August 2026, with the bill still to proceed through the next legislative stages. The Lesotho Times reports that a 2021 version was withdrawn from Parliament and the 2024 Computer Crime and Cyber Security Bill was referred to Parliament but not enacted. In August 2026 the Director General of ICT said both bills were ready and waiting for approval by the National Assembly.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact concerns the draft text. The Computer Crime and Cyber Security Bill, 2024 would commence on gazettal and be cited as the Act once enacted. In January 2026 the Principal Secretary at the communications ministry said it was working on the Cybersecurity Bill.

Not found. No source found says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2020 cybersecurity law is in force, and police counted 13,643 cybercrime cases in 2025. No count of cases under the law is published.
MAR.summary:
Law in force. Morocco's Loi n° 05-20 on cybersecurity was promulgated by dahir n° 1-20-69 of 25 July 2020 and published in Bulletin officiel n° 6906 of 6 August 2020. Its article 53 makes it operative on publication of its implementing texts. The same page records that décret n° 2-24-921, applying article 25, was in force by the Bulletin officiel of 20 February 2025, so the law has implementing texts in place alongside the 2020 text.

Use of the law. Morocco's national police, the DGSN, counted 13,643 cybercrime cases handled in 2025, in the annual report it presented on 17 December 2025. In the same year 415 people were arrested and referred to court for technology-related crimes and online blackmail, the DGSN says. Both figures are the police's own and cover offences committed through computers and networks.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

MDG.short: A 2014 cybercrime law is in force; a replacement bill was postponed in September 2026. No use of the law is known.
MDG.summary:
Law in force. Madagascar's cybercrime framework still rests in part on loi n°2014-006, adopted in June 2014, which defined offences such as fraudulent access to information systems and data breaches. The government tabled bill n°042/2026 on combating cybercrime at the National Assembly on 28 August 2026, with penalties of two to ten years and fines of 100,000 to 100 million ariary. The Council of Ministers had adopted the draft bill recasting the law on 7 July 2026. On 4 September deputies voted to postpone adoption of the 96-article text, and it was not among the 17 bills on the agenda of the extraordinary session opening 17 September 2026. By 24 October it was back on the Assembly's agenda, with committee examination set for 2 November.

Use of the law. The 2026 bill would create the Upin digital police. A digital-law specialist interviewed by Midi Madagasikara says it would require suspicious-transaction reports on Mobile Money transfers of 10 million ariary or more and tighten SIM identification.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MLI.short: Cybercrime provisions in force since December 2024 were used against journalists in 2026, with prison sentences; the cybercrime pole handled 1,338 files in 2025.
MLI.summary:
Law in force. IPI states that Mali amended its Penal Code in December 2024, incorporating provisions previously contained in the 2019 cybercrime law, and that journalists have been arrested and imprisoned under the new penal code. Human Rights Watch says articles 20 and 21 of the 2019 cybercrime law criminalise online "threats" and "insults" with up to 10 years in prison, and RSF says the law was applied to journalist Youssouf Sissoko in March 2026.

Use of the law. Journalist Chahana Takiou, founder-director of the newspaper 22 septembre, was sentenced on 3 August 2026 to 12 months in prison, 6 suspended, for undermining the credit of the State, after the cybercrime pole summoned him. IPI reports that journalist Abdrahamane Keita of Le Témoin was detained on 9 June 2026 and charged with undermining national unity and the credibility of the state and spreading false information, with his trial postponed from 17 to 31 August, and that the trial of commentator Mohamed Youssouf Bathily began on 10 August 2026. The criminal chamber of the cybercrime pole had 4 cases involving 8 accused on its roll on 21 May 2026. Human Rights Watch reports that editor Youssouf Sissoko was arrested on 5 February 2026 under the 2019 law, charged with spreading false information and insulting a foreign head of state, and RSF says he was sentenced on 23 March 2026 to two years in prison and a 1 million CFA franc fine.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

MOZ.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime laws were signed in 2026. No use of the law is known.
MOZ.summary:
Law in force. President Chapo promulgated the Cybersecurity Law in June 2026, protecting networks, information systems and critical infrastructure, with a regulatory body and penalties up to 160 minimum wages. Lusa reports that the president enacted the Cyber Security and Cybercrime Acts on 12 June. Africa AI News states that Mozambique already has a Cyber Security Act and a Cybercrimes Act as part of its legal foundation. The Penal Code (Law 24/2019, amended by Law 17/2020) also provides cybercrimes such as database intrusion, punishable by up to two years, and electronic fraud, punishable by one to five years. UNESCO's December 2025 profile lists a draft Cybersecurity Law among the country's instruments.

Use of the law. On 28 July 2026 the communications minister said the government has approved the Cybersecurity Law and the Cybercrime Law and that implementation is mandatory for companies operating critical infrastructure. In April 2026 Parliament unanimously approved the Cyber Security Law, making INCM technical coordinator for cyberspace security and creating a Cyber Security Fund, a proposal the government had submitted the previous Thursday.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MRT.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2016. No use of the law is known.
MRT.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2016-007 on cybercrime was adopted by the National Assembly and the Senate and promulgated by the President of the Republic. It has 52 articles covering offences, search and interception powers, and international cooperation. The year, 2016, is taken from the law number, and the law is cited as Loi n° 2016-007 relative à la cybercriminalité. Its provisions on offences sit beside its provisions on how investigators may search and intercept, and its provisions on how the state cooperates with other countries.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the content of the same 2016 cybercrime law: its 52 articles give search and interception powers, alongside the offences it defines and its provisions on international cooperation. Both chambers of the legislature adopted it before the President promulgated it, so the text that gives investigators those powers is a promulgated law and not a draft.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

MUS.short: A cybercrime and cybersecurity law has been in force since 2021; police made 130 arrests under it by January 2026, with no conviction yet.
MUS.summary:
Law in force. The Cybersecurity and Cybercrime Act 2021 (Act No. 16 of 2021) was passed on 19 November 2021 and assented to on 24 November 2021. The retrieved text records it as proclaimed in force on 10 December 2021, repealing the Computer Misuse and Cybercrime Act. In June 2026 regulations designating critical information infrastructure came into operation under the Act. On 7 October 2026 the Ministry of Technology, Communication and Innovation discussed proposed amendments to the Act with Meta in Ebene.

Use of the law. Le Mauricien reports that the police Cybercrime Unit handled 930 cases from January 2023 to January 2026, leading to 130 arrests. Of those cases, 177 were closed and 660 were under investigation. Another 33 awaited advice from the Director of Public Prosecutions, and 7 were before court. In November 2025 the Prime Minister gave a count of 837 cases to that date. That count included 120 arrests and no conviction.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

MWI.short: Malawi's 2016 cyber law is in force; a man was charged under it in 2026 for hacking phones. No yearly count of cases is published.
MWI.summary:
Law in force. Malawi's Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act, Act 33 of 2016, criminalises offences related to computer systems and ICT. It was gazetted on 4 November 2016 and commenced on 1 June 2017. In October 2026 the Justice Minister said a new cybercrime bill should go to Parliament in the February to April 2027 session. The ICT Minister said the 2016 Act would be reviewed alongside the new bills.

Use of the law. Nyasa Times reports that Collins Magalasi was charged in court in September 2026 under section 83(1), read with section 89, of the 2016 Act. The charge is aiding the hacking of the President's and senior officials' phones. In August 2024 police charged a Mzuzu man with cyber spamming under section 91. They also arrested the politicians Kamlepo Kalua and Bon Kalindo over voice notes said to breach the cyber law.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

NAM.short: Only a cybercrime bill is known, under consultation in 2026; no law in force is known, so no use of one.
NAM.summary:
Law in force. Namibia's proposed cybercrime law is the Cybercrime Bill. In December 2024 the regulator CRAN said Namibia lacks dedicated cybercrime legislation. A draft bill was presented to stakeholders in Windhoek on 18 February 2026, where the country was said to have no law yet that directly governs cybercrime. The Windhoek Observer, citing the 2026/27 budget estimates, reports that drafting is complete. It says the bill was due to go to Parliament in March 2026, after a validation workshop.

Use of the law. The nearest fact is the consultation on the bill. In February 2026 the ICT ministry consulted stakeholders at Rundu from Kavango East, Kavango West and Zambezi. The response team NAM-CSIRT, in its 2025 landscape report published in April 2026, asks the government to expedite the bill. In July 2025 the ICT Minister said drafting had been delayed by a lack of local cyberlaw expertise.

Not found. No source found says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force.

NER.short: A 2019 cybercrime law is in force; it was used to charge six journalists in October 2025 and a lawyer in September 2026.
NER.summary:
Law in force. Niger's cybercrime law is law no. 2019-33 of 3 July 2019. It was amended on 12 June 2024 to set penalties for online defamation, insults and harmful data. Human Rights Watch says the amendment restored prison terms of up to five years. They apply to disseminating data likely to disturb public order. In April 2026 a panellist cited the law among the texts in force that regulate cybersecurity.

Use of the law. The law was used against journalists and a lawyer. Police in Niamey arrested six journalists on 30 October 2025, Human Rights Watch reports, and they were charged under the 2019 law over an invitation to a state press conference. The lawyer Lirwana was charged and detained from 21 September 2026. On 13 October 2026 the Niamey High Court convicted him under Article 31 and sentenced him to two years and a 2 million CFA franc fine. In September 2026 the judicial police's cybercrime division arrested suspects in three fraud and blackmail cases.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

NGA.short: A cybercrime law is in force and was used in 2026 against activist Omoyele Sowore, and in 2024 against journalists and critics.
NGA.summary:
Law in force. The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act is an enacted law of 2015 and was amended in 2024. The amended Act contains interception provisions, and SERAP says the 2024 amendment retains ambiguous cyberstalking wording in section 24. Section 24 prescribes up to three years' imprisonment or a fine for sending a message known to be false. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre said on 15 October 2026 that section 24 is repeatedly used to arrest journalists for their reporting.

Use of the law. In December 2024 activist Olamide Thomas was arrested and charged for allegedly insulting the President's son on Facebook. The Department of State Services is prosecuting activist and presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore over his description of the President as a criminal, and its Director-General announced on 30 August 2026 that the prosecution would be suspended until after the 2027 election. SERAP says authorities continue to use section 24 to arrest and charge journalists, bloggers, activists and ordinary citizens. Reporters Without Borders reported in 2024 that at least eight journalists had been arrested, prosecuted or detained under the Act.

Not found. The number of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law in a period ending in the last two years.

RWA.short: A cybersecurity law is in force, and the Supreme Court upheld one article in June 2025. No source found says whether it has been used.
RWA.summary:
Law in force. Rwanda has a cybersecurity law in force. The East African Policy Observer, drawing on the Carnegie Endowment's Africa Technology Policy Tracker, says in a commentary of 30 July 2026 that Rwanda's binding legal instruments include cybersecurity law. The law is the 2018 Cybercrime Law, and on 5 June 2025 Rwanda's Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of its Article 39, which criminalises publishing rumours through digital platforms, according to CIVICUS Monitor.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact is the court's ruling of 5 June 2025, in which the Supreme Court upheld Article 39 of the 2018 Cybercrime Law, as reported by CIVICUS Monitor. It is a ruling on the article's constitutionality, and it leaves the article in force. The ruling does not record an arrest, charge or conviction under the law, and it is the only held fact about the law in the courts.

Not found. Any arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years.

SDN.short: A cybercrime law is in force and was used in 2026 to jail a pharmacist over anti-war messages and to arrest a journalist.
SDN.summary:
Law in force. Sudan has a Cybercrime Law, and courts apply it: a criminal court in El Obeid convicted a defendant under Articles 19 and 24 in August 2026. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate cites the Cybercrime Act as the basis of a live arrest and calls for its repeal. The SudaPass terms cite the Cybercrime Law as the basis of criminal penalties of up to twelve years for electronic sabotage or forgery, and refer to a Cyber Security Act of 2025.

Use of the law. The law has been used against an anti-war critic and a journalist. In August 2026 a criminal court in El Obeid sentenced pharmacist Ahmed Suleiman Ahmed Al-Waqi to six years in total, two of them under Article 19 and one under Article 24 of the Cybercrime Law, after a phone search found anti-war messages, according to his lawyer. In August 2026 criminal investigation police arrested journalist Gurashi Awad in River Nile State on a complaint by a General Intelligence Service lieutenant colonel, the Sudanese Journalists Syndicate said.

Not found. The number of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law in a period ending in the last two years.

SEN.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2008, and police recorded 3,902 cybercrime complaints in 2024. No count of cases under it is published.
SEN.summary:
Law in force. Senegal's Cybercrime Law, Law 2008-10 of 25 January 2008, completes the Penal Code and the Penal Procedure Code and lists offences with penalties of six months to 10 years. The same 2018 practitioner source says no separate cybersecurity act had yet been adopted. In August 2026 the Ministry of Telecommunications and Digital Economy submitted a bill on the protection of critical information infrastructure and digital security to the National Assembly's Intercommission, which would set up a National Cybersecurity Authority and CERTs.

Use of the law. Senegal's national police recorded 3,902 cybercrime complaints in 2024, it said on 16 April 2025. It cleared 223 and referred 194 people to prosecutors. Le Soleil, citing the same police report, puts these at 3,902 of 18,951 offences recorded that year. It also reports that Moustapha Diakhate was sentenced on 28 November 2024 to two months in prison. The offence was an insult made through a computer system.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

SLE.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2021; people were charged under it in 2024 and 2025. No yearly count is published.
SLE.summary:
Law in force. Sierra Leone has a cybercrime law in force. The Cyber Security and Crime Act, 2021 was published as a supplement to the Gazette dated 25 November 2021, setting up a response coordination centre, an advisory council and a fund, and defining offences. The national development plan lists the Cybercrime Act 2021 among its sector milestones, and the digital development strategy says the bill drafted in 2018 was signed into law in 2021.

Use of the law. A Freetown councillor was charged at Pademba Road Court in November 2025 with cyberstalking and cyberbullying under sections 44(1)(b) and 44(2)(b) of the Act. The councillor pleaded not guilty and was granted bail. On 5 August 2025 Joseph Sesay was arraigned at the same court on two counts of cyberstalking under section 44(1)(a). Hawa Hunt was arrested on 22 December 2024 and charged with two counts of sending insulting messages through a computer system, Amnesty International reports.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

SOM.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime bills have moved through parliament since 2025; no law in force is known, and no use is known.
SOM.summary:
Law in force. Somalia has bills before parliament. The National Communications Authority states the House of the People approved the Cybersecurity Law on 26 January 2026. On 29 August 2026 the Senate held first reading of a six-chapter, 33-article cybersecurity bill, which still needs second and third readings before final approval. The House of the People concluded first reading of the Cybercrimes Bill on 8 December 2025 and sent it to committee.

Use of the law. The nearest held facts concern the bills. A news report says the House approved the Cybersecurity Law on 26 January 2026 and that the government approved a draft cybercrime bill in August 2025. A second report says parliament approved the Cybersecurity Law in January 2026 and that a cybercrime bill passed in August 2025. A third report, on the launch of the national incident response team, also says parliament approved the Cybersecurity Law in January 2026 and that a cybercrime bill was approved in August 2025.

Not found. No source says a cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force. No use of any such law is known.

SSD.short: A cybercrime law was signed in February 2026 and put into operation in July 2026; no case under it is known.
SSD.summary:
Law in force. South Sudan has a cybercrime law in force. Radio Tamazuj reports that President Kiir signed the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 on 18 February 2026 and that it came into force on signature. Its offences and penalties sit in Chapter Six, and Chapter 5 sets critical infrastructure designation, 24-hour incident reporting and administrative penalties. The Information Minister said the law is in effect. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre says section 6(3) lets the National Communication Authority order service providers to hand over data without judicial authorisation. Parliament had passed the bill on 25 November 2025.

Use of the law. Eye Radio reports that the government announced implementation of the Act in July 2026, amid free expression concerns. Under Presidential Directive No. 03 of 2026 the National Cyber-Security Task Force held its first operational meeting on 16 July 2026. In September 2026 more than 20 civil society, security and media participants were trained in Yei River County on the Act, which the report treats as current law.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

STP.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2017; no case under it is known.
STP.summary:
Law in force. Sao Tome and Principe has a cybercrime law in force. Lei n.º 15/2017, the Lei sobre Cibercrime, was passed by the Assembleia Nacional on 28 June 2017, promulgated on 3 August 2017 and published in the Diário da República on 6 October 2017. It creates computer-crime offences and procedural powers, and it enters into force 30 days after publication, about 5 November 2017.

Use of the law. The same law is the nearest held fact on use. It gives the Polícia Judiciária a round-the-clock contact point, available twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, for the procedural powers it creates, and the Assembleia Nacional passed the law itself. The law was passed in June 2017 and published in October 2017, and it creates computer-crime offences and procedural powers that apply from about November 2017, when it enters into force.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

SWZ.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2022; a court convicted a woman under it in 2025. No yearly count of cases is published.
SWZ.summary:
Law in force. The Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act, 2022 (Act No. 6 of 2022) was published in the Government Gazette Extraordinary on 4 March 2022 and, by section 1(2), came into operation on the date of publication. On 1 October 2026 the Director of Public Prosecutions described the Act as the legal framework for offences committed through or against computer systems. In April 2026 the minister said the Act is already the legal groundwork, with its regulations at an advanced stage. The Prime Minister had spoken of it in October 2025 as passed in 2022 and among the cyber laws now in force.

Use of the law. A Mbabane woman was convicted by the Magistrates Court in August 2025 over a WhatsApp message. She was sentenced to three years or a E3,000 fine. In September 2025 two accused appeared in Manzini Magistrates Court on 30 fraud charges, some of them under the Act. A woman arrested by the police in July 2025 faces counts under the Act. The High Court denied her bail.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

SYC.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2022 and was widened in December 2025; no case under it is known.
SYC.summary:
Law in force. The Cybercrimes and Other Related Crimes Act 2021 (Act 59 of 2021) was assented on 15 December 2021 and repeals the Computer Misuse Act (Cap 254). Act 23 of 2025 amends it. The National Assembly passed that amendment on 15 December 2025 and the President assented to it on 22 December 2025. It widens the offences and amends an Act already in operation, so Seychelles has a working cybercrime statute that was extended at the end of 2025.

Use of the law. The 2025 amendment, assented on 22 December 2025, adds search and interception powers to the Act alongside the wider offences. These are powers for investigating offences under it. The amendment states no commencement date of its own. Both texts are published in the official gazette. They sit on top of the 2021 Act, which replaced the earlier Computer Misuse Act, Cap 254.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TCD.short: A cybercrime law from 2015 is listed among Chad's laws; no source found says whether it has been used.
TCD.summary:
Law in force. The sector regulator ARCEP's register of laws lists Loi N°009/PR/2015 on Cybersecurity and the Fight against Cybercrime among Chad's laws. The register names the law as Loi N°009/PR/2015 portant sur la Cybersécurité et la Lutte Contre la Cybercriminalité. The year 2015 is the year in the law's number. Chad's regulator therefore carries a national cybersecurity and cybercrime law on its list of the laws that apply in the country. On 16 February 2026 the National Assembly approved, by 160 votes to 1, the ratification of Ordinance 001/PR/2026 of 22 January 2026, which reforms the agency ANSICE to modernise the legal framework on cybersecurity and cybercrime.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on how the law is applied is its place in the same ARCEP register of laws, where the regulator lists it among Chad's laws alongside the rest of the legal framework for the sector. The law is presented there as part of the framework the regulator works within, in the 2015 numbering, under the title covering both cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TGO.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2018, amended in 2022; no case under it is known.
TGO.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2018-026 of 7 December 2018 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime was promulgated and published in the Journal officiel, setting the cybersecurity framework and defining and punishing cybercrime offences. Loi n° 2022-009 of 24 June 2022, adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President, amends articles 2, 3 and 6 of it. The 2018 text was issued as a special number of the Journal officiel and remains the base text that the 2022 law modifies.

Use of the law. The visas of Décret n° 2022-094/PR of 9 September 2022 cite the 2018 law as modified by the 2022 law, treating it as standing law. The government thus relies on it in later regulation, which is a use of the text as a legal basis. The decree cites both the 2018 law and the 2022 amendment as current, within three months of the amendment.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TUN.short: Tunisia's cybercrime and cybersecurity decree-laws are in force; six journalists were prosecuted under one by April 2026. No yearly count is published.
TUN.summary:
Law in force. Decree-law no. 2023-17 of 11 March 2023 on cybersecurity, published in JORT no. 26, is in force. It sets audit, labelling, classification, incident-response and critical-infrastructure duties for public and private bodies, with fines of 50,000 to 100,000 dinars. Decree-law 54 of September 2022 makes spreading falsehoods by electronic means an offence. An amendment replacing jail with fines of 10,000 to 20,000 dinars for a first offence took effect on 30 September 2026, Al Jazeera reports.

Use of the law. The journalists' union SNJT recorded six prosecutions of journalists under Decree 54 between April 2025 and April 2026. In January 2025 a National Guard spokesperson said 2,000 cybercrime cases had been recorded since the start of 2024. Most were referred to the courts and 800 had passed through all legal stages. Detention warrants were issued against several defendants.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

TZA.short: A cybercrime law has been in force in Tanzania since 2015; no case under it is known.
TZA.summary:
Law in force. The Cybercrimes Act (Cap. 443, Revised Edition 2023, originally Act No. 14 of 2015) states that it commenced on 1 September 2015 under GN No. 528 of 2015. It applies to Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, and it criminalises illegal access, interception, data interference, fraud and forgery. The consolidated text is the Revised Edition 2023 held by the Office of the Attorney General, and the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology cites the Act in 2026.

Use of the law. The ICT Minister said on 19 August 2026 that section 29 of the Cybercrimes Act provides a fine of not less than 100m/- or three times the damage, imprisonment of at least five years, or both, for damaging critical ICT infrastructure. The Ministry of Information and Communication Technology owns the Act in that report. The minister's statement concerns owners and operators of critical ICT infrastructure, for whom the Ministry has set up a registration system.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

UGA.short: The Computer Misuse Act is in force, and in 2026 police arrested three men over alleged fake news and personal data posts.
UGA.summary:
Law in force. Uganda's Constitutional Court struck down Sections 11, 23, 26, 27, 28 and 29 of the Computer Misuse Act and Sections 162 and 163 of the Penal Code Act (criminal libel), leaving the rest of the Act standing. Nilepost says the cyber-offence framework is anchored in the Computer Misuse Act, 2011 as amended in 2022, with some offences carrying up to 10 years in prison. The Nilepost account is dated 1 September 2026. A July 2026 joint UPR submission urges repeal or amendment of sections 24 and 25.

Use of the law. In September 2026 Kampala Metropolitan Police arrested and held three men over alleged fake news and unlawful obtaining or disclosure of personal data on social media, in an investigation the report places under the Computer Misuse Act. The incidents date to July 2026, and charges were not disclosed.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is held.

ZAF.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2021; a court convicted a fraudster under it in 2025. No yearly count of cases is published.
ZAF.summary:
Law in force. South Africa's Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020 was signed into law on 26 May 2021, and ITWeb says it came into partial operation on 1 December 2021. On 12 October 2026 Fritz and Limpitlaw state that the Act criminalises a range of online wrongdoing and provides investigative powers and evidence preservation. Michalsons says no separate cybersecurity act exists. In October 2025 a Hawks cybercrime head said a Cybersecurity Bill was still forthcoming.

Use of the law. On 3 June 2025 the Bellville Specialised Commercial Crimes Court convicted Lucky Erasmus on 17 Cybercrimes Act charges. It sentenced him to eight years, three of them suspended. A parliamentary reply of 29 November 2024 put 37 cases with 88 charges under the Act on the prosecutors' court rolls. In October 2026 the Acting Minister of Police told Parliament that the Hawks had made one arrest. They had registered eight cyber fraud, extortion and ransomware cases over three years.

Not found. No count of cases under the law has been published for a period ending in the last two years.

ZMB.short: Two cyber laws passed in 2025 are in force; a journalist was arrested under one in August 2026; no count of cases is known.
ZMB.summary:
Law in force. Zambia has a Cyber Crimes Act and a Cyber Security Act, both of 2025, which replaced the 2021 Cyber Security and Cybercrime Act. On 5 August 2026 Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition noted the enactment of both. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre says the 2025 Cyber Crimes Act made it an offence to use a computer to publish information damaging a person's reputation. In July 2026 the opposition running mate Makebi Zulu said that, if elected, his government would repeal the Cyber Crimes and Cyber Security Act. CAJ News Africa reports that the Cyber Security Act and the Cyber Crimes Act were enacted in 2025.

Use of the law. Paradigm Initiative, citing the African Union's preliminary report, says ZNBC journalist MacPherson Mukuka was arrested under section 10 of the cybercrime law, for recording a private conversation, during the August 2026 elections. On 5 August 2026 Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition urged the government not to let the two Acts become tools to suppress expression. At a rally before 4 July 2026, Makebi Zulu said the Act had gagged Zambians since its enactment.

Not found. No count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under the law, for a period ending in the last two years, is known.

ZWE.short: Cybercrime offences in the criminal code, amended 2021, are in force, and officials describe a wider law in 2026; no case of use is known.
ZWE.summary:
Law in force. On 24 January 2026 the Director General of POTRAZ stated that Zimbabwe has no standalone cyber crimes act. Cybercrime offences are in force instead in Part VIII of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], as amended in 2021. They cover hacking, data interference, cyber-bullying, child abuse material and others, in sections 163 to 168. On 15 October 2026 a POTRAZ official described a Cybersecurity Act as holding cybercrime definitions alongside cybersecurity provisions in one piece of legislation.

Use of the law. The cybercrime provisions in force are the offences in Part VIII of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, sections 163 to 168. The POTRAZ Director General set them out on 24 January 2026. A POTRAZ official on 15 October 2026 spoke of the same subject in the context of critical infrastructure.

Not found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is known.

AGO.short: A data centre ran on dedicated power lines from the substation in 2025; no source found reports power set aside for data centres.
AGO.summary:
A secured supply in service, and power reserved for data centres. Raxio Group runs data centres in Angola, as in five other African countries. In December 2025 its chief technology officer said Raxio builds medium-voltage lines direct from the substation to each of its facilities. He said it always uses two power lines, each able to carry the load, plus diesel generators. In none of its markets does it rely on the old local grid. No source found says power is set aside for data centres.

A PUE of 1.6 or less published. No PUE is on record for a data centre in Angola. The nearest fact is the supply design. Raxio says its facilities take dedicated medium-voltage lines from the substation, backed by standby diesel.

Water use published, or cooling that uses no water. No water figure, and no cooling that uses none, is on record for a data centre in Angola. The nearest fact is again Raxio's: two independent power lines and standby diesel at each facility.

Not found. No source found says power is set aside for data centres. None names a signed contract, a plant built for them, or a tariff or zone in force.

BDI.short: Nothing found says how data centres get power or water, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how any data centre is supplied with power or water.

BEN.short: A data centre on a secured power supply by 2026; no power set aside for data centres is known.
BEN.summary:
A secured supply in service, and power reserved for data centres. CIO Mag reports Benin's data centres run on dual power feeds from the SBEE, plus standby generators. These place a data centre on a secured supply. No source found says power is set aside for data centres.

A PUE of 1.6 or less published. No source found from the past three years states a PUE of 1.6 or less for Benin data centres (ASIN) or any other data centre in service.

Water use published, or cooling that uses no water. No source found from the past three years states the water use of Benin data centres (ASIN) or any other data centre in service, or cooling that uses none.

Not found. No source found says power is set aside for data centres by a signed contract, a plant built for them or a tariff or zone in force.

BFA.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how any data centre is supplied with power or water.

BWA.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how any data centre is supplied with power or water.

CAF.short: Nothing found says how data centres get power or water, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how any data centre is supplied with power or water.

CIV.short: A data centre has run on two independent substation feeders since 2024; no source found reports power set aside for data centres.
CIV.summary:
A secured supply in service, and power reserved for data centres. Raxio's CIV1 data centre in Abidjan opened in September 2024. Its chief technology officer says it is fed by two independent 15kV feeders direct from the CIE substation. Each feeder can carry the whole load. In December 2025 he said Raxio always uses two such lines, plus diesel generators, in every market. No source found says power is set aside for data centres.

A PUE of 1.6 or less published. No PUE is on record for a data centre in Cote d'Ivoire. The nearest fact is CIV1's supply: two 15kV feeders, each able to carry 100% of the load.

Water use published, or cooling that uses no water. No water figure, and no cooling that uses none, is on record for a data centre in Cote d'Ivoire. The nearest fact is Raxio's design: dedicated medium-voltage lines and standby diesel at each facility.

Not found. No source found says power is set aside for data centres. None names a signed contract, a plant built for them, or a tariff or zone in force.

CMR.short: A data centre had two utility feeds and a PUE under 1.5 in 2024; no source found reports power set aside for data centres.
CMR.summary:
A secured supply in service, and power reserved for data centres. ST Digital's Douala01 data centre has two utility feeds, one power transformer and three backup generator sets. The operator gives these figures in its 2024 OCP Ready self-assessment. Two utility feeds place a data centre on a secured supply. No source found says power is set aside for data centres by contract, plant, tariff or zone.

A PUE of 1.6 or less published. The same 2024 self-assessment gives Douala01 a design PUE and a current yearly PUE both under 1.5. It is the operator's own figure.

Water use published, or cooling that uses no water. No water figure, and no cooling that uses none, is on record for a data centre in Cameroon. The nearest fact is Douala01's annual PUE of under 1.5, from the same 2024 document.

Not found. No source found says power is set aside for data centres. None names a signed contract, a plant built for them, or a tariff or zone in force.

COD.short: A data centre ran on dedicated power lines from the substation in 2025; no source found reports power set aside for data centres.
COD.summary:
A secured supply in service, and power reserved for data centres. Raxio Group runs data centres in DR Congo, as in five other African countries. In December 2025 its chief technology officer said Raxio builds medium-voltage lines direct from the substation to each of its facilities. He said it always uses two power lines, each able to carry the load, plus diesel generators. In none of its markets does it rely on the old local grid. No source found says power is set aside for data centres.

A PUE of 1.6 or less published. No PUE is on record for a data centre in DR Congo. The nearest fact is the supply design. Raxio says its facilities take dedicated medium-voltage lines from the substation, backed by standby diesel.

Water use published, or cooling that uses no water. No water figure, and no cooling that uses none, is on record for a data centre in DR Congo. The nearest fact is again Raxio's: two independent power lines and standby diesel at each facility.

Not found. No source found says power is set aside for data centres. None names a signed contract, a plant built for them, or a tariff or zone in force.

COG.short: Power cuts and diesel shortages disrupted data centres in October 2026; the solar farm for the national data centre is not yet built.
COG.summary:
A secured supply in service, and power reserved for data centres. On 27 October 2026 the regulator ARPCE said nationwide power cuts and scarce diesel were badly disrupting data centres, with network sites and core networks. A plant for data centres is being built, not yet in service. On 22 September 2026 the government said works on the national data centre stood at 82%. The 12 MW Kintelé solar farm, with 19,354 panels, is being built to keep its power stable.

A PUE of 1.6 or less published. No PUE is on record for a data centre in Congo. The nearest fact is the national data centre, 82% built in September 2026.

Water use published, or cooling that uses no water. No water figure, and no cooling that uses none, is on record for a data centre in Congo. The nearest fact is ARPCE's warning that power cuts and diesel shortages were disrupting data centres in October 2026.

Not found. No source found says a data centre in service has a secured supply. That would be two grid feeds, its own substation or line, or its own plant.

COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how any data centre is supplied with power or water.

DJI.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how any data centre is supplied with power or water.

DZA.short: A data centre on a secured power supply by 2026; no power set aside for data centres is known.
DZA.summary:

BWA.summary:

A report of November 2025 says the Data Protection Act, in effect since January 2025, allows data to be transferred abroad only to approved countries and requires a copy of the data to remain in Botswana. CIV.summary:
Rule in force. Côte d'Ivoire has a rule in preparation and none in force. The Ministry of Digital Transition's national data governance strategy to 2030 sets as a principle that all data classified as critical information infrastructure must be processed and stored inside Côte d'Ivoire. It adds that the staff handling it should be at least 20 per cent Ivorian, and that a copy of data must be kept in the country for law enforcement. The strategy carries no date of its own and was published in 2024. No law, decree or regulation enacting the principle has been found.

Enforcer named and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the strategy itself, which states the storage principle and names no body to enforce it. No source found names a regulator or agency given that job, and none reports the principle applied to any organisation.

At Camtel's Cloud Days on 10 December 2025, speakers said the personal data protection law requires local storage. They said it also sets strict rules on consent and on the duties of those who handle data. The event offered Camtel's Zamengoé data centre to businesses and government agencies as a place to meet those requirements.

Enforcer named and rule applied. In June 2025 ST Digital's chief executive said the local hosting duties are neither checked nor applied. The December 2025 report names the storage duty and no body that enforces it. No order, penalty or exemption under it has been found.

Not found. No source found names a body that enforces the rule. No source found gives the law's date, the wording of its storage duty or the data it covers.

The report does not give the law's date or the article. The same account says some public data still sat on private servers at that date.

Enforcer named and rule applied. The nearest held fact is that account, which states the hosting duty and names no body that checks it. No source found names a body that checks compliance with the rule or grants exemptions from it. No source found names or counts the public bodies that have moved their data to the government data centre, and none reports an order or penalty.

DJI.short: Since 2020 a decree requires the national register of persons' data to be stored in Djibouti; no body is known to enforce it.
DJI.summary:
Rule in force. Decree 2020-146/PR/MI, issued after the Council of Ministers of 7 July 2020 and published on 13 July 2020, states in Article 9 that the processed data of the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) are stored only on national territory. The decree governs access to, exploitation of and communication of the register, and Article 9 applies to that one register. The text gives its publication date and no separate date of entry into force.

Enforcer named and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same decree, whose title sets the terms for access to, use of and communication of the register's data, with Article 9 as its storage provision. The register is a relational database run by the Direction Generale de la Population et de la Famille (DGPF), with ANSIE responsible for its development and security. Its users are public authorities, public and private bodies under Djiboutian law, and their subcontractors.

Not found. Nothing found names a body that enforces the rule, checks compliance or grants exemptions.

DZA.short: Algeria's telecoms regulator has required public cloud data to be hosted in the country since 2017; no order under the rule is known.
DZA.summary:
Rule in force. Algeria's rule sits in its personal data law. The United States government's country commercial guide of 2024 states that data localisation is mandatory in Algeria under Law No. 18-07, with data to be stored in the country. The law came into force on 10 August 2023. The guide does not say whether the requirement reaches all data or only personal data. It gives no exemption procedure.

Enforcer named and rule applied. In November 2017 the Regulatory Authority of Post and Electronic Communications required public cloud computing operators to build their infrastructure in Algeria and host and store their data there. It issued the rule for the operators it licenses, and cloud data hosting providers must hold its authorisation. Since December 2024 the Law on Audiovisual Activity has also required online audiovisual services to be hosted on servers in Algeria. No order, penalty or exemption under either rule has been found.

Not found. No source from the last three years names an organisation ordered, penalised or exempted under the rule. None counts those that have moved data to comply.

EGY.short: Egypt's Cloud First Policy, in force since August 2024, requires secret data to be hosted only in Egypt; no source found reports the enforcer.
EGY.summary:
Rule in force. Egypt's rule covers classified data. The Cloud First Policy, adopted by the Supreme Council of Digital Society on 13 March 2024, entered into force on 22 August 2024 and requires data classified top secret or secret to be hosted exclusively within Egypt. The record of the policy does not say where data of lower classifications may be held, and names no date by which existing systems must move.

Enforcer named and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same record, which sets out the hosting requirement and names no body that checks compliance. No source found names a body that checks compliance with the rule or grants exemptions from it. No source found names an organisation ordered to bring data into Egypt, penalised or exempted, and none counts public bodies that have moved classified data to hosting inside the country.

Not found. No source found names a body that enforces the rule: a regulator, agency or ministry unit that checks compliance or grants exemptions.

ETH.summary:
Rule in force. Ethiopia's rule covers personal data. Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024 entered into force on 24 July 2024. It requires data controllers and processors to store locally collected personal data on servers in Ethiopia. In October 2025 Birr Metrics reported that it lets data leave the country only under strict conditions. A July 2025 market brief by Xalam Analytics says it requires companies to host Ethiopian citizens' data in the country.

Enforcer named and rule applied. The Ethiopian Communications Authority's consumer rights directive of August 2021 requires telecom providers to process consumers' personal data only in Ethiopia. The authority issued it for the operators it licenses. It also oversees compliance with the data protection proclamation. No order, penalty or exemption under either rule has been found.

Not found. No organisation is known to have been ordered, penalised or exempted under the rule. No count of those that have moved data to comply is known.

GAB.summary:

Article 27 of Law No. 027/2023 on cybersecurity and cybercrime requires data judged confidential or sensitive to be hosted exclusively on national territory. The law was promulgated on 11 July 2023 and published in the official journal of 15 July 2023. Which data count as confidential or sensitive is set by the law's own article 22.

Enforcer named and rule applied. The law allows an exception: the competent administrative authority may grant a written derogation. The text held does not say which authority that is. No source found names a body that checks compliance with the rule or grants exemptions from it. No derogation granted or refused has been found, and no source names an organisation ordered to bring data into Gabon or penalised under the article.
