Rule in force. The Central African Republic's Loi n° 24.001 on the protection of personal data is the law that governs sending personal data abroad. Jurist Laurent-Fabrice Zengue wrote on 16 September 2025 that the law conditions a transfer to a state outside CEMAC or ECCAS on a sufficient level of protection in the recipient state. He added that other transfers face further requirements. The rule rests on the recipient country's level of protection, and it applies to any state outside those two regional groupings.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same 2025 account of the law, which describes the conditions the law sets on transfers and says nothing of a published list of countries, model terms, a permission procedure or guidance, or of the rule being applied to a named organisation.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

CIV.short: Decree 2015-79 of 2015 requires the telecoms regulator's prior authorisation to send personal data abroad; no source found says whether any transfer has been authorised.
CIV.summary:
Rule in force. Côte d'Ivoire has a rule in force on sending personal data abroad. Decree 2015-79 of 4 February 2015, issued under law 2013-450, requires prior authorisation from the telecoms regulator ARTCI before personal data is transferred to a third country. The receiving country must give protection equal to or higher than that of Côte d'Ivoire, and the requirement is set out in article 6 of the decree. The regulator publishes the decree on its own website, and the decree is the only instrument held on this point.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same decree, which sets sanctions for non-compliance with the transfer rule in article 8. Its title states that it fixes how declarations are filed, how requests are presented, and how authorisations are granted and withdrawn for the processing of personal data, so the decree itself is the one published procedure held. Nothing found shows the rule being applied to a particular transfer.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

CMR.short: Cameroon's December 2024 law requires the authority to authorise every transfer of personal data abroad, after a grace period; no source found reports guidance.
CMR.summary:
Rule in force. Cameroon's Law No. 2024/017 relating to personal data protection, dated 23 December 2024, requires all cross-border transfers of personal data to be authorised by the data protection authority, according to African Law & Business in its account of the law's key features, published on 17 July 2025. The same account says the Act becomes enforceable only after an 18-month grace period. The condition the rule sets on sending personal data out of the country is therefore the authority's authorisation, and it applies to every such transfer.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the requirement itself: under the Act of 23 December 2024, the data protection authority must authorise each cross-border transfer of personal data, and that duty takes effect once the 18-month grace period has run.

Not found. No list of countries, model contract terms, permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad is held from the authority. No application of the rule has been found.

COD.short: Transfers abroad need the data protection authority's approval under the digital code, exercised by ARPTIC since 2024; no source found reports any published procedure.
COD.summary:
Rule in force. The Code du numérique, in articles 262 to 270, creates a data protection authority whose duties include authorising or refusing cross-border transfers of personal data to third states. The authority itself is not yet set up, so since 17 August 2024 a ministerial order has given those duties to ARPTIC, the regulator for posts and telecommunications. The source is dated to 2025.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is that the decision on any transfer of personal data to a third state sits, for now, with ARPTIC rather than with a separate data protection authority. That is the whole of what is held on how an exporter would comply, and on how the rule is applied in practice.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

COG.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

COM.short: The 2021 data protection law governs sending personal data abroad on a risk-based model, and no source found says whether the rule has been applied.
COM.summary:
Rule in force. The Protection of Personal Data Law, enacted on 29 June 2021, governs international transfers of personal data, according to TechHive Advisory's review of the Comoros data protection law, published on 23 July 2025. The review describes a risk-based model for sending data abroad. Under it, a transfer can rest on an adequacy finding about the receiving country, on appropriate safeguards, or on one of the derogations the law provides.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the model itself: the 2021 law sets three routes for an international transfer, which are adequacy of the receiving country, appropriate safeguards and derogations. The 2025 review sets out these three routes as the law's way of governing transfers, and it dates the law to 29 June 2021, the day of its enactment. That date is the latest one held for the rule on sending data abroad.

Not found. Nothing found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad, or has applied the rule to a transfer.

CPV.short: Cape Verde law since 2013 lets personal data go abroad only to countries judged adequate or on listed grounds; no source found reports its application.
CPV.summary:
Rule in force. Cape Verde's Data Protection Law (Law 133/V/2001, amended by Law 41/VIII/2013 and Law 121/IX/2021) permits international transfer of personal data, as published in January 2025, only to a country with an adequate level of protection, or otherwise with the data subject's consent or in listed situations such as contract necessity or vital interests. Law 41/VIII/2013, published on 17 September 2013, made article 19 allow transfer abroad only to a country assuring an adequate level of protection, with the national data protection commission (CNPD) deciding which foreign states do.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same 2013 amendment lets the CNPD permit a transfer to any other country on consent, contract necessity, public interest, vital interests or a public register. Article 20 also lets the CNPD authorise a transfer where the controller gives sufficient guarantees, such as adequate contractual clauses.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

DJI.short: Djibouti's digital code, published in September 2025, bars sending personal data abroad without equivalent protection; whether the authority has published means of complying is unknown.
DJI.summary:
Rule in force. Djibouti's Code Numérique, Loi n° 019/AN/23/9ème L, was published in the Journal Officiel on 18 September 2025. Under article 99, a controller or processor may not transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation unless it ensures an equivalent and sufficient level of protection. Article 102 sets exceptions: the person's consent, a contract, public interest, legal claims or vital interests, or authorisation by the Commission nationale de protection des données.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same law: the Code Numérique of 18 September 2025 sets the conditions in articles 99 to 103 and gives the Commission nationale de protection des données the power to authorise a transfer.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

DZA.short: Algeria's 2025 amendment requires an adequacy assessment before data go abroad for criminal-justice purposes; no source says whether any list, contract terms or procedure exists.
DZA.summary:
Rule in force. Law 25-11 of 24 July 2025, published in the Journal Officiel that day, amends Law 18-07 with a new article 45 bis 13. Before data are transferred to a foreign State or international organisation, the competent authority assesses whether it gives an adequate level of protection. This applies to transfers for criminal-justice purposes. Transfer on insufficient safeguards is allowed only in listed cases: vital interests, a threat to public security, and individual criminal cases. The Authority's Délibération n° 04 of 15 July 2026 extends the law's rules to images published on social platforms and treats publication on foreign-run platforms as a transfer abroad.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the Authority's Délibération n° 04 of 15 July 2026, which applies the transfer rule to images published on foreign-run platforms. It is a ruling on one kind of transfer, and the law's article 45 bis 13 is the assessment it rests on. Digital Policy Alert said in April 2025 that the ANPDP had not issued the list of adequate countries or the declarations for transfer authorisation.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

EGY.short: Sending personal data abroad needs the data protection authority's permit, with a grace period ending in 2026; no source found reports published guidance or use.
EGY.summary:
Rule in force. Legal 500 says that under the Executive Regulations of Law 151 of 2020, issued in November 2025, personal data may not leave Egypt without prior authorisation from the Personal Data Protection Center. The regulations carry a grace period that ends in 2026. Shura Law Firm wrote on 13 October 2026 that a transfer abroad requires a licence or permit from the Centre and the consent of the data subject.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The Personal Data Protection Center assesses the adequacy of the destination before it permits a transfer, as Shura Law Firm described the procedure on 13 October 2026. Legal 500 describes the Centre's authorisation as prior to any transfer of personal data out of Egypt. The Centre is the authority named for the permit, and the permit applies from the end of the grace period in 2026.

Not found. Nothing found says the Centre has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

ERI.short: Eritrea had no rule on sending data abroad as of 2026, and no source found says whether any draft or sector rule exists.
ERI.summary:
Rule in force. The UNECA digital trade profile, published on 1 January 2022, states that no legal regime in Eritrea deals with the general flow of data and that no conditions are made for the flow of data. Levellers, in a legal-status page last reviewed on 8 June 2026, states that Eritrea has no data protection legislation and no restriction on cross-border transfer of data in its law.

Means of complying published and rule applied. Eritrea's law places no restriction on cross-border transfer of data, according to Levellers on 8 June 2026, and the UNECA profile of 2022 records no conditions on the flow of data. Those are the nearest held facts to a means of complying or a rule applied: in neither source is a sender asked to meet any condition before sending data abroad.

Not found. No source found says whether any draft rule on sending data abroad exists, and whether any sector rule applies,. No published means of complying and no case of a rule applied has been found.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's 2024 data protection law conditions sending data abroad, and about 10 requests were approved in 2025; no source found reports published means of complying.
ETH.summary:
Rule in force. Techhive Advisory reports that Ethiopia's Personal Data Protection Proclamation was published in the Federal Negarit Gazette on 24 July 2024, bringing it into effect. Articles 18-21 make international transfers depend on an adequacy decision by the Authority, the data subject's explicit consent, necessity, or public registry purposes, and transfers of sensitive data need the Authority's prior authorisation.

Means of complying published and rule applied. In November 2025 the Ethiopian Communications Authority's Director General told Shega the Authority had received about 10 requests to transfer data abroad and had approved them as a temporary measure; the article records no sanction and no published count of decisions. Officials previewed a forthcoming registration portal for data controllers and processors at a workshop co-hosted with Huawei.

Not found. The evidence does not show a published list of countries data may go to, model contract terms or guidance on transfers. It gives no count of decisions and no refusal or penalty tied to sending data abroad.

GAB.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2012 law was being amended in 2025 to add transfer rules; no source says whether any rule on sending data abroad is in force.
GHA.summary:
Rule in force. A roundup of data protection in Africa, published in January 2026, says amendments to the Data Protection Act 2012 are in process. It says they would add rules on international transfers, alongside rules on children's and sensitive data, retention limits, impact assessments and privacy by design. The same roundup says a draft Data Protection Act, 2025 was published, with no month given for the draft.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same roundup's account, dated 2025, of the draft Data Protection Act, 2025 and of the amendments to the 2012 Act that would add rules on international transfers. Both are described as a draft and as amendments in process, and the roundup is the only source found that speaks to Ghana's rule on sending data abroad.

Not found. No source says a rule on sending personal data abroad is in force. Nothing says what the authority has published to help organisations comply, or that the rule has been applied.

GIN.short: A 2016 law gives the data protection authority a transfer approval function; no source says whether any procedure or guidance on sending data abroad exists.
GIN.summary:
Rule in force. Guinea's law on cybersecurity and the protection of personal data, published in July 2016, defines a data protection authority, the Autorité de Protection. It gives that authority functions covering declarations and authorisations, transfer approval, investigation and guidelines. Article 5 sends processing declarations to the competent authority "designated by regulation". The law lists transfer approval as one of the authority's own functions, alongside investigation and guidelines.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same 2016 law, which lists authorisations, transfer approval and guidelines among the authority's functions. The law names no constituted body or appointed members, and it leaves the designation of the competent authority to regulation, so the body that would approve transfers is not identified in the law itself.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2025 data protection Act lets its Commission set conditions on sending data abroad; no source found says whether guidance or permissions exist.
GMB.summary:
Rule in force. The Gambia has the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2025 (Act No. 11 of 2025), and a February 2026 legal commentary on its key features describes the Act as setting up a data protection authority, called the Commission. The commentary says the Commission assesses cross-border transfers of personal data and may impose conditions on them. The full text of the Act is published as Act No. 11 of 2025.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the Commission's role in transfers. As described in the February 2026 commentary, the Commission is the body that assesses transfers of personal data out of the country and decides whether to attach conditions. That is a power the Act gives it, and it is the closest the held material comes to the way the rule is carried out in practice.

Not found. No source found says the Commission has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad. No source found names an approval, refusal or penalty under the rule.

GNB.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

GNQ.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2019 Data Protection Act governs sending personal data abroad, with authority guidance published in 2026; no source found says whether it has been applied.
KEN.summary:
Rule in force. ITWeb Africa reported on 9 September 2026 that the Data Protection Act (2019), the Constitution and the Kenya Cloud Policy (2025) govern the cross-border transfer of personal data in Kenya. The same report says the guidance of the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) sets out the legal obligations and conditions for lawful transfer abroad. The conditions therefore rest on a statute, the Constitution and a cloud policy, with the ODPC guidance stating the conditions for sending personal data out of the country, as reported in September 2026.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same ITWeb Africa report of 9 September 2026 says the ODPC, through Data Commissioner Immaculate Kassait, has issued guidance on cross-border data transfers. That guidance covers the conditions for lawful transfer, the safeguards required and the mechanisms for adequate protection. A controller or processor in Kenya therefore has published guidance from the data protection authority on how to meet the rule before sending personal data abroad, and the report presents it as the authority's own statement of the safeguards expected.

Not found. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

LBR.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

LBY.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

LSO.short: Lesotho's 2012 Data Protection Act sets rules on sending data abroad, in force as of 2025; no source found says whether any authority applies them.
LSO.summary:
Rule in force. Z. Mayet and Associates says that Lesotho's Data Protection Act (Act No. 5 of 2012) is the law in force, in a piece published on 31 October 2025. It says the Act carries rules on cross-border data transfers inspired by the SADC model, and that those rules need modern adequacy tools. The piece is the firm's own commentary on what should change next in the Act.

Means of complying published and rule applied. As at 31 October 2025, the same firm says the Data Protection Commission and Commissioner have not been appointed, so no authority exists to approve cross-border mechanisms or issue guidance. It adds that standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules are not yet in place.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

MAR.short: Morocco's law sets a condition on sending personal data abroad, as stated in 2012, with a 2015 country list; no source found reports recent application.
MAR.summary:
Rule in force. Morocco's Act 09-08, named in Morocco as Loi n° 09-08 and overseen by the supervisory authority CNPD, lays down protection of transfers of personal data to foreign countries, according to the Council of Europe Consultative Committee in a document of 18 October 2012. Its articles 43 and 44 apply that protection in particular where the receiving country does not provide an adequate level of protection, the same document states.

Means of complying published and rule applied. A DIAL expert comment states that Morocco's 2015 adequacy list, a list of countries personal data may be sent to, did not recognise a single African country. The year is the only date the comment gives for the list, so a published list of receiving countries is the means of complying that the evidence dates.

Not found. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

MDG.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

MLI.short: Mali's 2013 data protection law sets the rule on sending data abroad; no source says whether the authority has published lists, model terms or guidance.
MLI.summary:
Rule in force. Law no. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on the protection of personal data was adopted by the National Assembly on 9 May 2013 and promulgated. Article 11 lets a data controller transfer personal data to a foreign state when the data protection authority finds the receiving state's protection sufficient. The law as held gives no repeal, so it is the rule on sending data abroad that the 2013 law sets today.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is in the same law. Article 11 also covers a transfer made under contract clauses or internal rules, and for that case the authority's decision is what allows the transfer. The law names these two routes, a finding of sufficient protection and a decision on clauses or rules, and places both with the data protection authority.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

MOZ.short: A bill approved in March 2026 would let personal data leave only where protection is equivalent; no source says whether any rule is in force.
MOZ.summary:
Rule in force. On 3 March 2026 the Council of Ministers approved the Personal Data Protection Bill, the Proposta de Lei que estabelece o Regime Jurídico de Protecção de Dados Pessoais, for submission to the Assembly of the Republic, according to INTIC. INTIC published its report on 5 March 2026 under the headline that the bill goes to the Assembly for debate. The bill sets strict rules for international transfers of personal data, allowed only where equivalent protection is assured.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same bill. As INTIC reported on 5 March 2026, once before the Assembly it would allow transfers of personal data abroad only where equivalent protection is assured, and the rule is the bill's, dated 3 March 2026.

Not found. No source found says a rule on sending personal data abroad is in force, or that the authority has published the means of complying with one or applied one.

MRT.short: Mauritania has barred sending personal data abroad without adequate protection since 2017 and published a country list in 2025; no case applied is known.
MRT.summary:
Rule in force. Articles 20 to 25 of Law 2017-020, of 22 July 2017, bar a controller from sending personal data to a third country unless it ensures a sufficient level of protection, with authorisation by the data protection authority (APD) on guarantees such as contract clauses. Deliberation 004/2025, adopted by the APD on 14 July 2025, sets the conditions, rules and procedures for sending personal data abroad. Deliberation 005/2025, adopted on 30 July 2025, requires controllers using cloud services abroad to obtain prior APD authorisation.

Means of complying published and rule applied. Deliberation 005/2025 refers to a list of countries, published in deliberation 004/2025, that determines which host countries offer adequate protection. Where the host country is not on that list, a separate foreign-transfer authorisation request is required, in the text amended and published on 30 April 2026. The APD's monthly meeting of 29 April 2026 listed amending both deliberations on its agenda.

Not found. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

MUS.short: Mauritius's Data Protection Act 2017 governs sending data abroad, and in 2024 the regulator authorised 112 transfers and rejected 12; wider framework not known.
MUS.summary:
Rule in force. Mauritius enforces the Data Protection Act 2017. The Data Protection Office's annual report for 2024 sets out that enforcement for the year, and cites the Act's sections on complaints, transfers, registration, certification and appeals. Transfers abroad are therefore one of the duties the Office reports on within the Act, alongside its other functions such as registration and certification.

Means of complying published and rule applied. For January to December 2024 the Data Protection Office reports 112 cross-border transfers authorised and 12 rejected under section 36 of the Act. In the same year it reports 179 new complaints, 158 of them on CCTV, and 39 complaints closed. It also reports 105 personal data breaches notified, 10 impact assessments received and four compliance inspections during 2024.

Not found. Nothing further is held on the rule beyond the Office's 2024 report, so the wider framework for sending data abroad is not described here.

MWI.short: Malawi's Data Protection Act, in force since 2024, restricts sending personal data abroad; no source found reports any approved country list or permission procedure.
MWI.summary:
Rule in force. The Data Protection Act came into force on 3 June 2024, and sections 38 to 40 restrict transfers of personal data outside Malawi unless the receiving country has adequate data protection laws or a mechanism such as binding corporate rules is in place. The Act, No. 3 of 2024, assented on 31 January 2024, bars a controller or processor from transferring personal data unless the recipient is under a law, binding corporate rule, contractual clause, code of conduct or certification affording adequate protection, or consent or a contract condition applies.

Means of complying published and rule applied. On 17 October 2025 the Authority published a compliance guideline and checklist covering the Act's duties, data subject rights, breach notice and cross-border transfers, and a registration requirement for controllers of significant importance. No decision or sanction is reported.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

NAM.short: Namibia had no rule on sending data abroad in August 2026, according to an opposition MP; no source says whether a draft would set one.
NAM.summary:
Rule in force. In an article published on 4 August 2026, Rodney Cloete, the opposition IPC's shadow minister of international relations and trade, told the Windhoek Observer that Namibia has no data protection statute, and so no rules govern cross-border transfers of data. This is the stated position of a named opposition member of parliament, not a statement from the government. He made it while raising concerns about data control of a smart-city grant from China.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the same one: the August 2026 statement by the opposition shadow minister that no rules govern cross-border transfers of data. With no rule stated to be in force, there is no published means of complying and no application of a rule to describe.

Not found. Whether any law or draft sets a rule on sending data abroad is not shown by what is held. Nor is how any such rule would be applied.

NER.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria's 2023 data law governs sending data abroad, and in 2025 the regulator ordered Meta to stop unapproved transfers; no source found reports published model terms.
NGA.summary:
Rule in force. The Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023 was signed on 12 June 2023. Its Part VIII, sections 41 to 43, governs sending personal data abroad. It sets the basis for a transfer, the test of adequate protection, and other grounds. Vanguard reports the National Commissioner saying the Act has the Commission judge other countries' protection as a basis for transfers.

Means of complying published and rule applied. On 18 February 2025 the Commission found that Meta had sent Nigerians' data abroad without authorisation. Its orders, with a $32.8 million fine, told Meta to stop such transfers without approval. In April 2025 the National Commissioner said the Commission approves binding corporate rules, codes and certification as means of transfer, Vanguard reports.

Not found. No source says the Commission has published a list of countries, model contract terms or a permission form.

RWA.short: Rwanda's 2021 data protection law sets the rule on sending personal data abroad; model clauses came in 2024; no source found reports use.
RWA.summary:
Rule in force. A document dated February 2024 states that transfers of personal data from Rwanda must comply with Article 49 of Law No 058/2021 of 13/10/2021. The rule therefore rests on a law dated 13 October 2021. The same document ties its own contractual clauses to that Article, so the Article is the standard against which a transfer is measured, as the National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA) set out in February 2024.

Means of complying published and rule applied. In February 2024 the NCSA published standard contractual clauses for personal data transfer outside Rwanda under Article 49 of Law No 058/2021. A controller sending personal data abroad therefore has model terms from the authority to use in meeting the rule. The clauses are the means of complying that the authority itself put out, and they are issued under the same Article that sets the condition for transfers abroad.

Not found. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

SDN.short: A July 2026 source says Sudan has no statutory rule on sending data abroad; no source found says whether any draft law or guidance exists.
SDN.summary:
Rule in force. The Sudanese Center for Policy Studies, in July 2026, says mobile banking data in Sudan transits infrastructure the country neither owns nor regulates. It says no statutory requirement governs data localization or cross-border transfer, and it proposes localisation only as a first legislative tranche. The piece introduces a series on Sudan's privacy gap and the balance between digital transformation and data laws.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same July 2026 statement that no statutory requirement governs cross-border transfer of data in Sudan. With no rule stated, nothing has been found on published means of complying or on a rule being applied, and that statement is the only source found that speaks to the country's rule on sending data abroad.

Not found. No source states a rule on sending personal data out of Sudan, or a data protection law that covers it. Nothing says what guidance exists on complying or that any rule has been applied.

SEN.short: Senegal's 2008 data protection law bars sending data abroad unless the receiving country protects it enough, reported in 2018; no source reports the authority's practice.
SEN.summary:
Rule in force. Senegal's Data Protection Act, Law 2008-12 of 25 January 2008, sets the rule in Article 9. As a law-firm note of 11 May 2018 reports, a data owner cannot transfer data to another country unless the receiving country gives sufficient protection. The condition falls on the data owner, and it sits in the country's general data protection law rather than in a separate transfer instrument.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the same note of 11 May 2018 on Article 9: the data protection authority, the CDP, must be informed before any transfer, and its authorisation must be sought. That places the authority at the centre of every transfer, as the route a data owner has to follow before sending data out of Senegal.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

SLE.short: Since 2020, telecom regulations bar sending subscribers' registration information abroad without the regulator's approval; no source found says how approval is sought or granted.
SLE.summary:
Rule in force. Regulation 22(3) of the Telecommunications (Subscribers Identification and Registration) Regulations 2020, Statutory Instrument No. 35 of the Gazette of 6 November 2020, says subscribers' registration information shall not be transferred outside Sierra Leone without prior approval by the National Telecommunications Commission. The document is dated 6 November 2020 and gives no commencement date or later repeal. The rule is set in telecommunications regulations and applies to subscribers' registration information, not to personal data generally.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same regulation 22(4) requires any request to the Commission for approval to justify the purpose of the transfer. Beyond that requirement in the 2020 text, the sources found state nothing on how approval is sought, what the Commission decides, or whether any approval has been given.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

SOM.short: Somalia's 2023 data protection law bars sending personal data abroad without adequate protection or a stated exception; no source found reports published guidance and enforcement.
SOM.summary:
Rule in force. Somalia's Data Protection Act, Law No. 005 of 2023, is dated 22 March 2023, the presidential signature date. Articles 30 and 31 bar a data controller from transferring personal data outside Somalia unless the recipient country, organisation or sector gives adequate protection, or a stated exception such as the person's consent or a contract applies. The law takes effect on adoption by Parliament, promulgation by the President and publication in the Official Bulletin.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is in the same Articles 30 and 31 of the 2023 Act, which accept a recipient bound by a law, binding corporate rules or contractual clauses that give adequate protection as a way to send data abroad. They set out the means in law; they do not show a list or model terms published by the authority.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad. No application of the rule to a transfer is known.

SSD.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

STP.short: A 2016 law limits sending personal data abroad to places with adequate protection, in force as of 2022; no source reports published ways to comply.
STP.summary:
Rule in force. Law No. 03/2016, called Lei n.º 03/2016 in the country, was passed on 15 February 2016 and promulgated on 18 March 2016. It allows personal data to leave the national territory only where the receiving legal system ensures an adequate level of protection, with the National Data Protection Agency (ANPDP) deciding adequacy under Article 19. Article 20 sets exceptions: notification to the ANPDP for unequivocal consent or contractual necessity, and ANPDP authorisation backed by contractual clauses. Breaching Articles 19 and 20 carries fines of 45 to 90 million dobras. A factsheet dated 24 June 2022 lists the law as in place, with the authority operational.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is that the ANPDP decides adequacy and grants authorisation backed by contractual clauses, under Articles 19 and 20 of the law. The authority is listed as operational as of 24 June 2022.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

SWZ.short: In 2024 the data protection authority required its permission before personal data leaves Eswatini and published an application form; no approvals or penalties are known.
SWZ.summary:
Rule in force. The Eswatini Data Protection Authority (EDPA) requires authorisation before personal data leaves Eswatini, according to its application form for transfers, dated 2024. The form asks the applicant to supply the law of the recipient country, the contracts that govern the transfer and a data protection impact assessment. Sending personal data abroad is therefore a matter for the regulator's prior permission, and not for the sender alone to decide.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The EDPA has published an application form and a procedure for authorisation to transfer personal data outside Eswatini, in 2024. An organisation that wants to send personal data abroad has a document to complete and a stated route to the regulator, set out in the same 2024 form. The form is the means of complying that the authority itself makes available to controllers and processors.

Not found. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data. None names an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

SYC.short: Seychelles has had a rule on sending personal data abroad in force since December 2023; no source found says whether means of complying are published.
SYC.summary:
Rule in force. The Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023) came into force on 22 December 2023. DLA Piper states, in its summary of the country's data protection law that it permits transfer of personal data outside Seychelles provided the transfer ensures an adequate level of protection, with appropriate safeguards or legal mechanisms.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact, dated 2025, is in the Information Commission's annual report for 2025: it received and handled 14 cases under the Act in 2025, 6 of them data transfers, 5 breaches, 2 refused deletion requests and 1 a consultation. The report describes the handling as guidance, assessment and corrective advice, with no decision or sanction on a named controller and no count of cases settled.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

TCD.short: A 2026 source says the data protection law requires safeguards and notification or authorisation to send personal data abroad; no source reports means of complying.
TCD.summary:
Rule in force. Chad has a rule in force on sending personal data out of the country. The law firm Cabinet Thomas Dingamgoto wrote on 6 July 2026 that articles 29 to 32 of Loi n°007/PR/2015 require a legal basis and adequate safeguards for sending personal data out of Chad. Its analysis adds that the sender must either notify or obtain prior authorisation from ANSICE, the national agency named in the law. The rule is therefore a condition on each transfer, set in the data protection law itself, and it applies to organisations sending data from Chad to a head office or other recipient abroad.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same 2026 analysis of the law, which describes the conditions that articles 29 to 32 set and the notification and authorisation steps they require. It says nothing of a published list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance from the authority, or of the rule being applied to a named organisation.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

TGO.short: Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2004 law bars sending personal data abroad without the authority's prior permission; no source says whether any transfer has been approved, refused or penalised.
TUN.summary:
Rule in force. Tunisia's Organic Law 2004-63 of 27 July 2004, in articles 50 to 52, bars sending personal data abroad where it would harm public security or Tunisia's vital interests. It allows a transfer only to a country with an adequate level of protection. In every case it requires the prior authorisation of the data protection authority, the INPDP, which must decide within one month. The source notes that no replacement law had been adopted when it was retrieved in 2026. A Tunisian lawyer wrote in October 2026 that the 2004 regime for transfers abroad is outdated, and that organic bill No. 095/2025, before the Assembly's Rights and Freedoms Committee, contains a revised framework for them.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The published means of complying is a list of countries judged adequate. A DIAL article of 15 June 2026 says Tunisia's 2018 adequacy list of countries for data transfers identified only five African countries. The 2004 law leaves the authorisation of each transfer to the INPDP, the authority it names as owner of the rule.

Not found. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, an organisation given or refused permission, or an order or penalty for sending data abroad.

TZA.short: Tanzania's 2023 data protection law sets rules for sending personal data abroad; no source found says whether the authority has published guidance or country lists.
TZA.summary:
Rule in force. The Personal Data Protection Act, Chapter 44, published in the Gazette on 13 June 2023, has a Part V on transborder data flow: section 31 covers transfer to a state with adequate data protection and section 32 transfer to a state without it. A journal study of August 2026 cites the Act as Cap. 44 R.E. 2023 alongside the Data Protection (Collection and Processing Personal Data) Regulations, GN No. 349 of 2023.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The Personal Data Protection Commission reported in August 2026 that its preliminary assessments found unlawful data transfers abroad, and listed rectification directives, warning letters and fines as remedies. The 24 August 2026 study finds the framework on cross-border transfers progressive on paper, with gaps in institutional capacity and enforcement.

Not found. No source found says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

UGA.short: Uganda's 2019 Act sets safeguards for sending data abroad and the regulator applied them in 2025 and 2026; no source reports published guidance for complying.
UGA.summary:
Rule in force. Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 carries safeguards governing international transfers of personal data. The Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO) applies Regulation 30 on cross-border transfers, and Regulation 48 sets a fine of up to three currency points a day or six months' imprisonment for offences.

Means of complying published and rule applied. In a decision of 20 February 2026 the PDPO partly upheld a complaint against WhatsApp LLC and Meta Platforms, Inc. and ordered, within 90 days, a Regulation 30 adequacy assessment and an intra-group data protection impact assessment. On the same day it directed both companies to ensure lawful safeguards for transfers of Ugandan users' personal data. On 18 July 2025 it found Google in breach for transferring data abroad without adequate safeguards, and gave it 30 days to register and submit transfer-compliance evidence.

Not found. No published list of approved countries, model contract terms, application form or guidance on transfers is held.

ZAF.short: Since July 2020 the law bars sending personal data abroad without adequate protection or consent, but no approved country list or guidance is known.
ZAF.summary:
Rule in force. South Africa's Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) prohibits transfers of personal information outside the country unless the recipient is under adequate legal protection, the data subject consents, or a contract or the data subject's interest requires the transfer. The Act took effect in July 2020, with a grace period to 30 June 2021, so the rule has applied in full since mid-2021. It is a single statutory rule covering every responsible party that sends personal information out of South Africa, and the conditions for a lawful transfer are set out in the Act itself.

Means of complying published and rule applied. An article published on 17 January 2024 states that POPIA does not name the countries with adequate protection and creates no mechanism for the regulator to recognise such countries. On that account the party sending the data has to judge adequacy for itself, case by case, since the Act supplies no approved list to rely on.

Not found. No source found says the Information Regulator has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

ZMB.short: Zambia's Data Protection Act, passed in 2021, sets conditions for sending personal data abroad; no source found says whether it has come into effect.
ZMB.summary:
Rule in force. Zambia's Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021, enacted on 24 March 2021, sets the conditions for sending personal data outside the Republic in Part X, sections 70 and 71. The Act says it commences on a date the Minister appoints by statutory instrument, and the published text gives no date.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The Act sets out three routes. The first is the data subject's consent together with standard contracts or intragroup schemes approved by the Commissioner. The second is a transfer to a country the Minister has prescribed, on a test of an adequate level of protection. The third is a transfer the Commissioner approves where it is necessary, case by case.

Not found. No source found says a rule on sending personal data abroad is in force.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's data protection authority issued a transfer rule in 2024 and reported 24 authorisations by 2025; no source found says which organisations and destinations.
ZWE.summary:
Rule in force. On 13 November 2024 POTRAZ, the designated data protection authority, issued guideline CDPG 5 of 2024 under sections 6(1)(a) and 28(3) of the Cyber and Data Protection Act. It took effect on publication and bars data controllers from sending personal data abroad unless they have notified the Authority and met stated conditions: an impact assessment, the data subject's consent, adequate protection in the destination country and a data-sharing agreement.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same guideline sets out the notification, impact assessment, consent, adequacy and agreement steps, includes a letter requesting prior authorisation from the Authority, and gives a contact address for complaints and guidance. In a report published on 26 December 2025, POTRAZ said 24 cross-border transfers of personal data have been authorised.

Not found. The dates of the 24 authorisations, the organisations that received them and the countries data went to are not held. No list of approved destination countries or model contract terms has been found.

AGO.short: A rural connectivity programme had connected a stated number of sites or people by 2024; rural and urban use is not measured.
AGO.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. MINTTICS says its Conecta Angola project, launched in June 2023 to bring voice and internet to remote areas operators do not serve, has reached more than 300,000 people previously without communications, per GGPEN director-general Zolana João. President Lourenço says programmes such as N'gola Digital, Escola Conectada and Conecta Angola brought connectivity to communities including remote areas via ANGOSAT-2, and that strengthening connectivity in rural communities is a priority for coming years. On 20 October 2026 the President authorised US$50 million and a tender for the Programa Conectividade, which takes broadband to less-served areas, schools and community centres first, under the World Bank-financed Angola Digital Acceleration Project.

Gap measured. No source found since October 2023 gives internet use in rural and in urban areas. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Gap narrow. No source found since October 2023 gives rural internet use of 80 per cent or more of the urban rate. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 gives internet use in rural and in urban areas.

BDI.short: A programme to bring internet to rural areas was under way in 2026; sites connected are not counted.
BDI.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. ARCT acting director Hermalas Nahimana said the government has created a universal service fund that will help the rural population to have access to the internet. SETIC (also PAFEN coordinator) signed a $5,907,000 contract with ONATEL to deploy infrastructure across 92 rural hills lacking 2G or 3G coverage, expected to benefit about 372,035 people, said Burundi Times. PAFEN, the government digital-inclusion programme, and Lumitel signed a USD 10 million contract to extend 4G broadband in rural areas, co-financed 44 per cent by the government through PAFEN, says SETIC.

Gap measured. No source found since October 2023 gives internet use in rural and in urban areas. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Gap narrow. No source found since October 2023 gives rural internet use of 80 per cent or more of the urban rate. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says: is one delivering, with sites counted.

BEN.short: Nothing found since 2023 names a programme to connect rural areas, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not found. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether a programme to connect rural areas is under way.

BFA.short: Rural and urban internet use were measured in 2026, rural use below four-fifths of urban.
BFA.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. The digital-transition minister said on 8 October 2026 that 750 villages would get calls, internet and mobile money for the first time by end-2026 and 750 more by 2028, with FCFA 25 billion mobilised by the State, under a zero-white-zone target for 2030. PactDigital, a government digital project, is set to extend mobile and internet connectivity to 1,000 underserved communities in 2026 under the 'Zero White Zones' initiative, benefiting 1.5 to 2 million people, mostly rural, per TechAfrica News citing the project. The minister said the State had subsidised the commissioning of 223 sites since 2020.

Gap measured. Data presented at the National Forum on the Digitalization of Justice showed internet access of about 72% in urban areas and 27% in rural areas.

Gap narrow. No source found since October 2023 gives rural internet use of 80 per cent or more of the urban rate. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 gives rural internet use of 80 per cent or more of the urban rate.

BWA.short: A rural connectivity programme had connected a stated number of sites or people by 2025; rural and urban use is not measured.
BWA.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. The Universal Access and Service Fund reports 51 more villages given 4G mobile network connectivity in 2024-25, bringing 279 villages connected by March 2025, plus 37 highway sites. Minister Segokgo says the government's village connectivity project, aimed at over 500 villages, had in its first phase connected 1,138 public facilities across 144 villages. The Ministry of Communications and Innovation says the government continues to expand high-speed internet access to rural communities, schools and healthcare facilities through the Village Connectivity Project.

CAF.short: A programme to bring internet to rural areas was under way in 2026; sites connected are not counted.
CAF.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. Agence Ecofin reports that the Central African Republic plans to finalise implementation of its universal service fund in 2026, a priority ARCEP unveiled on 15 April 2026, to extend access to telecom services including broadband internet, with operators deploying infrastructure in uncovered areas. Agence Ecofin reports that the Central African authorities launched the activities of the CDCE, the body that oversees the universal service fund meant to extend basic telecom access across the territory, funded by a 2% operator revenue contribution.

Gap measured. No source found since October 2023 gives internet use in rural and in urban areas. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

CIV.short: Rural and urban internet use were measured in 2025, rural use below four-fifths of urban.
CIV.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. A government communique of 2026-08-24 says Cote d'Ivoire is continuing its FCFA 38 billion Programme national de connectivite rurale to bring mobile network and internet access to 575 localities, with phase two (FCFA 18 billion, 240 localities) and phase three (FCFA 10 billion, 160 localities) following. ANSUT's director general said on 2026-08-11 that the universal service agency is working to connect 300 localities to reach 300,000 inhabitants, citing that 70% of rural households have no internet. ANSUT's Honoré Aka said 300 new localities are to be added to the rural digital connectivity effort in 2026.

Gap measured. Citing ITU DataHub, the article gives internet penetration of 52.7% in urban areas against 24.6% in rural areas.

CMR.short: A programme to bring internet to rural areas was under way in 2025; sites connected are not counted.
CMR.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. Business in Cameroon reports that the Posts and Telecommunications Minister opened bidding on 31 October 2025 for the rural connectivity component of the World Bank-backed PATNUC, funded with 55 billion XAF, to connect 328 unserved 3G localities by 2028. It is the only fact held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

COD.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. On 12 February 2026 the universal service fund (FDSU) presented its National Connectivity Strategy 2026-2035. It plans a subsidised, TowerCo-led roll-out in five zones and three phases, to connect about 68 million rural Congolese. In August 2026 the FDSU signed subsidy agreements with Vodacom, Airtel, Africell and Orange for at least 40 towers in peri-urban and rural areas. About 300 sites are to follow, and 3,000 settlements by 2030. No count of sites already connected is on record.

COG.short: A rural connectivity programme had connected a stated number of sites or people by 2026; rural and urban use is not measured.
COG.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. FASUCE officially connected two localities, Miaba and Ehota, with inauguration ceremonies attended by the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications. FASUCE committee chair Luc Missidimbazi said that in five years the fund deployed 254 sites in 244 localities, connecting more than 500,000 people, and the minister said the government will continue the policy. The PATN steering committee adopted a 2026 budget of 21.872 billion FCFA on 26 February 2026 with rural-area connectivity as a 2026 axis, and the project plans to serve white zones by 2027.

Webdo reports that the 2017 white-zones project, with Tunisie Telecom alone, connected 94 white zones, 164 schools and 59 health centres, benefiting over 180,000 citizens (2017, before the three-year window).

For 2026/27 Tanzania's Ministry of Communication and Information Technology proposed a budget of about $84 million, about 94 per cent for development projects, with key initiatives including extending connectivity to rural and underserved communities. The UCSAF programme is described as a government-led initiative extending telecommunications infrastructure to areas where connectivity has been limited or commercially unviable, per Tech Review Africa.

Uganda operates the Uganda Communications Universal Service and Access Fund (formerly the Rural Communications Development Fund), financed by a 2 per cent operator revenue levy to support digital inclusion. The Uganda Communications Commission says its Universal Service and Access Fund (UCUSAF), financed by a 2% levy on operator revenue, supports communications services in unserved and underserved areas and will be used to expand ICT infrastructure there.

The Sunday Times reports that through the SA Connect programme government is expanding broadband infrastructure, public Wi-Fi access and connectivity to households, schools and healthcare facilities, particularly in underserved communities. The Smart Zambia Institute's rollout connected three rural community institutions in Moomba Chiefdom: Moomba Rural Health Clinic, Choonzo Primary School and Kalamba Primary School. Machiya Tower in Mpongwe District, built in 2021 under the 24 Towers Project, provides broadband coverage to over 9,500 people, and Lisomona Tower in Masaiti District, completed in 2025 under the 51 Towers Project, delivers 2G, 3G and 4G within 15 km, per ZICTA's inspection. The Smart Zambia Institute's Electronic Government Division installed Starlink satellite internet kits in Moomba Chiefdom, Kazungula District, as part of the government's efforts to bring internet connectivity to rural communities.

ZWE.summary:
Rural connectivity programme. ICT Minister Mavetera said at Digital UNGA that more than 10,000 remote sites have been connected under Zimbabwe's digital inclusion initiatives. ICT Minister Mavetera said the government introduced infrastructure sharing and mandated tower relocation using the Universal Service Fund as interventions to bridge the digital divide for underserved rural and remote communities, and wants the fund to yield 100% coverage of marginalised wards. Free Wi-Fi has been rolled out at rural business hubs under the Presidential Internet Scheme, and Community Information Centres modernised into Digital Centres. MISA Zimbabwe states the Universal Service Fund finances network expansion into economically disadvantaged areas. On 23 October 2026 the minister directed POTRAZ to set Universal Service Fund targets for schools, clinics, chiefs' courts and rural business centres, and to publish coverage and uptake figures every quarter.

AGO.short: Angola's identity law, amended in 2017 and 2021, gives each citizen a unique number on a chip card. No rules since 2023 are known.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. Angola's identity card rests on Lei n.º 4/09, the law on civil identification and the issue of the citizen's identity card. The National Assembly amended it in August 2017 and again in January 2021, each amendment in force on publication. On 29 April 2026 the Council of Ministers reviewed a civil and criminal identification bill that would gather the rules on the identity card and criminal records into one law.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The law as amended gives each identity card a number that acts in law as the unique citizen number, and the card carries an encrypted QR code. Since 2017 the card has also carried a microprocessor holding the holder's tax, social security, birth-record and voter numbers, so that it can be read by public and private institutions.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

BDI.short: Burundi's identity card runs on ministerial orders of 1978 and 1986; in 2026 the texts for a national identification file were still to be adopted.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi's identity card runs on two ministerial ordinances, of 1978 and 1986, with no law behind them. The government's procedures page for the card lists those ordinances as its main texts and names no identity law. The page is held as published in January 2026 and says further texts remain to be adopted before the national identification file is instituted.

Digital identity covered and rules made. With no law in force, none provides for a digital identity. The same page says the national identification file still awaits its instituting texts, and the card it describes rests on the two ordinances alone. Burundi therefore answers the first question only: an identity system run on orders, with the texts for its register still to be adopted.

Not found. No source found says a national identity law is in force.

BEN.short: Benin's 2017 identification law, amended in 2025, sets up a biometric register and a personal number. No rules made under it since 2023 are known.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Benin's law no. 2017-08 of 19 June 2017 on the identification of natural persons is the law behind the national register and the personal identification number. In June 2025 the National Assembly adopted law no. 2025-12 amending its article 6, extending who the law covers, and the 2017 law stands as amended.

Digital identity covered and rules made. Article 6 as amended provides for a national biometric population register and a personal identification number for each person entered in it. The 2025 amendment adds special numbers for foreigners and for naturalised persons of African descent, so the register and the number now reach beyond citizens. The number is the one each person keeps for life in the register. No regulation or decree made under the law since September 2023 is on record.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso's assembly adopted a unique electronic identification bill in October 2024. No source found says whether it has been promulgated.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. Burkina Faso's transitional legislative assembly adopted the bill on unique electronic identification of the natural person on 11 October 2024. On 19 August 2025 the minister for digital transition said the law had been adopted the previous year. Neither source says the law has been promulgated.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The adopted text underpins a system giving each resident a random unique identifier, issued against biographic data, fingerprints and iris, and linked to the national identity card, the passport, the driving licence, the patient file and the bank account. Until a source says the law is promulgated, that provision is a bill's and not a law's. The identifier is to be issued once to each resident and kept for life, by the text as reported in October 2024.

Not found. No source found says a national identity law is in force.

BWA.short: Botswana's 1986 National Registration Act, amended in 2025, is in force. No source found says whether it provides for a digital identity.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. Botswana's National Registration Act commenced on 31 December 1986 and has been amended up to 2017; it has the Registrar of National Registration keep a national register of citizens aged 16 or over and issue identity cards. The National Registration (Amendment) Act, 2025 followed: in July 2026 the minister told Parliament what it changes.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The 2025 amendment lets a passport or a driving licence serve as identification while a defaced, lost or expired identity card is being replaced. That is the newest change to the law on record. The Act itself provides for the national register and the card, and the minister described the amendment in March 2026 as now in effect. No other change to the Act since 2017 is on record.

Not found. No source found says the law in force provides for a biometric register, an identity number unique to each person, or an identity that can be checked electronically.

CAF.short: Nothing found names a national identity law or bill for the Central African Republic, or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a national identity law or bill, or says there is none.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire's 2019 law on digital identification is the basis of its biometric identity card. No rules made under it since 2023 are known.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Côte d'Ivoire's biometric identity project is backed by the Law on Digital Identification, no. 2019-566, an enacted law of five articles. A 2025 study of ten African identity systems records the law with an executive decree and the 2013 data protection law alongside it, and treats the three together as the legal basis of the system.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The same study says the 2019 law establishes the legal basis for the biometric digital identity and that its second article describes the identity document as a secure card serving several applications. It is the one law in the country's framework that the study names as written for the digital identity itself, and it is short: five articles in all. No regulation or decree made under the law since September 2023 is on record.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

CMR.short: Cameroon's 2024 civil registration law provides a unique personal identification number for every citizen. No rules made under it since 2023 are known.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. Cameroon's Law 2024/016, the new civil registration law, is the law the national civil status office is implementing, as reported in October 2025. It is an ordinary law of 2024 and replaces the earlier civil registration regime. The report describes the office as working under it, with the registers being moved onto digital systems.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The law authorises digital birth, marriage and death certificates and a unique personal identification number for every citizen. The number is the part of the law that makes it an identity law as well as a civil registration one: each citizen is to hold one number, issued from the civil register, and the certificates drawn from that register may be digital. No regulation or decree made under the law since September 2023 is on record.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

COD.short: The DRC's population file rests on a 2022 decree; a bill on identifying persons was tabled in parliament in June 2026.
COD.summary:
Law in force. The Democratic Republic of the Congo's population file was created by the Prime Minister's decree no. 22/07 of 2 March 2022, with no identity law among its legal bases. On 12 June 2026 two deputies tabled a private member's bill on the general rules for identifying natural persons, which is to go to committee.

Digital identity covered and rules made. No law is in force. The 2022 decree gives the population file a national identification number and biometric data and puts the national identification office in charge of it, on the strength of a decree alone. The bill tabled in June 2026 describes the present arrangements as resting on decrees, which is what it sets out to change. The bill had not been debated by the end of September 2026.

Not found. No source found says a national identity law is in force.

COG.short: Congo's identification number and identity card rest on decrees of 2004 and 2009, the latter amended in 2024; no identity law is known.
COG.summary:
Law in force. The Republic of the Congo's unique identification number was instituted by decree no. 2004-469 of 3 November 2004, and no law is named behind it. The national identity card rests on a 2009 decree, which decree no. 2024-2692 of 13 November 2024 amended. Both instruments are decrees.

Digital identity covered and rules made. No law is in force, so the rules that follow are made under decrees. An order of 12 March 2020 added the capture of iris and fingerprints to the identification number, and an order of 12 October 2022 made the number mandatory for eight economic transactions and five administrative formalities. The 2024 decree provides a card holding both thumbprints. No bill for an identity law is on record.

Not found. No source found says a national identity law is in force.

COM.short: The Comoros's 2014 law institutes a biometric identity card. No rules made under it since 2023 are known.
COM.summary:
Law in force. The Comoros has a law instituting its identity card: law no. 14-023/AU of 24 June 2014, promulgated by decree no. 14-137/PR. The decree is held from the Ministry of Justice's site, which lists it as the instrument that brought the law into force. The law is an act of the Assembly of the Union.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The Ministry of Justice describes the 2014 law as instituting the Comorian digital, biometric identity card. That description, in the title under which the ministry publishes the promulgating decree, is what is held on the law's content: it is a law for a biometric card, and the ministry calls the card digital. No regulation or decree made under the law since September 2023 is on record. The card it institutes is the national identity card Comorians hold.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2013 law and 2014 decree-law set up an electronic identity card; the last rules known under them date from 2017.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. Cabo Verde's national civil identification and authentication system was created by Lei n.º 43/VIII/2013 of 17 September 2013. The national identification card was then created by Decreto-Lei n.º 19/2014 of 17 March, which also governs its issue, replacement, use and cancellation. The card was launched on 23 January 2018.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The card is an electronic one whose chip holds a digital certificate and applications for identification, authentication and digital signature. Rules were made under the decree-law in 2017: Portaria n.º 21/2017 of 15 June regulates the capture of biometric data and Portaria n.º 35/2017 of 2 September sets how long the card is valid. Those rules all date from before September 2023, and none made under the law since then is on record.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

DJI.short: Djibouti's 2019 identification law sets up a unique number and biometric register; the last rules known under it date from 2020.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. Djibouti's law no. 39/AN/19 on the identification of natural persons was published on 21 January 2019. It creates the national identification number and the national register of natural persons, which the population directorate runs. A decree of 13 July 2020 was made under its article 9.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The law creates a unique national identification number and a central register of biographic and biometric data, the single reference for the identity card and travel documents. Decree no. 2020-150 sets the number's composition and requires administrations, hospitals, schools, utilities and traders to carry it on their documents. A second 2020 decree governs access to the register. Those rules all date from before September 2023, and none made under the law since then is on record.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

DZA.short: Algeria's February 2026 law covers electronic identification, with a national number required since 2010. No rules made under the law are known.
DZA.summary:
Law in force. Algeria's Council of Ministers approved a draft law on trust services and digital identification on 2 November 2025. It became law no. 26-02 of 17 February 2026, which fixes the general rules on trust services for electronic transactions and on electronic identification and is published by the ministry of post and telecommunications. The Ministry of the Interior lists law 14-03 of 24 February 2014 on travel titles and documents among the texts governing issuance of passports and identity cards.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The law sets the rules for electronic identification. Reports on its draft say it introduces a national digital identification framework built on the existing biometric identity card and updates the 2015 electronic signature law. The identity it provides for is therefore one that is checked electronically, tied to the card citizens already hold. The Ministry of the Interior says executive decree 10-210 of 16 September 2010 instituted the national identification number and requires it on official identity, circulation and travel documents.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's 2023 Digital Identification Proclamation sets up a biometric identity database. No rules made under it since 2023 are known.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. Ethiopia's Digital Identification Proclamation, no. 1284/2023, was signed by the President on 18 April 2023 and came into force on its publication in the Federal Negarit Gazette. It is a proclamation of the federal parliament, written for the digital identity and for nothing else, and it is the law the identity system runs under.

Digital identity covered and rules made. The proclamation sets up a digital identification system that collects demographic and biometric data in a central database. The system it describes is digital from the start: a person is enrolled with biometric data and identified from the central database. The proclamation's second article sets out the terms the rest of the text relies on. No regulation or decree made under the law since September 2023 is on record.

Not found. No regulation or decree applying the law, and no rule made under it that others must check identity against the system, dated in the last three years, is held.

GAB.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a national identity law or bill, or says there is none.

GHA.short: Ghana's identity Acts of 2006 and 2008 are in force; 2026 regulations require biometric verification against the national register.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Ghana's identity system rests on two Acts of Parliament that the National Identification Authority lists as its laws: the National Identification Authority Act, 2006 and the National Identity Register Act, 2008. The Authority is the statutory body the 2006 Act set up to create and maintain the national identity register.

Digital identity covered and rules made. Regulations made under the 2008 Act, gazetted on 27 March 2026 and in force from 9 June 2026, require organisations to verify identity through the Authority's biometric verification system, in real time against its database. An earlier notice under the same laws, of 15 February 2024, specifies the portable card readers that may be used. The 2026 regulations amend the register regulations of 2012.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

GIN.short: Guinea's 2023 identification law is in force, and an April 2025 decree applying it set up a biometric register with an identification number.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. Guinea's Law L/2023/019/CNT of 25 October 2023 on the identification of physical persons is the law under which a decree of April 2025 is made. On 26 February 2026 the head of the identification office named it at a workshop where officials said the country now has two new laws, on identification and on civil status. The minister's declaration of 10 August 2026 lists their adoption and dissemination among the year's achievements.

Digital identity covered and rules made. Decree D/2025/052 of 14 April 2025, in effect from its signature, fixes how people are entered in and kept on the national register of natural persons, in application of the 2023 law. The decree sets up a register of biographic and biometric data with a personal identification number, and a jurist writes that under the law fingerprints, face and iris may be taken from the age of ten. A workshop at Kindia in January 2026 reviewed and validated further draft decrees and orders applying the identification and civil status laws.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.
