ZAF.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The fund's own figures, given in a ministerial reply, show 1,087.9 million rand spent in 2025/26. The 2026 Estimates of National Expenditure raise the digital and postal access subprogramme of Vote 30 from 742.9 million rand in 2025/26 to 767.2 million for 2026/27. The digital lines held for both years total 8,082.2 million rand for 2026/27 against 7,685.6 million for 2025/26.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The Universal Service and Access Fund is paid for by operators' mandatory contributions. ICASA collected 281.2 million rand for it in 2025/26, and its administrator spent 1,087.9 million rand that year, leaving about 652.1 million unspent. The fund collected 1.2 billion rand over the five years to 2025/26. It has not been abolished. The 2026 Estimates put 146.0 million rand of 2026/27 towards the universal service and access bodies.

Not found. Nothing: all four questions are answered.

ZMB.short: The digital lines in Zambia's 2026 budget total more than in 2025, with 843.4 million kwacha spent in 2025; no fund or levy is known.
ZMB.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. Zambia's budget tables publish 843.4 million kwacha as spent on digital lines for 2025. The digital lines held for both years total 1,792.9 million kwacha for 2026 against 1,594.5 million for 2025, a rise. The Appropriation Act, 2025 authorises 1.15 billion kwacha for Smart Zambia e-government for 2026, with 566.8 million kwacha for ICT development. The Supplementary Appropriation Act of 2025 added 162 million kwacha for Smart Zambia e-government and 194.3 million for ICT development for 2025. In May 2026 the minister announced approval of 255 million kwacha to upgrade digital infrastructure, mainly in rural areas.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The budget document linked names no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes. The nearest budget fact is that the budget for 2026 gives 1,942.9 million kwacha to 45 digital lines.

Not found. Whether the government has said digital transformation must be paid for from its own resources and acted on it: no fund, levy or assigned tax is shown created, collecting or paying.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's ICT ministry budget rises about 3 per cent to 763.5 million Zimbabwe Gold for 2026; no source found reports spending and any fund.
ZWE.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The Budget Statement gives the ICT ministry's Vote 23 budget as 763.5 million Zimbabwe Gold for 2026 against 741 million for 2025, a rise of about 3 per cent. The digital lines held for both years total 4,503.5 million Zimbabwe dollars for 2026 against 5,703.9 million for 2025, 21.0 per cent lower. The Appropriation Act gives 258.3 million Zimbabwe Gold to the ministry's policy and administration programme and 505.2 million to ICT development and promotion for 2026. No figure for what was spent has been found.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The budget document linked names no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes. The nearest budget fact is that the 2026 budget gives 4,675.6 million Zimbabwe dollars to 31 digital lines.

Not found. What was actually spent on digital programmes, and whether the government has said they must be paid for from its own resources and acted on it: no fund, levy or assigned tax is shown created, collecting or paying.

AGO.short: Angola's 2011 presidential decree on information society services covers e-signatures and contracts; no rules made under it are known, and a 2026 regime awaits enactment.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. Angola's Presidential Decree 202/11, published in the Diário da República I Série no. 139 on 22 July 2011, approves the Regulamento das Tecnologias e dos Serviços da Sociedade da Informação. It covers information society services, electronic documents and legal acts, with qualified electronic signature, certification and electronic contracts, and electronic advertising. It enters into force 30 days after publication.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact concerns a further e-signature regime. On 30 July 2026 the Assembleia Nacional unanimously approved, with 166 votes in favour, a bill authorising the President to legislate the Regime Jurídico da Assinatura Electrónica e da Certificação Digital, valid for 90 days after publication. Angop reports that the regime would set e-signature validity, evidential value and the Infra-Estrutura de Chaves Públicas de Angola. The regime itself is not yet enacted.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2011 decree has been found, and the new e-signature regime is not yet in force.

BDI.short: Burundi's 2024 communications code governs e-commerce, and the regulator issued guidelines and a conformity call in 2026; no licence or penalty is known.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi's Loi N°1/22 of 22 August 2024, the code des communications électroniques et postales, was promulgated. The regulator ARCT states that e-commerce activity on Burundi's territory is subject to a prior conformity obligation, applying the provisions of that code. The obligation was set out in an ARCT communiqué of 26 June 2026, which applies to e-commerce platforms and merchant sites.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. On 29 May 2026 ARCT published national e-commerce ecosystem guidelines, drawn from the regulation in force, which set technical, operational and organisational standards for interoperability, transaction security and consumer protection. On 26 June 2026 it issued a communiqué calling e-commerce platforms and merchant sites to declare their conformity, with a procedures manual, a conformity checklist and a declaration form annexed.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the code has been found for the last three years, and no declaration of conformity is shown to have been received.

BEN.short: Benin's 2018 digital code is in force with a 2025 decree on electronic archiving providers; no use of it since 2023 is known.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Benin's Loi n° 2017-20, the Code du numérique, was promulgated by the President on 20 April 2018 after adoption by the National Assembly and review by the Constitutional Court. The code is Benin's main digital law and includes a title on the obligations of trust service providers. Decree 2025-363 of 2 July 2025, in force on signature, gives an electronic archive the same legal value as a paper document where it is signed with a qualified electronic signature and time-stamped.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree 2025-363 was made in application of the Code du numérique, as amended in 2021. It sets the conditions for providers of electronic archiving, who must be qualified by the competent authority as trust service providers, for three years at a time, renewable after review. Articles 305 and 306 of the code give trust service providers freedom of establishment and a duty to declare themselves.

Not found. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the code in the last three years has been found.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso's 2009 law on electronic services and transactions is in force with implementing decrees; no source found reports accreditations or licences under it.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. Burkina Faso's Law n°045-2009/AN regulates electronic services and transactions, covering electronic signatures, electronic formalities, e-commerce contracts and trust service providers. The National Assembly adopted it on 10 November 2009 and it was promulgated by Decree n°2009-824/PRES on 4 December 2009. No repeal is given in the document held.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The law has implementing decrees: a report on the launch of FasoSign on 15 September 2026 says the platform gives effect to law 045-2009 and its implementing decrees, which together give a digital signature the legal value of a handwritten one. The platform already signs official mail, mission orders and land deeds in three government systems. Wearetech reports that the law presumes reliable a secure signature based on a qualified certificate.

Not found. The implementing decrees are not named, and no accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found.

BWA.short: Botswana's 2014 electronic communications and transactions act has been in force since 2016 and covers contracts, signatures and online buyers; no rules are known.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. Botswana's law is the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act, 2014 (Act No. 14), which Parliament enacted and which was assented to on 14 May 2014. The Act gives electronic communications, contracts and signatures legal effect, and it covers the protection of consumers who buy online. It did not start on assent: commencement was by an Order of the minister published in the Gazette, and the regulator BOCRA records the Act as in force since 1 April 2016.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The one instrument held that was made under the Act is the ministerial Order that brought it into force, which the Act itself provides for. No regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online is named in the text held, and no accreditation, licence or penalty under the Act is recorded.

Not found. No regulation or order made under the Act, other than the commencement Order, has been found.

CAF.short: The Central African Republic's regulator lists a 2022 electronic transactions law among the country's laws; no rules made under it are known.
CAF.summary:
Law in force. The Central African Republic has a law on electronic transactions. The regulator ARCEP lists Loi 22.002 of 11 January 2022, regulating electronic transactions in the country, among the laws on its official index of laws and ordinances. The index page was published on 21 February 2024, two years after the date the law carries, and it presents the law as one of the country's laws and not as a bill or a draft.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The regulator's index names the law and gives its date, and it shows no decree, regulation or order made under it. No rule on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online is named there, and no accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law is recorded in the index.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found, and the text of the law is not held.

CIV.short: A 2013 electronic transactions law is in force with 2014 and 2016 decrees, but no use of it is dated in the last three years.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Côte d'Ivoire's Loi n°2013-546 of 30 July 2013 on electronic transactions is the law that a decree of 12 March 2014 states it implements. APA reports that the ANSSI CI national public key infrastructure launched in July 2026 rests on this law, which it says gives electronic signatures legal value. AIP, citing an ANSSI-CI communiqué, reports the same, in an article of 25 July 2026.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree 2014-106, signed by the President on 12 March 2014, sets rules on secure electronic signatures, qualified electronic certificates and the approval of certification service providers by ARTCI. Biometric Update reports further decrees of 2014 and 2016 that accompany the law and cover cryptology, electronic signatures and digital archiving.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated in the sources found.

CMR.short: A 2010 e-commerce law is in force with a 2011 application decree, but no use of it is dated in the last three years.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. Law No. 2010/021 of 21 December 2010, adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President, governs electronic commerce in Cameroon. It defines electronic signatures, certificates and certification authorities. The Prime Minister's decree of 15 June 2011 describes it as a made law and fixes its application rules. At a CENADI workshop on 14 August 2024, Professor Jean Louis Fendji listed the e-commerce law among the local texts that frame aspects of data protection.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree no. 2011/1521/PM of 15 June 2011 fixes the modalities of application of law no. 2010/021 on electronic commerce. It defines the scope of e-commerce activity under the law. The decree was issued by the Prime Minister and is published on the Ministry of Commerce website, where the law is also published. It follows the law of 21 December 2010 that it implements, by about six months, and is the rule-making instrument for e-commerce in Cameroon.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated in the sources found.

COD.short: A 2023 digital code governs e-signatures, with a March 2026 order on authorisation, but no licence under it is dated in the last three years.
COD.summary:
Law in force. Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 of 13 March 2023, the Code du Numérique, governs electronic writings, electronic signatures, trust service providers and digital services. Under article 108, a qualified signature has the evidential force of a handwritten one. ACP reports that a ministerial order of March 2026 is made to implement the Code, which the order treats as the operative law for digital services.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The ministerial order of 11 March 2026 sets an authorisation regime for qualified trust-service providers, marketplaces and e-commerce platforms, and enters into force on signature, with full application from 1 July 2026. ACP reports it was published on 17 March 2026, with a transition to 30 June 2026.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated in the sources found.

COG.short: A 2019 electronic transactions law is treated as in force in 2026, but no rule made under it is known.
COG.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 37-2019 of 12 December 2019 on electronic transactions is treated as an existing law by the four arrêtés of 9 July 2026, which cite it as a legal basis. Décret n° 2026-101 of 31 March 2026 cites the same law as a legal basis, again treating it as existing. Both instruments concern the certified electronic invoicing system and appeared in the Journal officiel in 2026.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The four arrêtés of 9 July 2026 and Décret n° 2026-101 of 31 March 2026 are the nearest held instruments. Each names the 2019 law on electronic transactions among its legal bases, and each treats it as already in force. The law is dated 12 December 2019, while the decree and the arrêtés citing it are dated March and July 2026.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named in the sources found.

COM.short: A 2021 law on cyber security gives electronic signatures legal effect; nothing is known of rules made under it or of its use.
COM.summary:
Law in force. The UNECA Digital Trade Regulatory Integration profile, published in 2024, states that the 2021 law on cyber security and the fight against cybercrime, Law No. 21-012/AU, fills gaps in electronic transactions, notably by giving electronic signatures the same legal effect as handwritten ones. The same profile states that the Comoros has no stand-alone law on electronic transactions, no consumer protection framework and no UNCITRAL-based legislation for online transactions.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the profile's account of that law, which names no decree, regulation or order made under it and no provider accredited under it. Before the law, the national digital strategy drawn up in December 2018 stated that the telecommunications-centred legal framework leaves a legal vacuum on digital transactions and electronic signature. In March 2021 ANADEN's legal affairs officer listed a law on e-commerce among legislation still to be drafted, to be part of a digital code targeted for 2024.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2021 law, and no use of it in the last three years.

CPV.short: Cape Verde was said in 2025 to have a law on digital transactions, but no rule made under it is known.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. The Secretary of State for the Digital Economy, Pedro Lopes, cited Cape Verde's modern laws on data protection and digital transactions among its regulatory progress, in a report published on 31 July 2025. The article is about the country's digital start-up ecosystem, and the law on digital transactions is one of the regulatory advances it lists.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the same statement: the Secretary of State for the Digital Economy cited Cape Verde's laws on data protection and digital transactions as regulatory progress in July 2025. It is the only statement held on the law on digital transactions. The statement dates from 31 July 2025 and comes from the Secretary of State, who presents the laws as part of the regulatory progress the country has made.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named in the sources found.

DJI.short: Djibouti's National Assembly passed a Digital Code covering e-commerce in June 2025; no source found says whether it is in force or has implementing rules.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. Djibouti's National Assembly adopted the Digital Code unanimously on 30 June 2025, a text of nearly 800 articles that covers the regulation of online commerce among other areas. TechAfrica News describes it as the country's first Digital Code, in eight books including Book IV on e-commerce and Book V on consumer rights, announced by the Ministry of Digital Economy and Innovation. Jones Day reports that the law was still to be promulgated by the President and published in the Journal Officiel.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Jones Day reports that the Digital Code, which covers e-commerce, cryptology service providers, data protection and cybersecurity in eight volumes, is to be supplemented by regulatory decrees. The Code passed the National Assembly on 30 June 2025, and the decrees are the rules that are to follow it.

Not found. Whether the Digital Code has been promulgated, is in force or has regulatory decrees is not held.

DZA.short: Algeria's e-commerce Law 18-05 and a 2026 trust-services law are in force; no source found reports rules made under either.
DZA.summary:
Law in force. Algeria's Law No. 18-05 on e-commerce is in force: in August 2026 the head of the national consumer-guidance organisation for e-commerce said most online sellers operate without the obligations it lays down. The Minister of Post and Telecommunications described Law 15-04 of 1 February 2015 on electronic signature and certification as the text in force in December 2025, covering certification and electronic signatures only. Law 26-02 of 17 February 2026, on general rules for trust services for electronic transactions and identification, is now in force; the Council of Ministers approved a draft on that subject on 2 November 2025.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. As a draft, the trust services law was presented to the National People's Assembly in December 2025 to recognise electronic contracts and documents as equal to paper, create the ANCE authority and set sanctions. Since March 2026 the public procurement portal signs documents electronically in line with law 26-02, under a ministerial order made under the procurement law. For the e-commerce law, the consumer-guidance organisation describes sellers operating without its obligations.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named.

EGY.short: Egypt's Law 15/2004 on e-signatures is in force and has executive regulations, per 2025 legal guides; no dated licence or penalty is known.
EGY.summary:
Law in force. Egypt's Law No. 15/2004 regulating e-signatures establishes ITIDA, and its confidentiality duties bind licensed certification authorities, as an ICLG chapter written by a law firm lists it in July 2025. A Chambers guide of March 2025 also cites the law as part of Egypt's framework and states what it requires of applicants for e-signature services. Biometric Update states that digitally signed contracts are legally binding in Egypt.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The law has executive regulations. The ICLG chapter states that they require applicants for e-signature services to implement systems securing the confidentiality of information, and the Chambers guide states that applicants must keep a secure system preserving the confidentiality of customers' data. Both statements date from 2025.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years is held.

ERI.short: A 2022 UN Africa commission profile said Eritrea had no e-commerce or e-signature law; nothing newer is held, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. No law or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has none.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's e-signature Proclamation 1072/2017 is in force and its regulation was approved by the Council of Ministers in 2025; no source reports publication and use.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. Ethiopia's electronic signature law is Proclamation No. 1072/2017 and its amendment, as the Ethiopian News Agency described it in November 2025. The agency reported that a regulation under the proclamation was a step toward fully operationalizing the law. The proclamation is the existing legal basis for electronic signatures in the country, and the regulation is the step the agency named toward putting it fully into operation.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Council of Ministers unanimously approved the Electronic Signature regulation under Proclamation No. 1072/2017 in November 2025. The regulation is to take effect on publication in the Federal Negarit Gazette. It is the rule made under the proclamation that the Ethiopian News Agency reported as the means of putting the law into operation.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years is held.

GAB.short: Gabon's Law 025/2021 regulates electronic transactions, and in September 2026 ministers adopted a draft trust-services decree; no source found reports use of the rules.
GAB.summary:
Law in force. Gabon's Law No. 025/2021 of 28 December 2021 regulates electronic transactions and was published in Journal Officiel no. 145 of 1 January 2022. It gives electronic acts, writings, signatures and invoices the same probative force as paper, and sets rules for e-commerce, distance contracts and consumer withdrawal.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. On 18 September 2026 the Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree setting how the qualified electronic signature certificate and other trust services are issued. It covers electronic signature and seal, website authentication, electronic invoice, and the approval conditions and duties of providers, to secure the legal value of electronic transactions. The decree sits alongside the 2021 law, whose rules on e-commerce, distance contracts and consumer withdrawal are in force.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years is held.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2008 Electronic Transactions Act is in force; no source found reports a November 2023 notice required e-commerce platforms to register, and later enforcement.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Ghana's 2008 Electronic Transactions Act is in force. The US Country Commercial Guide, published 20 September 2024, calls it the baseline for e-commerce and e-signature in the country. Digital Policy Alert describes it as setting fair business practice requirements for suppliers, consumer rights and liability protections for intermediaries. A MyJoyOnline op-ed of 16 October 2026 names the Act as part of Ghana's existing legal foundation.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Act has been put to work. In November 2023 the Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation issued an enforcement notice under the Electronic Transactions Act, requiring all e-commerce platforms and digital delivery companies to register by January 2024, as Digital Policy Alert reports. The notice set a registration duty for every platform of those two kinds, with a deadline about two months after it was issued.

Not found. No source found shows a licence, penalty or court case under the Act after the 2023 notice, or lists further rules made under it.

GIN.short: Guinea has a 2016 transactions law, a 2021 decree and a 2026 e-signature decree; no source found says how far they are applied.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. Guinea has two layers of law. Law L/2016/035/AN of 26 July 2016 on electronic transactions applies to all electronic transactions including online commerce, and covers electronic signature, digital archiving, system certification, consumer information duties, fines and prison terms, according to ANSSI's summary. A presidential decree signed on 19 August 2026 also gives an electronic signature the same probative force as a paper writing, covering public, private and person-to-person acts.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree D/2021/092/PRG/SGG, signed on 25 March 2021, sets rules for electronic transactions including e-commerce, names the ARPT as regulator with sanction powers, and provides fines and penalties. The August 2026 decree requires every electronic-certification service provider to be approved by the competent authority, names the national digital agency ANDE as that authority for approval, control and audit, and refers technical standards to a joint order of the telecommunications and justice ministries.

Not found. No source found dates an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years.

GMB.short: The Gambia's Communications Bill 2025 covering electronic transactions passed second reading in March 2026; no law in force is known.
GMB.summary:
Law in force. The Gambia has a bill and no law in force that has been found. The National Assembly approved the Communications Bill 2025 at second reading on 2 March 2026, after a first reading on 19 November 2025, and sent it to a committee. The Minister said the bill will create a legal framework for electronic transactions, recognising electronic signatures and contracts, and will cover electronic commerce services.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No rules made under an e-commerce law have been found, because the bill is still before the National Assembly. The Minister described the bill as the framework for electronic signatures, contracts and electronic commerce services, so any rules under it would follow its passage. No application of such a law has been found.

Not found. No source found says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau put a draft Electronic Transactions Law to consultation until 28 May 2026; no law in force is known.
GNB.summary:
Law in force. Guinea-Bissau has a draft law and no law in force that has been found. In May 2026 the national regulator ARN-TIC put the draft Electronic Transactions Law out for public consultation, with responses due by 28 May 2026; it covers electronic communications and transactions, trust services and e-government. The 112-article text would give data messages, electronic records, contracts and electronic signatures legal effect, license trust-service providers and set e-commerce consumer rules.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No rules have been found, because the draft has not been enacted. The text enters into force only on a date the Minister designates, so any rules under it would follow later. The regulator ARN-TIC ran the consultation and is the body named in the notice.

Not found. No source found says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea enacted a law on electronic signature and documents on 10 January 2017; no rules made under it or application are known.
GNQ.summary:
Law in force. Equatorial Guinea has a law on electronic signature and documents. The official gazette compilation, published 10 January 2017, lists Ley Núm. 2/2.017, of 10 January 2017, on Firma y Documentos Electrónicos, a law of the country. The passages held give its title and date, so what the law requires is not described here. The entry names it as the country's law on electronic signature and documents, and it is the only fact held on the law.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found. The compilation of electronic laws, published 10 January 2017, lists the 2017 law, and nothing found shows the law being applied. The nearest held fact is the law's own listing, which carries a title and a date and no text.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

KEN.short: Kenya gave electronic signatures legal effect and made certification rules by 2020; nothing is known of licences or penalties in the last three years.
KEN.summary:
Law in force. The Business Laws (Amendment) Act, 2020 came into force on 18 March 2020 and allows advanced electronic signatures in place of wet-ink signatures in nearly all legal documents, amending among others the Law of Contract Act. Under the Kenya Communications Act 1998 as amended in 2009, an advanced electronic signature has the same legal effect as a handwritten one.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Kenya Communications (Electronic Transactions) Regulations, 2009 set licensing, operating and liability rules for certification service providers. Valid advanced electronic signatures are issued by providers licensed under the Kenya Information and Communications (Electronic Certification and Domain Name Administration) Regulations 2020. On 1 September 2020 the Communications Authority required all foreign electronic certification providers to apply for recognition within 30 days. As at October 2020 only two certification service providers were licensed, and neither had yet started issuing advanced electronic signatures.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years.

LBR.short: Liberia's 2002 Electronic Transactions Law gives electronic contracts and signatures legal effect, but no regulation under it is known.
LBR.summary:
Law in force. Liberia's Electronic Transactions Law, Chapter 13 of Title 14 of the General Business Law, was approved on 8 January 2002 and published on 19 June 2002. It took effect on publication in handbills. The law gives electronic records, contracts and signatures legal effect, so a contract concluded electronically is recognised in Liberian law. It is a chapter of the General Business Law rather than a stand-alone act, and it dates from 2002.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The law applies at once to matters under Titles 5 and 21 of the General Business Law. Anywhere else it applies only as regulations of the Minister of Foreign Affairs bring it into effect. That makes the Minister's regulations the route by which the law reaches the rest of the commercial code, and the nearest held fact on rules made under it is this delegation, not a regulation itself.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

LBY.short: Libya's 2022 electronic transactions law is in force and covers online sellers; its executive regulation was unpublished in 2023, and no later rules are known.
LBY.summary:
Law in force. Libya's Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions was issued by the House of Representatives on 4 October 2022. It gives electronic signatures, records and contracts legal effect. The repository that holds it lists it as in force, and its Article 87 makes it effective from the date of issue. The law is not limited to signatures: it also sets pre-contract disclosure and return rules for online sellers, so it reaches the sale of goods and services over the internet as well as the validity of electronic documents. Eltumi Partners also states that Libya passed the law in October 2022.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is Article 87, which makes the law effective from issue, so it applied from the date of issue. The same text sets the return rules that online sellers must follow. In December 2023 Eltumi Partners stated that the government had not yet published the executive regulation to the law. No regulation, order or decision made under the law is named, and none is described as applying its rules to a particular seller or platform.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

LSO.short: Lesotho had no electronic transactions law in 2026 and a revised bill was in draft, so no source found says when it will pass.
LSO.summary:
Law in force. The ministry responsible says Lesotho lacks a legal and regulatory framework for electronic transactions, which leaves government, businesses and consumers uncertain over electronic contracts, signatures, records, online services and digital commerce. A bill is in draft: the Electronic Transactions and Communications Bill, 2026 revises a 2022 bill of the same name. The government opened a two-day validation workshop in Maseru on 28 September 2026 to gather stakeholder views.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No rules exist yet, because there is no law to make them under. The nearest held fact is the bill's progress: after the workshop, which was held with the United Nations Development Programme, the draft goes to the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel for refinement. The FinMark Trust said in June 2026 that Lesotho, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zimbabwe, lacks comprehensive legislation on electronic transactions.

Not found. No source found says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2020 trust services law is in force, with a 2023 decree and three approved qualified providers listed in September 2026.
MAR.summary:
Law in force. Morocco's Law 43-20 on trust services for electronic transactions sets the rules for trust services, cryptology means and services, and trust service providers and certificate holders. It also sets the powers of the national trust services authority. The law covers trust services, meaning signatures and certificates, rather than online selling. The DGSSI applies it, and its register of regulated services cites the law's Articles 8, 17, 46, 52 and 53 as the basis for what it regulates.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree 2-22-687 was made to apply the law. It sets transitional periods running from 13 July 2023, including six months for non-qualified trust service providers under its Article 33. Under Article 53 the DGSSI publishes a list of approved trust service providers, which as of September 2026 names three at the qualified level: EURAFRIC INFORMATION, Barid Al Maghrib and DamaneSign. It also lists the conformity certificates it has issued for qualified signature and seal creation devices, six of them current, the latest dated 18 March 2026.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

MDG.short: Madagascar has had electronic transactions and signature laws since 2014, and no source found says a 2025 draft decree on electronic signature has been adopted.
MDG.summary:
Law in force. Madagascar has a law on electronic transactions and a law on electronic signature, both dated 10 December 2014 and cited by a presidential decree as the legal basis it is made under. The transactions law, Loi no. 2014-024, has 35 articles in four parts, defines electronic signature and regulates e-commerce. Newsmada describes the signature law as the legal equivalent of the handwritten signature. Decree 2024-1911, published on 13 November 2024, gives documents signed through a certified electronic signature device the same recognition as paper.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The 2024 decree is the nearest rule held that is made under the laws, and its Article 10 on certified electronic signatures is the part that applies them. In September 2025 Newsmada reported that a draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability was in preparation, and that the ministry held a validation workshop on the regulatory framework on 13 September 2025. The evidence does not say the draft decree has since been adopted.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law, other than the 2024 decree, and none says the draft decree has been adopted.

MLI.short: Mali's 2016 law on electronic transactions regulates e-commerce and is cited by the state in 2025, but no source found reports rules made under it.
MLI.summary:
Law in force. Mali's Law no. 2016-012 of 6 May 2016 on electronic transactions, exchanges and services regulates electronic commerce. It gives legal effect to electronic writings, electronic signatures, electronic certificates and electronic archiving, and it was published in the Journal officiel of 27 May 2016. A second text, consumer protection law no. 2015-036 of 16 July 2015, sets rules for distance sales including by electronic means and bans email advertising without consent. It covers online selling only in part, and it states that an electronic contract is validly concluded under the law on electronic exchange of legal data.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact on application is a statement from the state. In November 2025 the Director General of Taxes cited the law on electronic transactions as part of a solid legal framework for digitalising public payments. The evidence names no decree, regulation or order made under the 2016 law, and no case of its provisions being applied to a particular seller or platform.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

MOZ.short: In 2026 Mozambique's electronic transactions law is applied through 19 operator licences, with about 170 companies under evaluation; no source found reports wider enforcement.
MOZ.summary:
Law in force. Mozambique's Electronic Transactions Law, Law no. 3/2017 of 9 January, is listed among its laws in force and sets rules on electronic marketing consent, intermediary service providers and personal data, with fines for breach. Licences to digital operators began under it on 8 June 2026. Decree No. 40/2026 of the Council of Ministers gives the electronic signature the same legal standing as a handwritten one.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree no. 59/2023 of 27 October, amended by Decree no. 44/2025 of 28 November, requires intermediary electronic service providers and digital platform operators to register and be licensed with INTIC. Decree 59/2019 of 3 July, the Regulation of the Digital Certification System, is made under the law, INTIC says. On 8 June 2026 INTIC's board president said 19 licences had been issued, with about 170 registered companies under evaluation.

Not found. No further rule or enforcement figure has been found beyond the above.

MRT.short: A 2018 law on electronic exchanges is in force, with a draft decree reported in 2024; no source found says whether any decree was adopted.
MRT.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2018-022 of 12 June 2018 on electronic exchanges is the law under which Tech Rek reports a draft decree in April 2024. Ordinance No. 2006-031 of 23 August 2006 on payment instruments and e-commerce operations is, per the minister's account to the National Assembly reported by AMI on 30 January 2018, the law covering banking operations and some aspects of e-commerce. On 30 January 2018 the National Assembly adopted a 102-article bill on electronic transactions, covering electronic writing equal to paper, e-commerce provider liability and a national certification authority.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Tech Rek reported on 23 April 2024 a draft decree made under the 2018 law, headed as approving a national agency for cybersecurity and electronic certification. The minister told the Assembly in 2018 that the 2006 ordinance operates with implementing texts, none of which is named.

Not found. Whether the draft decree was adopted, any decree, regulation or order made under the 2018 law or the ordinance, and any use of either in the last three years.

MUS.short: In 2026 Mauritius enacted an electronic transactions amendment act, to start on a date set by Proclamation; no source found reports rules made under it.
MUS.summary:
Law in force. Act No. 5 of 2026, the Electronic Transactions (Amendment) Act, was passed by the National Assembly on 19 May 2026 and assented to by the President on 25 May 2026, six days later. On 29 July 2026 the ICT minister referred to amendments to the Electronic Transactions Act 2006 meant to modernise digital commerce frameworks and strengthen consumer protection. That was ten weeks after the Act was passed.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The 2026 Act comes into operation on a date to be fixed by Proclamation, and different sections may be brought into operation on different dates. The same minister's July 2026 statement treats the 2006 Act as existing law and gives no date for its entry into force.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found, and nothing shows the law applied in practice.

MWI.short: Malawi's electronic transactions act has been in force since June 2017; rules made under it and no source found says how it is applied.
MWI.summary:
Law in force. The Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act (Act 33 of 2016, Chapter 74:02) was published in the Gazette on 4 November 2016 and commenced on 1 June 2017, seven months after Gazette publication. Part III of the Act gives legal recognition to electronic writing, electronic signatures and digital signature certificates, and the Act defines electronic commerce and distance contracts.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Act is held in the MalawiLII version, which includes amendments published up to 31 October 2021. That version is the nearest held statement on how the Act has been changed or applied since it commenced in June 2017, and it names no regulation made under the Act. In that version the Act sits as Chapter 74:02. In February 2024 the government put draft regulations on cryptography and certification authorities under the Act to stakeholders, alongside a 2023 bill to amend it.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found beyond drafts, and nothing shows the law applied in practice.

NAM.short: Namibia's 2019 e-transactions law was applied in 2026, with a first certification provider accredited in September; the consumer protection chapter is not yet in force.
NAM.summary:
Law in force. Namibia's Electronic Transactions Act 4 of 2019 was promulgated in Government Gazette 7068 on 29 November 2019, covering legal recognition of data messages, electronic signatures, contracts, consumer protection and accreditation of security services. It was brought into force on 16 March 2020 by GN 75/2020, except section 20 (electronic signatures), Chapter 4 (consumer protection) and Chapter 5 (accreditation). Section 20 and Chapter 5 came into force on 15 June 2026 by GN 182/2026; Chapter 4 is annotated as not yet in force.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Government Notice 335 records the Electronic Signature Regulations under section 20, signed 27 November 2025. CRAN also made regulations on accreditation of security products and services and certification service providers, published 17 December 2025. In the week of 3 September 2026 CRAN accredited the Ministry of Home Affairs as Namibia's first Certification Service Provider under the Act, for four years. DigiNam, the national public key infrastructure, was launched on 31 August 2026 under the Act, with CRAN as Root Certification Authority.

Not found. No count of accredited providers beyond the first, and no date for Chapter 4.

NER.short: Niger's 2019 electronic transactions law is presented by the ministry as governing; no source found reports rules made under it and its application.
NER.summary:
Law in force. The ministry's page presents Loi 2019-03 of 30 April 2019 on electronic transactions in Niger as governing electronic transactions. The law covers electronic signatures, contracts and payments, data retention and sanctions, so one text carries both the rules for electronic dealings and the penalties for breaching them. It dates from April 2019 and is presented on the page as the current text.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The same ministry page is the nearest statement on rules made under the law: it presents Loi 2019-03 as the governing text for electronic transactions in Niger No decree, regulation or order made under it is named, and no figure for how the law is applied is given.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found, and no date of entry into force has been found.

NGA.short: Nigeria's electronic-signature rules are in a bill the House approved by May 2026 and the Senate had not passed; no source found reports the rules.
NGA.summary:
Law in force. Nigeria has a bill, not yet a law. TechCabal reports that the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, introduced in July 2024, gives qualifying electronic signatures the same validity as handwritten ones. By May 2026 the House of Representatives had approved the bill, and it was waiting for the Senate. In July 2026 the Senate ICT committee chair said the bill was at third reading, with assent expected within weeks.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Because the bill has not passed, no rules are yet made under it and nothing is applied. The nearest held fact is its design: as TechCabal describes it, the bill empowers the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) to accredit certification authorities, the bodies that vouch for electronic signatures. That power sits in a bill that was still before the Senate in May 2026.

Not found. No source found says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

RWA.short: Rwanda's consumer law has had an e-commerce chapter in force since 4 March 2026; no source found reports rules made under it.
RWA.summary:
Law in force. Rwanda regulates e-commerce through its consumer law. Law 011/2026 of 26 February 2026 on competition and consumer protection carries a chapter on e-commerce, from Article 41 onward, setting obligations for an e-commerce enterprise and for an online intermediary. It came into force on its publication in the Official Gazette on 4 March 2026.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the content of the law itself. Its e-commerce chapter, set out in the Official Gazette of 4 March 2026, places duties on two kinds of party, the e-commerce enterprise and the online intermediary, and has applied from that date. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found, so the duties are stated at the level of the law.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

SDN.short: Sudan's Electronic Transactions Act of 2007 is the law cited in the May 2026 SudaPass terms; no source found reports rules made under it.
SDN.summary:
Law in force. Sudan's Electronic Transactions Act of 2007, with its amendments, is the law the national digital identity service relies on. The SudaPass terms of use, published on 21 May 2026, treat it as the governing law. They state that a digital signature meeting its requirements is equivalent to a handwritten signature (Article 8).

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The same SudaPass terms show the Act applied in a government service: they cite its Article 28 for punishing forgery and its Article 8 for the standing of digital signatures. This is the only application held, dated 21 May 2026. No decree, regulation or order made under the Act has been found, so the rules are stated at the level of the Act itself.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

SEN.short: Senegal's 2008 law on electronic transactions and its 2008 implementing decree are in force; no source found reports any use of them since 2023.
SEN.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2008-08 of 25 January 2008 on electronic transactions gives electronic records and signatures equivalence with paper and sets rules for electronic commerce. The National Assembly adopted it on 30 November 2007. It is the law that gives electronic contracts and signatures their legal effect in Senegal, and the decree below is made to apply it.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree no. 2008-718 of 30 June 2008 on electronic commerce was made to apply law no. 2008-08. It sets supplier information duties on what sellers must tell buyers, contractual liability, electronic advertising and electronic contract rules. The nearest held fact on application is that the decree was made in 2008; nothing found dates an application of the rules since.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's Electronic Transactions Act has been in force since 2019, but in July 2026 its enforcement was not fully set up.
SLE.summary:
Law in force. Sierra Leone's Electronic Transactions Act, Act 89 of 2019, is in force. The SierraLII record gives assent and commencement on 5 December 2019 and promulgation on 14 January 2020. Sierra Loaded reports that it gives legal recognition to electronic signatures, consumer protection and digital communications in courts. The UNECA digital trade profile lists it among the country's frameworks, with intermediary safe-harbour and consumer-protection provisions.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Sierra Loaded reports that at a government dialogue on implementing the Act on 27 and 28 July 2026, its enforcement structures were not yet fully established. These include digital certification authorities, electronic evidence procedures, dispute resolution and penalties. The law is in force, but the machinery for applying it was still being set up in July 2026.

Not found. No source found names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

SOM.short: Somalia's E-Transactions Law was described in August 2026 as moving through the legislative process; no law is known to be in force.
SOM.summary:
Law in force. Somalia has a draft, not a law in force. A Ministry of Information adviser, writing in a personal capacity in an article published on 19 August 2026, says an E-Transactions Law is moving through the legislative process, alongside a Data Protection Act and a Cybersecurity Bill. No date is given for the stage it has reached. In October 2026 the communications ministry said the House of the People had approved the Digital Transactions Bill by 137 votes; the Senate stage and assent are not stated.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Because the E-Transactions Law is still moving through the legislative process, as the adviser writes, no rules are made under it and nothing is applied. The same article names the Data Protection Act and the Cybersecurity Bill as companion measures in the same process, which places the law among three pieces of digital legislation under way in August 2026.

Not found. No source found says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

SSD.short: No law on electronic transactions or e-commerce, or draft of one, is known for South Sudan as at 2026, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce or a draft of one, or says there is none.

STP.short: São Tomé and Príncipe passed an e-signature law, reported in 2025; no rules made under it or use of it are known.
STP.summary:
Law in force. São Tomé and Príncipe has an E-Signature Law, the name the project report gives it. The World Bank's April 2025 implementation status and results report for the Digital Sao Tome and Principe project states that the law was passed. The report was published on 11 April 2025 and gives no date of passage or of entry into force, so that publication date is the latest date at which the law is stated to exist.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the passing of the E-Signature Law, which the World Bank's implementation status and results report for the Digital Sao Tome and Principe project records in a report published on 11 April 2025. It states that the law was passed, and the page for the country stops at that statement.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found.

SWZ.short: Eswatini has had an Electronic Transactions Act since 2022, named by ministers in 2025 and 2026; no rules made under it are known.
SWZ.summary:
Law in force. The Prime Minister said in October 2025 that the Electronic Transactions Act was passed in 2022, and the same article's highlights say three major cyber laws are now in force. On 29 April 2026, Minister Savannah Maziya listed the Electronic Transactions Act of 2022 among Eswatini's existing legal groundwork. APC, in an article published on 22 July 2024, lists the Electronic Communications Transactions Act of 2022 among the ICT laws the regulator ESCCOM oversees. The same article says the four 2022 ICT Acts were tabled in Parliament under certificates of urgency.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the Act itself. The Prime Minister placed its passage in 2022, and APC's article of 22 July 2024 lists it among the laws ESCCOM oversees, the regulator named there. In April 2026, Maziya counted the Act among the country's existing legal groundwork.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found.

SYC.short: Seychelles has had an electronic transactions act in force since 2001, recognising electronic records and digital signatures; no source found reports rules made under it.
SYC.summary:
Law in force. The Electronic Transactions Act, 2001 (Act 8 of 2001) commenced on 20 December 2001 and gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. The consolidation published by SeyLII shows the Act as amended and current to 29 March 2018. The Act is the law that governs electronic dealings in Seychelles, and it has been in force since 2001.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The consolidated text lists one further amendment as outstanding, Statutory Instrument 12 of 2024, which is not yet worked into it. It names no regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online, and it records no accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the Act.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law on signatures, certifiers or online sellers is held, and the 2024 amendment is not held.

TCD.short: Chad has a 2015 law on electronic transactions, and electronic signatures count in finance ministry correspondence from 2026; no source reports rules under the law.
TCD.summary:
Law in force. Chad has Law No. 008/PR/2015 on electronic transactions, which the regulator ARCEP's register of laws lists among the country's laws; the register gives the law's year, 2015, and no other date. A second provision gives electronic signatures force: Article 53 of Law No. 008/AN/SENAT/2025, the finance law for 2026, makes electronic signature compulsory for administrative correspondence in the finance ministry from 1 January 2026 and states that it has the same legal value as a handwritten signature.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is Article 53 of the 2026 finance law, which sets the electronic signature in the finance ministry's administrative correspondence from 1 January 2026, and it states that this signature has the same legal value as a handwritten one.

Not found. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found.

TGO.short: Togo's 2017 electronic transactions law, amended in 2023, and its 2018 decree on sellers, signatures and trust providers are in force.
TGO.summary:
Law in force. Decree 2018-062/PR of 21 March 2018 is made in application of Law 2017-007 of 22 June 2017 on electronic transactions, which it cites as the law governing electronic contracts, written records, electronic signatures and online selling. Law 2023-012 of 19 July 2023, published in Journal officiel no. 55 bis, amends the 2017 law. It redefines its terms and adds rules on electronic seals, digital safes and 20-year retention of electronic copies and signatures, and a penalty for usurping the status of trust service provider.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The same Decree 2018-062/PR, adopted by the Council of Ministers on 21 March 2018, has 105 articles. It regulates electronic transactions and services under the 2017 law: formalities for e-commerce sellers in Article 6, electronic signatures and qualified certificates, trust service providers and the accreditation procedure.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TUN.short: Tunisia has had an electronic exchanges and commerce law since 2000, with certification decrees reported, but no dated use of it is known.
TUN.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2000-83 of 9 August 2000 on electronic exchanges and commerce was published in the Journal Officiel no. 64 of 11 August 2000 and gives electronic documents and signatures legal effect. Decree-law 2020-31 of 10 June 2020 (JORT no. 54) took effect on publication. It gives a reliable electronic signature the same evidentiary force as a handwritten one, and electronic documents the same force as paper.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The ID4Africa country playbook of May 2026 reports that decrees of 2000-2001 organise certification, set the conditions for accrediting certification service providers and fix the technical specifications. Law 2000-83 creates the national electronic certification agency (ANCE) and licenses certification providers. The same law sets consumer rules for online sales: disclosure duties, a 10-working-day withdrawal right and fines.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated.

TZA.short: Tanzania's Electronic Transactions Act is in force and was amended by the Finance Act of June 2026; no source found reports rules made under it.
TZA.summary:
Law in force. Tanzania's Electronic Transactions Act, Chapter 442 of its laws, is in force. Parliament amended it in 2026: Part III of the Finance Act, 2026, published on 30 June 2026, amends section 13 of the Act. The Finance Act treats the Electronic Transactions Act as an existing law of Tanzania and changes one section of it, leaving the rest of the Act standing as it was before.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Finance Act, 2026 is an act of parliament amending the law, and it is not a regulation or order made under it. The text held names no regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online, and it records no accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the Electronic Transactions Act.

Not found. No regulation or order made under the Act has been found.

UGA.short: Uganda's 2011 Electronic Transactions Act and its 2013 regulations are in force; no source found reports any application of them in the last three years.
UGA.summary:
Law in force. The Electronic Transactions Act (Act 8 of 2011, now Chapter 99) was assented to on 17 February 2011 and commenced on 15 April 2011. It gives data messages, electronic signatures and electronic contracts legal effect and sets consumer rules for online sellers. In October 2026 the Daily Monitor said Uganda relies on a piecemeal framework including the Act.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Minister responsible for ICT made the Electronic Transactions Regulations, 2013 (S.I. 2013 No. 42) on 10 September 2013 under section 35 of the Act, gazetted on 30 September 2013. They cover the authenticity of data messages, disclosures by sellers and service providers, commercial communications and provider liability. They set offences with fines up to six currency points for sellers who fail to give the required information and for unsolicited commercial communications.

Not found. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

ZAF.short: South Africa's 2002 electronic communications and transactions act is in force, and three signature providers held accreditation under it in September 2026.
ZAF.summary:
Law in force. South Africa's law is the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act of 2002. TechCentral reported on 11 September 2026 that it is the law under which the South African Accreditation Authority accredits providers whose signatures qualify as advanced electronic signatures. The Act has stood since 2002 and no bill to replace it is named.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Act is being applied. Under it the South African Accreditation Authority accredits providers of advanced electronic signatures, and three hold accreditation: Altron Security, TrustFactory and Impression Signatures, as TechCentral reported on 11 September 2026. The report gives no date for any of the three accreditations, and it names no regulation made under the Act.

Not found. No regulation made under the Act has been found, and the dates of the three accreditations are not held.

ZMB.short: Zambia's 2021 electronic communications and transactions act is in force, with the regulator named root certification authority under it; amendments are in consultation.
ZMB.summary:
Law in force. Zambia's law is the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act No. 4 of 2021, which gives a legal framework for electronic transactions and secure electronic signatures. It is under review: the Ministry of Technology and Science began consulting stakeholders on amendments to the Act, which Cabinet approved in principle in September 2025, as reported on 30 September 2026. The Act stays in force while the amendments are prepared.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Act has been applied to set up the country's certification system. The regulator ZICTA was designated National Root Certification Authority under the Act, as reported on 30 September 2026. When the national public key infrastructure was launched, the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Technology and Science said the Act provided its legal foundation, as reported on 7 September 2026. No regulation made under the Act is named.

Not found. No regulation made under the Act has been found, the date of the regulator's designation is not held, and the text of the amendments is not held.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe had no electronic transactions law in June 2026 and relies on other laws; no published draft of one is known.
ZWE.summary:
Law in force. Zimbabwe has no law on electronic transactions. FinMark Trust said on 18 June 2026 that Zimbabwe, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Lesotho, does not have comprehensive legislation of the kind an Electronic Transactions Act provides. It is the one dated statement held on the question, and it names no bill or draft before cabinet or parliament.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. With no law, there are no rules under one. FinMark Trust says existing laws on financial services, data protection and cybersecurity are adapted instead to cover electronic dealings. No decree or regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online is named, and no accreditation, licence or penalty is recorded.

Not found. No published draft of an electronic transactions or e-commerce law has been found.

AGO.short: A link between education systems was under way in 2025; none in service is on record.
AGO.summary:
Education systems exchanging data. LBC, the contractor, says the SIETP technical-vocational education system was designed for integration with SIGE, Angola's Education Information and Management System. It is the only fact held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited included, and the systems themselves were not examined.

One learner identifier across education systems. No source found since October 2023 says one learner identifier is used across education systems. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Linked to the national ID or another sector. No source found since October 2023 says learner records are linked to the national ID or another sector. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says two education systems exchange data in use.

BDI.short: A link between education systems was under way in 2024; none in service is on record.
BDI.summary:
Education systems exchanging data. The ministry and UNESCO held a workshop on 29 July to 2 August 2024 for the project, agreed in December 2022 and running 35 months to 14 February 2026, to build a human resources module integrated into the central SIGE and compatible with the STATEDUC application, for teacher recruitment, deployment and posting; activities were planned over 12 months and user profiles validated. The Panel says the ministry of education is developing a human resources module to be integrated in the education management information system.

One learner identifier across education systems. No source found since October 2023 says one learner identifier is used across education systems. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Linked to the national ID or another sector. No source found since October 2023 says learner records are linked to the national ID or another sector. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

BEN.summary: Not found. Nothing found names education systems exchanging data, or says there is none.

BFA.short: A link between education systems was under way in 2025; none in service is on record.
BFA.summary:
Education systems exchanging data. La Tribune du Faso, citing the digital transition ministry, reports that on 25 June 2025 the digital transition and basic education ministers reviewed progress on the national pupil file, online enrolment and school identity cards, built with WURI support to track pupils from primary to university, with progressive enrolment due from the next school year. The ministry's February 2024 report on the pilot phase of the national pupil file, online enrolment and school identity cards (FIUE-BF) records a pilot of the unique pupil identification file; the passages read give only the contents list, with no figures.

One learner identifier across education systems. No source found since October 2023 says one learner identifier is used across education systems. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Linked to the national ID or another sector. No source found since October 2023 says learner records are linked to the national ID or another sector. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

BWA.summary: Not found. Nothing found names education systems exchanging data, or says there is none.

CAF.short: Two education systems exchanged data in 2026; no source found reports a shared learner identifier.
CAF.summary:
Education systems exchanging data. The World Bank ICR says the HRMIS built under the Education Sector Plan Support Project is now linked to the payroll, with 98.01 percent of teachers on payroll recorded in it with a certificate of presence (target 95 percent), and is used under the CARE project for teacher recruitment and deployment, while also saying it was developed, validated and piloted and that nationwide routine use is to be consolidated under CARE.

One learner identifier across education systems. No source found since October 2023 says one learner identifier is used across education systems. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Linked to the national ID or another sector. No source found since October 2023 says learner records are linked to the national ID or another sector. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

CMR.short: A link between education systems was under way in 2026; none in service is on record.
CMR.summary:
Education systems exchanging data. UNESCO and Cameroon's PAEBC project unit signed an agreement on 2026-07-31 for 8 million euros of technical assistance over 36 months that includes updating the MINEDUB WebSIG platform and interconnecting the education databases. It is the only fact held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited included, and the systems themselves were not examined.

One learner identifier across education systems. No source found since October 2023 says one learner identifier is used across education systems. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Linked to the national ID or another sector. No source found since October 2023 says learner records are linked to the national ID or another sector. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

COD.short: A 2026 source says the country's education systems exchange no data.
COD.summary:
Education systems exchanging data. The SERNIE director writes that other education departments in the DRC collect teacher and school-infrastructure data separately from SERNIE's learner records, with no link between them stated. It is the only fact held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited included, and the systems themselves were not examined.

One learner identifier across education systems. No source found since October 2023 says one learner identifier is used across education systems. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Linked to the national ID or another sector. No source found since October 2023 says learner records are linked to the national ID or another sector. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

The study's lines are 30, 20, 10 and 2 per cent, the frame's own cuts, and the latest figure for 2023 or later sets the stage, so a rise is a rise. The gap is men's rate of internet use less women's, as a share of men's; below zero, women's use is the higher. It measures the difference between women and men, not how many use the internet: a country where few people are online stands high if women and men are online alike, and one where most are online stands low if women lag.

AGO.short: Clinics report on paper, and municipal or provincial offices enter the figures into the national reporting system (2025).
AGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The health ministry's Office of Studies, Planning and Statistics, GEPE, oversees the health information system and has been moving it onto DHIS2 since 2015, as an article of June 2025 states. WHO supported the drafting in 2024 of a strategic plan for the system running to 2030, and the European Union finances that plan's preparation. The World Bank's appraisal of 4 November 2025 proposes US$5 million to extend DHIS2's functions and geographic coverage.

Tiers in use. A technical mission in March 2026 found the DHIS2-based national system had more than 4,700 registered users.

Where data is digitised. Health facilities collect and report their data on paper, and the figures are aggregated and entered into DHIS2 at municipal or provincial level, as the June 2025 article states.

Last twelve months. In March 2026 a joint WHO Angola and HISP UiO mission with Saudigitus assessed the platform, and the ministry and its partners agreed to upgrade it, harmonise data across information flows, build dashboards for decision-makers and train staff at all levels.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Health facilities report in paper format, and entry into DHIS2 is made at municipal or provincial level, on the June 2025 article's account.

Not found. No source names the tiers using the system, and no count or share of primary clinics entering their own reports is published. The strategic plan is not reported as adopted, and no domestic budget line is tied to the system by name.

BDI.short: Health centres enter their own reports into the national reporting system (2023), but no figure shows how many of them do.
BDI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The health ministry's Direction du Système National d'Information Sanitaire manages the health information system, and its IT cell administers DHIS2, as the ministry's statistical yearbook of July 2024 states. In a memorandum signed with the United States on 6 February 2026 the government commits to use DHIS2 as its national health data warehouse, and the United States plans $188,526 for it in 2026.

Tiers in use. The ministry collected its 2023 data through the national DHIS2 platform from health centres, district hospitals and national hospitals, with report forms set for the community, the health centre and the hospital.

Where data is digitised. Facilities record by hand in paper registers and the entry into DHIS2 is made at the facility, by the deputy head of a health centre and by a hospital's information officer, the World Bank reported in March 2023. Community health workers' monthly reports go to the health centre for entry, by the method note of the ministry's 2023 yearbook.

Last twelve months. The memorandum of 6 February 2026 runs to 31 December 2030 and costs United States support for DHIS2 at about $609,872 over the term, for linking it with SIDAinfo and other systems and for bringing in supply chain and laboratory data.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Reports in DHIS2 were more than 95% complete for health centres at 30 June 2022, in the World Bank's assessment of March 2023.

Not found. No share or count of health centres keying their own reports, with a denominator, is published, and nothing on the point is dated inside the last three years. The one community application described as interfaced with DHIS2 was still in test in 2023.

BEN.short: Health zone offices entered clinics' paper reports into the national system in 2022; how many clinics enter their own is not published.
BEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The health ministry's 2022 statistical yearbook says the ministry adopted DHIS2 from 2014 as its platform for managing health data, under what it calls the Système National d'Information et de Gestion Sanitaires (SNIGS). The ministry's programme budget for 2024-2026 puts its Direction des Systèmes d'Information in charge of the information systems action and funds that action from domestic resources alone, at 590,406,313 FCFA in 2024. The same document sets targets of 80 per cent in 2024 and 85 per cent in 2025 and 2026 for health facilities whose statistics are integrated in SNIGS.

Tiers in use. In 2019 SNIGS collected a monthly return from health centres and another from hospitals, on standard paper forms, and reported indicators for the national teaching hospital.

Where data is digitised. In 2022 a facility sent its paper report to the zone sanitaire before the 5th of each month and the zone keyed it into DHIS2 before the 20th, in every zone sanitaire. Certain equipped facilities and community relays keyed their own monthly forms directly into the data warehouse.

Last twelve months. The programme budget of December 2023 allocates the information systems action the same 590,406,313 FCFA in 2026 as in 2024 and 2025.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Abt Global, in November 2023, names one private facility, the Minonkpo Clinic in Cotonou, as recording its data directly into DHIS2 since 2020, against 752 private health facilities in the country.

Not found. No number or share of primary clinics entering their own reports is published, and no tier below the health centre is named. No dated event falls in the last twelve months.

BFA.short: Clinics and hospitals reported into the national system in 2024, entered at district or facility; the share of clinics entering their own is not published.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health's Direction générale des études et des statistiques sectorielles coordinates the national health information system, under its procedures manual of July 2023. Enabel reported in July 2026 that a strategic plan for the system for 2026-2030 is being implemented. The ministry's digital health strategy of January 2025 is costed at 42.6 billion FCFA, against 2.8 billion FCFA of available funds.

Tiers in use. In 2024 Endos-BF, the ministry's name for its health data warehouse, took the monthly activity reports of public and private health facilities and of the units of the regional and university hospitals. The Countdown to 2030 country team states that 83% of expected monthly facility reports were received nationally through DHIS2 in 2024.

Where data is digitised. In 2024 health facilities sent their monthly reports to the district, where data managers keyed them into Endos-BF. The ministry's strategy of January 2025 lists the scaling-up of decentralised entry of routine data in health facilities among the health system's innovations.

Last twelve months. Enabel reports that district management teams and head nurses of health posts were trained in data analysis and use, including quality control of DHIS2 data, at Dédougou and Tenkodogo in July 2026.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. In 2024, in the health districts implementing decentralised entry, the heads of health facilities entered their own monthly activity reports. In 2021 entry by the primary health centres themselves was operational in the Boucle du Mouhoun, one of 13 regions.

Not found. No number or share of primary clinics, or of districts, keying their own monthly reports is held. Who finances the system is not stated, and no community system is shown exchanging data with Endos-BF.

BWA.short: All public health facilities reported into the national system in 2016-18; they report on paper (2025), and it is unclear where the figures are entered.
BWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. WHO's country office report for 2024-2025 describes DHIS2 as the Government's selected "gold standard" platform for aggregate data. The Ministry of Health and Wellness's roadmap, dated 2019, set one integrated DHIS2 as the default reporting system for the sector, under the ministry's stewardship.

Tiers in use. MEASURE Evaluation's country profile of August 2019 records a national deployment of DHIS2 aggregating health data from all facilities in the country.

Where data is digitised. WHO's report for 2024-2025 lists facilities' heavy reliance on paper-based reporting as a challenge and recommends revising the DHIS2 dashboards and trackers "to enable onsite data capturing".

Last twelve months. WHO's report for 2024-2025 has DHIS2 used to monitor HIV, immunisation and reproductive, maternal and child health across districts.
