UGA.summary:
Framework adopted. Uganda has a framework issued and renewed. The published Uganda e-Government Interoperability Framework, issued by the ICT ministry and the national IT authority and dated 6 May 2021, sets twelve principles and six interoperability layers for e-government systems. The renewal was launched with a multi-agency workshop in Kampala in February 2026, and by May 2026 the government had renewed the Government Enterprise Architecture and the framework, with World Bank support.

Required and followed. The Ministry of Health's guidelines of January 2023 say the government has spelled out how sectors exchange information in the framework. No source names an instrument that makes the framework compulsory or counts the bodies following it. No source names the body that enforces the renewed framework.

Not found. No source found says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

ZAF.short: Government has published minimum interoperability standards, being updated in 2026; no source found says whether any rule makes them compulsory.
ZAF.summary:
Framework adopted. The Department of Public Service and Administration told Parliament in a reply to a question of 28 August 2025 that it had published the Minimum Interoperability Standards to guide departments in achieving system interoperability. The standards are under revision: the Operation Vulindlela report for the first quarter of 2026/27, from the National Treasury and the Presidency, says work progressed during the quarter on updating the Minimum Interoperability Standards and the Government-Wide Enterprise Architecture.

Required and followed. The same report says the updated standards are to be progressed and tested in priority digital services by September 2026. It cites no instrument that makes the standards compulsory for departments and names no body that enforces them, and no department is reported as certified against them. The DPSA reply presents the standards as guidance. Exchange systems named in the same reporting are noted below, since no source ties them to the standards.

Not found. No instrument held makes the Minimum Interoperability Standards compulsory and names who enforces them, and no department is reported following them.

ZMB.short: Zambia issued a public service interoperability standard in 2019; no decree or law making it compulsory has been found.
ZMB.summary:
Framework adopted. Zambia has a standard issued. The government, through the electronic government division in the Office of the President, issued the Public Service ICT Electronic Government Interoperability Standard, first edition, in a final version dated February 2019. The text describes itself as the electronic government interoperability framework for all ministries, provinces and spending agencies.

Required and followed. The standard is a government-issued document and cites no decree or law behind it. It says of itself that the division enforces it and that systems must comply to join the government's ICT infrastructure. No source dated since 2019 names a law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory, or counts the ministries and agencies whose systems have been checked against it.

Not found. No source found says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe handed an enterprise architecture blueprint to government ICT directors in May 2026; nothing says it is published or binding.
ZWE.summary:
Framework adopted. Zimbabwe has an architecture written and not published. A supplier says it completed an enterprise architecture framework, roadmap and change plan for the government in a project running from September 2023 to September 2024, with staff from over 40 ministries, departments and agencies in its workshops. In May 2026 the Enterprise Architecture Model blueprint was officially handed over, and is expected to guide the integration of government digital systems and public services.

Required and followed. The ICT minister said the blueprint was handed to the nation's ICT directors at an e-Government Unit conference on 7 May 2026, with a government service bus planned so that ministries share data once. No source names an instrument making the blueprint compulsory.

Not found. No source found says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

AGO.short: A 2018 presidential decree makes a national interoperability plan binding on public services; no source found says whether it requires them to share data.
AGO.summary:
Law or decree in force. Angola's Presidential Decree 46/18 of 14 February 2018 approves the national plan for a global interoperability architecture across the central and local administration of the state. It took effect on publication and is a binding act of the President. The plan it approves says that the measures it needs at the level of law are still to be legislated.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2018 decree states that adherence to the plan is mandatory for the services of the public administration. What is made mandatory is the plan and its architecture; the decree is not recorded as obliging a public body to hand data to another, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking people for what the state already holds. No regulation or order made under it since 2023 is recorded.

Not found. No source found says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

BDI.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Burundi, or a draft, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

BEN.short: A 2020 decree sets up the national data exchange platform; no source found says whether public bodies are required to use it.
BEN.summary:
Law or decree in force. Benin's Decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020, issued by the Presidency, sets up XRoad BJ, the national interoperability platform through which public bodies exchange data. The decree is the founding instrument of the platform, and no later text is recorded as amending or replacing it.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2020 decree is recorded as setting up the platform, with nothing on an obligation for ministries and agencies to connect to it or to exchange their data through it. No regulation or order made under the decree since 2023 is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because the decree requires it. The platform is run for the Presidency by the agency for information systems and digital technology.

Not found. No source found says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

BFA.short: A 2018 order of the Prime Minister sets interoperability rules for public administrations; no source found says whether it requires them to share data.
BFA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Burkina Faso adopted its general interoperability reference, the Référentiel général d'interopérabilité, by an order of the Prime Minister dated 23 May 2018. The order fixes the rules that make the information systems of the different public administrations compatible with each other. It is a regulation of the head of government and not an act of parliament or a decree.

Sharing required and the law applied. The reference was the subject of a training seminar for the IT directorates of ministries from 15 to 17 October 2019, a year after the order was signed. Nothing recorded says the order obliges administrations to exchange data or to connect to a common platform, and no regulation or order made under it since 2023 is recorded. No administration is named as exchanging data because the order requires it.

Not found. No source found says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

BWA.short: A 2025 act tells public bodies not to collect what another body already holds; no rules made under it are recorded.
BWA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Botswana's Digital Services Act, 2025 (Act No. 22 of 2025) was passed by the National Assembly on 14 August 2025 and assented to on 17 October 2025. It provides for public bodies exchanging data through an information gateway and under a framework for the secure exchange of information, and for one body to retrieve data from another. The Act starts on a date the minister sets by order in the Gazette.

Sharing required and the law applied. The Act says a public or private body shall avoid collecting information that another body already holds, and that citizens and businesses are to give the same information only once, to be shared and reused as needed. A body that does not comply with the directions of the authority the Act sets up can be fined up to P500,000. No regulation or order made under the Act is recorded.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

CAF.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Central African Republic, or a draft, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

CIV.short: A 2017 ordinance binds every administrative authority to connect to the state's exchange platform; no source found says whether it has been applied since 2023.
CIV.summary:
Law or decree in force. Cote d'Ivoire's Ordinance 2017-500 of 2 August 2017, made by the President in the Council of Ministers, governs electronic exchanges between users and administrative authorities and between the administrative authorities themselves. It has a chapter on the interoperability of electronic services, and no repeal is recorded.

Sharing required and the law applied. Chapter V of the ordinance says the state sets up an interoperability platform for electronic services to which every administrative authority is bound to connect, and that the authorities must follow the general interoperability framework. The ordinance also bars an authority from asking a user again for information the administration already holds. No decree or order applying the ordinance since 2023 is recorded, and no authority is named as connected to the platform because the ordinance requires it.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

CMR.short: A draft e-government law described in 2025 would have administrations share data; it has not been passed.
CMR.summary:
Law or decree in force. Cameroon has a bill and no law in force. The government's digital transformation project described in November 2025 a draft e-government law on access to public information and the digital transformation of the administration, one of the texts examined at a workshop in Ebolowa. No promulgation is recorded, and no decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is recorded as in force.

Sharing required and the law applied. The draft, as the project describes it, provides that administrations must make their information systems compatible so that they can share data securely, and gives a body named GovTech Cameroun the task of steering interoperability. These are terms of a bill that has not been passed. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no administration is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

CPV.short: A 2020 government resolution requires state bodies to share data; no source found says whether any regulation or application has followed.
CPV.summary:
Law or decree in force. Council of Ministers Resolution 54/2020, approved on 19 March 2020 and published in Boletim Oficial no. 37 of 27 March 2020, took effect the day after publication and applies to all direct and indirect State administration services. It is a government resolution, not a law. Its measure e orders a legal diploma on interoperability of public administration information systems to be drafted and approved, and its measure f orders an interoperability framework.

Sharing required and the law applied. Measure g of the resolution establishes that public administration services and bodies must share among themselves the public data and documents needed for a given process or service, subject to personal data protection rules. Measure r orders steps to operationalise the once-only principle, with the citizen's consent. The resolution was published on 27 March 2020.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under the resolution, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

DZA.short: A December 2025 decree makes one national system the only channel for data exchange between public bodies; no order made under it is known.
DZA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Algeria's Presidential Decree 25-320 of 30 December 2025, published in Official Journal no. 87, sets up a national data governance system. Within it, a national interoperability system secures the exchange of data between public institutions and administrations. In September 2026 a further presidential decree on a secure digital interoperability plan was reported as being drawn up on the President's instruction. An earlier measure, Executive Decree 23-316 of 6 September 2023, is also in force.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2025 decree makes the national interoperability system the exclusive framework for exchanging digital data between public institutions and administrations, over a secure national interconnection network set aside for the purpose. Each body must classify and catalogue its data to gain access. No order made under the decree is recorded, and no institution is named as exchanging data through the system because the decree requires it. Separately, the Interior Minister says public bodies are required under Executive Decree 23-316 to connect their IT systems to the automated national identification number generation system.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

ETH.short: The Council of Ministers sent a draft data governance proclamation to parliament in September 2026; nothing is in force.
ETH.summary:
Law or decree in force. Ethiopia has a bill and no law in force. On 28 September 2026 the Council of Ministers referred a draft National Data Governance Proclamation to the House of Peoples' Representatives, a text designed to make government services work through interoperable systems. The same meeting is reported as approving a draft National Data Management Proclamation meant to ease data sharing, interoperability and reuse.

Sharing required and the law applied. The draft is described as designed to facilitate data sharing, interoperability and the reuse of data across government. Whether it would oblige public bodies to share is not stated in either report, and the House had not passed it by the end of September 2026. With no proclamation in force, nothing has been made under one and no public body is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

GAB.short: A 2025 ordinance makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect and exchange information; no source found says whether it has been applied.
GAB.summary:
Law or decree in force. Gabon's Ordinance 0006/PR/2025 regulating digitalisation was signed by the President on 12 August 2025 and published in the Official Journal on 30 August 2025. It applies to all services of the state and to public and private bodies, and sets a legal framework for e-government for the first time.

Sharing required and the law applied. The ordinance makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect, so that they exchange information and procedures are simpler, and puts the interoperability of information systems at its centre. It also requires public administrations to digitise their services. No decree or order applying the ordinance is recorded, and no administration is named as exchanging data because the ordinance requires it. The ordinance was published in the Official Journal within three weeks of its signature.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

GHA.short: A data harmonisation bill went to public consultation in November 2025 and a data exchange act is proposed; nothing is in force.
GHA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Ghana has a bill and no law in force. The National Information Technology Agency's draft Data Harmonisation Bill 2025 would give a legal basis for data sharing, common standards and the integration of systems across public and private institutions. The agency put it out for public consultation on 19 November 2025, with Cabinet and Parliament to follow. In July 2026 a representative of the communications minister said a Data Exchange Act was also proposed.

Sharing required and the law applied. The proposed Data Exchange Act is described as a law to improve interoperability and allow secure data sharing among government agencies. The draft bill would set a framework for data sharing, standardisation and interoperability through a National Data Exchange Platform. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no public body is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

GIN.short: A 2019 arrêté between the health and territorial administration ministries covers vaccination and birth certificates; no source found says whether any wider law requires sharing.
GIN.summary:
Law or decree in force. UNICEF Guinea lists a government interoperability arrêté between the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation (MATD), published in May 2019, for promoting vaccination and obtaining birth certificates. Its scope is health and civil registration only. The arrêté is authored by the government, and UNICEF Guinea gives only the month of publication, May 2019, for a text covering the Ministry of Health and MATD.

Sharing required and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the same May 2019 arrêté, which UNICEF Guinea describes as running between the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation. It is listed for two purposes, promoting vaccination and obtaining birth certificates, and UNICEF Guinea dates it to May 2019.

Not found. No source found says a law requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

GNB.short: A decree of October 2025 approved a national interoperability regulation; no source found says whether it requires public bodies to share data.
GNB.summary:
Law or decree in force. Guinea-Bissau's national regulation on the interoperability of the digital systems and platforms of public and private services was approved by Decree 27/2025 and published in the Official Bulletin of 31 October 2025. The Council of Ministers had approved it in draft on 10 July 2025. The regional digital project again announced the regulation's approval in August 2026.

Sharing required and the law applied. The regulation is described as one that lets public bodies share information securely. The reports do not say that it obliges public bodies to share data, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking people for what another body already holds. No order made under the regulation is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because the regulation requires it.

LBR.short: An executive order of April 2026 mandates interoperable government systems, with legislation due within a year; no law is in force.
LBR.summary:
Law or decree in force. Liberia has an executive order and no law. Executive Order No. 163, signed by President Boakai on 22 April 2026, creates a national digitalisation and modernisation initiative and an office of technology, digitalisation and innovation. Draft legislation to make the arrangement permanent is due within twelve months of the order.

Sharing required and the law applied. The order mandates interoperable digital systems across ministries, agencies and commissions and introduces a government interoperability framework. It provides that data sharing between them be governed by formal agreements on access, use and accountability. These are the terms of an order that legislation is meant to replace. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no ministry is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

MAR.short: A framework bill covering interoperability between government institutions was under government review in November 2025; nothing is in force.
MAR.summary:
Law or decree in force. Morocco has a bill and no law in force. A framework bill known as Digital X.0, covering artificial intelligence, data governance, digital identity and interoperability, was under review by the General Secretariat of the Government in November 2025. It was still being worked on before going to parliament, and the minister delegate for digital transition said it clarifies how data moves between government institutions.

Sharing required and the law applied. The bill is described as setting a model in which any exchange of information between public agencies is authorised by the user, through consent that can be traced. That is a condition on sharing and not a duty to share. The bill had not been passed by the end of September 2026. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no agency is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

MDG.short: A draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability was validated at a workshop in September 2025; nothing is in force.
MDG.summary:
Law or decree in force. Madagascar has a draft decree and no law in force. In September 2025 the ministry of digital development held a workshop to validate a draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability. The text would set up a regulatory framework for interoperability of its own, with a digital governance unit and a national interoperability committee. No adoption by the government is recorded.

Sharing required and the law applied. The draft is described by what it would set up: a framework, a unit and a committee. The report does not say the decree would oblige public bodies to exchange data or to connect to a common platform. The decree had not been adopted by the end of September 2026. With nothing in force, no rule has been made under it and no public body is named as exchanging data because a decree requires it.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

MOZ.short: A 2017 decree obliges public bodies to share data and use one exchange platform; a revised regulation was still in consultation in June 2026.
MOZ.summary:
Law or decree in force. Mozambique's Decree 67/2017 of 1 December 2017, made by the Council of Ministers under the Electronic Transactions Law, approves the regulation of the e-government interoperability framework. It applies to every institution of the public administration and took effect 180 days after publication. A revised regulation went to its final consultation at a national workshop on 11 June 2026, and the regulator described the review in December 2025.

Sharing required and the law applied. The decree obliges public administration bodies to share the data they hold and to reuse data held by other state bodies. They must reuse data a citizen has already supplied through the interoperability platform, and must use the single platform. The revised regulation had not been approved by the end of September 2026, so no rule made under the decree since 2023 is recorded, and no body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

MRT.short: A 2022 decree governs electronic exchanges between administrative authorities; no source found says whether it requires them to share data.
MRT.summary:
Law or decree in force. Mauritania's Decree 2022-009, made by the Prime Minister and published in Official Journal no. 1505, governs electronic exchanges between users and administrative authorities and between the administrative authorities themselves. The Council of Ministers heard it on 3 November 2021. It applies to any information exchanged electronically between administrative authorities.

Sharing required and the law applied. The decree sets a general security reference that the authorities' information systems must meet when they exchange information electronically. It governs how exchanges are made; it is not recorded as obliging an authority to share its data, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking users for what another authority already holds. No order made under it since 2023 is recorded, and no authority is named as exchanging data because the decree requires it.

Not found. No source found says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

MUS.short: A 2022 Civil Status Act amendment lets the Bank of Mauritius share population data for Central KYC; no source found reports any wider sharing law.
MUS.summary:
Law or decree in force. On 15 April 2022 the Bank of Mauritius Governor said, in opening remarks at the signing of memoranda of understanding, that legislative amendments to the Civil Status Act enable the Bank to share information retrieved from the Central Population Database with Central KYC participants. The amendment is limited to the Central KYC purpose, and the Governor named the Central Population Database as the source of the information shared.

Sharing required and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the same speech of 15 April 2022, in which the Governor of the Bank of Mauritius says the amendment to the Civil Status Act enables sharing between the Bank and Central KYC participants. The Governor describes the amendment as enabling sharing from the Central Population Database for Central KYC.

Not found. No source found says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

MWI.short: A government data sharing regulation was proposed in June 2026; nothing in force requires public bodies to exchange data.
MWI.summary:
Law or decree in force. Malawi has a draft regulation and no law in force. In June 2026 the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology proposed a Government Data Sharing Regulation to govern the national data exchange platform, Boma Lathu. The regulation had not been made by the end of September 2026.

Sharing required and the law applied. The minister said in June 2026 that government institutions still share citizens' data by email, on USB drives and on paper, and that a binding regulation on exchange through the platform is the missing piece. No instrument in force requires public bodies to exchange data. With no regulation in force, nothing has been made under one and no institution is named as exchanging data because a rule requires it.

Not found. No source found says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

NER.short: A 2019 electronic transactions law lets administrations exchange data and sets a framework they must use; no source found reports later use under it.
NER.summary:
Law or decree in force. Niger's Loi 2019-03 of 30 April 2019 on electronic transactions was promulgated and published in the Journal Officiel. Its Title VII on electronic administration lets administrations exchange information, documents and acts electronically (Art. 29). Art. 35 institutes a General Interoperability Framework for administrative information systems, to be set by decree.

Sharing required and the law applied. The same law exempts an applicant from supplying a supporting document when the administration can obtain it directly from the administration or services concerned (Art. 33), replacing it with a sworn declaration. The framework's data directories, norms and standards are those the administration must use (Art. 35). No regulation or order made under it is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under the law, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

SEN.summary:
Law or decree in force. Senegal has a draft decree and no law in force. The digital ministry said on 26 March 2026 that the first phase of its interoperability work had delivered a national interoperability framework, a draft decree and a platform. On 4 May 2026 it announced that the draft decree governing the interoperability platform would be presented the next day. No adoption is recorded.

Sharing required and the law applied. The decree is described only as the text that will govern the interoperability platform. The ministry's posts do not say that it would oblige public bodies to connect to the platform or to exchange data through it. It had not been adopted by the end of September 2026. With nothing in force, no rule has been made under it and no public body is named as exchanging data because a decree requires it.

SOM.short: GovStack stated in September 2024 that Somalia has no data sharing law; no source found says whether a draft has appeared since.
SOM.summary:
Law or decree in force. In September 2024 GovStack stated that Somalia has no enabling legislation for data sharing and data analysis. No law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is recorded as in force, and no draft of one is recorded. The statement is dated 29 September 2024 and comes from GovStack's spotlight on Somalia's digital leaders, which sets out the country's position on data exchange.

Sharing required and the law applied. With no such law recorded, nothing requires public bodies to exchange data, to connect to a government exchange platform or to stop asking people for what another body holds. TUN.short: A 2020 decree-law and decree require public bodies to exchange data electronically, in force in 2026 per the Presidency; no rules since 2023 are known.
TUN.summary:
Law or decree in force. Tunisia's Decree-Law 2020-31 of 10 June 2020 on the electronic exchange of data between public structures, and between them and their users, was approved by Law 14 of 7 April 2021. Government Decree 2020-777 of 5 October 2020 sets the conditions and procedures for applying it, and took effect on 1 January 2021. The Presidency of the Government gave the decree-law as in force in October 2026.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2020 decree says public structures must use electronic exchange among themselves and with their users. They must give the interoperability operator the list of the data flows they can supply, and may not ask for more than one electronic copy of a document. The Presidency says the decree-law sets the principle that users are not asked for data or documents public bodies already hold. The decree itself is the rule made under the decree-law, and sets up a strategic committee and a coordination committee; it dates from 2020. No rule made under the decree-law since 2023 is recorded.

Not found. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

TZA.short: The 2019 e-government act has a section on data sharing and exchange; no source found says whether it requires public institutions to share.
TZA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Tanzania's e-Government Act, No. 10 of 2019, started on 19 September 2019 by Government Notice 964 of that year, and applies to all public institutions. Part VIII of the Act deals with the management of electronic government data, and its section 48 is headed Data sharing and exchange. The Act defines interoperability as systems exchanging data.

Sharing required and the law applied. The Act provides for data sharing and exchange between public institutions in its section 48. The e-Government Authority says section 48(2) requires it to set up and run a system through which government ICT systems exchange data. Nothing found says the Act obliges other public institutions to share data or connect to that system. Nothing found says it stops them asking people for what another institution already holds. No regulation or order on data sharing made under the Act since 2023 is recorded. No institution is named as exchanging data because the Act requires it.

Law or decree in force. They bind all public bodies in Uganda and are a statutory instrument issued by the ICT Minister. They provide for inter-operable systems, a national data centre, mandatory use of the shared government backbone and e-government infrastructure, and information sharing in e-government services.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2015 regulations make use of the shared government backbone and e-government infrastructure mandatory for public bodies (reg. 10). On information sharing, regulation 13 says public and private bodies may share. No source found says they must share data, connect to an exchange platform, or stop asking a person for what another public body holds.

They took effect on 1 August 2016 and are consolidated to 11 April 2019. Chapter 6 of the regulations lists a regulation 97 headed Minimum interoperability standards. The regulations are a national instrument of the public service, issued by the Minister under section 41.

Sharing required and the law applied. The nearest fact held is the same consolidated regulations, made by the Minister for the Public Service and Administration, which carry the regulation 97 heading on minimum interoperability standards in Chapter 6. They took effect on 1 August 2016 and are consolidated to 11 April 2019, as the Department of the Public Service and Administration publishes them.

ZMB.summary:

It provides for public bodies sharing data: one public body may retrieve a document from the body that issued it, with the consent of the person concerned, and public bodies may run joint automated procedures. Sharing required and the law applied. The Act allows sharing between public bodies and does not require it: each of the two provisions says a public body may act, and neither obliges it to exchange data or to connect to a platform. The amendment bill is described as giving legal standing to electronic submissions and digital authentication. No regulation made under the Act since 2023 is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because the Act requires it.

Terms of reference issued by the government agency IMA on 9 February 2026 report that a seven-month study with 25 public institutions produced a Framework and Roadmap of Interoperability for the public administration, with organisational, semantic, technical and infrastructure guidelines and a phased roadmap. The document names no instrument adopting the framework. The same study found that 27% of the institutions' systems were interconnected, mostly point to point, that governance was fragmented and that the institutions shared no common standards.

Standards required and checked. The terms of reference name no decree making the framework compulsory. They were issued to hire a consultant to put interoperability into effect across the public administration, on the basis of the framework and its roadmap.

A legal note from ASIN in July 2026 treats the framework as in place and says it sets the registration, technical and contractual conditions for connecting to the government's exchange platform. A consultation workshop in Cotonou on 30 June 2026 examined a draft policy on the architecture of the State's information systems, which sets technical rules and standards for making public systems interoperable.

Standards required and checked. The framework was instituted by decree in 2020 and is addressed to administrations that provide a public service.

Burkina 24 described it in October 2019 as a normative collection of protocols, covering communication rules and the exchange of voice and files, that keeps the information systems of public administrations compatible with one another. A training seminar on the referential was held from 15 to 17 October 2019.

Standards required and checked. The decree on the public administration's digital platforms, published by August 2024, makes a favourable opinion a condition of putting a platform into service. The file submitted for that opinion includes a check that the platform respects the interoperability referential, which the decree says is adopted by order of the Prime Minister. The decree leaves the procedure for obtaining the opinion to a joint order of three ministers.

It names both aims together: systems that work with one another, and data that passes between agencies.

It sets nine areas of technical standards for government systems to exchange data: interconnection, data integration, access, collaboration, application design and development, application integration, system standards, metadata and security. Data integration covers character encoding, data exchange formats and a data modelling language.

Standards required and checked. The framework carries the agency's document number eGA/EXT/GIF/001 and is written for public institutions. The national IT authority's e-Government Interoperability Framework, e-GIF-2026, dated 15 April 2026, sets the prerequisites and guidelines for integrating government systems, offering services online and sharing data across government; it is the country's second national e-GIF. Among its standards are DCAT for metadata, so that systems describe data the same way, machine-readable ODRL policies stating how, when and by whom data may be used, and the reuse of data meanings from the base registries. It covers all ministries, departments, agencies and local governments, and states that interoperability is a prerequisite of every new IT project.

STP.summary: Not found. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether land rights are registered digitally.

SWZ.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2026; no source found reports national coverage.
SWZ.summary:
Digital register in service. The Ministry's Deeds Registry page says that since 1995 the Registry has done away with manual land, debts and miscellaneous contract registers because the information is computerised and retrievable within seconds, with registers updated daily. Registrar of Deeds Nozipho Vilakati said Eswatini is working to upgrade its manual registration and storage of deeds into a fully electronic system, after benchmarking visits to Kenya's Ardhisasa platform. 2 facts are held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. No source found since October 2023 says land can be searched or registered online. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

SYC.short: Nothing found names a digital land register or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found says how land rights are recorded.

TCD.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2023; no source found reports national coverage.
TCD.summary:
Digital register in service. ATPE reports the Direction générale des Domaines put E-Conservation (SIDCF) into production on 2 October 2023, with the first 5,000 secured land deeds distributed and a database for managing land files. Portail de la Renaissance du Tchad reports Chad's land ministry signed an accord with IGNFI covering modernisation of geographic information systems and digitalisation of cadastral data. ATPE reports the land ministry signed a partnership with Géo Consult on 5 December 2025 with priorities of modernising the cadastre and developing an urban and land information system.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. No source found since October 2023 says land can be searched or registered online. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

TGO.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2024; no source found reports national coverage.
TGO.summary:
Digital register in service. Togo Officiel says land title procedures are fully dematerialised, with all cadastre procedures done remotely via an online portal. The OTR says it is georeferencing land titles created before 2007, with surveyors measuring parcels and the data entered into a digital database, to modernise the cadastre; the Directorate of Cadastre and Land Conservation leads the operation.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. Togo Officiel says citizens can now carry out all cadastre procedures for a land title remotely through an online portal. Togo-Presse reports that, through an online portal, citizens can now carry out all Cadastre procedures for a land title remotely, and that a unique parcel number (NUP) has been introduced.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

TUN.short: Land searches or registrations could be made online in 2025.
TUN.summary:
Digital register in service. The Minister of State Domains and Land Affairs said the ministry has completed digitisation of over 10,000 state properties into a unified database, with the Office of Topography and Cadastre and the National Remote Sensing Centre. The OTC signed a USD 50m, three-year contract with the Samsung C&T Consortium for the Tunisian land information system, to digitise all OTC archives, build a land database and an integrated cadastral information system, with infrastructure in the OTC's 24 arrondissements, per OTC head Ahmed El Kamel. Land conservator Wadii Rhouma said the digital land register is already operational.

Nationwide. The Minister says the ONPF's IT system has been generalised to all its regional administrations.

Online services. Land conservator Wadii Rhouma said the operational digital land register lets users consult land titles remotely. The Minister says ONPF publicity services are now delivered online, including certificates of ownership, co-ownership, non-ownership and registration, via the updated cpf.gov.tn site.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

TZA.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2026; no source found reports national coverage.
TZA.summary:
Digital register in service. The Ministry of Lands' e-Ardhi system, covering planning, surveying, allocation, registration and valuation, is already in use in Dodoma, Arusha, Tanga, Mbeya and Mwanza regions and several municipal and district councils, per TanzaniaInvest. Deputy Minister Kaspar Mmuya said the National Land Data Infrastructure project is building a national land database to centralise official land records and geographic information, during an inspection visit in Dodoma. IGN FI reports the Land Administration and Registration Information System (LARIS) project was officially launched in Zanzibar on 27 July 2026, with aerial mapping starting to provide the foundation for Zanzibar's Digital Land Information System.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. A Ruvuma assistant commissioner for lands said citizens can sign their title deed through e-Ardhi while in any region, without travelling to the region where the service originated.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

UGA.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2025; no source found reports national coverage.
UGA.summary:
Digital register in service. The Minister of Lands, Housing and Urban Development, Judith Nabakooba, described the Uganda National Land Information System (UGNLIS) as a public portal where citizens can check land status, confirm ownership and track transactions. Minister Ntabazi said that with the new digitalisation system applicants enter their data in the computer at district level and have their title printed. Lands Minister of State Harriet Ntabazi said the ministry's survey, mapping and registration departments have been equipped with upgraded digital systems, a blockchain-based land records system has been developed, and satellite and drones will be used to capture parcels.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. The Minister said citizens can check land status and confirm ownership on the UGNLIS public portal, and the author urged landowners to check land interests through digitalised land services before transactions.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

ZAF.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2025; no source found reports national coverage.
ZAF.summary:
Digital register in service. The Minister's reply says 16,911,328 deeds documents have been digitised and made publicly accessible through the eDRS Information Provisioning Module, live since 1 April 2025, and all deeds registered after 2014 are in electronic format. It is the only fact held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. No source found since October 2023 says land can be searched or registered online. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

ZMB.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2024; no source found reports national coverage.
ZMB.summary:
Digital register in service. SMART Zambia Institute says the Zambia Integrated Land Administration System (ZILAS) is deployed and 100% digital, handling land administration in Zambia. A Ministry of Lands ICT officer says ZILAS, deployed by the SMART Zambia Institute and hosted on the Government Service Bus, is in use and issuance of title deeds is now digitally processed. 3 facts are held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. SMART Zambia Institute says users can apply for any land-related matter through ZILAS web and mobile interfaces, accessed via the Government Service Bus.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

ZWE.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2025; no source found reports national coverage.
ZWE.summary:
Digital register in service. Zimbabwe launched the Digital Land Administration Platform for electronic processing of title deeds, per a Government Gazette notice announced by Justice Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi. Justice Minister Ziyambi told Parliament that the programme begun in July 2025 requires all urban freehold stands, sectional titles and agricultural land to be digitised, with the Digital Land Administrative Platform to become the sole authoritative title register after the 24-month validation period ends in July 2027 (Open Parly).

Nationwide. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Online services. The Permanent Secretary said conveyancers submit the title deed information through the DLAP system to the Deeds Registry for processing, after which a securitised title deed is issued. The eCadastre portal states property can be searched online from anywhere, with property cards available after payment, and surveyors can e-lodge surveys.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country.

AGO.short: In 2026 counters in municipal administrations work in a national database, in the 11 municipalities of one province; no source found reports the national count.
AGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A presidential order reported on 8 June 2026 created an interministerial commission, coordinated by the Minister of State and head of the Casa Civil, to reinforce the network of Balcões Únicos de Atendimento ao Público (BUAP), as the Government names its public service counters, and charged it with the network's power, computing equipment, communication systems and connectivity. The Ministry of Territorial Administration runs a national programme of V/SAT satellite antennas for commune seats.

What the office does over it. Since 15 June 2026 adult citizens confirm their electoral data at counters installed in municipal and commune administrations, feeding the national database of adult citizens. In Zaire province more than 24,000 adults updated their data at the counters between 15 July and 14 August 2026.

How the office is connected. The ministry's antennas are to guarantee communications and internet at commune seats so that the counters there can work, and ten Zaire commune seats with no UNITEL network were to get them in the days after 14 August 2026.

Last twelve months. The data update began on 15 June 2026 with 254 counters in a first phase and 634 intended. The Cubango provincial government approved on 18 December 2025 a project that provides for internet access in all its municipal administrations, to start in January 2026.

Local governments connected. Twelve counters were working in the 11 municipalities of Zaire province on 14 August 2026, on the provincial director's word.

Not found. No source found says how the counters at municipal seats are connected, or how many municipalities nationally have a working counter. The finance of the counter network is not stated.

BDI.short: A commune began keeping its accounts in a national financial platform in 2026; no source found says how many commune offices are connected.
BDI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The sector strategy for the National Development Plan 2018-2027, issued by the Ministry of Communication, Information Technologies and Media in February 2021, names the extension of the government's fibre-optic interconnection to the communes under its e-government project. In Rumonge commune the routers and other equipment for the civil registry service's connection are to come from the local NGO FVS-Amade under a one-year project, as announced on 19 July 2024.

What the office does over it. In October 2026 Butihinda commune's accountants and tax collectors were entering its revenue and spending into AK-SOFT, a financial-management platform; they said they need a stable Internet connection.

How the office is connected. FVS-Amade said on 19 July 2024 that it will give Rumonge's civil registry service computers, tablets, solar panels and routers to ease its connection.

Last twelve months. In October 2026 the Primature trained communal finance officers on AK-SOFT. On 18 July 2026 the interior ministry's Director General for territorial administration said that many civil registration centres have no reliable internet connection for digital services and are poorly equipped with computers.

Local governments connected. The strategy of February 2021 states that about a hundred public institutions are interconnected by a fibre-optic link and that the project needs to be extended to the communes not yet connected. One commune, Rumonge, was named for a connection on 19 July 2024.

Not found. No source found says how Butihinda's office is connected, whether Rumonge's routers were delivered, or how many communes are connected.

BEN.short: Twelve more communes' town halls joined the state's administration network in 2024, of 77 communes; no source found reports the total connected.
BEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Government Action Programme 2021-2026 schedules the connection of communes to the administration's network for 2023-2026, under the Ministry of Digital Affairs and Digitalisation, and costs its local-government digital project at FCFA 21 billion, FCFA 7 billion of it from the national budget. The finance ministry's 2025 report allocates EUR 6.43 million of the 2021 sovereign Eurobond to digitalising the administration.

What the office does over it. The national land platform, which Benin calls e-Foncier Bénin, has been operational since 1 January 2025 with the participation of town halls, and a parcel is sold at the mairie with every operation done directly in the platform (March 2026).

How the office is connected. Town halls use the services of the Réseau National de l'Administration, the state's own network (2024). The 2021 programme reported a network dedicated to the public administration interconnecting 187 decentralised sites, town halls among the kinds of office it lists.

Last twelve months. The state agency ASIN presented at Bantè's town hall the connecting of the mairie to the network, reported on 18 July 2026. On 11 September 2026 a connection failure in several of Cotonou's arrondissement offices stopped the registering of taxi-duty payments for the day.

Local governments connected. The finance ministry counts 12 new town halls using the network's services in 2024, in a country of 77 communes. KfW reported on 31 May 2023 that 187 authorities were on the network and that connecting all municipalities was the next step.

Not found. No cumulative total of town halls on the state's network is published, and the 2024 count names no system their staff work in over it. Whether the mairies working in the land platform do so over that network is not stated.

BFA.short: Town halls are on the state's network and 78 civil status centres were networked in 2025; no source found reports the share of the 351 communes.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The government network, RESINA, is built and run by ANPTIC, a state establishment under the ministry of the digital economy, and the State financed its reinforcement and extension with FCFA 346.2 million in 2020. The national civil status strategy for 2023-2027, steered by the territorial administration ministry, counts the networking of principal civil status centres among its 2025 results.

What the office does over it. ANPTIC says the connection gives interconnected structures, local governments' buildings among them, access to the government intranet's computing resources, to email and to the web (January 2024).

How the office is connected. ANPTIC lists the interconnection of local governments' buildings to RESINA, with internet access at no monthly fee over WiMAX or LTE, microwave or fibre (January 2024). In 2020 its regional antennas gave the Dédougou town hall a local network and RESINA access and connected sites of the Ouagadougou town hall by fibre.

Last twelve months. The strategy's results for 2025, validated on 25 June 2026, report 78 principal civil status centres networked and the declaration software deployed in 30 principal and 140 secondary centres; the ministry names insufficient financing and too few qualified staff as brakes.

Local governments connected. The territorial administration ministry gives 78 principal civil status centres networked in 2025. ANPTIC's report for 2020 names five town halls on RESINA or being put on it: Dédougou, Fada N'Gourma, Tenkodogo, Manga and Ouagadougou.

Not found. No share of the 351 communes' town halls connected is published: the 78 centres networked in 2025 are a count with no total. Nothing found says commune staff work in a national system over the connection, or how the connection has been financed since 2020.

BWA.short: Four councils had partnerships to deploy office Wi-Fi in 2022/23; no source found says whether any council office's connection is in use.
BWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The premises Wi-Fi for council centres is recorded as partnerships between BoFiNet and four local authorities, in the company's annual report for financial year 2022/23.

What the office does over it. District officials uploaded beneficiary data to the national social registry every month as at May 2021, the World Bank says; its review names the registry the Single Social Registry.

How the office is connected. By the end of financial year 2022/23 BoFiNet had partnered with four local authorities for the deployment of premises Wi-Fi in their Rural Administration Centres.

Last twelve months. The four deployment partnerships stood at the end of financial year 2022/23, in March 2023.

Local governments connected. The four are Serowe and Mahalapye District Councils and Bobirwa and Boteti Sub District Councils, as BoFiNet lists them for 2022/23. The local government ministry ran the social registry pilot in four districts in 2019 and 2020, Gaborone, Kweneng, Kgatleng and South East, and had uploaded beneficiary data in six districts by May 2021, the World Bank says.

Not found. No source states that a council's own office has a connection in use, or gives the total of councils. Nothing dated after March 2023 is held on the councils' connection, nor who plans and pays for it.

CAF.short: A fund meant to bring broadband to town halls was still being set up in April 2026; no source found says how many communes are connected.
CAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The universal service fund (Fonds du service universel) is supervised and managed by the Comité de développement des communications électroniques, a body set by law, with the regulator ARCEP selecting the operators it pays. It is fed mainly by a levy of 2% of telecom operators' turnover of the previous year. ARCEP listed finishing the fund's set-up among its priorities for 2026 when it presented a draft budget of 6.2 billion FCFA on 15 April 2026, Agence Ecofin reports.

What the office does over it. The fund's framework provides for broadband internet access in mairies.

How the office is connected. The fund was not yet in operation on 15 April 2026.

Last twelve months. The committee that manages the fund began its activities in July 2025, and on 15 April 2026 ARCEP said the fund's effective set-up was planned for 2026.

Local governments connected. Mairies are in the fund's scope alongside schools, health centres, libraries and post offices, under law 18.002 of 17 January 2018 and a decree of February 2019.

Not found. No source states that any mairie's office is connected, how, or what its staff do over a connection, and no count or share of communes has been found. There is no dated statement that local government offices have no connection of their own.

CIV.short: A loan-financed programme to connect the communes' town halls was ratified in February 2026; no source found says how many are connected.
CIV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Digital Transition and Digitalization implements phase 1 of PADCI, with the Republic as borrower. The project runs from 2025 to 2030 and carries US$45 million for broadband to targeted public institutions, town halls among them, in Abidjan, Yamoussoukro and twelve regions. In September 2025 a separate project for the connectivity of town halls was funded by the European Union and implemented by CIVIPOL.

What the office does over it. ONECI's civil-status project lead said on 11 August 2026 that birth data entered by health staff on new digital terminals is transmitted in real time to the civil-status office, notably the mairies or sous-préfectures.

How the office is connected. The digital ministry's plan for PADCI, dated May 2025, targets public facilities, mairies among them, that have electricity but no internet, and gives the government's ambition as broadband for all mairies.

Last twelve months. Côte d'Ivoire and IDA concluded the loan agreement for PADCI phase 1 on 17 October 2025. On 4 February 2026 the Council of Ministers ratified the loan of 84,356,070,200 FCFA by decree.

Local governments connected. The World Bank's appraisal document of 18 September 2025 says the project aims to connect more than 1,300 schools, hospitals, courts and municipalities to high-speed internet, phase 1 covering selected regions and phase 2 the country. The ministry's plan sets the connection of mairies for 2025 to 2030 ANSUT said in September 2024 that its national broadband network aims to link town halls.

Not found. No source states a town hall connected and in use, and none gives a count or share of town halls connected or to be connected. The national broadband network's link to town halls is an aim, with no town hall named as reached. The civil-status data sent to the mairies is not described as arriving over a connection of the mairie's own.

CMR.short: Two commune offices in the East Region had an internet connection in August 2026; no source found says how many of the 360 communes are connected.
CMR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. On 2 June 2026 the government presented DIGI-CoR, a CFA 92 billion programme over three years to improve connectivity and equip decentralised local authorities, and was still seeking its financing from partners. The Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications is contracting authority for PATNUC, whose connectivity for local authorities is paid from a World Bank loan of US$100 million. In August 2026 the commune of Bertoua 1er had a budget line of its own for maintenance and the internet connection.

What the office does over it. APC's policy brief of 2023 says the pilot networks at Mayo-Oulo and Bibemi give the connected sites, the two town halls among them, internet access and offline access to the GOON platform of local content.

How the office is connected. UNDP Cameroon reported in August 2026 that Bertoua 1er budgets for the internet connection of its digitised civil status service. The town halls of Mayo-Oulo and Bibemi were each fitted with a Wi-Fi access point on a long-distance Wi-Fi link, by APC's brief of 2023.

Last twelve months. On 3 October 2025 the posts ministry sought a consultant for a 120-day needs assessment under component 2 of PATNUC. DIGI-CoR went to funders in Yaoundé on 2 June 2026.

Local governments connected. UNDP Cameroon's monitoring of six East Region sites in August 2026 states an internet connection at two commune offices: Bétaré-Oya, where it is available but unstable, and Bertoua 1er. Cameroon has 360 communes and 14 urban communities.

Not found. No share or total of communes connected is published; the two offices are those one region's monitoring names. Who pays for the connection at Bétaré-Oya, what staff do over the connection, and whether any commune office works in a national system held elsewhere are not stated.

COD.short: In March 2026 one province handed satellite internet kits to 45 chiefdoms and sectors; no source found says whether any office works over them.
COD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The provider is a provincial government: the governor of Haut-Uélé handed the kits to the heads of the province's decentralised territorial entities at Isiro on 17 March 2026.

What the office does over it. The kits are for the heads of the entities to send security alerts to the provincial capital in real time, in the governor's words.

How the office is connected. By satellite: the entities were given Starlink internet kits, in a province where the lack of a telecom network remains a problem.

Last twelve months. The handover of 17 March 2026 followed the recommendations of the 2025 forum on security governance.

Local governments connected. 45 chiefdoms and sectors of Haut-Uélé received kits on 17 March 2026, beside 6 territories and the security services, according to the provincial information note.

Not found. No source says any chiefdom, sector or commune office is working over a connection: the kits in Haut-Uélé are reported handed over, not installed or in use, and who pays the subscription is not stated. The 45 comes with no total of entities, and no plan naming the connection of local governments or budget line is on record.

COG.short: In February 2026 a World Bank-funded project was asked to extend internet access to town halls; no source found says how many communes are connected.
COG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Internet access for town halls falls under the Projet d'accélération de la transformation numérique (Patn), which the World Bank finances for US$100 million and whose 2026 work plan and budget was adopted at XAF 21.872 billion on 26 February 2026, according to ACI. The Bank's appraisal of May 2022 expects shared connectivity to be supplied to decentralised local authorities.

What the office does over it. The access is meant to let public administrations interconnect with the state's digital platforms.

How the office is connected. The project is to provide internet access within the public administrations themselves, town halls included.

Last twelve months. At its fifth session on 26 February 2026 the Patn steering committee recommended continuing and intensifying the extension of internet access and approved reallocating funds towards the connectivity component.

Local governments connected. Town halls are named with ministries and hospitals among the administrations to be given access. The May 2022 appraisal planned fibre for 22 ministries, departments and agencies in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, national and local government service providers alike.

Not found. No source says any town hall is connected: no count, share or place is given, and no use over a connection is named. Who owns the connection is not held within the last three years.

COM.short: Only civil-status and central systems are held, the latest from 2026; no source found says whether the communes' offices are connected, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether the office of any of the 54 communes is connected. No published count of connected communes was found.

CPV.short: Municipal councils worked in national systems in 2025, 21 of 22 supplied with state digital services; no source found says how many offices are connected.
CPV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. NOSi, a public enterprise, supplies the municipal councils with what it calls Local Digital Governance services, under a contract signed with each council, on its communiqué of 6 October 2025. The councils pay it current invoices under those agreements. Its plan for 2019-2022 budgeted ECV 25,000,000 for the state's private network.

What the office does over it. The social development ministry, on a page published in September 2018, says registration in the Cadastro Social Único, a national system, is done locally by the municipal councils. Until 17 December 2025 the registry's declaration was issued and printed at the councils. Councils on Sal, Boa Vista, Maio and rural São Vicente use the shared land platform SIGTP, on Ministry of Finance terms of reference published in March 2022.

How the office is connected. NOSi's strategic plan of March 2020 lists the municipal councils' local area networks among those served by basic access to the state's private network, which it calls the Rede Tecnológica Privativa do Estado.

Last twelve months. By 6 October 2025 NOSi's services to the Mosteiros council were not in regular supply, over unpaid invoices. The association of municipalities said it was indignant at the suspension of services, and NOSi reported a very low payment rate across the councils.

Local governments connected. NOSi says 21 of the 22 municipalities, all but Mosteiros, were receiving its services regularly on 6 October 2025.

Not found. No share of councils connected: the 21 of 22 are councils supplied with NOSi's services, and that source does not say how their offices are connected. The connection rests on one plan of March 2020 that gives no count of councils, and no plan covering 2026 has been found.

DJI.short: In 2024 Djibouti city's three communes recorded civil status in the city's system; no source found reports connection of local governments outside the capital.
DJI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The system the commune centres work in belongs to the city: the PROGOUV terms of reference of February 2024 describe Djibouti city's computerised civil-status system, which the city calls SIGEC, with its data held on a central server in a room of the town hall.

What the office does over it. At February 2024 the civil-status centres of Djibouti city's three communes recorded civil-status events in SIGEC, as did five maternity antennas.

How the office is connected. The records the commune centres enter sit on a central server at the town hall, as the terms of reference of February 2024 describe it.

Last twelve months. In February 2024 three commune centres and five antennas in health facilities were working in SIGEC.

Local governments connected. Three commune civil-status centres worked in SIGEC at February 2024, one in each of Balbala, Ras Dika and Boulaos, the three communes of Djibouti city. All three are in the capital.

Not found. No source found states how the commune civil-status centres are connected or who provides and pays for the link, and none places a local government office outside Djibouti city on a connection. No national total of local governments has been found, nor anything on governance or on the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

DZA.short: All 1,541 communes worked in national systems over the interior ministry's network in 2019; no source found reports a later count and the rural share.
DZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The network linking the communes to the national civil-status database is the interior ministry's own, on its presentation of June 2019. It was on the ministry's directives that municipal services moved onto the national vehicle-registration platform on 5 April 2026. The commune of Bouira bears its own annual internet subscription, the Court of Accounts found in September 2023.

What the office does over it. Communes and their annexes issue birth, marriage and death acts from any commune in the country, from commune databases linked to a national one (June 2019). Since 5 April 2026 municipal services work in the national vehicle-registration system, a centralised platform that replaced local applications. In September 2023 Bouira used 55 applications, 41 of them the ministry's.

How the office is connected. The ministry's architecture slide of June 2019 shows commune, wilaya and ministry levels linked over its own network, which it labels "Réseau MICL". Bouira has no intranet and links its floors to the internet by Wi-Fi, the Court of Accounts found in September 2023.

Last twelve months. On 5 April 2026 municipal services began the third phase of generalising the national vehicle-registration system, ending manual and local procedures.

Local governments connected. The interior ministry's presentation of June 2019 shows 1,541 commune databases on the civil-status network: 1,541 of 1,541 communes, on its own account. The Court of Accounts says the ministry's human-resources system was placed at all communes and wilayas, in an audit covering 2019 to 2024.

Not found. No count of communes connected has been found after the interior ministry's of June 2019, and no source found gives a rural share. No current plan with a stated period has been found, and who pays for a commune's link is stated for one commune only.

EGY.short: In 2024 one governorate was the pilot for linking districts and local units; no source found says whether any local unit office is connected.
EGY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Egypt's project to automate local administration and governorate headquarters, as its minister of communications named it on 15 January 2024, is carried out by the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology with the Ministry of Local Development and the governors. It sits within the state's institutional digital transformation project.

What the office does over it. The project is to start at governorate headquarters, move to governorate capitals and districts, and end with local units.

How the office is connected. The minister expected the Minya governorate headquarters to be linked electronically to the governorate's districts and local units during 2024.

Last twelve months. The minister described the project and named its pilot on 15 January 2024.

Local governments connected. Minya was chosen as the pilot for the first digital governorate headquarters, with the rest of local administration to follow it.

Not found. Whether any governorate headquarters, district or local unit office is connected or works over a connection, and whether the Minya link expected for 2024 was made. What the offices would do over it, the kind of connection, a plan, a funder and any event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

ERI.short: No source found says whether any sub-zoba administration office is connected as at 2026, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Whether any sub-zoba administration has a connection. What is held concerns the zoba population registers and central systems.

ETH.short: Addis Ababa piloted a connection from the centre to its woredas in 2025; no source found says whether any woreda office outside the capital is connected.
ETH.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Addis Ababa City Administration runs the one-stop service centres it calls Addis Mesob and their digital system, on its director general's report of July 2026. The city's civil registration and residency system was launched by the city administration for its own agency and built by the state's Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute in December 2025.

What the office does over it. Over the Addis Ababa connectivity, family registration, vital events registration, resident services and verification are carried out through a digital system built with locally developed applications, a government statement published on 22 December 2025 says. Outside the capital, the World Bank said in October 2025 that 444 of the safety net programme's 492 woredas use its management information system for programme tracking, which is the programme's own system and not the woreda administration's.

How the office is connected. In Addis Ababa connectivity has been created from the central level down to the woreda level for civil registration and citizenship services, the deputy director general of the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute said in the statement of 22 December 2025.

Last twelve months. Addis Ababa's mayor launched the Integrated Civil Registration and Residency Service Technology on 5 December 2025 and said implementation would start in 50 of the city's woredas on 8 December 2025.

Local governments connected. The central-to-woreda connectivity is a major pilot, in Addis Ababa only, on the statement of 22 December 2025.

Not found. No woreda office outside Addis Ababa is put on a connection provided to it, and no count of woredas connected or total of woredas is given. No plan naming the connection of woredas and no source of finance for it is stated.

GAB.short: One commune's town hall, at Oyem, was on the state administration network in 2026; no source found says how many of the communes are connected.
GAB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Réseau de l'Administration Gabonaise, the RAG, is a public network dedicated to the administrations and controlled by the State, activated at Oyem by ANINF, the State's operational arm for public digital infrastructure, Gabon Review reported on 1 April 2026.

What the office does over it. The connection at Oyem improves the working conditions of the public services and prepares the progressive integration of new digital uses in the administrations on it, on Gabon Review's account of April 2026.

How the office is connected. The Mairie Centrale d'Oyem is among the administrations of the town already on the RAG, a fibre-optic network that ANINF has brought into service there, as reported on 1 April 2026.

Last twelve months. The RAG fibre at Oyem, installed in 2010 and inactive since, has been brought into service by ANINF, Gabon Review reported on 1 April 2026.

Local governments connected. One town hall is named on the network, the Mairie Centrale d'Oyem in Woleu-Ntem, beside the town's police station and courthouse, with activation to continue to other administrations of the locality and then to other public entities, as at April 2026.

Not found. No total of communes connected or to be connected is given, and no system the town hall's staff work in is named. No plan and no source of finance is stated, and the activation at Oyem is not dated.

GHA.short: The government network connected all 274 planned sites of metropolitan, municipal and district assemblies in 2024; no source found says how many of the 261 assemblies.
GHA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation tendered the government network it calls eGovNet in September 2021, awarded it to AirtelTigo and Ascend Digital Solutions in September 2022 and signed a 10-year contract in December 2022.
