Not found. No figure for assemblies recording in dLRev is dated after February 2020: the 2021 figure is a roll-out and the 2026 figures are staff trained. No current plan for the software has been found, and nothing on its hosting is dated after 2017.

GIN.short: A revenue tool was presented in March 2025 for a pilot in communes of Conakry, Coyah and Kindia; no source found says whether the pilot began.
GIN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The president of Kindia's special delegation said on 25 March 2025 that financing for the tool remained to be found.

What is recorded. The tool presented on 25 March 2025 is one for digitalising the management of communes' revenue.

Where the record is held. The tool comes from Benin, where it was in use before its presentation in Guinea in March 2025.

Last twelve months. On 25 March 2025 the tool was presented at the Conakry governorate to the communes that are to receive it and to officials of the ministry of territorial administration and decentralisation, ahead of a pilot.

Local governments recording. The pilot presented in March 2025 is for Conakry's 13 urban communes, with Coyah and Kindia, which are to experiment with the tool.

Not found. Whether the pilot began, what the tool records and where its record is held. No owner or plan is named, and nothing is dated after March 2025.

GMB.short: One council outside the capital keeps a digital tax register, reported in 2024 and 2025; no source found reports the share of councils recording.
GMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The evaluation of the 2021–2025 public finance strategy says most of the funding for revenue reform comes from the councils, with support from donors. Kuntaur Area Council had a budget line for a pilot of digital collection in September 2025. A UN agency tendered in June 2026 for a property tax digital management system for Kanifing Municipal Council; the award is not held.

What is recorded. Basse Area Council implemented a digital tax register in 2024. Kanifing Municipal Council holds a property rates database, by its Rates Manager in June 2026. In Banjul market stalls were registered by QR code in three of five pilot zones by August 2022.

Where the record is held. Basse's system runs beside the government accounting system, with the link between the two pending in September 2025. Kanifing's database is the council's own.

Last twelve months. The evaluation, dated April 2026 and covering the period to 2025, reports the Digital Tax Collection System largely unimplemented in Banjul City Council, and its link to the accounting system incomplete in Kanifing and Janjanbureh.

Local governments recording. The ministry of finance's report of September 2025 names one council, Basse, as operating the system, and says Janjanbureh has none and Brikama no digital platform for collections.

Not found. The total of councils is not stated beside any count, so no share of councils recording is established. No plan for the system has been found from the last three years.

GNB.short: Only national tax declaration and online payment systems are named (2022); no source found reports local governments' revenue records, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not found. Whether any local government keeps a digital revenue record. Neither system held is stated as serving a local government.

GNQ.short: Only the finance ministry's national tax systems are named (2023 to 2026); no source found reports municipalities' revenue records, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. Whether any municipality keeps a digital revenue record. No municipal system is named.

KEN.short: Thirty-three of 47 counties had automated revenue collection by 2020, issuing electronic receipts; no source found says whether they hold a register of payers.
KEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. On 7 February 2019 the President directed a task force to deliver one revenue management system for all 47 counties, and none had been delivered by September 2020. A 2018 policy brief says most counties that had automated did not own their system. Standards for county revenue automation, gazetted on 27 July 2026, say counties are to own their systems and revenue data. An October 2026 commentary puts about 70 per cent of counties on contracts that pay a vendor up to 15 per cent of collections, on the writer's own figures.

What is recorded. A 2020 paper describes automation as the move from paper receipts to an electronic system, with point-of-sale machines. In 2018, 97 per cent of the 34 counties with a system used only its collection module.

Where the record is held. A 2020 survey of 24 counties found that most could not host their revenue data, which the vendor hosted. In 2018, 14 of the 34 counties used one vendor's cloud service.

Last twelve months. The Vision 2030 Delivery Secretariat's review of all 47 counties, dated 23 February 2026, names five with well-established systems and cashless collection: Murang'a, Nairobi City, Machakos, Laikipia and Nyeri.

Local governments recording. Thirty-three of the 47 counties, 70 per cent, had automated their revenues, some of them in part, by a paper in the European Scientific Journal of September 2020. In February 2026 six of the 47 relied heavily on manual and cash-based systems, by the Secretariat's review.

Not found. No source says counties hold a register of payers, and no count of counties recording is dated after 2020. No source says any county has complied with the July 2026 standards.

LBR.short: A pilot revenue database was planned in June 2023 for two city corporations; no source found says whether it was built.
LBR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Terms of reference of June 2023 put a revenue advisor under the project unit of the Ministry of Public Works, and the work is financed by the World Bank under the Liberia Urban Resilience Project.

What is recorded. The June 2023 terms of reference plan a revenue collection database built on a map, and a digital payment system.

Where the record is held. The data collected is to be owned by the municipalities and the Republic of Liberia, by the terms of reference of June 2023.

Last twelve months. The terms of reference, of June 2023, set the pilot within an advisor's contract of 36 months.

Local governments recording. The pilot planned in June 2023 is for two city corporations, Monrovia and Paynesville.

Not found. Whether the pilot database was built, and whether any local government records on it. Nothing is dated after June 2023.

LBY.short: A 2024 ministry programme signed by 27 municipalities includes electronic collection; no source found says how many municipalities use its local revenue system.
LBY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Local Government of the Government of National Unity runs the National Programme for Activating Local Revenues. Its action plan for municipalities covers economic-activity revenue, electronic collection, revenue regulations and a forum.

What is recorded. The programme's projects include an electronic collection system and a database of municipal economic activities, as reported in June 2024.

Where the record is held. The local revenue system and the electronic collection project both sit under the ministry's national programme.

Last twelve months. On 10 June 2024, 27 municipalities signed a sponsorship document committing them to implement the programme.

Local governments recording. The programme director said in June 2024 that it targets both municipalities where the local revenue system is already activated and those where it still needs activating, and gave no count of either.

Not found. What the local revenue system records, where its record is held, and how many municipalities use it or which they are. The 27 signatories are not said to use it; 21 municipalities were given access and training in October 2025.

LSO.short: Nothing is held on local governments' revenue records, digital or paper, and no system is named, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not found. No source on local government revenue records has been found, and no system of any class is named. Nothing is shown either way, including absence.

MAR.short: Communes issue local tax bills in a national system, in more than 100 large municipalities in August 2025; no source found reports the share recording.
MAR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. GIR-CT, the integrated revenue management system for local authorities, is run by the Interior Ministry's directorate for local authorities with the national treasury, as reported on 29 May 2025. The minister's circular of 19 May 2020 told authorising officers to equip their revenue offices and work with the treasury on extending it.

What is recorded. Communal tax officials issue the annual bills for local taxes in GIR-CT, and the treasury's accountants take the payments, as reported on 29 May 2025.

Where the record is held. The World Bank's status report on its mission of August 2025 has GIR-CT operating at national level, interfaced with local systems. In May 2025 the ministry told local authorities to upload their revenue orders in GIR-CT alone and to drop software they had bought or built, as the minister had told communal councils in October 2024, with revenue orders sent electronically to the public accountants. The treasury collects all municipal revenues except the professional tax, the World Bank said in November 2021.

Last twelve months. On 29 May 2025 taxpayers were being urged to declare and pay local taxes through the online platform set up with the treasury.

Local governments recording. The World Bank's status report of August 2025 puts GIR-CT in place in more than 100 large municipalities and gives no total of municipalities. The Interior Ministry's circular had it deployed in 969 of 1,590 local authorities on 19 May 2020.

Not found. How many local authorities record in GIR-CT, as a share: the newest count has no total and the only figure with one is a deployment figure of 2020. No plan or finance for the system, and nothing dated in the twelve months to September 2026.

MDG.short: One commune outside the capital was handed property-tax software in 2021; no source found says whether it or any other commune records payers digitally since.
MDG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In September 2021 UNDP, through its GBCI project with the Ministry of Economy and Finance, supported and developed the G-IFPB property-tax software and installed it.

What is recorded. UNDP states that G-IFPB, fed by a 2019 taxpayer census, was handed over on 13 September 2021 to manage collection of the built-property tax in Toamasina.

Where the record is held. The software was installed at the Commune Urbaine de Toamasina and at the Direction Régionale des Impôts Atsinanana, the regional tax office.

Last twelve months. UNDP reported the software's operational launch and official handover in Toamasina on 13 September 2021.

Local governments recording. In September 2021 only Toamasina commune used the software, and staff were trained to replicate the process in the city's other arrondissements.

Not found. Whether Toamasina went on to bill from the software after the handover, and whether any other commune was equipped. Nothing dated between September 2021 and 30 September 2026 shows a commune recording its payers or their payments in a system.

MLI.short: Communes tested tax registers in 2023 and Koutiala began a pilot in March 2026; no source found says whether any uses one as routine.
MLI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. ReCoDe, the communes' software, was chosen by the national local finance committee and rolled out by the DGCT and the treasury, a Pro-ARIDES note of July 2024 says. The Koutiala project launched on 6 March 2026 is financed by the Embassy of the Netherlands and carried with the NGO ID Sahel Afrique.

What is recorded. ReCoDe's local tax module follows a census of taxable matter, with an electronic ticket coded for each taxpayer and a payment terminal that feeds the town hall's server; Bamako's Commune VI collected 250 million CFA francs with it in 2023. In a test at Koulikoro reported in June 2023, about 100 vendors were registered and each ticket was entered at once in the town hall's database.

Where the record is held. In July 2024 the data of the 13 Pro-ARIDES communes using ReCoDe were centralised on a server at the DGCT. Market fees were collected by hand, the agent writing each ticket, UNDP Mali said in June 2023.

Last twelve months. A project launched on 6 March 2026 is to give pilot communes a digital solution and equipment for financial management and the collection of communal taxes, starting with Koutiala.

Local governments recording. ReCoDe was deployed in 680 communes for testing, the July 2024 note says. After training in 27 of the programme's communes, only Kava was willing to carry tax digitalisation through.

Not found. Whether any commune outside Bamako uses the local tax module as routine, and how many of the 680 communes use it at all. No plan for the system is stated.

MOZ.short: Only Maputo's municipality is shown keeping a taxpayer register, on a 2020 assessment; no source found says whether any other municipality records its revenue digitally.
MOZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. CEDSIF, the state's information systems centre, specifies e-SGA, a single integrated municipal management system of 22 modules, with ANAMM named as client, on a page published on 8 August 2026.

What is recorded. A September 2020 assessment for the Ministry of Economy and Finance describes SISPGIA, the Maputo municipality's property tax system, built in 2009, with modules for a taxpayer register, taxpayer queries and the payment of taxes and fees.

Where the record is held. The e-SGA specification includes modules for municipal revenue management, markets and street trading, and commercial rents.

Last twelve months. CEDSIF's page setting out the e-SGA modules was published on 8 August 2026.

Local governments recording. The September 2020 assessment describes a property tax system in one municipality, Maputo.

Not found. Where the record is held, how many municipalities record, and whether e-SGA is in use anywhere. No plan or finance is stated, and no dated event falls in the twelve months to September 2026.

MRT.short: One commune, Sebkha, kept a digital register of taxpayers in 2020 and eight were installing it; no source found says how many communes record now.
MRT.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. El Mouhassil was tested and provided to communes by the Interior Ministry's directorate for local authorities, with support from Germany, France and the World Bank, the directorate's report of November 2022 says.

What is recorded. In Sebkha a seven-week census found 10,564 taxpayers against the 2,000 officially recognised, as reported in April 2020. The software, launched there in April 2019, issues numbered, barcoded fiscal stamps and tracks each from stock to sale to payment into the commune's Treasury account; agents with tablets scan a trader's stamp to see whether it is paid or overdue.

Where the record is held. Sebkha's mayor describes the system as completely independent and run by the commune with its own stamps, as reported in April 2020.

Last twelve months. On 11 July 2023 the commune of Rosso held a training session on integrating civil-status records into its El Mouhassil programme.

Local governments recording. In April 2020 El Mouhassil was live in one commune, Sebkha in Nouakchott, and being installed in eight others. On 23 May 2023 the commune of Zouerate launched its own digitised tax collection programme, built on a census of the town's commercial activities.

Not found. Whether any commune other than Sebkha records in El Mouhassil, and how many communes use it. Nothing is dated after July 2023.

MUS.short: Permit and document systems run in local authorities (2024); no source found says whether any council keeps a digital revenue record, so no stage is set.
MUS.summary: Not found. Whether any council keeps a digital revenue register or receipt record. Nothing found says the national tax portal collects any council revenue.

MWI.short: Five of 35 local governments recorded revenue digitally by 2025, three with registers of payers; no source found reports the cities' position since 2022.
MWI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In 2022 the four city councils' systems were supplied by vendors under revenue-share contracts, Blantyre's and Mzuzu's by Technobrain and Lilongwe's and Zomba's by Nitel. Mwanza District Council adopted its system with the support of the United Nations Development Programme, as stated in February 2025. In August 2024 Lilongwe City Council said the United States had agreed US$24 million in grant funding for property records and billing in four cities.

What is recorded. In 2022 the systems in Blantyre, Lilongwe and Mzuzu held property and business owners with their payments and liabilities in one database per city, used to produce demand notices and business licences. Zomba's covered market rates, bus depots and parking only in March 2022. In February 2025 Mwanza issued electronic tickets for market fees, vehicle parking and border entry fees.

Where the record is held. In 2022 each of the four city councils ran its own cloud-hosted system from a different vendor, none of them integrated with the treasury's system, banks or mobile money. Mwanza's is built and run by the council's own systems analyst, as stated in February 2025.

Last twelve months. In February 2025 Mwanza District Council was using every component of the system it calls LORMIS.

Local governments recording. Revenue management systems had been introduced in all four city councils since 2017, of 35 local governments, the International Growth Centre's study found in 2022. The United Nations Development Programme named one district council, Mwanza, in February 2025.

Not found. No figure for the four cities after 2022, and no system named in the other 30 local governments. No current plan naming the systems, and no event in the last twelve months.

NAM.short: The capital city billed water accounts to named customers in its own system in 2024; no source found says whether any other local authority records revenue.
NAM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The City of Windhoek's billing system is its own, with the vendor BCX supplying the financial management software, The Namibian reported for February 2024.

What is recorded. The City of Windhoek bills water accounts for named customers in the system it calls Solar, with payments and arrears recorded against each account. A city memo of February 2024 found accounts imported from the financial system with wrong customer information, and a payment history missing from one account.

Where the record is held. In February 2024 the billing system ran on the city's own servers.

Last twelve months. On 2 July 2024 the City of Windhoek confirmed irregularities in its water billing system, with forensic investigators appointed and nine accounts found with wrong figures. The system keeps its logs for 30 days.

Local governments recording. The Namibian's report of July 2024 covers the City of Windhoek's billing system, the capital's, and names no other local authority.

Not found. Any local authority outside Windhoek, a total of those recording, and any of the city's accounts other than water. Nothing on who plans or pays for the systems, and no event in the last twelve months.

NER.short: The capital registers its taxpayers digitally and one commune outside it began in December 2025; no source found says how many communes record.
NER.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The City of Niamey launched the platform it calls Naneye Yarda under its 2025-2027 strategic plan, with the national information society agency building the architecture, Le Sahel reported in January 2025. The city's delegated administrator called it the main pillar of that plan at the launch on 3 October 2024.

What is recorded. In Diffa the system covers a digital census of taxable establishments by agents with tablets, automatic tax calculation, tax notices with QR codes and payment by electronic terminals, from 11 December 2025. In Niamey 50 field agents with mobile devices had geolocated over 2,000 taxpayers by January 2025.

Where the record is held. In Niamey municipal tax payments through Al Izza and Nita were integrated with real-time revenue tracking and an automated audit of each transaction, the city's administrator said in January 2025.

Last twelve months. The commune urbaine of Diffa put the system into service on 11 December 2025, replacing manual collection with incomplete taxpayer files.

Local governments recording. The platform launched in the City of Niamey in January 2025. The United Nations Development Programme named Diffa in December 2025 as the first outside the capital to deploy it in full. On 21 August 2025 Niamey received 100 electronic payment terminals.

Not found. Where the record is held, in Niamey or in Diffa, and who pays for the system. No count of communes recording, no report of use in Diffa since it was put into service, and no statement that Niamey's 100 terminals are in use.

NGA.short: Two local government areas in one state registered payers digitally from 2017; no source found says how many record across the country.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In March 2017 the Edo State government, with the local councils, introduced an automated revenue collection system under the Edo Jobs Initiative.

What is recorded. A journal article of November 2018 describes an app in which local government revenue agents register payers, businesses and vehicles and collect and print receipts. Before it, the authors say, revenue from drivers, traders and others was collected on manual receipts, with no data of collection.

Where the record is held. The agents' entries go onto a taxpayers' database.

Last twelve months. The system in the two local government areas of Edo State was introduced in March 2017.

Local governments recording. The authors say two of Edo State's local government areas, Oredo and Egor, use the system, as at November 2018.

Not found. Whether the two local government areas still use the system, and how many local government areas across the country keep a digital revenue record. Nothing on a local government area's own record is dated after 2018.

RWA.short: The national revenue authority collects for the districts and keeps their tax register (2024); no source found reports districts' own records, so no stage is set.
RWA.summary: Not found. Whether any district keeps a revenue record of its own. What is held is the national revenue authority's record, kept on the districts' behalf.

SDN.short: One locality began electronic collection as a model site in May 2026; no source found says whether it keeps a register of payers.
SDN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In Sennar State, Isali electronic collection is run by the state finance ministry's unified collection department, as reported in May 2026.

What is recorded. The Sennar state finance ministry launched Isali electronic collection on 12 May 2026 at the transport and petroleum department and Sinja locality, with collectors, auditors and accountants equipped and trained.

Where the record is held. The state's governor described Isali as a national programme covering all Sudanese states.

Last twelve months. The launch of 12 May 2026 followed preparation from January 2026, in stages of networking, account opening and training.

Local governments recording. Sinja locality was one of two model sites in Sennar State at the launch. The state's finance director general said all state institutions would be covered at the start of the second half of 2026.

Not found. Whether collection in Sinja ran past its model stage, whether a register of payers is kept and where the record is held. No other locality is named as collecting electronically.

SEN.short: More than 20 communes were equipped with a vendor's municipal software by November 2025; no source found says whether any records its revenue in it.
SEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The municipal software named in Senegal's communes is a product of the vendor Linking Development, supplied to communes, on the vendor's own account in November 2025.

What is recorded. The vendor says the software, which it calls Terlink, includes accounting and taxation modules covering the recovery and management of communal taxes. Its other modules are for civil status and for planning and land.

Where the record is held. Linking Development describes Terlink as all-in-one municipal management software, supplied together with a website for the commune.

Last twelve months. In November 2025 the vendor published its account of the software and of the communes it had equipped with it.

Local governments recording. Linking Development, the vendor, states that more than 20 communes in Senegal are equipped with Terlink, as at November 2025.

Not found. Whether any commune uses the software it was equipped with, what the software records of payers, and where the record is held. No total of communes beside the count, no plan or finance, and no event in the last twelve months.

SLE.short: Three of 22 local councils had a property tax system by December 2025, with billing shown only in the capital; no source found reports use elsewhere.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Finance runs the rollout through its Fiscal Decentralization Division, with the Ministry of Local Government, as at May 2026, under a 2025-2029 strategy for property tax roll-out pilots and scaling-up plans. The rollout is financed by a US$50 million IDA grant and US$6.73 million of GEF co-financing under the Resilient Urban Sierra Leone Project.

What is recorded. The Municipal Property Tax System covers a georeferenced property roll, valuation, billing, demand notices and payment reconciliation, the ministry said on 20 May 2026. Freetown City Council's database held more than 160,000 properties and billed each a Rate Demand Notice in 2020.

Where the record is held. The ministry's notice of 20 May 2026 says the system, which it calls MOPTAX 2.0, is integrated with the Central Government Monitoring and Reporting System.

Last twelve months. Freetown City Council was upgraded to MOPTAX 2.0 in December 2025. On 20 May 2026 the ministry invited firms to roll the system out in Bo and Koidu New Sembehun City Councils over fifteen months.

Local governments recording. In December 2025 Freetown became the third local council, after Kenema and Makeni, to have the upgraded system, of 22, the Ministry of Finance says: 14 per cent of local councils given the system. Makeni's was deployed in April 2025, and the ministry called Kenema's a pilot in May 2026.

Not found. Whether Kenema or Makeni bills from the system each was given, and any council recording outside Freetown past a pilot. The ministry's 2025 progress report still expected in 2026 the integration that its May 2026 notice describes as made.

SOM.short: Four Puntland local governments kept a digital register of payers and payments in 2022; no source found reports the share of all local governments.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. As of September 2023 the property tax work was run by the UN Joint Programme on Local Governance with state ministries of interior. In Puntland the system was implemented through the Ministry of Interior with the telecom firm Golis, on programme support, in August 2021.

What is recorded. In Garowe, Qardho and Galkacyo properties were mapped and registered in the local government financial system, which generates the tax invoices and receipts payments made through mobile money, on fieldwork of October 2022. The system, which the local governments call FMIS, replaced printed receipts and books, from 2019 in Garowe and from 2021 in three others.

Where the record is held. In June 2021 the programme described the Puntland districts' system as moving to a coherent financial system from district to state level, deployed through the state Ministries of Interior and Finance.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is in the period to September 2023, when three of five targeted Puntland districts had completed the demonstration phase of a mobile-payment tax collection system.

Local governments recording. Four Puntland local governments, Galkacyo north, Garowe, Qardho and Bosaso, used the system to collect taxes in October 2022. In Galmudug and Benadir no local government or district had a financial management system; Benadir's districts collect no taxes, and the regional administration's agents collect property taxes, permits and licences, in November 2022.

Not found. No total of local governments is given, so the four counted are a floor and not a share. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months, and whether district records reach the state system since 2021 is not established.

SSD.short: A digital revenue system was launched for Juba City Council in September 2026; the council is still leaving manual collection. No other council is named.
SSD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Stateman Software & Telecom Ltd is named as the developer, implementer and managing company of what Juba City Council calls its Digital Revenue Collection & Management System, working in partnership with the council, in October 2022. In September 2026 the Central Equatoria State Government launched a digital revenue collection system and e-services for the council; no vendor or funder is named.

What is recorded. A council notice of 21 October 2022 invites all businesses within the council and its blocks to register their data on the new system. Registration and access to services had started, and manual payments for council services are to end.

Where the record is held. Businesses register their data at the council's block headquarters offices, by the notice of October 2022.

Last twelve months. The state government launched the council's digital revenue system in September 2026, and the council's first executive meeting under its caretaker mayor, reported on 8 October 2026, put the move from manual to digital collection at the centre of its priorities.

Local governments recording. The roll-out covers Juba City Council and its blocks, and was announced as just started in October 2022. In October 2026 the council was still described as moving from manual collection to a digital system.

Not found. Where the record is held is not stated, and no local government other than Juba City Council is named. Whether the system of October 2022 stayed in use is not established, and no figure for collection on the system launched in September 2026 has been found.

What is recorded. For 2024/2025 the council issued rates bills to individual ratepayers by post, email and bulk SMS, and keeps their contact and ownership details; payments carry the plot or account number. In December 2020 it said rates had been billed in April 2020 and some property owners had not paid since.

Where the record is held. Ratepayers check their rates balance and pay on the USSD code *440#, as of April 2024.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is of April 2024, when the council introduced the USSD code for checking balances and paying, alongside bulk SMS of bill amounts, for the 2024/2025 billing year.

Local governments recording. One council, the Municipal Council of Manzini, billed its ratepayers for 2024/2025, as it did in April 2020.

Not found. Where the record is held, who finances the billing, and whether any local government other than Manzini keeps such a record are not established; no total of local governments is given. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

Where the record is held. Payments are to be recorded in the commune's management system, which it calls the système de gestion communal, by the account of April 2025.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is of 2 April 2025, when Mongo launched the ten-day taxpayer census, to move local tax collection to a digital system.

Local governments recording. One commune, Mongo, began the census in April 2025 as the start of its digital tax system.

Not found. Whether any commune records its payers or their payments in a system, and where such a record is held, is not established. No commune other than Mongo is named, and nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

What is recorded. After a visit on 27 May 2021, UNDP and the commune of Lacs 1, at Aného, were said to have initiated a project to digitalise the registration of municipal taxes, alongside one for civil-status acts.

Where the record is held. The project to digitalise the registration of municipal taxes belongs to the commune of Lacs 1 and UNDP, on UNDP's account of May 2021.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is the visit of 27 May 2021, after which the tax project was initiated.

Local governments recording. One commune, Lacs 1, had the tax digitalisation project in May 2021, among the about sixty that UNDP says it equipped from 2020.

TUN.short: Communes entered their business-tax rolls in a system shared with the Ministry of Finance in 2022; no source found says how many communes do so.
TUN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The municipal revenue system GRB 2.0 was developed by the GIZ-run REMO project in partnership with the Ministry of the Interior, which ran from 1 May 2022 to 30 April 2026 as a German-Tunisian cooperation programme.

What is recorded. For the business tax, the commune president lists the taxable persons and the amounts due and enters the list in the commune's GRB system, a GIZ study said in March 2022. Ceremony fees were then receipted from a stub book at the commune's cash office.

Where the record is held. The commune's entry is visible on the GRB network to the regional treasurer and the municipal receiver of the Ministry of Finance, who follow collection (March 2022).

Last twelve months. The REMO project, which produced GRB 2.0, ended on 30 April 2026.

Local governments recording. In 2024 a cooperation project in Bizerte was developing GRB 2.0 and electronic payment of municipal fees for that commune. The 2022 study calls GRB the communes' system.

Not found. No count or share of communes entering their rolls in GRB is given, and what is known of its use dates from March 2022. No plan naming the system has been found.

TZA.short: By February 2023, 169 of 184 councils had started using a centrally hosted billing system; no source found reports the share recording today.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The local government ministry, PMO-RALG, manages TAUSI, the revenue system the councils use, the Controller and Auditor General recorded for 2024/25, and the 2026/27 budget speech assigns its development to that ministry. In his report on 2023/24 the auditor recommended that the ministry secure funding for TAUSI's full rollout in all 184 local government authorities.

What is recorded. The auditor reviewed the bills issued through TAUSI to 30 June 2025 and found TZS 1.22 billion issued by seven authorities unpaid; the revenue manual he cites requires a bill to update the taxpayer's record on payment. A ministry official said on 10 September 2025 that some councils issue receipts that do not come from the system.

Where the record is held. TAUSI is a centrally hosted application (audit of 2024/25). Some councils and village governments still keep forest-product revenue in books and hard-copy documents, the forestry division said in August 2026.

Last twelve months. The budget speech of 11 June 2026 commits the ministry and the revenue authority to finish linking TAUSI to the national tax system, and to add modules for buildings and for registering traders.

Local governments recording. By February 2023 169 councils had started to use TAUSI, the minister told the National Assembly; the auditor counts 184 local government authorities. In 2023/24 16 of them collected through the older LGRCIS instead, and by December 2024 the property tax module was in 47 of the 184.

Not found. No share of local government authorities recording in TAUSI has been published since February 2023; the newer figures concern one module or the authorities still on the older system. No domestic budget line for the system is stated.

UGA.short: A revenue system was in use in nine cities in late 2024; no source found reports the share of local governments recording in it.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Local Government runs E-LogRev (March 2024), under a contract with Tucksee Pty Limited that does not clearly require the source code to pass to government, the Auditor General reported in December 2024. The system is funded by both the finance ministry and URA TREP, and the local government ministry has no IT strategic plan.

What is recorded. In IRAS, the mayor of Nansana said in March 2024, the system fixes the assessment and records payments against a catalogue of fees.

Where the record is held. The Auditor General found no formal access policy for the E-LogRev database (December 2024).

Last twelve months. At the half-year of 2024/25 local governments' own revenue reached 37 per cent of the annual budget, against 24.35 per cent at the same point of 2019/20, which the finance ministry attributes to the IRAS rollout.

Local governments recording. The finance ministry's monitoring covered IRAS in nine cities in the first half of 2024/25, with the tenth, Jinja, still on E-LogRev. In March 2024 IRAS was reported rolled out in 98 districts, 21 municipalities and nine cities and E-LogRev operational in 48 local governments. The Auditor General's report on 2022/23 counted 124 activated local governments, 39 of them without the equipment to run the system.

Not found. Where the record is held is not stated, and no total of local governments is given against which the counts can be set. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

ZAF.short: Municipalities bill property rates per property and owner from their own billing systems, as described in 2023; no source found says how many do so.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. National Treasury's budget circular of 7 December 2023 has each municipality reconcile its valuation roll to its billing system and send the reconciliation to the Treasury every quarter, within 10 working days of the quarter's end.

What is recorded. The circular says every municipality's property-rates billing report holds, for each property, the market value, the category, the amount billed, the owner and any rebate, exemption or reduction, with a unique identifier that ties the property to the valuation roll (December 2023).

Where the record is held. The billing record stays in the municipality's own billing system; what goes to National Treasury, through its GoMuni upload portal, is the reconciliation (December 2023).

Last twelve months. National Treasury set the quarterly reconciliation in its circular of 7 December 2023.

Local governments recording. The circular describes the billing report of every municipality, on the ground that all municipal financial systems take the valuation roll as their basis (December 2023).

Not found. No count or share of municipalities billing from a system is given. Nothing is held on who owns, plans or pays for the billing systems, and nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

ZMB.short: A council revenue system was at proof of concept in eight councils in March 2026; no source found says whether it is live anywhere.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Smart Zambia, the state digital agency, announced the e-Council system in March 2026 as part of the national e-government plan.

What is recorded. The e-Council system is planned to let councils identify their revenue streams and track collections in real time (March 2026). A policy brief of May 2024 found councils' property tax administration weakened by outdated cadastres and poor record keeping, with many tax maps covering a fraction of rateable properties.

Where the record is held. The same brief says most local councils still run on manual systems, and the few partly digitalised work in silos at department or section level (May 2024).

Last twelve months. In March 2026 the government's chief technical officer said all 116 local authorities were connected to the government network and had solar power, ahead of an e-Council rollout planned for 2026.

Local governments recording. The first phase is a proof of concept in eight councils, among them Ndola, Kitwe, Solwezi, Chingola, Kalulushi, Kalumbila and Chilanga, with a demonstration of the system expected by 19 June 2026 before it is extended to the rest (March 2026).

Not found. Nothing shows the e-Council system live in any council, or that the June 2026 demonstration took place. No plan period and no finance are stated, and the statement that most councils work manually dates from May 2024.

ZWE.short: In 2024 about 83 of 92 local authorities used a shared digital system; no source found says whether most record revenue payers in it.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In May 2023 the Deputy Minister of Local Government and Public Works said LADS would become a business unit of her ministry, with the Harare Institute of Technology as consultant, and that its further development would be paid for from a government devolution grant.

What is recorded. Kwekwe City Council bills on the Promun package, with sections for utility billing, accounts receivable, cashiering and credit control (August 2026). Mutare's finance department runs the LADS debt management module (October 2021). At Gwanda, the Auditor-General reported for 2024, 27 stands sold in 2019 were still not billed.

Where the record is held. The Harare Institute of Technology says LADS links local authorities' financials and billing to the national public financial management system (November 2024). The Auditor-General's report on 2024 says most local authorities had no ERP system for revenue collection and ran processes that were manual or partly automated.

Last twelve months. In June 2025 the institute said its InstaPark parking system was in use in 15 municipalities.

Local governments recording. Around 83 of Zimbabwe's 92 local authorities use at least one LADS module, the institute told the Harare Commission of Inquiry in November 2024.

Not found. Which LADS modules the 83 local authorities use, and whether any of them records revenue, is not stated. No fact on governance is dated inside the last three years, and no event inside the last twelve months.

AGO.short: In 2025, 5 GB of mobile data for a month cost 1.89 per cent of average monthly income, on a stated price.

The cost is within 2 per cent and 0.89 points above 1 per cent. Average monthly income is gross national income per person divided by 12, so the figure says nothing of what the poorest pay against what they earn. The stage rests on that one figure, the newest held for 2024 or later, whoever published it.

These place a nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above in service. A second at Tier III is not stated.

NGA.short: Two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above by 2026, and the state's own data hosted with a national provider.

Galaxy Backbone, a government-owned technology services company, operates an Uptime Institute Certified Tier III national shared services centre and data centre in Abuja, per its communications head, who says it would host financial institutions' data. 21st Century Technologies' Lagos data centre is Tier IV certified and holds a Capitoline Certificate of Conformance for Constructed Facilities; it names no Uptime Institute certificate. Together these place two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service, the first three of the study's questions.

Owned in the country. Rest of World describes Galaxy Backbone as a privately held company established by the Nigerian government, which provides cloud services to government agencies and private companies and runs two data centres, one in Abuja and one in Kano; the article gives no further ownership detail. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. The Galaxy Backbone data centre in the National Shared Services Centre, Abuja, commissioned on 20 December 2022, serves government as well as corporate customers.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

RWA.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire in service by 2025, none found at Tier III or above.
RWA.summary:
In service, Tier III, and two of them. TransAfrica Communications (TrAC), a Rwanda-based ISP, is stated to offer data centre collocation services to customers (no facility named, no tier given). The ministry's ICT Sector Strategic Plan lists, among the initiatives that improved local hosting, the introduction of the TransAfrica Communications (TrAC) data center in Rwanda. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire in service. No source found states one at Tier III or above: built so that power and cooling can be maintained without shutting the data centre down, as the Uptime Institute defines it.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: TrAC data centre colocation (TransAfrica Communications (TrAC)). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

SDN.summary:

Sudatel itself states, on its operator page and with no certification body named, that the Sudatel Data Center (SDC) is a Tier IV data centre with 99.995% availability. Sudani's deputy director general says the company lost its Tier-4 data centre that hosted state government and institutions, along with other assets, in damage exceeding USD 70 million. Sudani's deputy director general says the company restored its core data centre, now fully operational and serving government bodies, private institutions and citizens. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above in service. A second at Tier III is not stated.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: Sudani core data centre; Sudani Tier-4 data centre; Khartoum State data centre (Ministry of Digital Transformation and Communications). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

Not found. No source found names a second nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

SEN.short: Two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above by 2021; state hosting with them not known.

ADIE states that the Diamniadio national Datacenter, inaugurated 22 June 2021 and in service, is the state's first Tier 3 data centre (operator's own statement, no certifier named). Sonatel reports its Rufisque (Senegal) Datacenter holds Uptime Institute Tier III Design certification and obtained Tier Certification of Constructed Facility (TCCF) in December 2019, renewed in 2020 until 4 December 2021; the passage does not say whether it sells space to outside customers. Together these place two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service, which answers the first three of the study's four questions.

Owned in the country. CIO Mag reports the Diamniadio national data centre, tier 3, was built by ADIE (the state IT agency) and inaugurated 22 June 2021 by President Macky Sall; it is to host administration and private-sector data. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

Not found. No source found says the government hosts its own data in a nationally owned data centre in the country.

SLE.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above by 2026; no second one held.
SLE.summary:

These place a nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above in service. A second at Tier III is not stated.

Owned in the country. The data centre is operated by the Sierra Leone Ministry of Finance's own directorate, the DFMST. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

Not found. No source found names a second nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

SOM.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire in service by 2026, none found at Tier III or above.
SOM.summary:

These place a nationally owned data centre for hire in service. No source found states one at Tier III or above: built so that power and cooling can be maintained without shutting the data centre down, as the Uptime Institute defines it.

These place a nationally owned data centre for hire in service. No source found states one at Tier III or above: built so that power and cooling can be maintained without shutting the data centre down, as the Uptime Institute defines it.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: Trinity Technologies Tier 2 Datacenter, Hai Malakal, Juba (Trinity Technologies Limited). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

SWZ.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above by 2023; no second one held.
SWZ.summary:
In service, Tier III, and two of them. The operator's brochure describes the National Data Centre as a Tier III facility with 99.982% uptime, on its own word. It sells colocation, dedicated servers and cloud services to clients. A blogger who visited in late 2019 found it already at Tier III level, selling colocation and basic cloud services. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above in service. A second at Tier III is not stated.

Owned in the country. The Times of Eswatini reports that the Royal Science and Technology Park runs the National Data Centre. It describes the park as a parastatal under the Ministry of ICT. In 2019 a visiting blogger found the centre run much like a state-owned enterprise. In April 2025 the ICT minister said the park earns money by storing data. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country. A facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. In September 2026 an incident at the National Data Centre disrupted at least 12 government services, the Times of Eswatini reported. They included the e-Visa, company registration, IFMIS, the elderly grant and deeds registration. The park first acknowledged the outage on 18 September.

Not found. No source found names a second nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

SYC.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above by 2026; no second one held.
SYC.summary:
In service, Tier III, and two of them. Cable & Wireless Seychelles states it has the country's first Tier IV certified data centre (certifier not named; operator statement), which it says lets local businesses, banks and government run on onshore infrastructure. Cable & Wireless Seychelles inaugurated its Bon Espoir Data Centre on Friday 2024-11-15 (inferred from the 2024-11-22 article); the free lede does not say whether space is rented to others. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above in service. A second at Tier III is not stated.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: Cable & Wireless Seychelles Tier IV data centre; Bon Espoir Data Centre (Cable & Wireless Seychelles). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

TGO.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above by 2026; no second one held.

Connecting Africa reports that the state-owned SIN operates the Lomé Data Centre, where SIN and ST Digital are launching private cloud services, with SIN's director saying firms can rent half or full racks for data hosting. SIN and ST Digital state that the SIN-operated Lomé Data Centre is Tier 3 certified with a 99.982% SLA; operator statement, certifying body not named. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above in service. A second at Tier III is not stated.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: Lomé Data Centre (Société d'Infrastructures Numériques (SIN), state-owned); Lomé data centre (SIN) (Société d'infrastructures numériques (SIN), state; transfer to a private operator authorised 2022-12-21). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

Not found. No source found names a second nationally owned data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

TUN.short: Two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above by 2025; state hosting with them not known.
TUN.summary:

DataXion states it is the only Tunisian data centre certified Tier IV by the Uptime Institute (operator claim, undated beyond the page date 2024-05-31). Tunisie Telecom's CEO presented the operator's hosting and storage solutions and its data centres, which he said meet international standards and certifications. Orange Tunisie inaugurated its Kalaa Kebira (Sousse) data centre, 1,000 sqm, serving Orange's own needs and customers with hosting, cloud computing and backup. Together these place two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service, which answers the first three of the study's four questions.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: Data Center Carthage (Tunisie Telecom); Orange Tunisie Kalaa Kebira data centre; Data Center Kalaa Kebira (Sousse) (Orange Tunisie). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted. EO Data Center, a Tunisian hosting provider, received the government cloud label in July 2024.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres.

Not found. No source found says the government hosts its own data in a nationally owned data centre in the country.

TZA.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire in service by 2026, none found at Tier III or above.
TZA.summary:

TTCL's National Internet Data Centre (NIDC) offers cloud computing, virtual server and colocation services to businesses and public institutions, as briefed to Zanzibar's president at the Kizimkazi Festival 2026. The TTCL data centre at Kijitonyama, Dar es Salaam, described as Tanzania's largest, was operating and offering services to both public and commercial organisations, though barely occupied; operated by Tanzania Telecommunication Company Limited (TTCL); It is described as built to Tier Three specifications, with no certification or operator statement. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire in service. No source found states one at Tier III or above: built so that power and cooling can be maintained without shutting the data centre down, as the Uptime Institute defines it.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: TTCL Kijitonyama data centre; National Internet Data Centre (NIDC) (TTCL). Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. Nothing found says the government hosts its own data beside the national data centres. NIDA's 2026 deck says government data centres provide secure hosting for the national ID systems.

UGA.short: A nationally owned data centre for hire in service by 2024, none found at Tier III or above.

NITA-U sells colocation and data centre services to ministries, local governments and private clients. It forecast UGX 2.54 billion from them in FY2024/25. Xalam Analytics lists a state agency selling colocation among Uganda's providers in 2024. These place a nationally owned data centre for hire in service. No source found states one at Tier III or above: built so that power and cooling can be maintained without shutting the data centre down, as the Uptime Institute defines it.

Owned in the country. The plan describes the National Data Centre and its recovery site as infrastructure built by NITA-U, the government's IT authority. The government and the World Bank paid for them. NITA-U runs them and pays their revenue into the Consolidated Fund. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country. A facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The state's data hosted nationally. The World Bank reports 162 government applications hosted at the data centre in June 2024, against a target of 400. By July 2026 NITA-U said the centre and its recovery site hosted over 308.

Not found. No source found says a nationally owned data centre for hire is Tier III or above.

ZAF.short: Two nationally owned data centres for hire at Tier III or above by 2026, and the state's own data hosted with a national provider.

Owned in the country. Nationally owned: Digital Parks Africa; xneelo Samrand data centre; Digital Parks Africa Centurion. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

The ministerial statement says the Government established and commissioned the Tier 3 Zambia National Data Centre (ZNDC), commercialised it and opened it to the private sector at a fee, with banks and mobile providers already using it. Owned in the country means by the state, a state enterprise or a company owned mostly in the country; a facility a foreign group controls is not counted.

President Mnangagwa said the Zimbabwe Centre for High Performance Computing (ZCHPC) national HPC data center at the University of Zimbabwe, run by ZCHPC as custodian of national HPC infrastructure, already hosts the Ministry of Health and Child Care's Impilo Electronic Health Records and Telemedicine platform, and the Civil Registry is integrated with it (date is the commissioning of Phase 2, 2025-08-15, as the article gives no other). In January 2025 the minister said government email and other platforms are hosted in the national data centre.

AGO.short: Private money reached Anda and Africell in 2026, but no source found says whether earlier years saw any.
AGO.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In March 2026 BFA Asset Management put $1.2 million from its Kimbo Fund into Anda, an Angolan motorcycle-taxi mobility start-up. Breega, Speedinvest and 4DX Ventures had put $3.4 million into Anda in total, with no round dates given. In 2026 EXIM Bank of the United States committed $100 million to Africell for technology investment in Angola.

Money raised inside the country. The $1.2 million for Anda came from BFA Asset Management of Luanda, a firm spun off from Banco de Fomento Angola, announced in March 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The state is selling a 15% stake in the mobile operator Unitel in 2026.

Not found. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year, and nothing earlier is held.

BDI.short: Lumitel put about USD 5.6 million into a rural 4G contract in 2026; no source found says whether private money came in other years.
BDI.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026 Lumitel Burundi, a subsidiary of Vietnam's Viettel group, signed a USD 10 million contract with the PAFEN project to extend rural 4G, and financed 56 per cent of it itself, about USD 5.6 million. That is the only amount held from 2024 onward, and it is dated to the publication on 3 March 2026, as the page itself carries no date.

Money raised inside the country. The money came from a foreign group's subsidiary, Lumitel, which pays 56 per cent of the rural 4G contract from its own funds, and no local raise is stated in that source.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The government of Burundi, through the PAFEN project, co-finances the remaining 44 per cent of the USD 10 million rural 4G contract, and so brought Lumitel's private 56 per cent, about USD 5.6 million, into a public connectivity project in 2026, with the state and the company sharing the cost of the same contract.

Not found. Only one amount is held from 2024 on, so no source found says whether private money came in more than one year.

Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2025 MTN Group committed over USD 215 million of its own money in Benin through 2026, spent on a 5G rollout, fibre expansion and a new MTN Benin headquarters. The commitment was announced at the Benin Investment Forum in May 2025 and is the only private amount held for the country from 2024 on.

Money raised inside the country. No money raised inside Benin has been found; MTN, a South African group, put in the USD 215 million itself, dated 2025.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No private money brought in by the government has been found; The MTN commitment was self-funded and approved by MTN.

Not found. The amount held was signed or started in the same year, 2025, so no earlier or later private money is shown. Nothing shows money raised inside Benin, or private money the government brought into a public project.

BFA.short: No private money put into a digital business in Burkina Faso has been found, and none is reported absent, so no stage is set.
BFA.summary: Not found. Nothing found names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

BWA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In April 2026 Pula Investments, the family office of UK financier Stephen Lansdown, anchored Botswana Tech Fund, which TechCabal reports has GBP 10 million (USD 13.5 million) in committed capital, with a first close of GBP 5 million (USD 6.7 million). The fund is run from Botswana with Launch Africa.

Money raised inside the country. Nothing from 2024 on is held; In May 2021 members of Angel Network Botswana, a Botswana investor network, put P250,000 (USD 22,000) into the online marketplace Ponatshego, per the World Bank.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. There is a government-backed startup programme launched in March 2026 with Scalar International, which states no private amount.

Not found. Only one amount is held from 2024 on, so no source found says whether private money came in more than one year.

CAF.short: No private money put into a digital business in the country is known for 2024 or later, so no stage is set.

CIV.short: Development finance institutions put money into two Ivorian firms in 2024; no source found says whether Ivorian investors or public projects drew private money.
CIV.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. The Dutch development bank FMO approved an equity investment of EUR 2.40 million in Hub2 (Connekt 4 SAS), effective August 2024. Hub2 is a fintech providing mobile wallet and payment services in Francophone Africa, and the investment sits under FMO's Ventures Program 2. Invest International approved a concessional loan of USD 0.325 million to PAIX Indigo B.V., part of the Paix Group, in 2024. The loan paid for a feasibility study for a data centre in Côte d'Ivoire.

Money raised inside the country. The equity in Hub2 came from outside the country: FMO is a Dutch development bank, and the investment was made under its own Ventures Program 2.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The 2024 money went to a payments fintech and a data centre developer, both private companies, and not to a government project.

Not found. Any investment in an Ivorian digital business since 2024 beyond the two above, any money from investors of the country itself, and any private money in a public digital project.

CMR.short: Private companies committed $75 million in September 2026 and $225 million over three years from 2025; no source found reports money raised inside Cameroon.
CMR.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In September 2026 the US company Cybastion committed $75 million to digital infrastructure in Cameroon, including an AI-ready data center in Douala with a dedicated power plant, as Biometric Update reports. In 2025 MTN Cameroon said it is investing US$225 million over three years in its own operations, chiefly its fintech division and national network coverage.

Money raised inside the country. No amount raised on a Cameroonian market or put in by a Cameroonian bank, fund or investor is held for 2024 or later. The MTN Cameroon pledge is financed by the company itself, in its own network and fintech operations, with no separate recipient named.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No public digital project with a stated private amount has been found for 2024 or later, and no government co-investment is recorded. There is the private data center commitment in Douala, a US company's investment in which no public project is named and no government money is stated.

Not found. No source from 2024 on names an amount put in by a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Cameroon itself, or raised on the country's own market.

COD.short: A fund lent USD 32.8 million and Helios Towers committed over USD 100 million to towers in 2026; no source says where it was raised.
COD.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026, EAAIF, a PIDG fund managed by Ninety One in London, signed a USD 32.8 million senior secured loan to Eastcastle Infrastructure DRC, within an upsized USD 179 million facility, to build 728 towers. On 31 March 2026, Helios Towers DRC signed an investment agreement for more than USD 100 million in shared telecom towers, which the company says it is investing itself.

Money raised inside the country. No fact held says where any of this money was raised. Vodacom Congo says it spends on average USD 140 million a year on its network in the DRC and plans a USD 670 million long-term programme, stated on 8 October 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No amount has been found. The national investment promotion agency ANAPI was the counterparty to the Helios tower agreement in March 2026.

Not found. Where the money was raised, and any private money in a public digital project, is not established.

COG.short: Private money went into Congolese digital businesses in 2024 and 2025; no source found says whether any came from Congolese investors.

Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In June 2024 Uma Ventures, a Hong Kong-based venture capital firm, led a USD 3 million seed round for Noki Noki, a delivery platform based in Brazzaville. The money went into a privately owned company that operates in the Congolese capital, and the investor who led the round is based abroad. Trendtype reported the round on 24 June 2024. In December 2025 Fondation BantuHub and L'Archer Group committed EUR 1 million in equity to Congolese startups and small firms, about USD 1.1 million, to be invested during 2026 through a 24-month incubation and acceleration programme in fintech, artificial intelligence and business services.

Money raised inside the country. The one 2024 round, Noki Noki's USD 3 million seed round, was led by Uma Ventures of Hong Kong, so that money came from outside Congo and was not raised on the Congolese market.

LBY.short: Libya presented a draft open government data policy in November 2025 and opened a portal with it; no source found says whether the policy is adopted.
LBY.summary:

On 14 October 2026 the authority met ministries and sectoral information centres to finish the final draft of a National Policy for Open Data and Artificial Intelligence.

Portal run and data published. The authority opened the Open Government Data Platform on the same day, with a first set of datasets. By February 2026 it reported 91 datasets from nine government bodies in eight sectors. The policy the platform came with is still a draft. In February 2026 the authority launched new indicators across the 91 datasets.

The agency manages the portal and monitors the national Open Data action plan, which a steering committee set up in December 2019 oversees, and that committee debated a 2026 action plan that includes maintaining and enriching the portal. The agency itself publishes datasets there, such as one listing 1,028 Moroccan startups, updated in January 2025. None of these ties the portal to a policy, since none has been adopted.

The OGP Malawi Secretariat announced on 3 September 2025 that Malawi had officially launched its new Open Data Portal as part of the Third OGP National Action Plan, giving citizens access to government budget, development project and public service delivery data through dashboards and downloadable datasets. In November 2025 the CSEA brief states that most government datasets stay in PDF reports.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2021 open data decree is in force and its portal carried data from 23 public producers in 2024; the follow-on strategy is not adopted.
TUN.summary:

Government decree 2021-3 of 6 January 2021, issued by the Head of Government after the Council of Ministers deliberated, organises the publication of public data on the principle that it is open by default. A national strategy for governing, opening and using public data, written under the decree, was presented in final draft at a workshop with the PAGOF programme on 26 March 2026 and still awaited the government's endorsement in August 2026.

Portal run and data published. A new version of the national open data portal, built to the decree's specifications, opened in early March 2023, and in April 2024 it carried datasets from 23 data producers across six themes, according to the Open Government Partnership's review. The e-administration unit of the Presidency of the Government said in July 2024 that it had built the national public data register in application of the decree and of Circular 4 of 2024 on open public data.

It was handed to the Ministry of Finance for submission to Cabinet in December 2016 and presented to the Permanent Secretary of Finance in February 2017. By June 2017 it had not been officially adopted.

Portal run and data published. The same report says the national open data portal opendata.go.tz, launched in September 2015 and managed by the eGovernment Agency, held 163 datasets (755 resources) from 11 institutions in 4 sectors by June 2017, double the year before. The portal ran under the Chief Secretary's January 2015 circular as the interim directive.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block has been found for Angola. On 23 January 2026 UNITA abstained when the National Assembly approved the cybersecurity bill in general, saying it feared internet cuts on election and protest days.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest or charge for speech has been found. The Law Against False Information on the Internet, Lei n.o 6/26, was published in the Diario da Republica on 4 August 2026 with prison of up to 10 years, and the bar association cited sanctions of 2 to 10 years for executives.

Not found. Nothing found says whether anyone in Angola was punished for what they said or published in the last twelve months, or that no one was.

BDI.short: A journalist was jailed over messages in 2024-2025 and a media coalition suspended in 2025; criticism of policy and internet cuts are unknown.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, or that the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

BEN.short: Journalists were jailed over posts in 2025-2026; no source found reports public criticism and internet cuts, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, or that the internet was cut.

BFA.short: In 2026 a student union criticised the government and was suspended, and TV5 Monde was suspended; no source says whether anyone was jailed for speech.
BFA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. In May 2026 the General Student Union of Burkina Faso (UGEB) issued a statement criticising the government's security record and the military authorities' failure to restore security, as the CIVICUS Monitor reports. No other criticism of a government policy inside the country has been found.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. The Centre national de presse Norbert Zongo reported that in 2024 the online platforms of RFI, France 24, Jeune Afrique and Le Monde, among others, remained inaccessible in Burkina Faso. No law or court ruling barring such cuts has been found.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 5 May 2026 the Higher Council for Communication indefinitely suspended TV5 Monde broadcasts, and Human Rights Watch says the regulator accused the broadcaster of disinformation and apology of terrorism. On 26 May 2026 the Minister of Territorial Administration suspended UGEB for three months after its statement, and the Ouagadougou prosecutor opened an investigation into its authors. An August 2026 report relayed by The Nation also cites the suspension of international broadcasters over alleged bias.

Not found. Nothing found says who ordered the block on foreign media websites, or whether the internet was cut in the last twelve months. Nothing found says whether anyone was arrested or jailed for what they said or published in that time.

BWA.short: In February 2026 a civil society chairperson called for fuller consultation on a court process; no source reports any cut, block or punishment for speech.
BWA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The chairperson of the civil society body BOCONGO told the minister on 9 February 2026 at a dialogue that the Constitutional Court process must rest on meaningful, structured and inclusive participation, that consultations must go beyond mere formality, and called for clear public information and more time.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing on a cut or block is held. The nearest held fact is the dialogue between civil society and the minister on the Constitutional Court process, reported on 10 February 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Nothing on punishment for speech is held. The nearest held fact is the same dialogue, at which BOCONGO's chairperson called for more time and clear public information.

Not found. Nothing found says whether anyone in Botswana was punished for what they said or published in the last twelve months, or that no one was. No cut or block has been found either.

CAF.short: The government set up a communications monitoring unit in 2026; no source says whether criticism, cuts or speech punishments occurred, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

CIV.short: In 2025 Côte d'Ivoire's opposition denounced an activist's arrest and courts jailed people for social-media speech; no source found says whether any internet cut occurred.
CIV.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The opposition party PPA-CI, speaking through Justin Kone Katinan, publicly denounced the arrest of one of its activists as a violation of freedom of expression on 3 September 2025. The activist had spoken in a social-media video about the Constitutional Council's deliberations on the candidate list.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block has been found. The nearest held fact is the Ministry of Communication's national campaign against disinformation and its local information integrity committee in Tonkpi, reported in September 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. RFI reports that PPA-CI activist Mamadou Zigui was arrested on 2 September 2025 and that the Abidjan court sentenced activist Gala Kolebi on 30 June 2025 to 18 months and a 500,000 CFA franc fine for spreading false news. The prosecutor says a nurse received 36 months and a 5 million fine on 18 July 2025 over a social-media comment about a state institution.

Not found. Nothing found says the internet was cut, or that any offence of speech was repealed.

CMR.short: In October 2025 Cameroon restricted internet access during its presidential election; no source found says who ordered the cuts and when they ended.
CMR.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Civic Watch Cameroon's head and other participants at a workshop in Yaounde on 8 and 9 June 2026 on the 2010 cybercrime law said it contains provisions limiting free expression, and legal experts and civil society called the October 2025 election-time internet restrictions a rights violation.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Le Jour reports that on 23 October 2025, during the presidential election, internet restrictions blocked a blogger's access to Facebook and publishing, described as a government decision. Access Now's #KeepItOn report counts 4 internet shutdowns in Cameroon in 2025, one a cross-border cut that reached the Central African Republic through the WACS cable.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest or charge for speech has been found. The nearest held fact is the 2010 cybercrime law, law n°2010/012 of 21 December 2010, whose provisions workshop participants said limit free expression.

Not found. Nothing found says who ordered the 2025 shutdowns or when they ended, and no source says whether a bar on such cuts exists.

COD.short: A rights group criticised government policy in public in 2026, but a journalist was jailed over a post in September 2026.
COD.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. At a side event of the African Commission's 89th session in October 2026, Fidèle Mbilizi Mutimanwa of the National League of Indigenous Pygmy Associations of the Congo (LINAPYCO) criticised the state for leaving the Commission's 2022 Batwa decision and national law 22/030 on Pygmy peoples' rights largely unapplied, and condemned the clearance operations in national parks.
