Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut in the last twelve months is counted. The nearest held fact is that Access Now lists an internet shutdown at Goma, in the M23 conflict area, among the shutdowns of 2025, without saying who ordered it, when it began or whether it ended.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Committee to Protect Journalists says journalist Tresor Muntu was detained on 15 September 2026 and charged with defamation and publishing false news for sharing a post criticising a provincial politician, and was jailed the next day.

Not found. A journalist was jailed for what he shared inside the last twelve months; no law repealing a speech offence, and no bar on cutting the internet, has been found.

COG.short: In May 2026 police arrested a rights defender after a passport campaign and held him in pre-trial detention; no source says how his case ends.
COG.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The platform Congo Droit et Justice pour Tous et par Tous ran a campaign, including through members' social media, denouncing the difficulty citizens have in obtaining a passport, and announced a press conference for 29 May 2026 on the causes.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. The UNESCO assessment says access to the internet and to social networks was restricted nationwide during the presidential election of 21 March 2021, citing NetBlocks.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Police in plain clothes arrested the human rights defender Ghislain Ondele Kanga at his home on 30 May 2026 and took him to the intelligence service in Brazzaville. He was referred to the prosecutor 56 days later, reportedly charged with false dissemination and with declaring an unauthorised demonstration, and held in pre-trial detention.

Not found. The evidence does not say whether anyone else was punished for what they said or published in the last twelve months, nor who ordered the 2021 cut or when it ended.

COM.short: Police arrested a journalist over a Facebook post in November 2025; no source found reports a year without arrests or closures.
COM.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. In December 2025 the Comorian press mobilised against a ministry and CNPA proposal to amend article 169 of the Information Code on source protection, and the journalists' union SNJC obtained its withdrawal. CIVICUS Monitor reports that the union, media and rights defenders opposed the draft, which would have let a judge compel journalists to reveal sources, and that MPs rejected it on 26 December 2025.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block has been found. The nearest held fact is law 25-021/AU, promulgated by decree on 2 February 2026, whose article 124 lets the regulator order internet providers.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Mayotte Hebdo says police arrested Al-Watwan correspondent Abdou Moustoifa on 17 November 2025 over a Facebook post about migrants held in a Moroni police station, and questioned him for over two hours to learn his source. Article 361 of the penal code makes defamation a criminal offence.

Not found. Nothing found says a year has passed with no one arrested, charged or jailed, and no outlet suspended or closed, for what was said or published. Nothing found says the internet was cut or a service blocked.

CPV.short: Rights groups criticised prosecutions of journalists in August 2025; no internet cut is known, and no source found says whether anyone was punished since.
CPV.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The RECADDH human-rights network publicly denounced an escalation of judicial prosecutions and intimidation of journalists in Cabo Verde on 8 August 2025. It called for the cases against the journalists to be dropped, so criticism of how the state treats the press is voiced openly inside the country.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block of the internet, a social media service or a news site has been found for Cabo Verde, and no law or ruling barring one. The nearest held fact is the same RECADDH statement, which names prosecutions and intimidation of journalists, not any cut.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. RECADDH says journalists Herminio Silves and Daniel Almeida are accused of qualified disobedience over reports on a death, as of 8 August 2025, and demands that the cases be dropped. No repeal of an offence of defamation, false news, sedition or insulting the head of state is held.

Not found. Nothing found says whether anyone in Cabo Verde was punished for what they said or published in the last twelve months beyond the accusations of August 2025, or that no one was.

DJI.short: In 2024 to 2026 Djibouti's state media stayed uncritical, opposition sites were blocked and journalists were arrested; no source says whether anyone criticises policy publicly.
DJI.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The US State Department's 2024 human rights report says the government owned the only radio and television stations and the newspaper La Nation held a monopoly on authorized print media. It adds that official media generally did not criticise government policy.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Exiled journalist Zineb Haddaji told CIVICUS Lens in July 2026 that opposition and exiled media websites are blocked in Djibouti and social media access is restricted at times of political tension. No law or ruling barring such cuts has been found.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The opposition party RADDE says police arrested a journalist and a cameraman of its citizens' rights programme at their homes on 20 November 2025. The US State Department says authorities arrested Farhya Houssein on 25 June 2024 for online criticism of the government, and a court sentenced her on 17 July 2024 to one month in prison and two years' probation.

Not found. Nothing found says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside Djibouti criticised government policy in public in the last three years, or that a law or court barred internet cuts.

DZA.short: Algeria confined its exam internet shutdowns to exam centres in June 2026; no source found says whether policy is criticised in public.
DZA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. No paper, party or group inside Algeria has been found criticising a government policy in public. The nearest fact is Access Now's review of the 2026 exam season. It reports how the Education Minister explained the government's own exam measures.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. When the Baccalaureate began on 7 June 2026, Algeria confined its exam shutdown measures to the inside of exam centres. The rest of the country stayed connected, Access Now says. Education Minister Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui explained that the cuts would apply only inside the centres from then on. No law or court ruling barring cuts has been found.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The nearest fact is the same Access Now review of exam shutdowns, dated October 2026. It covers connectivity during the exams, not arrests or charges for what people said.

Not found. No source found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country. None says anyone was punished for what they said.

EGY.short: In February 2026 Egypt was still blocking independent news sites, at least 630 websites; no source says whether the journalists arrested since 2025 were charged.
EGY.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Khaled Elbalshy, head of the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate, was quoted by Al Manassa on 13 April 2026 rejecting all blocking of news websites. He also rejected the licensing justification the regulator gave for its move against the news site Egyptke.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Freedom House reports that the news site Cairo 24 was blocked in November 2024 and the outlet Zawia3 in February 2025, within a wider blocking of news websites by the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. In February 2026 Access Now and other groups said the authorities were still blocking independent media sites, at least 630 websites in all. No bar on cuts or blocks has been found.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Human Rights Watch says security forces arrested the six journalists of the Matsda2sh newsroom on 28 and 29 September 2026, and the Interior Ministry said they were suspected of preparing fabricated news. Al Manassa reports that security forces arrested Egyptke's editor-in-chief and CEO in December 2025 after a complaint over a poultry story. Freedom House, citing Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, reports more than 100 people detained in June and July 2024 after calling for protests on social media, and two years added to the sentence of the blogger Alaa Abdel Fattah in September 2024.

Not found. Nothing found says whether the journalists arrested in 2025 and 2026 were charged or jailed, or whether any outlet was suspended or closed for what it published.

ERI.short: In 2026 UNESCO states that the state runs all media and private outlets ended after a 2001 ban; no source found reports cuts and punishments.
ERI.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. UNESCO states, in a document dated January 2026, that the Ministry of Information runs all television, radio and newspapers in Eritrea, and that privately owned outlets effectively ceased to exist after a government ban in 2001. It presents that position as continuing, so no outlet independent of the state has been found as carrying public criticism.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing is held on a cut to internet access or a block on a platform or outlet in Eritrea, or on any bar against such a cut. The nearest held fact is the 2001 government ban on privately owned media, which UNESCO states ended private outlets.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Nothing is held on a person arrested or an outlet punished for what was said, nor on a law repealed. The nearest held fact is again the 2001 ban, after which UNESCO says the Ministry of Information runs all television, radio and newspapers.

Not found. No source says whether anyone in Eritrea has been cut off, arrested or charged for speech in the last twelve months, or whether any law has been repealed.

ETH.short: Journalists were abducted or suspended in 2025 and 2026; nothing found shows policy criticism or an internet cut, so no stage is set.
ETH.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country. Nor does anything show the internet cut in the last twelve months.

GAB.short: The regulator suspended social media in Gabon from February to October 2026; no source found says whether anyone was punished for speech.
GAB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Nine civil-society organisations, including ROLBG, SOS Prisonniers, Tournons la Page Gabon and the Ligue nationale des droits humains, met in Libreville on 11 July 2026 and called the suspension unconstitutional and disproportionate, demanding its repeal. On 25 July 2026 the group APSAD presented a report finding self-censorship among public-debate actors and urged an end to blanket suspensions.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. The communications regulator, the HAC, suspended social media in Gabon by decision no. 0002/HAC/2026, until further notice. The Presidency's spokesman defended the suspension as temporary and conservatory on 17 July 2026, with no lifting date given. The HAC lifted the suspension, ordered on 17 February 2026, on 24 October 2026, citing cooperation with TikTok, Meta and YouTube. Maroc Telecom lists temporary restrictions on certain internet uses in Gabon for February 2026. No bar on such cuts has been found. The communication authority suspended Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp across Gabon in February 2026 without express legal basis, Village de la Justice says.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Nothing is held on a person arrested or an outlet closed for what was said, nor on a law repealed. The nearest held fact is the APSAD finding of self-censorship among public-debate actors and rules short of international standards.

Not found. Nothing found says anyone in Gabon was arrested or charged for speech, or that any law was repealed. No source says a court or other body has barred such cuts.

GHA.short: In September 2026 a nursing officer was arrested and charged over alleged false-news videos; no source says whether anyone else was punished or access cut.
GHA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 19 September 2026 Democracy Hub, a civil-society group, through its adviser Oliver Barker-Vormawor, criticised on JoyNews the police detention, the denial of bail and the evidence-gathering in the Salomey Awiti Bafoh prosecution. The same day the MP John Ntim Fordjour said that Section 208 is applied selectively against government critics.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing is held on a cut to internet access or a block on a platform in Ghana, or on any bar against one. The nearest held fact is the Presidency's letter on a national stakeholder engagement on hate speech and abusive online content.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Senior nursing officer Salomey Awiti Bafoh was arrested on 13 September 2026 and charged at the Adentan Circuit Court with abetment of publishing false news under sections 20(1) and 208 of the Criminal Offences Act, for allegedly helping redistribute videos from a UK-based TikTok account. She pleaded not guilty and was denied bail and remanded. The National Commission for Civic Education chairperson said, as reported on 1 September 2026, that the repeal of criminal libel and seditious laws in 2001 strengthened democratic development.

Not found. Nothing found says an outlet was suspended or closed for what it published in the last twelve months, or that any access to a platform was cut.

GIN.short: In September 2026 the regulator barred France 24, and social media have been restricted since 28 July; no source found says who ordered the restrictions.
GIN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Union pour la defense des consommateurs, through its president Bany Sidibe, denounced the social media restrictions on 4 August 2026 as a state decision harming the right to information. It and the Association des blogueurs de Guinee demanded the return of access to all social networks.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Facebook, YouTube and TikTok were blocked from 28 July 2026, according to the bloggers association ABLOGUI, and Jeune Afrique reported WhatsApp difficulties too. On 17 September 2026 the HAC ordered the telecoms regulator ARPT to block all France 24 digital access points and Canal+ Guinée to cut its signal. The ECOWAS Court found that restrictions on internet access from October to December 2020 violated rights to information and expression.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 17 September 2026 the HAC revoked the national broadcasting authorisation of France 24 and withdrew its correspondents accreditations. The Media Foundation for West Africa report, as reported on 14 August 2026, cites the suspension of critical media outlets in Guinea. No repeal has been found.

Not found. No source says who ordered the social media restrictions of July 2026, or when they ended. Nothing found says a person was arrested for speech in the last twelve months.

GMB.short: In May 2026 the Gambia Press Union criticised new laws, and courts struck down criminal defamation; no source found reports cuts and punishments.
GMB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 14 May 2026 the Gambia Press Union spoke to the African Commission's 87th session in Banjul. It called the Cybercrime Bill 2023, the Communications Bill 2025 and the Criminal Offences Act 2025 threats to media freedom. In March 2025 the Union and the Edward Francis Small Center for Rights and Justice criticised the Criminal Offence and Procedure Bill 2025. They objected to its power to ban publications and its false-publication offence.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut, block or bar on either is on record for the Gambia. The nearest fact on file is a regulator's draft. The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority put its draft Broadcasting and Online Content Regulations, 2026 out for consultation in April 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 24 March 2025 the National Assembly passed the Criminal Offence and Procedure Bill 2025. It dropped the offences of criminal defamation and sedition. The Press Union said in May 2026 that the Supreme Court had struck down criminal defamation and false publication online, with no date for the ruling. In October 2024 the High Court charged The Voice's editor and a reporter with false publication. The charge followed an article on the president's successor.

Not found. Nothing found says the internet was cut in the last twelve months. Nothing found says anyone was punished for speech in that time. No law, court ruling or undertaking from the last three years bars the government from cutting the internet.

GNB.short: On 26 November 2025, the day the military took power, social media access was restricted; no end date is known.
GNB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. No source found reports public criticism of government policy in the window. The nearest held fact is that on 26 November 2025, the day the military seized power, citizens reported restrictions on social platforms.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. On 26 November 2025, citizens reported widespread restrictions on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, which the Media Foundation for West Africa says the military imposed. The source gives no end date, and no held source names a bar on such cuts.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No source found reports a person punished for speech, or a punishing law removed. The nearest held fact is the same report, which says the military imposed restrictions on social platforms on the day it took power.

Not found. No source found says when the social media restrictions ended, or that anyone criticised policy in public or was punished for speech.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea arrested the author of a viral video about the vice-president in 2026; no source found reports policy criticism, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

KEN.short: A journalist was charged over a WhatsApp message in February 2026; courts struck down false-publication offences in March; no source found reports a bar on cuts.
KEN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Bloggers Association of Kenya returned to court in 2025 to challenge the amendment to the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act. In February 2026 it argued before the courts that the 2018 cybercrimes law violates freedom of expression. On 4 September 2026 the Consumer Federation of Kenya won a High Court order quashing the Attorney-General's opinion clearing the Digital Superhighway tenders. On 24 August 2026 an opposition leader said the electoral commission's contract specifications were tailor-made for one company. On 8 October 2026 a KICTANet dialogue named the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act a threat to online expression.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Access Now counts three internet shutdowns in Kenya in 2025, including an exam-time block of Telegram, the third year running, now being litigated. KICTANet's network ran its first rapid-response protocol during a 2024 Telegram shutdown. No held source gives a law or court ruling that bars cuts.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In March 2026 the Court of Appeal struck down two sections of the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act on false publication. The case was brought by the Bloggers Association of Kenya. The sections carried fines up to KSh 5 million. The National Assembly has appealed to the Supreme Court. On 25 February 2026 journalist Peter Mwita was charged under the Act over a WhatsApp message. It linked a Mombasa politician to a gang.

Not found. No law, court ruling or undertaking from the last three years bars the government from cutting the internet.

LBR.short: In September 2026 police arrested a man under the Cybercrime Act over posts about the Vice President; no source found reports the court outcome.
LBR.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 24 September 2026 the Press Union of Liberia, the Center for Media Studies and several civil society groups called the Cybercrime Act's provisions on false information and offensive communication vague and a weapon to silence critics. On 31 August 2026 the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia and other groups pressed the Liberia Telecommunications Authority chairman to disclose revenue from the gateway monitoring system, which he has refused to do. In October 2026 the Press Union called for the withdrawal of the Civil Service Agency's confidentiality agreement for civil servants.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No held source reports a cut or block of internet access, or a law or ruling that bars one. The nearest held fact is the Liberia Telecommunications Authority's temporary management of the International Gateway Monitoring System.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In September 2026 police arrested Jerry Nyanti Wratto in Monrovia, charged him and sent him to court under the Cybercrime Act over Facebook and TikTok posts about the Vice President. The Vice President asked for his release, and no court outcome is given. A 2019 law, the KAK Act, decriminalised sedition and criminal libel against the President.

Not found. No source found gives the outcome of the Wratto case, a cut or block of internet access, or a bar on one.

LBY.short: An activist was arrested over online posts in August 2026 and a draft cybercrime law was criticised in 2025; no source found reports cuts.
LBY.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. In 2025 a representative of Internet Society Libya said Article 39 on defamation in the draft cybercrime law could be used to suppress activists and journalists, and proposed civil rather than criminal defamation.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No held source reports a cut or block of internet access, or a law or ruling that bars one. The nearest held fact is a 2025 session on the draft law on cybercrime and digital evidence.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 14 August 2026 the Committee for Justice documented that Internal Security Agency personnel arrested Benghazi activist Aziz Al-Orfi over Facebook and TikTok posts on public affairs. He says he was held five days on accusations of incitement.

Not found. Nothing found gives a cut or block of internet access, a bar on one, or a person arrested, charged or jailed for what was said in the last twelve months beyond the one arrest above.

LSO.short: Courts struck down criminal defamation, reported in October 2026 without a date; no source found reports public criticism of policy and any internet cut.
LSO.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Nothing on public criticism of government policy is held. The nearest held fact is the Southern Africa Litigation Centre's oral statement on the human rights situation in Africa, published on 15 October 2026, which says that courts in Lesotho struck down criminal defamation.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing on a cut or block is held, and no bar on cutting the internet has been found either. The nearest held fact is the same oral statement from the Southern Africa Litigation Centre, which concerns criminal defamation and not access to the internet.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre said in October 2026 that courts in Lesotho struck down criminal defamation. It gave no date for the ruling, so the removal of the offence has been found without a year.

Not found. No law, ruling of the country's own court or undertaking given in court in the last three years is held that bars the government from cutting the internet. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, or that the internet was cut.

MAR.short: Nationwide protests criticised policy from September 2025 and a man was jailed in October 2025 for posts; no source says whether the internet was cut.
MAR.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Human Rights Watch says the youth movement GenZ212 called nationwide protests from 27 September 2025, criticising public spending on mega-sporting events and demanding more for health care and education. No other criticism of a government policy inside the country has been found. Opposition members proposed deleting part of Article 51 bis of Organic Law 53.25 as a threat to free expression; the government rejected the amendment (December 2025).

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No internet cut, no blocked service and no law or court ruling barring one has been found. The nearest held fact is the set of nationwide protests that began on 27 September 2025, as Human Rights Watch reports.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Human Rights Watch reports that on 4 October 2025 the Agadir Court of First Instance sentenced a man to four years in prison and a 50,000 dirham fine for "inciting minor offenses and crimes via social media". No repeal of an offence of criminal defamation, false news, sedition or insulting the head of state is held.

Not found. Nothing found says the internet was cut in the last twelve months, or that the country went a year with no one punished for what they said or published.

MDG.short: In September 2026 a news site questioned the cybercrime bill's digital police powers; no source found reports it whether anyone was punished for speech.
MDG.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 3 September 2026 Madagascar-Tribune questioned the government's cybercrime bill n°042/2026, saying the permanent access powers of its new digital police raise issues of public freedoms and of balance with freedom of expression, and contrasting it with the stalled access-to-information bill.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No held source reports a cut of internet access or a bar on one. The nearest held fact is the Council of Ministers decision of 8 July 2026 to block pornographic websites, which is a block of named sites and not of access.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No held source reports a person punished for speech, or a punishing law removed. The nearest held fact is the same bill n°042/2026, whose digital police unit would hold permanent access powers.

Not found. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

MLI.short: In 2026 Mali's press bodies criticised journalists' arrests while two journalists were sentenced and a radio programme suspended; no source says whether any cut occurred.
MLI.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. In June 2026 the Maison de la Presse sharply criticised the detention of two journalists, Reporters Without Borders says. The private print publishers' association denounced the 5 February 2026 arrest of the editor Youssouf Sissoko. In June 2026 the editor Chahana Takiou criticised the authorities for trying journalists under the cybercrime law. He said the press-offence law should apply instead.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block has been found for Mali. The restrictions held run through the cybercrime provisions of the Penal Code amendment of December 2024, not through the network.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The cybercrime tribunal sentenced the journalist Abdrahamane Keita to two years in prison on 14 September 2026. Takiou, arrested on 8 June 2026, was sentenced on 3 August to 12 months, six suspended. Sissoko was held in Bamako's central prison. The HAC suspended the radio programme Allo Kledu for two months from 19 June 2026. On 27 October 2025 the former prime minister Moussa Mara got two years, one firm, over posts in support of political prisoners.

Not found. Nothing found says the internet was cut in Mali. Nothing found shows twelve months with no one punished for speech.

MOZ.short: In March 2026 civil society and opposition criticised telecommunications regulations as allowing internet shutdowns; no source found says whether anyone was punished for speech.
MOZ.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. In March 2026 civil society bodies and opposition parties attacked the new telecommunications regulations. They said the rules allowed internet shutdowns on national security grounds. The journalist Tomas Vieira Mario condemned the minister's defence on Facebook and called for the rules to be overhauled.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. After the October 2024 election, OONI measurements show internet providers blocked Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The block ran from 29 October to 14 November 2024. Human Rights Watch says mobile and internet access was restricted from 25 October, and operators said it was restored on 18 November. No cut is on record from the last twelve months. In March 2026 the minister denied any attempt to restrict use of the internet.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest, charge or sentence for speech has been found. The nearest held fact is that a named journalist publicly condemned the minister's defence of the regulations in March 2026, the day after the minister spoke.

Not found. No source says the country went twelve months with no one punished for speech.

MRT.short: Two MPs were arrested in 2026 and a news site closed in 2025; policy criticism and internet cuts not known, so no stage is set.
MRT.summary: Not found. Nothing found dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, or that the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

MUS.short: Social media was suspended for a day in November 2024 amid public outcry; whether anyone was punished for speech in the last year is unknown.
MUS.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Civil society groups and businesses opposed the November 2024 social media suspension, and members of the party Linion Reform protested in front of the National Assembly on 1 November 2024. Human Rights Watch reports swift and widespread outcry from business, civil society and opposition politicians inside Mauritius.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. On 1 November 2024 the Information and Communications Authority directed internet service providers to suspend access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X; the ban was lifted on 2 November after 24 hours. Human Rights Watch says the suspension was to run until after the 10 November elections and the government rescinded it a day later.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In August 2026 the ministry reminded the public of the sanctions for unwanted content online.

Not found. Nothing found says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

MWI.short: Civil society criticised budget and surveillance plans in 2026; no source found says whether anyone was punished for speech in the last twelve months.
MWI.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Civil society groups told parliamentary committees on 9 March 2026 that the proposed 2026/27 education budget falls short of the 20 percent UNESCO benchmark. A group calling itself the Concerned Citizens of Malawi People Power Movement publicly criticised the communications regulator MACRA by January 2026 for not briefing the public on its social media monitoring system procurement.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block has been found. The nearest held fact is that civil society groups challenged the legality of MACRA's $1.5 million social media monitoring contract and called for its suspension.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest or charge in the last twelve months has been found. The nearest held fact is that journalist Joshua Chisa Mbele was arrested in January 2022 after sharing on Facebook a document alleging corruption involving government officials.

Not found. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

NAM.short: A think tank criticised a draft data bill in 2022; nothing found shows internet cuts or punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
NAM.summary: Not found. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

NER.short: In 2026 Niger suspended nine foreign outlets and charged journalists and a lawyer for their words; no source found reports public criticism of policy.
NER.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Maison de la Presse, the umbrella body of journalists' associations, spoke out against post-coup press violations and was forced by the Ministry of the Interior to shut down in January 2024, as ModernGhana reports. No criticism of a government policy inside the country in the last three years has been found beyond that.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Niger's National Communication Observatory suspended nine outlets from reaching audiences in Niger on 8 May 2026, and a France 24 channel screen showed "program blocked", as the Committee to Protect Journalists reports. The signals of RFI and France 24 were cut within a week of the July 2023 coup. No law or court ruling barring such cuts has been found.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 21 September 2026 the lawyer Abrourahamane Lirwana was charged and detained over comments about the army, and prosecutors sought five years on 6 October, Human Rights Watch says. Niamey police arrested six journalists on 30 October 2025 and charged them under the 2019 cybercrime law. The editor Ali Soumana was jailed in September 2025 after a complaint from the Prime Minister. The regulator suspended nine France-based outlets on 8 May 2026, citing a threat to public order.

Not found. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

NGA.short: In 2026 the State Services department prosecuted Omoyele Sowore for criticising the president, then paused the case; other recent arrests are not dated.
NGA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project and the Nigerian Guild of Editors called in August 2026 for enforcement of Section 24 of the Cybercrimes Act to be suspended. On 18 July 2026 the Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre urged the National Assembly to withdraw or revise parts of the Data Protection (Amendment) Bill that could let regulators shut digital platforms.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut in the last twelve months is counted. The nearest held fact is that the federal government announced an indefinite suspension of Twitter on 5 June 2021 and telecom providers were directed to block it.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Department of State Services is prosecuting Omoyele Sowore under the Cybercrimes Act for describing President Tinubu as a criminal; its Director-General announced on 30 August 2026 that the prosecution would be suspended until after the 2027 election. On 31 August 2026 SERAP and Sowore's lawyer demanded that the DSS withdraw the charges. In an oral statement dated 15 October 2026 the Southern Africa Litigation Centre said section 24 of the Cybercrimes Act is repeatedly used to arrest journalists for their reporting.

Not found. Nothing found dates an arrest, charge or jail term, or an outlet suspended or closed, for what was said or published, to the last twelve months, other than the Sowore prosecution.

RWA.short: Nothing found says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
RWA.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

SDN.short: In August 2026 a court in El Obeid jailed a pharmacist for six years over a private call opposing the war; no repeal is known.
SDN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate condemned the detention of journalist Gurashi Awad on 14 August 2026. It called for the repeal of the 2007 Cybercrime Act. In October 2026 it rejected a decree extending a Criminal Act provision to electronic publishing. In October 2025 its secretary general called the cabinet's changes to the Informatics Crimes Law a threat to press freedom.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. MTN Sudan suspended internet service in the afternoons of 13 to 15 April 2026, on government directives. Those were the days of the national school examinations. The source calls it the sixth year running of exam-period shutdowns. Access Now says the government ordered 10 internet shutdowns during exams between 13 and 23 April 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In August 2026 a criminal court in El Obeid sentenced pharmacist Ahmed Suleiman Ahmed al-Waqi to six years in prison. His offence was a private phone conversation opposing the war. He was tried under the Criminal Act and the Cybercrime Law.

Not found. Nothing found says a cut was barred or a penalty for speech repealed.

SEN.short: In 2026 23 MPs challenged the media regulator law in court; no source found says whether anyone was punished for speech last year.
SEN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 10 March 2026, 23 MPs lodged a constitutional challenge to the media regulator law, citing risks of administrative censorship. APPEL, the Senegalese online press body, backed it with Paradigm Initiative. The Conseil constitutionnel ruled on the law on 7 April 2026, in Decision n° 2/C/2026.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. RSF says internet shutdowns in early 2024 undermined the right to inform. It does not say who ordered them or for how long. CIPESA says shutdowns were imposed during the 2023 unrest. A court later found they violated freedom of expression.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In July 2025, Le Soleil reports, journalist Bachir Fofana was tried for spreading false news. The commentator Badara Gadiaga was jailed over remarks about Ousmane Sonko. No arrest for speech is on record from the last twelve months. The deputies adopted the media regulator bill on 3 March 2026 as Loi n° 2026-09.

Not found. No source says the country went twelve months with no one punished for speech.

SLE.short: Parliament repealed the criminal libel provisions in 2020, but nothing recent is known on public criticism or internet cuts, so no stage is set.
SLE.summary: Not found. No source from the last three years says a paper, broadcaster, party or group criticised a government policy in public. None says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

SOM.short: Police shut Risaala Media and arrested five journalists in March 2025; Amnesty reports arrests in 2026; no source found says who was punished since.
SOM.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Defenders Coalition Somalia, a Somali civil-society group, with DefendDefenders, criticised the Official Information Bill approved by the Council of Ministers in March 2024 in a joint UN review submission dated 28 October 2025. They objected to its broad confidentiality and national-security exemptions, its lack of independent oversight and the secrecy in which it was drafted.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut of a connection has been found. The nearest held fact is that the government closed 82,000 social media pages it called extremist-linked in 2026, as Hiiraan reported on 4 September 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 18 March 2025 armed police stormed the Risaala Media station in Mogadishu, took it off air and arrested five named journalists without a court warrant, after it was first to report the bombing of the president's convoy. Amnesty International said in May 2026 that journalists in Somalia were subjected to arbitrary arrests and prosecution as the government stepped up attempts to censor reporting on insecurity, corruption and forced evictions.

Not found. No source names a person charged or jailed, or an outlet closed, for what was said or published inside the last twelve months.

SSD.short: A media body criticised the January 2025 social media block publicly; no source says whether anyone was punished for speech in the last twelve months.
SSD.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 28 January 2025 AMDISS, a South Sudanese media body, criticised the block on Facebook and TikTok. It said the block restrained press freedom and public debate.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. On 22 January 2025 the National Communication Authority directed all internet service providers to block all social media accounts for 30 to 90 days. Zain and MTN told users Facebook and TikTok were no longer accessible, and CPJ's sources said both were unreachable without a VPN on 23 January. AMDISS urged the regulator in January 2025 to expedite lifting the ban. CPJ says that in 2025 the authorities also suspended social media to block news from neighbouring Sudan.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No punishment for speech is on record. The nearest fact is the law. President Kiir signed the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 on 18 February 2026.

Not found. Nothing found says whether anyone was punished for speech in the last twelve months. Nothing found says when the social media block ended.

STP.short: Nothing found says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

SWZ.short: In April 2026 an outlet published an investigation holding the ICT ministry to account; a 2009 speech charge still stands untried.
SWZ.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. An opinion piece in Independent News Eswatini says that the Swazi Bridge outlet published an investigation on 12 April 2026 holding the ICT ministry to account for how its memorandum of understanding with Google Cloud EMEA was communicated, which the piece calls a failure of communication.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block of a connection or a site has been found. The nearest held fact is that MISA, the media body, engaged the Eswatini government on expression and media freedom, in a blog dated 27 February 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre says that Mphandlana Shongwe was charged under the Suppression of Terrorism Act in 2009 for shouting political slogans at a meeting, and that the charge still stands untried. No removal of such an offence has been found.

Not found. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

SYC.short: Nothing found says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

TCD.short: Internet access in Lac province has been cut since October 2024 and was still limited in September 2026; no source found says who ordered it.
TCD.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Internet Society Chad, a civil-society chapter, called on the authorities in a communique of 11 February 2025 to restore access in Lac province and said alternatives to a total cut exist. The Association des Médias en Ligne du Tchad (AMET) said on 5 August 2026 that the regulator HAMA's suspension of applications to create new media must respect press freedom and citizens' right to pluralistic information, while backing action against fake pages.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Internet access in Lac province has been cut since 28 October 2024 and was still off on 11 February 2025, with security reasons mentioned as possible. A citizen's open letter to the president, reported on 10 September 2026, says connectivity in Lac has been heavily limited for nearly two years and was still limited. Neither source names who ordered it or gives an end date.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest, charge or sanction for speech has been found. The nearest held fact is that HAMA suspended the examination of applications to create online newspapers, reported on 4 August 2026.

Not found. Who ordered the cut of internet access in Lac province, and when it ends, are not held.

TGO.short: Access Now reports 2025 protest throttling in Togo, but not where, who ordered it or when it ended, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not found. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

TUN.short: Messaging apps were disrupted across Tunisia during the June 2026 exams, and journalists were jailed for speech; no source found says whether any law bars cuts.
TUN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The National Union of Tunisian Journalists, with Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and RSF, denounced Decree-Law 2022-54 as a tool of repression. Their report is dated 16 July 2026. The union called for the El Mekki judgment to be annulled. In October 2026 it and civil society groups demanded that Decree 54 be scrapped.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Access Now, citing OONI data, says mobile internet disruptions hit messaging apps across Tunisia during the Baccalaureate from 3 June 2026. They came back during the resit session of 29 June to 2 July. Access Now counts Tunisia among exam-shutdown offenders for the first time. No law or ruling barring cuts has been found.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 15 July 2026 the Sfax Court of Appeal sentenced journalist Haythem El Mekki to one year in prison. His offence was a post about a Sfax hospital. Journalists Borhen Bsaies and Mourad Zeghidi got one year, cut to eight months, under Decree-Law 54. On 25 May 2026 Sonia Dahmani was convicted again under Decree-Law 54 and sentenced to two years. Journalist Ghassen Ben Khelifa got two years in March 2026.

Not found. Nothing found shows twelve months in which no one was punished for speech. No law or court ruling bars the government from cutting the internet.

TZA.short: The internet was cut nationwide around the 29 October 2025 election; no source found says who ordered it and whether another cut has followed.
TZA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Nothing is held on public criticism of policy. The nearest held fact is that the Legal & Human Rights Centre filed a case at the East African Court of Justice on 8 December 2025 alleging a nationwide internet shutdown by the government.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Access Now reports a five-day nationwide internet blackout during the 29 October 2025 election, and counts 8 internet shutdowns in Tanzania in 2025. The Legal & Human Rights Centre alleges a total shutdown from 29 October to 4 November 2025. Amnesty International says the authorities imposed a partial internet shutdown during the October 2025 general elections, and the Southern Africa Litigation Centre says the network was switched off around the election and the protests that followed. The Internet Governance Project puts the cost at an estimated US$250 million in losses during the 2025 election period.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority suspended the online content licence of JamiiForums for 90 days from 6 September 2025 over content it called misleading and insulting to the Government and the President, and blocked access to the platform; Amnesty International also reports the ban. A complaint filed in August 2026 alleges the leader of the opposition was jailed on capital charges in 2025 for calling for electoral reforms.

Not found. Nothing found shows a twelve-month stretch with no cut or block of the internet or a service, or who ordered the October 2025 blackout.

UGA.short: The government cut the internet for four days in January 2026, and Facebook stayed blocked in March; no source found reports a bar on cuts.
UGA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Uganda Law Society condemned the shutdown as illegal and unconstitutional. Its vice president said no state of emergency had been declared. On 27 February 2026 UGANET and other groups criticised blanket internet shutdowns and urged legal safeguards. Unwanted Witness and Amnesty International criticised the continued Facebook suspension in March 2026.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. The Uganda Communications Commission ordered operators to suspend public internet access from 18:00 on 13 January 2026. That was two days before the presidential election. Access Now describes it as a cut of internet and social media. The blackout lasted four days. On 18 January the Commission said social media and messaging stayed restricted. They were still blocked more than a week later. On 27 March 2026 the ICT minister of state said the Facebook suspension, in place since January 2021, would stay until Meta meets the government's conditions.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In December 2025 a student was jailed for six months for TikTok posts claiming President Museveni was ill. In August 2025 a magistrate convicted NUP member Juma Musuuza of hate speech and malicious information. His TikTok posts were about the President, his son and the Speaker. A CIPESA submission to the UN review names sections 24 and 25 of the Computer Misuse Act.

Not found. Nothing found shows twelve months with no cut or block of the internet or a service.

ZAF.short: Nothing found says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
ZAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

ZMB.short: A vlogger got nine months in September 2026 over a post about a presidential aide; whether any year passes without such cases is unknown.
ZMB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 8 August 2026 the Net Rights Coalition said arrests of journalists under the Cyber Crimes Act signal a chilling climate. It called for the cyber laws to be amended. In March 2025 eleven groups, MISA among them, said the cyber bills still lacked safeguards against abuse. In July 2026 the Law Association of Zambia and Chapter One Foundation asked the court to strike down parts of both laws.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block is on record from the last twelve months. The nearest fact is older. Access Now says the authorities reportedly blocked WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter and Instagram in the August 2021 elections. The block was lifted after civil society went to court.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 15 September 2026 a Lusaka court sentenced vlogger Joseph Chishimba to nine months over a screenshot about a presidential aide. Journalist MacPherson Mukuka was detained from 17 July 2026 over an audio recording of a campaign committee. Police in Mansa arrested Kennedy Mwansa for insulting the president on TikTok. The EU observers said the August 2026 elections took place amid arrests for online speech.

Not found. Nothing found shows twelve months in which no one was punished for speech.

ZWE.short: Journalists were reportedly arrested on cyberbullying charges in 2026 and the data protection law was criticised; no source found says whether any outlet was closed.
ZWE.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 23 June 2026 MISA Zimbabwe, a media-freedom body inside the country, published an analysis criticising the National AI Strategy 2026-2030. It found the strategy's truth-checking platform short of legal safeguards for free expression. On 15 October 2026 the Media Alliance of Zimbabwe held a dialogue criticising the Cyber and Data Protection Act as a tool to silence journalists.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. CIPESA says the state security minister ordered an internet shutdown in January 2019 amid fuel-price protests. The order went to mobile operators as an intercept directive. That month the High Court ruled that the minister had no authority to order it under the Interception of Communications Act.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Media Alliance of Zimbabwe's coordinator said four journalists were reportedly arrested in 2026 on cyberbullying charges over their stories. Amnesty International says a Bulawayo24 journalist has been in custody since 18 February 2026, charged with cyberbullying after a story alleging corruption. Paradigm Initiative's Londa 2025 report says arrests of journalists and rights defenders continued in 2025, under sedition and false-news laws. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre says Zimbabwe's courts struck down criminal defamation, giving no date.

Not found. Nothing found says whether an outlet was suspended or closed in the last twelve months. Nor does anything say whether access was cut in that time.

AGO.short: Angola's 2020 payment system law is in force and since 2022 lets non-bank companies be authorised; no rule to connect providers is known.
AGO.summary:
Law or rules in force. Angola's payments law is Lei n.º 40/20 of 16 December 2020, the Lei do Sistema de Pagamentos de Angola, and the Banco Nacional de Angola makes binding notices under its article 6. Aviso n.º 2/22 of February 2022 sets the rules for access to payment service activity, Aviso n.º 4/25 of August 2025 those for opening and running e-money accounts, and Aviso n.º 1/26 of January 2026 those for acquirers that are not banks.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Aviso n.º 2/22 lets non-bank financial institutions based in Angola provide payment services, e-money issuance among them, as payment service companies authorised by the central bank. Since January 2026 only such authorised companies may act as non-bank acquirers of payment terminals and cash machines.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

BDI.short: Burundi's 2018 payment system law is in force, and a 2024 regulation licenses non-bank payment institutions; no rule to connect providers is known.
BDI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Burundi's Loi n°1/07 of 11 May 2018 on the national payment system is in force, and the central bank's oversight framework, published in November 2025, cites it as the current law, whose article 9 lets the bank issue regulations. Under it the bank made Règlement n°002/2024, revising a 2017 regulation on payment services and payment institutions: no one may provide payment services without the central bank's licence.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The central bank licenses payment institutions under the 2024 regulation, and its framework lists them apart from commercial banks and microfinance institutions as operators of e-money platforms. Every licensed payment service provider is to be inspected on site at least every two years. The regulation's date within 2024 is not given, and no rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

BEN.short: Benin is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
BEN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Benin is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, applied since January 2024, obliges every company offering payment services in the union to hold a licence or stop, and distinguishes payment institutions from banks, microfinance institutions and e-money institutions.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Four companies held payment institution licences in Benin at 31 August 2026: Julaya Bénin, Open SI, FedaPay Bénin and QOS Integrated Center Bénin. The union's banking commission counted three licensed e-money issuers there at the end of 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money institution and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September 2026, with microfinance institutions given until 30 June 2027.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
BFA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Burkina Faso is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Payment institutions are licensed under its instruction of 23 January 2024 on payment services, which sets them apart from banks, microfinance institutions and e-money institutions; the BCEAO counted 34 licensed across the union at 31 August 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Two payment institutions are licensed in Burkina Faso: INTOUCH Burkina, since 9 May 2025, and KERRY Payments Burkina, since 2 September 2025. The union's banking commission counted one licensed e-money issuer there at the end of 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September 2026. L'Oeil du Sahel reports a BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 requiring interoperable e-money transfers in the union to pass through PI-SPI from 2 November 2026, and the banking commission's figure of 314.8 billion FCFA of e-money outstanding at Orange Money Burkina Faso at the end of 2024.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

BWA.short: Botswana's electronic payment regulations, amended in April 2026, license payment companies that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
BWA.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Bank of Botswana regulates payments under the Electronic Payment Services Regulations. Amendments made by the Minister of Finance as Statutory Instrument No. 46 of 2026, under the Bank of Botswana Act, took effect on 2 April 2026, and providers had to comply at once. Operating a service without the Bank's licence is an offence.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The amended regulations require anyone operating an electronic payment service, e-money issuance and money transfer included, to hold a Bank of Botswana licence and to be a company incorporated in Botswana. They do not apply to banks licensed under the Banking Act, so the licence is one for companies that are not banks. The Bank told the public to use licensed providers.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

CAF.short: The Central African Republic is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, which licenses non-banks; none was licensed there by 2023.
CAF.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central African Republic is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which the regional central bank's financial inclusion strategy, published in February 2025, describes as governing payment establishments and mobile money across the six member states of the Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 regulation created payment establishments, licensed to provide payment services without being tied to a bank; subsidiaries of mobile operators and fintech companies can be licensed where they meet its requirements. The strategy lists six licensed across the region by July 2023: two in Cameroon, one in Chad, two in Congo and one in Gabon. None of the six was in the Central African Republic.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with ten non-bank payment institutions licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
CIV.summary:
Law or rules in force. Côte d'Ivoire is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, applied since January 2024, obliges every company offering payment services in the union to hold a licence or stop; payment institutions are licensed under it.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Ten payment institutions were licensed in Côte d'Ivoire at 31 August 2026, the newest on 27 April 2026, and in 2025 Djogana Pay became the country's fourth e-money institution after Orange Money, MTN Mobile Money and Moov Money. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money institution and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September 2026.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

CMR.short: Cameroon licenses payment institutions that are not banks under regional rules, the newest in July 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
CMR.summary:
Law or rules in force. Cameroon's regulatory framework lets payment institutions, and also banks and microfinance institutions, offer payment services under the conditions the regulation sets. A licence is granted by order of the finance minister on a decision of COBAC, the banking commission of the six-state Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Konoom Cameroun was licensed as a payment institution by arrêté n°681/MINFI of 21 July 2026, following COBAC decision n°D-2026/092; Orange Money Cameroun and Mobile Money Corporation, the MTN subsidiary, were already licensed. COBAC's 2025 annual report counts seven licensed payment institutions in the region, those two among them. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch, so Cameroon answers the first three questions and not the fourth.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

COD.short: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's 2018 payments law is in force; since 2024 all regulated payment providers must join the national switch.
COD.summary:
Law or rules in force. Loi n° 18-019 of 9 July 2018 on payment systems and securities settlement systems is the Democratic Republic of the Congo's payments law. It was published in the Journal Officiel on 23 July 2018. No regulation made under it by the central bank is named, and no amendment to it is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 law defines electronic money and payment orders. The central bank's Instruction No. 58 of 4 September 2024 obliges every regulated entity, from credit institutions to financial companies, postal services and aggregators, to connect to the National E-Payment Switch within six months, under sanction, and covers wallet-to-bank transfers between e-money institutions. Settlement runs through the central bank's SAREC system.

Not found. No payments-law source found names a non-bank provider licensed under the law.

COG.short: Congo has two licensed payment institutions that are not banks, reported for 2025; the rules they are licensed under are not named.
COG.summary:
Law or rules in force. Congo's payment institutions are licensed by COBAC, the banking commission of the six-state Central African Economic and Monetary Community, whose 2025 annual report covers the payment institutions licensed in the region. The commission reports each year on the institutions it supervises in the six member states.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Mobile Money Congo SA and Mobile Commerce Congo SA are the payment institutions operating in Congo, neither of them a bank, and their revenues rose 28.1% to FCFA 20.6 billion in 2025. No law or regulation is named as the one they are licensed under, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch. Congo therefore reaches the third question on the licences alone.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

COM.short: The Comoros has had central bank e-money rules since 2017, under a 2015 payments decree; no source found says whether they license non-banks.
COM.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of the Comoros issued Regulation n°01/2017/BCC/DSBR in 2017, setting the conditions for carrying on e-money activity. It rests on decree n°15-026/PR of 3 March 2015 on payment systems, means of payment and payment incidents. The regulation gives only the year it was made, and no later amendment is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2017 regulation sets conditions for e-money activity. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. The Comoros therefore answers the first two questions only: rules in force, with their reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not found. No source found says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2018 decree-laws on payments are in force and let the central bank authorise non-bank institutions; no rule to connect providers is known.
CPV.summary:
Law or rules in force. Cabo Verde legislated on payments in three decree-laws published on 28 November 2018. Decreto-legislativo n.º 7/2018 sets the regime for regulating and operating the payment system, and Decreto-legislativo n.º 8/2018 regulates payment services and the issue, distribution and redemption of electronic money. All three appeared in the same issue of the Boletim Oficial, n.º 78, and the Banco de Cabo Verde is the regulator under each.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Payment institutions and e-money institutions, financial institutions distinct from banks, are authorised by the Banco de Cabo Verde under the third, Decreto-legislativo n.º 9/2018, which governs access to their activity. The postal service, Correios de Cabo Verde, may also issue e-money. No licensed institution is named, and no rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

DJI.short: Djibouti's 2016 payment law is in force and the central bank has licensed two non-bank e-money issuers; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
DJI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Loi n° 118/AN/15/7ème L, the law creating the National Payment System, was adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated in 2016. It applies across Djibouti to every payment service and system. It is known as the Loi sur le Système de Paiement National. No regulation made under it by the central bank is named, and no amendment to it is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2016 law covers payment services and systems. The central bank's register of licensed institutions lists two e-money issuers beside the banks, D-Money (licensed 2020) and WAAFI (licensed 2022). No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

DZA.short: Algeria's 2023 banking law and 2025 regulation license payment providers that are not banks; the first mobile operator subsidiary was authorised in September 2026.
DZA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Algeria's Loi n° 23-09 of 21 June 2023 on money and banking provides for payment service providers and counts electronic money among payment instruments. Under it the Bank of Algeria made Regulation no. 25-02 of 14 April 2025 on their authorisation, licensing and operation, and instruction no. 06-2025 of 17 August 2025 on how they are organised.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2023 law lists payment service providers apart from banks, and the 2025 regulation lets a company be licensed as one by the Governor of the Bank of Algeria once the Monetary and Banking Council has authorised it. On 23 September 2026 the Council authorised Djezzy Payment Services, a subsidiary of a mobile operator, to set itself up as a provider; it has twelve months to apply for the licence.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

EGY.short: Egypt's central bank licenses payment companies that are not banks under 2025 rules; no source found says whether providers must connect to each other.
EGY.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Egypt issued Rules for Licensing and Registration of Payment System Operators and Payment Service Providers in June 2025, with transitional provisions for existing payment institutions. In September 2025 it issued regulations on governance, internal control and fit and proper criteria, with which operators and providers must comply within a year.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The rules of 19 June 2025 set licensing conditions, minimum capital and financial guarantees for payment institutions, domestic and foreign-based, that provide payment services or operate payment systems for customers in Egypt. Existing payment institutions had twelve months to apply for a licence. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

ERI.short: Nothing found names a payments law or e-money rules for Eritrea, or says there are none, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a payments law, e-money rules or a draft of either, or says there is none.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's 2020 central bank directives license payment operators and wallet issuers that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
ETH.summary:
Law or rules in force. The National Bank of Ethiopia introduced two sets of rules in 2020: the Payment Instrument Issuers directives and the Payment Systems Operators directive. Firms are licensed and operating under both. The Reporter gave this account of the two frameworks in July 2026. No act of parliament on payments is named.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The operators directive created four licence categories, for switch, point-of-sale, cash machine and payment gateway operators, under which companies that are not banks, Chapa, Arifpay, Santimpay and Kacha among them, were licensed. The issuers directives let telecom operators launch mobile wallets. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch, so Ethiopia answers the first three questions and not the fourth.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GAB.short: Gabon is under the 2018 regional payment regulation, with non-bank payment institutions operating; a national digital payments ordinance was before parliament in 2026.
GAB.summary:
Law or rules in force. Gabon is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which a BEAC instruction of 5 May 2026 supplements. A national text is in preparation: the Council of Ministers adopted a draft ordinance on digital payments on 29 January 2026, and on 22 May the digital economy minister defended the bill ratifying it before the National Assembly's finance committee.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The regional regulation governs payment institutions distinct from credit institutions, which must report monthly to the central bank. COBAC's 2025 report names Airtel Money Gabon and Clikpay Gabon in Gabon's payment institution sector, which earned FCFA 24.7 billion in 2025. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2019 payments act licenses e-money issuers that are not banks, and mobile money interoperability was mandated in 2018.
GHA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Ghana's Payment Systems and Services Act, 2019 (Act 987) has applied since February 2020. The Bank of Ghana acts under it: on 14 July 2026 it revoked a licence under section 13. The Act sets licensing requirements for payment service providers and electronic money issuers.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The Act requires payment service providers and electronic money issuers to hold a Bank of Ghana licence. Zeepay Ghana, a fintech company, held a dedicated electronic money issuer licence until the Bank revoked it in July 2026 over inadequate cash backing of its e-money. Ghana mandated mobile money interoperability in 2018; the rule that did so is not named. The Bank of Ghana assesses licence applicants on financial stability, technology, compliance with anti-money-laundering rules and consumer protection.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

GIN.short: Central bank decisions from 2015 license non-bank e-money companies; as of 2026 no rule is known requiring providers to connect to a switch.
GIN.summary:
Law or rules in force. The BCRG's Comite des agrements issued Decision D/2015/003/CAM of 31 March 2015 on e-money issuance and e-money establishments. It binds from its date of signature and was published in the Journal Officiel, as reproduced in the BCRG's December 2017 compendium of banking texts.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The decision places e-money establishments among financial establishments, not banks, and constitutes them as Guinean limited companies. It requires them to obtain a BCRG licence, with a decision due within 90 days of a complete file. Decision D/2015/008/CAM of 3 June 2015 sets their minimum share capital at GNF 2 billion, to be held in Guinean francs and employed in Guinea. Article 5 of banking law L/2013/060/CNT, promulgated by decree on 28 November 2013, allows service providers other than credit institutions to be authorised, in a limited way, to provide and manage means of payment under rules set by a Comite des agrements decision. At the 22 July 2026 NimbaPay launch the BCRG Vice-Governor called NimbaPay a strategic opportunity, not a regulatory constraint.

Not found. No rule has been found that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2011 mobile money regulation authorises providers that are not banks, beside a 2013 payments act; no rule to connect providers is known.
GMB.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Gambia has two texts. The central bank's Mobile Money Regulation, 2011, made under the Central Bank of The Gambia Act 2005, took effect on 15 October 2011. The Electronic Payments System Act 2013 defines the establishment and operation of the electronic payments system.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2011 regulation provides for retail transfers by persons not licensed as banks or financial institutions, and has the central bank authorise such payment service providers: limited liability companies registered in The Gambia, with core capital of GMD 10 million and a security deposit of GMD 5 million. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with two non-banks licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
GNB.summary:
Law or rules in force. Guinea-Bissau is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Payment institutions are licensed under its Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, and 34 were approved across the union at 31 August 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The banking commission's register lists one payment institution and one e-money institution in Guinea-Bissau, INTOUCH Guinée-Bissau and Finances Mobiles Bissau, neither a bank; the first was approved on 25 June 2025. The BCEAO required every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September; five institutions in Guinea-Bissau were authorised on the platform at 31 July 2026.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, which licenses non-banks; none was licensed there by 2023.
GNQ.summary:
Law or rules in force. Equatorial Guinea is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which the regional central bank's financial inclusion strategy, published in February 2025, describes as governing payment establishments and mobile money across the six member states of the Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 regulation created payment establishments, licensed to provide payment services without being tied to a bank; subsidiaries of mobile operators and fintech companies can be licensed where they meet its requirements. The strategy lists six licensed across the region by July 2023: two in Cameroon, one in Chad, two in Congo and one in Gabon. None of the six was in Equatorial Guinea.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2011 payment system act and 2014 regulations authorise mobile money operators; a replacement bill was published for comment in September 2026.
KEN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Kenya's National Payment System Act 2011 is the legal framework for payment systems and providers, and the National Payment System Regulations 2014 put it into operation.
