It is the current Act. In September 2026 the National Treasury and the Central Bank of Kenya published a draft National Payment System Bill, 2026 to repeal and replace it, with comments due by 9 October.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Mobile phone money transfer operators are authorised as payment service providers under the 2011 Act and the 2014 regulations, in categories that include e-money issuer and small money issuer. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Rwanda's central bank says a memorandum of March 2026 on licence passporting covers payment service providers licensed by the Central Bank of Kenya.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

LBR.short: Liberia's central bank mobile money regulations were in force in 2024; no source found says whether they license companies that are not banks.
LBR.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Liberia's Mobile Money Regulations are the framework governing electronic money and mobile money operators in Liberia, where more than 11 million mobile wallets operate. The Central Bank of Liberia is the regulator, and in June 2024 it fined Lonestar Cell MTN Mobile Money Inc. for persistent breaches of its mobile money regulations.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The regulations govern mobile money operators. It is not said that those operators are companies other than banks, or that they are licensed under the regulations, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Liberia therefore answers the first two questions only: rules in force, with their reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated. The year the regulations were made is not given. Nor is any payments act of parliament named.

Not found. No source found says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

LBY.short: Libya's 2022 electronic transactions law covers e-money, and the central bank licenses electronic payment companies; no rule to connect providers is known.
LBY.summary:
Law or rules in force. Libya's Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions defines electronic money and, in article 70, provides that it is issued by commercial banks and other financial institutions under controls set by the Central Bank of Libya.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The Central Bank's circular 18 of 2025 is addressed to electronic payment companies it has licensed, and binds them. It defines an electronic payment service provider as an entity licensed by the Central Bank to provide electronic payment services and e-wallets. The licence is therefore one a company that is not a bank can hold. No rule is named that requires those companies and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

LSO.short: Lesotho's 2014 payment systems act is in force; a bill to replace it and license all payment providers reached second reading in May 2026.
LSO.summary:
Law or rules in force. Lesotho's Payment Systems Act, 2014 was published in the Government Gazette on 12 September 2014 and came into operation that day. On 5 May 2026 the Minister of Finance moved the Payment System Bill, 2025 for second reading in the National Assembly, to repeal and replace it. The bill had first been presented on 2 May 2025 and approved by the portfolio committee with ten amendments.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The bill would license all payment service providers, fintech companies included. The 2014 Act frames interbank payment systems and the issue and use of payment instruments. It is not said that companies other than banks can be licensed under the Act in force, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No source found says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2014 banking law licenses payment institutions that are not banks, and they were active in 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MAR.summary:
Law or rules in force. Morocco's Law 103-12 on credit institutions, enacted on 24 December 2014, defines means of payment, electronic money among them, and payment services, and regulates payment institutions. Bank Al-Maghrib supervises them; in July 2026 it cut the cap on domestic card interchange fees from 0.65% to 0.50%, effective 1 October 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The law defines payment institutions as entities offering payment services, separate from credit institutions, and requires them to obtain Bank Al-Maghrib's approval before operating. Bank Al-Maghrib and the Competition Council said in July 2026 that newly licensed payment institutions and older ones were taking up card acquiring. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other. Payment institutions also open accounts remotely alongside banks, under a 2020 ruling of the data protection commission.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MDG.short: Madagascar's 2017 e-money law licenses non-bank e-money institutions, and since 2024 banks and e-money institutions must join the central bank's instant payment system.
MDG.summary:
Law or rules in force. Madagascar's Loi n°2016-056 on electronic money and electronic money institutions was adopted by both chambers in December 2016, cleared by the High Constitutional Court on 27 January 2017 and promulgated on 2 February 2017. The banking supervision commission, the CSBF, applies it: it issues instructions and audits the institutions.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The law requires any legal entity running e-money operations to be approved by the CSBF as an e-money institution, a limited company separate from credit institutions and microfinance institutions. The CSBF grants and withdraws those licences, and in June 2026 the central bank governor announced audits of the institutions. In October 2024 the central bank made connection to its instant payment system compulsory for banks and e-money institutions, with a deadline of 31 January 2025, and for the largest microfinance institutions.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

MLI.short: Mali is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
MLI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Mali is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Payment institutions are licensed under its Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, which sets them apart from banks, microfinance institutions and e-money institutions.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Two payment institutions are licensed in Mali: INTOUCH Mali, since 9 May 2025, and CAURIDOR, since 3 September 2025. The union's banking commission counted two licensed e-money issuers there at the end of 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June set 30 September 2026 as the new deadline. L'Oeil du Sahel reports a BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 requiring interoperable e-money transfers in the union to pass through PI-SPI from 2 November 2026, and the banking commission's listing of Orange Finances Mobiles Mali and Sama Money among Mali's e-money institutions, with 162.7 billion FCFA outstanding at the end of 2024. Orange Finances Money Mali is an e-money institution authorised by the BCEAO, it said in January 2024.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

MOZ.short: Mozambique passed a new payment system law in July 2026, licenses mobile operators' e-money institutions and requires them to join the instant payment system.
MOZ.summary:
Law or rules in force. Mozambique replaced its payments law in 2026. Lei n.º 15/2026 of 2 July approves the National Payments System Law and revokes Lei n.º 2/2008; parliament approved it in April and the president promulgated it in June. The central bank had made Aviso n.º 1/GBM/2026 under the 2008 law in February.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Three electronic money institutions authorised by the central bank, M-Pesa, e-Mola and M-Kesh, belong to the three mobile operators. Article 8 of the regulation annexed to the Aviso makes participation in the instant payment system compulsory for electronic money institutions and for credit institutions above a set size. A report of July 2026 likewise says participation by digital wallet operators in the instant payment system, which joins banks, microbanks and e-money institutions, is mandatory.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

MRT.short: Mauritania's 2021 electronic payments law and 2022 instruction license payment institutions that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MRT.summary:
Law or rules in force. Mauritania's Loi n°2021-014 of 5 July 2021 on electronic payment services and means regulates payment service providers and e-money issuers, and repealed a 2006 ordinance. Under it the central bank issued Instruction no. 03/GR/2022 of 31 March 2022 regulating payment institutions. The law has 113 articles and was published in Journal Officiel n°1490 of 30 July 2021.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The law bars anyone except banks from carrying on the business of a payment institution, or issuing and distributing e-money, without the central bank's prior licence. The instruction defines payment institutions as legal entities licensed by the central bank other than credit institutions, with minimum capital and a guarantee deposit of 20 million ouguiya each. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MUS.short: Mauritius's 2018 payment systems act licenses non-bank payment providers, with new rules for aggregators in 2026; no rule to connect providers is known.
MUS.summary:
Law or rules in force. The National Payment Systems Act 2018 was assented to on 29 November 2018 and makes the Bank of Mauritius the regulator of payment systems and payment service providers. It was last amended in April 2026, and the Bank's Guideline for Payment Aggregators, issued under section 17, took effect on 31 August 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Section 9(1) of the Act provides that no one other than the central bank or a bank may act as a payment service provider without the Bank's licence. The 2026 guideline requires non-bank companies that want to act as payment aggregators to obtain that licence, and gave existing ones until 31 August 2026 to apply. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MWI.short: A non-bank fintech was licensed under Malawi's payments law in 2026; no source found says whether providers must connect to a switch.
MWI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Malawi's Payment Systems Act, 2016 is in force: the Reserve Bank of Malawi issued a payment service provider licence under it on 30 September 2026. On 6 August 2026 Parliament passed an amendment to the Act removing its provisions on cheques, and the Finance Minister said detailed regulations would follow. Malawi's 2025 ID4Africa deck lists the Payment Systems Act, 2022, a revision of the 2011 act, and the E-Money Regulation, 2019 among the legal frameworks for payments.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Companies that are not banks are licensed under the Act. On 30 September 2026 the Reserve Bank granted the local fintech PayChangu Limited licence PSP-003/26 to run payment aggregation across the country, bringing mobile money, card payments and bank transfers onto one platform for businesses. No rule has been found that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not found. No source found says a rule requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a switch.

NAM.short: Namibia's 2023 payment system act licenses non-bank providers, and a 2025 directive requires e-money issuers to interoperate through the instant payment switch.
NAM.summary:
Law or rules in force. Namibia's Payment System Management Act 14 of 2023 was promulgated on 28 July 2023 and commenced on 8 August 2023. The Bank of Namibia makes determinations under its section 45: PSD-10 on fees and charges took effect on 24 December 2025, PSD-1 on licensing on 6 January 2026 and PSD-12 on operational and cybersecurity standards on 3 July 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. PSD-1 sets a licensing process for payment services by non-bank financial institutions and defines an electronic money issuer as a licensed payment service provider. PSD-10 applies to all payment service providers, defined as banking institutions and non-bank financial institutions, and binds e-money issuers and providers of e-money wallets and instant payments. Directive PSDIR-11 of 16 June 2025 requires every provider issuing payment instruments to make e-money interoperable through the instant payment switch by 26 February 2026. Directive PSDIR-10, in force from 31 March 2025, gives providers until 1 April 2027 to send low-value transfers within the Common Monetary Area through the regional TCIB scheme.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

NER.short: Niger is under the regional central bank's rules, with one non-bank e-money issuer licensed in 2025; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
NER.summary:
Law or rules in force. Niger is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union, which licenses e-money issuers and supervises them with the union's banking commission. The commission's 2025 report counts one licensed e-money issuer in Niger at 31 December 2025, among 18 across the union.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. That issuer is not a bank. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution in the eight states, Niger included, to be connected to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026. By a communiqué of 25 June it set 30 September 2026 as the new deadline for them, and 30 June 2027 for microfinance institutions. L'Oeil du Sahel reports a BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 requiring interoperable e-money transfers in the union to pass through PI-SPI from 2 November 2026, and the banking commission's figure of 4.6 billion FCFA of e-money outstanding at Airtel Money Niger at the end of 2024.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

NGA.short: Nigeria's central bank licenses mobile money operators and payment providers, reported in 2026; the rules it does so under are not named.
NGA.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Nigeria already licenses mobile money operators, payment service providers and digital banks, operators told a public hearing on 2 March 2026. The hearing was on the Nigerian Fintech Regulatory Commission Bill 2025, which would create a single regulator to license and supervise all fintech services and passed second reading in the House of Representatives on 28 October 2025.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The central bank's licences go to mobile money operators and payment service providers, OPay among the operators that said so at the hearing. The law or rules under which it grants them are not named, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Nigeria therefore reaches the third question on the licences alone.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

RWA.short: Rwanda's central bank directive of January 2026 requires banks and e-money issuers to route all transfers through one national platform from July 2026.
RWA.summary:
Law or rules in force. The National Bank of Rwanda issued Directive No. 45/2026 on 9 January 2026. It required domestic retail payments between banks and electronic money issuers to move to the eKash platform, the national instant payment rail. RSwitch gave the account of the directive that ITWeb Africa reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. From 14 July 2026 every transfer between bank accounts and electronic money issuers, account to wallet, wallet to account, account to account and wallet to wallet, is routed through eKash. The Rwanda Bankers' Association states that the directive took effect on that date, so that banks and e-money issuers all run on the single rail. The directive binds the e-money issuers with the banks; the law under which those issuers are licensed is not named.

Not found. Nothing on the four questions.

SDN.short: Sudan's 2020 central bank regulation licenses non-bank mobile payment companies; a 2026 circular asks them to connect to a switch not yet available.
SDN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Sudan's central bank regulates payments under its Regulation on Licensing and Organising Mobile Payment Financial Institutions 2020, approved on 28 December 2020 under the Banking Business Organisation Act, and a Payment Systems Regulation of 2013. Circular 7/2026 of 31 March 2026 cites both as its basis and sets binding minimum rules for financial services over USSD.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2020 regulation has the central bank license companies, not banks, to run mobile payment and open e-money wallet accounts; their names may not include the word bank. The 2026 circular lets those institutions and licensed electronic payment providers offer USSD financial services alongside banks. It asks providers to connect to a national switch once one is available, and sets no date.

Not found. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

SEN.short: Senegal is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with eleven non-bank payment institutions licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
SEN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Senegal is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Its instruction of 23 January 2024 on payment services is the rule under which payment institutions are licensed, and obliges every fintech offering payment services in the union to obtain a licence or stop.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Eleven payment institutions were licensed in Senegal at 31 August 2026, Flutterwave Sénégal and Julaya Sénégal among them, and the banking commission counted five licensed e-money issuers at the end of 2025; Wave has held an e-money licence since April 2022. SLE.short: Sierra Leone's 2022 payment systems act licenses non-bank providers, and since April 2025 banks and mobile money operators must route payments through the national switch.
SLE.summary:
Law or rules in force. Sierra Leone's National Payment Systems Act, 2022 was assented to on 2 June 2022, commenced on 23 June 2022 and repealed the Payment Systems Act 2009. The Bank of Sierra Leone's Guidelines for E-money have been completed and gazetted, with guidelines on remittance business and directives for the national switch.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Section 6 of the Act bars anyone from providing payment services or operating a system without a Bank of Sierra Leone licence, and sets conditions for e-money issuers; section 8 exempts only banks and financial institutions from needing a new licence. The licence is therefore one for companies that are not banks, and the Act gives mobile money operators a seat on its payments council. Directives issued in December 2024 require all commercial banks and mobile money operators to route instant, card and point-of-sale payments through the national switch from 1 April 2025.

SOM.short: Somalia's 2020 mobile money regulations are in force, and both houses had passed a payment system bill by January 2026; no source found reports its signing.
SOM.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Somalia made the Mobile Money Regulations, Amended 2020 under the Central Bank of Somalia Act 2012, setting out the licensing, conduct and supervision of mobile money service providers. A National Payment System Bill is before parliament: the House of the People passed it on 8 November 2025 and the Upper House passed its third reading on 11 January 2026.

It is not said that those providers are companies other than banks, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Whether the bill has been signed into law is not reported.

SSD.short: South Sudan's amended e-money rules took effect in 2026, licensing non-bank issuers and requiring every payment platform to connect through a licensed switch.
SSD.summary:
Law or rules in force. South Sudan's Electronic Money Regulation 2017 Amendment 2025 took effect as reported on 1 September 2026, issued under the Bank of South Sudan Act 2011 Amendment 2023 and binding licensed financial institutions and non-bank e-money issuers. A broader National Payment System Bill, 2025 is still a draft: the Bank of South Sudan opened a five-day workshop on 10 August 2026 to validate it, and at its close the governor called for faster progress.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Under the amended regulation non-bank e-money issuers are licensed: standalone payment providers must set up a separate company, seek the central bank's approval and pay a filing fee of 65 million South Sudanese pounds. The same rules require every digital payment platform to connect to the National Payment System through a licensed switch, so that customers can send money between providers.

São Tomé and Príncipe's Lei n.º 17/2018, published on 7 September 2018, sets the legal regime for regulating, overseeing and managing the National Payment System, and covers payment services, the issue of electronic money among them. The central bank's organic law, Lei n.º 03/2025, makes it responsible for regulating payment systems and lets its board adopt binding regulations.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 law lets the central bank authorise and license payment service providers, defined as any entity providing payment services, e-money issuance included. Banks are treated apart: they need no new authorisation to provide payment services. The licence is therefore open to companies that are not banks. No licensed provider is named, and no rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

The central bank said in November 2025 that licensing runs under it now and that it was finalising regulations on timelines and requirements.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. A new mobile money provider must go through the central bank's licensing process; three mobile money operators, MTN MoMo and Instacash among them, are in the interoperable system. At the launch of fast payments on the Eswatini Payment Switch on 11 December 2024 the Governor said participation is mandated for all payment service providers offering local payments, with the remaining participants expected to be live by the end of January 2025. A central bank directive binding all licensed payment service providers from 31 March 2025 gives them until 31 March 2027 to move low-value transfers within the Common Monetary Area to the TCIB scheme.

Under it the Central Bank made the Electronic Money Regulations, 2022, which commenced on 12 December 2022, and on 15 December 2025 amended its licensing and authorisation regulations. The Governor said in July 2025 that Seychelles had amended its main payment system Act.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2022 regulations set capital and liquidity rules for electronic money issuers other than banks, with initial capital of SCR 1,000,000, and treat issuers that are banks or credit unions as separate cases. The 2025 amendment sets the conditions on which the Central Bank may license any company incorporated under the Companies Act as a payment service provider. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other. The amended regulations exempt banks and credit unions from annual fees only.

In February 2026 the finance ministry signed conventions with four such operators on mobile money for state payments. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

TGO.short: Togo follows regional central bank rules; an e-money institution was licensed in 2025, and from 2026 all providers must connect and e-money limits rise.
TGO.summary:
Law or rules in force. Togo is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. A BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 sets binding terms for person-to-person e-money transfers through PI-SPI from 2 November: free sends up to FCFA 8,000 a day, a charge of 0 to 0.8% above that, and free receipt. A BCEAO instruction of 8 October 2026 raises the e-money balance cap to CFAF 4 million per issuer, from CFAF 2 million since 2015, and cuts the demand-deposit float floor from 75% to 65%, both from 2 November 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Tmoney was licensed as an e-money institution in September 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution in the eight states to be connected to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September, with microfinance institutions given until 30 June 2027. Nine institutions in Togo were authorised on the platform at 31 July 2026.

UGA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Uganda's law is the National Payment Systems Act, 2020. Bank of Uganda officials told a parliamentary committee on 14 September 2026 that the bank's oversight of wallet providers, payment firms and deposit-taking institutions rests on it. On 16 October 2026 the Daily Monitor reported that Uganda relies on a framework that includes the Act and guidelines issued by financial regulators.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The hearing was part of a committee inquiry into the central bank. Fintechs have since announced licences of their own: NALA, a Tanzanian firm, payment service provider and payment system operator licences from the Bank of Uganda in December 2025, and Payaza a payment system operator licence in February 2026.

ZAF.short: South Africa's 1998 payment system act is in force and non-banks are designated under it; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
ZAF.summary:
Law or rules in force. South Africa's National Payment System Act of 1998 regulates the payment system and gives the Reserve Bank responsibility for clearing and settlement; it is twenty-eight years old and still the law. The Reserve Bank governor said on 1 September 2026 that a National Payment System Bill, moving regulation from the kind of entity to the kind of activity, would soon go out for public comment. On 20 October 2026 he said the Reserve Bank had proposed an exemption notice and authorisation framework letting regulated non-banks carry out payment activities, to be published by the end of November 2026. Under the Act the Reserve Bank issued Directive No. 1 of 2025, binding on settlement participants from 1 April 2025, and in June 2026 published a draft directive on payments for offshore merchants; its May 2026 draft framework would let approved non-banks issue e-money.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The Reserve Bank says it regulates third-party payment providers and e-money providers, and has designated companies that are not banks as clearing system participants under the 1998 Act, among them Yoco Technologies in 2021 and Payfast in 2024. South Africa has no dedicated mobile money licence for non-banks, an MTN executive said in September 2026, and the Reserve Bank is preparing one through an authorisation framework and the bill. No rule has been found that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a switch.

BFA.short: A computerised occurrence book for police and gendarmerie stations was over 80% built in December 2023; no source found says whether any station uses it.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The computerised main courante platform, as the security ministry names its occurrence-book system, belongs to the Ministère de l'Administration Territoriale, de la Décentralisation et de la Sécurité, whose director of information systems reported on it to a delegation of the digital transition ministry in late December 2023.

Records made digitally. In late December 2023 the platform was not yet operational: the digital transition ministry put it at more than 80 per cent built.

How the record is made. The platform is to replace the physical registers in which main courantes are kept at police commissariats and gendarmerie brigades, and in late December 2023 those registers were still the record.

Last twelve months. The ministry's director of information systems said in late December 2023 that the platform would be operational by mid-January 2024, once amendments were taken in.

Stations doing the digital entry. In late December 2023 no commissariat or gendarmerie brigade was using the computerised main courante.

Not found. Nothing dated on or before 30 September 2026 says the platform went live in any commissariat or brigade. No plan, source of finance, count of stations or event in the last twelve months has been found.

BWA.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

CMR.short: A digital system for investigation and case information existed in 2020 and was barely used; no source found says which stations use it, if any,.
CMR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. GIZ's factsheet on its support to the Cameroonian police, status June 2020, presents the digitised investigations and proceedings system as the Délégation générale à la sûreté nationale's own, and says the DGSN must also overcome unreliable internet connection, electricity and computer equipment.

Records made digitally. In June 2020 the police had a digitised system for processing and transmitting information on investigations, criminal proceedings, arrest warrants, fines and current sanctions.

How the record is made. The system processes and transmits information on investigations and criminal proceedings, on the June 2020 factsheet's account.

Last twelve months. At June 2020, the date of GIZ's factsheet on its programme with the Cameroonian police, the digitised system for investigations and criminal proceedings was barely used.

Stations doing the digital entry. GIZ put the system's slight use down to weak institutional and management capacity at the Délégation générale à la sûreté nationale in its factsheet of June 2020.

Not found. Which units use the system, whether any is outside the capital, where and how entries are made and how many stations enter are not held. Nothing is held since June 2020.

COD.short: Police documents were typed or handwritten on paper in 2023; no source found says whether any station has had a digital system since.
COD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A police statement must by law be written out and signed by the officer who drafts it, on pain of nullity, the programme officer of the Ligue des droits de la personne dans la région des Grands Lacs told Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board on 15 March 2023.

Records made digitally. A case is referred to the Congolese National Police by a written and signed complaint, the Executive Secretary of Héritiers de la justice told the board on 9 March 2023.

How the record is made. Police documents in criminal proceedings are typed, and the record of the parties' hearings is handwritten in most cases, he said in March 2023 after consulting lawyers at the South Kivu Court of Appeal.

Last twelve months. The samples supplied to the board in March 2023 were blank paper forms of findings, arrest and witness testimony reports.

Stations doing the digital entry. The typed and handwritten police documents were described in March 2023 for the country as a whole.

Not found. Nothing dated after March 2023 is held on how stations record, and neither account of that month says in terms that no digital system exists. Nothing is held on a system for stations, its owner, plan or finance, or on the last twelve months.

COG.summary: Not found. The one statement that stations work by hand is a survey of commissariats in Pointe-Noire and Nkayi from January 2014; nothing is held on Brazzaville, the rest of the country or the gendarmerie beyond one brigade, and nothing dated since. CPV.short: Complaints ran digitally from national police stations to the courts by March 2026; no source found says how many stations use the system.
CPV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The criminal-process subsystem of what the Ministry of Justice calls the Sistema de Informação da Justiça was developed by the state's NOSi with the justice institute IMIJ and handed to the ministry on 16 March 2026. The order bringing it into phased operation was issued jointly by the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Internal Administration on 27 December 2024.

Records made digitally. The Ministry of Justice says the subsystem takes in the Polícia Nacional's stations and the Polícia Judiciária's delegations, so that the handling of complaints is essentially digital from the police to the courts. By 16 March 2026 it had processed about 25,000 police reports and more than 18,000 cases from end to end.

How the record is made. The ministry says the system integrates the stations and the delegations with the courts, complaints being handled digitally in the one system.

Last twelve months. On 16 March 2026 NOSi formally handed the subsystem over. The stated target is all courts fully digital within three years.

Stations doing the digital entry. The joint order of 27 December 2024 makes use of the electronic criminal process obligatory in the Polícia Nacional.

Not found. No count or share of Polícia Nacional stations using the system, and no account of how a station enters the complaint. No plan or finance for it, and nothing on rural stations.

ETH.short: A criminal records system covering crime report to sentence was still being built in January 2026; no station is known to use it.
ETH.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice says CRIMS, as it names its Criminal Records Information Management System, is being developed by the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute for the ministry, the Federal Police Commission and the Addis Ababa Police Commission to work in jointly, steered by a coordinating committee, in an item published on 20 January 2026.

Records made digitally. The system is under development and not yet in use, and is to record digitally everything from the crime report through investigation, charge, trial and sentence, the ministry said in January 2026.

How the record is made. Its modules cover report intake, investigation, juvenile offenders, offence type, biometric data, and prosecutors' and courts' decisions, on the ministry's account of January 2026.

Last twelve months. In January 2026 the ministry reported a coordinating-committee forum, with the minister and senior leaders of the three bodies, at which the system was said to be in development.

Stations doing the digital entry. In August 2023 the ministry was training federal investigating police and prosecutors, about 100 in all, in order to launch the system widely.

Not found. No station, place or way of making the record is given for the system, and no launch is recorded since the 2023 training. No plan or source of finance is stated.
