GHA.short: Case dockets were held digitally in 55 police stations across seven regions in 2022; no source found reports the total of stations, and anything since.
GHA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Government of Ghana launched what it calls the Case Tracking System in 2018, with the support of USAID, as a common platform for the Police Service, the Attorney General's office, the Prisons Service, the Legal Aid Commission, the Economic and Organised Crime Office and the Judicial Service.

Records made digitally. The Asokwa Municipal Police Commander said in May 2022 that the system had eliminated the use of paper as case dockets in the prosecution of criminal cases. The Legal Resources Centre reported in 2022 that 2,475 cases had been registered on it from December 2021.

How the record is made. The commander said he could monitor cases in all stations within his jurisdiction from his office through the system, with unstable internet and electricity hindering it. In the Volta Region, 104 laptops, 95 tablets and 93 connectivity units were given out to run it, by the centre's 2022 report.

Last twelve months. On 23 May 2022 the project was being supported by USAID, whose Justice Sector Support Activity also paid for an awareness campaign.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Legal Resources Centre reported in 2022 that 55 police stations and 3 prisons services were using the system, in seven regions and over 40 districts: Greater Accra, Ashanti, Northern, Volta, Bono, Western and Eastern. In July 2019 the West African Police Information System had more than 35 units in the capital, shared among police, immigration and prisons, and none in the regions.

Not found. No total of stations to set beside the 55, and nothing on the system since 2022. Whether the first report of an occurrence is recorded digitally, and whether rural stations use the system.

GIN.short: Ten police and gendarmerie units in Greater Conakry were equipped in 2021; no source found says whether any enters records, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: Not found. The facts held on a station system are a decree of 13 May 2019 creating the police data centre and its information system, which names no station, and an account dated 31 March 2021: ten police and gendarmerie units of Greater Conakry equipped, with no total of units, no statement that any was entering records, and the digitising of procès-verbaux stated as an intention. Nothing newer shows preparation, a pilot or a system running, and no dated statement says how stations record today.

GMB.short: The police chief said in March 2026 that documentation is on paper; no source found says what became of a 2021 pilot.
GMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNDP's terms of reference of 22 April 2021 state that the crime-reporting app will be owned by the Gambia Police Force, and UNDP reports that in 2020 it supported the work technically and financially with UN Peacebuilding Fund money.

Records made digitally. The Inspector General of Police, at a media briefing reported on 24 March 2026, described the force's documentation as paper-based. UNDP reports that in 2020 it supported a Mobile Data Collection App within the police's digitalised case management system and trained 24 officers to use it.

How the record is made. The Inspector General said the force needs to move from paper-based documentation to a digitalised mode, as reported on 24 March 2026.

Last twelve months. At the briefing reported on 24 March 2026 the Inspector General put digitalisation of police workflow and records management as work still to come.

Stations doing the digital entry. UNDP's terms of reference of 22 April 2021 describe a mobile app for crime reporting by police officers as in its pilot phase, to be extended to other police stations in phases.

Not found. What became of the case management system and the crime-reporting app after April 2021, and how many stations took part in the pilot. Who owns, plans or pays for digital station records has not been stated in the last three years.

GNB.short: A 2024 student project states that police stations have no system for recording occurrences; no source found says how stations record.
GNB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A steering committee of several entities oversees the centre for collecting and processing criminal information that Guinea-Bissau calls SIPAO, and INTERPOL accompanies it and the European Union finances it, the Minister of Justice and Human Rights said on 17 April 2023.

Records made digitally. Guinea-Bissau does not have a system for recording criminal occurrences in police stations, the author of an undergraduate final project at IFBA in Brazil stated in August 2024.

How the record is made. The author gave that absence as the first reason for building a prototype, a web application tested in 2024 by ten users of Guinean nationality.

Last twelve months. INTERPOL described the West African Police Information System on 12 September 2025 as strengthening information exchange and coordination among the region's law enforcement agencies.

Stations doing the digital entry. A new SIPAO service beside the Guarda Nacional command in Bissau was described in August 2024 as a centre where all police forces work and share information. The centre's director named extension to all law-enforcement institutions as the main challenge still ahead in 2024.

Not found. How stations record is not held, and the statement that no station system exists is one author's, with no source cited. No station is named as entering its cases at the criminal-information centre in Bissau, and nothing is held on a plan, on the last twelve months or on stations.

GNQ.short: A project to interconnect police stations is in the 2026 budget law; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

KEN.short: Seventy-six stations around Nairobi had a digital occurrence book in 2023; no source found reports in 2026 one was still being procured, and its use now.
KEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Police Service presented the programme that carries digital Occurrence Books to Parliament on 13 May 2026 as its own investment, and the Interior Cabinet Secretary said on 1 April 2026 that the government was itself procuring the digital occurrence book. On 26 March 2025 the service asked development partners for Sh20 billion for digitisation, the digital Occurrence Book included.

Records made digitally. The occurrence book. The service's annual report for 2022 says its Digital Occurrence Book was launched at Kasarani Sub-County, Nairobi, on 21 November 2019, and on 30 June 2023 the Interior Cabinet Secretary said complaints, statements and details of criminal activity made at stations are recorded in it.

How the record is made. On 30 June 2023 the Deputy Inspector General of Administration Police said reports entered at the station were open to monitoring by ward, county and regional commanders and the Inspector General.

Last twelve months. On 13 May 2026 the Inspector General told a parliamentary committee that digital Occurrence Books would come within three to four months. On 28 August 2026 the Interior Cabinet Secretary said they would accompany police communication centres set up first in Nairobi, Mombasa, Nyeri, Nakuru, Eldoret and Kisumu.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Star reports that 76 police stations in and around Nairobi had their Occurrence Books digitised by 30 June 2023. On 13 May 2026 the Inspector General told MPs the service did not yet have digital Occurrence Books.

Not found. What became of the Nairobi system after June 2023, and whether any station outside the capital area records digitally. No domestic budget line and no dated plan naming the system.

LBR.short: Six officers in the capital's county began entering crime reports on tablets in a 2021 pilot; no source found says whether any station outside it does.
LBR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Liberia National Police was the first to roll out the case management system under the Ministry of Justice, in 2021. The UN Joint Rule of Law Programme supported its design, development and roll-out, and the crime statistics system was developed with UNDP support.

Records made digitally. UNDP reported in March 2023 an officer entering crime reports into a tablet as they come in, with suspects' biodata, photos and GPS locations. The case management system records the parties, the offences, the proceedings and the outcome of a case, and was up and running at the police in June 2022.

How the record is made. The Crime Statistics Information System, as UNDP names it, is online and in two parts: a smartphone or tablet on which the officer enters the report, and a portal that aggregates the reports for police decision-makers. Case data is captured on a web and mobile application that works online and offline, by UNDP's account of April 2022.

Last twelve months. FrontPageAfrica reported in 2026 that Nyehn Town Police Station, the only police facility serving Todee District, has no computers.

Stations doing the digital entry. The crime statistics system went live at police headquarters on 25 January 2021, with training for 15 personnel. Six officers were chosen to pioneer it in Montserrado County, the seat of the capital, that month.

Not found. No fact shows either system in use at a station outside Montserrado County, and no count or share of stations entering records has been found; the newest facts on use are of 2021 to 2023. Nothing is held on who owns, plans or pays for the systems since 2022, or on any change in the last twelve months.

LBY.short: Tripoli's police stations got a digital system for investigation reports in December 2025; no source found reports use outside the capital.
LBY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Tripoli Security Directorate launched its digital transformation system itself at its headquarters on 31 December 2025, with the Attorney General, the security director and a representative of the acting Minister of Interior present, the Libyan News Agency reports.

Records made digitally. Among the components inaugurated that day is a system for the evidence-gathering reports of police stations and traffic sections. On 3 May 2025 Tripoli's security director told the heads of investigation of the police stations and traffic departments, whose officers receive reports and complaints and open the case minutes, to attend to the running of "the digital system".

How the record is made. The instruction of May 2025 names the digital system as a primary source for the database and for documenting legal rights.

Last twelve months. The directorate inaugurated its digital transformation system, including the police-station investigation-reports system, on 31 December 2025.

Stations doing the digital entry. The agency's report of the launch names the system as one for police stations and traffic sections of the Tripoli Security Directorate.

Not found. No station outside the Tripoli Security Directorate is shown using a records system, and no count of stations, plan or source of finance is given. How the record is made is not stated.

LSO.short: An inspection begun in 2023 found posts without stationery keeping registers by hand; no source found says what other stations do, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not found. The one fact on station records, from the Ombudsman's inspection begun in July 2023, shows named posts without stationery keeping registers and forms by hand; it does not say that stations record on paper only, nor what the other inspected stations do. No records system for stations is named, and nothing has been found on its owner, the records made, the stations or the last twelve months.

MAR.short: Police stations record complaints and cases in connected national systems, cases in 16 of 22 commands in 2025; no source found reports the share of stations.
MAR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Direction Générale de la Sûreté Nationale (DGSN), the national police, built GESTARR with its own technical staff and holds its data on a central DGSN server. Its own teams built the case-management system added to GESTARR in 2024.

Records made digitally. Complaints lodged at a police arrondissement are managed in GESTARR (October 2019). In 2024 the DGSN added a system for crime and misdemeanour cases at the arrondissements, each case followed through investigation to submission to the judicial authorities. Its 2025 review says the system it calls Qadaya handles crime and misdemeanour cases in real time.

How the record is made. In October 2019 the arrondissements' information was stored on a central DGSN server and shared between arrondissements across the Kingdom, on a platform that links the arrondissements to each other and to the Sûreté nationale's central services.

Last twelve months. The DGSN's review of 2025 says Qadaya's rollout continued during the year and reached 16 of the 22 police commands, with national coverage in view.

Stations doing the digital entry. GESTARR was in almost all the Kingdom's arrondissements in October 2019, and its generalisation was completed in 2023, when the DGSN counted 454 police arrondissements and had the case system on trial in 350 police posts. The case system was in use in 12 commands in 2024, among them the regional sûretés of Ouarzazate, Errachidia, Taza and Al Hoceima, and Qadaya covered 16 of the 22 commands in 2025.

Not found. The share of police arrondissements entering their records: the DGSN counts commands, not stations. No plan or finance for the systems is stated, and nothing dated places the Royal Gendarmerie's brigades in or out of a record system.

MDG.short: The police opened an online platform for reporting violence and disappearances in 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

MLI.short: An online criminal-record service opened in 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

MOZ.short: Police kept almost no digital records in 2007 and stations used no computers; no source found says whether any station records digitally now.
MOZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. An information technology plan for the Polícia da República de Moçambique had not been achieved at all by October 2007, its needs assessment waiting on a bilateral funding agreement with Spain, UNDP's evaluators stated.

Records made digitally. The evaluation mission, visiting stations and commands in September 2007, verified the almost complete absence of digital records of autos, case files or any other procedure across the force.

How the record is made. In 2007 piles of paper served as case file archives, and stations lacked paper and typewriter ribbons, the mission found.

Last twelve months. Club of Mozambique reported on 23 August 2024 a public security management information system for the Ministry of the Interior, described as nationwide in scope.

Stations doing the digital entry. In September 2007 the use of information technology was non-existent at district and police station level, and most stations the mission visited had a computer that did not work or outdated typewriters.

Not found. Nothing dated after 2007 is held on how stations record, so the owner, plan and finance of a station records system and the last twelve months are not held. No fact says that stations enter reports or cases in the gender-based violence register or in the public security information system.

MRT.short: A police information system launched in June 2025 runs in Nouakchott's commissariats, 34 centres linked; no source found reports use by stations outside the capital.
MRT.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The central office for collecting police information, in the judicial police directorate of the General Directorate of National Security, supervises the police information system, which the directorate calls WAPIS and which its Director General launched on 19 June 2025.

Records made digitally. The system is meant to digitise the work of police commissariats and to document the reports and complaints made at commissariats and their offices, a report of the launch states.

How the record is made. Central commissioners and heads of judicial police sections in the commissariats register in a database held by the central office, to which police centres are being linked, by the same report of 19 June 2025.

Last twelve months. On 19 June 2025 the Director General put the system to work for central directors, the regional directors of the Nouakchott wilayas, central commissioners and heads of judicial police sections in the commissariats.

Stations doing the digital entry. At the launch the director of the central office gave the centres linked as 27 of the National Police and 7 of the National Gendarmerie, and the report puts the rollout across Nouakchott's commissariats at 90 per cent complete.

Not found. No source shows the system in use at a station outside Nouakchott, and the 34 centres linked are given with no place and no total of stations. No plan or source of finance is stated.

MUS.short: All police stations had computers linked to the headquarters complaint and case system in 2025; no source found says how many stations enter records in it.
MUS.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Crime Occurrence Tracking System is the police's own, answered for by the Commissioner of Police through the Prime Minister as Minister of Home Affairs, with the government's Central Informatics Bureau working with the police on its replacement, as the National Assembly heard on 17 June 2025.

Records made digitally. The Prime Minister told the Assembly on 17 June 2025 that the system manages and tracks complaints and declarations from initial reporting to final case disposal, and has been operational since 2011. Défi Media reported in March 2023 that statements made at police stations, once handwritten in Occurrence Books, have been entered in it since 2015.

How the record is made. The system is a digital platform connecting all police stations to the main server at Police Headquarters, used on personal computers in the stations (June 2025). The entries are made directly on computers linked to a server (March 2023).

Last twelve months. On 17 June 2025 the Prime Minister said the system had been enhanced but never upgraded since 2011, and that the police had begun to replace it with a new case management system, with a special consultant to be retained.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Prime Minister said on 17 June 2025 that all police stations are equipped with personal computers for the system, which Défi Media's account of his reply also carries.

Not found. The number of police stations and the share of them entering records in the system: the one figure is of stations equipped. No plan or finance for the system is stated, and nothing is dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

MWI.short: Officers were trained in July 2026 for a crime management system's introduction, after a 2022 pilot in six districts; no source found reports stations using it.
MWI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Crime Management System is the Malawi Police Service's own platform, launched in partnership with UNDP, which said so in July 2026. The earlier case management system for sexual and gender-based violence was rolled out with support from the Spotlight Initiative, funded by the European Union from 2019 to 2023.

Records made digitally. The system covers a case from the moment it is reported until its final disposal, by UNDP's account of July 2026. In 2022 officers entered cases into a crime record system combined with the gender-based violence one.

How the record is made. At a conference in September 2024 the police said it was working towards digitising its processes, a crime management system among them, and UNDP's assessment found most justice-sector processes still on paper.

Last twelve months. On 29 July 2026 the police and UNDP opened a three-day training on the system in Lilongwe, for officers from across the country ahead of its introduction in stations.

Stations doing the digital entry. In 2022 the combined system was piloted in six districts: Mzimba, Nkhata Bay, Ntchisi, Dowa, Nsanje and Machinga. In July 2026 the Crime Management System was being introduced across stations and formations, with the trained officers as its early adopters.

Not found. No source names or counts a station using the Crime Management System, and whether the system piloted in six districts in 2022 stayed in use is not stated. How a record is entered in the new system, a current plan naming it and who pays for it are not held, and nothing found describes rural stations.

NAM.short: In 2026 the police said their case docket system reaches nearly all stations; no source found says how many enter cases there.
NAM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Safety and Security launched the E-Policing eco-system, as it names the force's system, in 2010 at a cost of N$22 million, the minister said on 8 July 2016.

Records made digitally. In October 2026 the Acting Inspector-General said the Force Case Docket Management System is part of an E-Policing System whose implementation began in 2014. In July 2016 the eco-system comprised 16 databases, case docket management among them. A paper of May 2022 says e-policing in Namibia records, stores and shares police information electronically.

How the record is made. A 2022 University of Namibia study of police stations in the Omusati region found that officers there record by hand, first in the station crime register and then in paper files kept in cabinets or boxes, and that no digital record system was in place in those stations.

Last twelve months. In October 2026 the force said it had begun an overhaul of the E-Policing System after slow processing and intermittent interruptions; no timetable or funding was given. In May 2022 officers at Okahandja police station saw storing the occurrence book electronically as duplication of data.

Stations doing the digital entry. According to the Acting Inspector-General in October 2026, the docket system is accessible at all Class A and Class B police stations and about 90% of Class C stations. In May 2022 implementation was immature, because not all units of the Namibian Police had been introduced to the system.

Not found. No source gives a count of stations, or says how many enter reports or cases in the system when they are taken; the one study of stations, in the Omusati region in 2022, found none doing so there. No plan or source of finance has been found.

NER.short: In 2019 a team of eight in Niamey entered cases into the police database; no source found says whether any station outside the capital records digitally.
NER.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The national police's Direction de la Police Technique et Scientifique in Niamey works the database, and its director is responsible for recording criminal acts in Niger, EUCAP Sahel Niger reported on 23 May 2019. The system, launched in Niger in 2012, is financed by the European Union under the Emergency Trust Fund for Africa and implemented by INTERPOL with EUCAP Sahel Niger.

Records made digitally. The database, which Niger calls the Système d'Information Policière en Afrique de l'Ouest (SIPAO), holds offences, criminals' identities and criminal proceedings, and the team recording criminal acts had entered more than 8,000 cases by May 2019.

How the record is made. Cases are entered by a team of 8 under the director in Niamey, while operators are being trained to record data directly from their own service, by the same report of May 2019.

Last twelve months. EUCAP Sahel Niger reported on 23 May 2019 that 700 new cases were recorded in the month.

Stations doing the digital entry. In May 2019 the entry was made in Niamey, by the team of 8.

Not found. Nothing since May 2019 says the system reached stations outside Niamey or still runs. No count of stations has been found, and what the Niamey team enters from is not stated.

NGA.short: Stations made statements, reports and the crime diary by hand in 2021 and 2022; no source found says whether that still holds.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Police Affairs' press unit said in June 2021 that divisional police stations lack basic ICT infrastructure.

Records made digitally. The ministry's press unit stated in June 2021 that statements and reports in police stations are made manually, and that most criminal records of offenders and property across the country are not made electronically. A paper by Jimoh, Wajiga and Garba, published in June 2022, found criminal records kept by hand in a crime diary or ledger at the stations its authors observed.

How the record is made. Sources writing to Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board in October 2020 described statements and police reports written on a standard paper form at the division, with some records kept electronically at state commands or police headquarters. In June 2021 the ministry said writing a statement, generating a report for citizens and entering biodata were done manually.

Last twelve months. The 2022 paper described crime reporting and detailing in stations as a manual method.

Stations doing the digital entry. A law-firm partner told the Board in October 2020 that use of computer networks and electronic databases was still very low among police formations.

Not found. No source found says whether stations still record by hand after 2022. What the Smart Police Station launched in Gombe State in June 2026 records, who owns and funds any station record system, and how many stations enter records digitally are not held.

RWA.short: The investigation bureau processes criminal case files in the justice ministry's electronic system, by its 2024 history; no source found says whether stations enter them.
RWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice manages the Integrated Electronic Case Management System, the Rwanda Investigation Bureau's history of its first years, published in October 2024, states.

Records made digitally. The bureau has incorporated the system to process criminal investigation files, by the same history, which the bureau wrote of its own work and which covers the years 2017 to 2023.

How the record is made. The handling of cases is digitalised from investigation to final judgment through the system, the bureau's history states.

Last twelve months. The bureau's history, published in October 2024, covers 2017 to 2023 and gives the system as the place its investigation files are processed.

Stations doing the digital entry. The history gives the entry of criminal investigation files as the bureau's own, in the system the justice ministry manages.

Not found. Whether the bureau's stations and posts enter the case file themselves, where and how the entry is made, and how many stations do it are not established. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

SDN.short: Police stations took reports on paper in 2022, before the war; no source found says how they record now.
SDN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The police plan for 2024 to 2030, as reported in June 2026, lists digital systems development among its 39 projects in 21 programmes.

Records made digitally. A thesis abstract from Sudan University of Science and Technology, of 2022, proposes converting the reports taken in Sudanese police stations to an electronic system.

How the record is made. The same abstract describes the system for reports in police stations as the old paper one. Its subject is the report that opens the legal procedure for medical treatment after an incident, known as Form 8.

Last twelve months. Police databases were reported in June 2026 as restored after the war, and as having helped settle administrative and financial matters and the payment of entitlements.

Stations doing the digital entry. The 2022 thesis reports no electronic report system in use in police stations.

Not found. No source found says how stations have recorded reports since 2022, and since the war began,. Which records any station system would cover, who owns and funds it, and how many stations use one are not held.

SEN.short: The gendarmerie showed a report-drafting tool still in design in October 2025; no source found says how stations record today, so no stage is set.
SEN.summary: Not found. No dated statement says how stations or gendarmerie brigades record today. The one records tool held was shown at a design workshop on 2 October 2025, its technical form not stated and its use in the units still under discussion; no training, delivery, plan or finance has been found for it.

SLE.short: Police records were paper-based in 2024 and statements still taken on stationery in July 2026; no source found says whether the planned case system has begun.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Sierra Leone Police's Strategic Development Plan 2025-2029 names what it calls an e-Case Management System, for case tracking and processing, as key intervention 4.3, with Crime Services the responsible directorate. The plan says government allocation, limited and late, remains the force's main funding.

Records made digitally. The plan sets the system against a 2024 baseline: a survey on the status of case management in 2025, implementation of its recommendations from 2026 to 2028 and an effective system as the 2029 target.

How the record is made. The plan lists a transition from a paper-based to a digital records management system among its priorities, on a 2024 baseline. A report of 27 July 2026 says stationery would be kept mainly for operational work such as statement-taking and physical record-keeping.

Last twelve months. The force handed 39 laptops to Local Unit Commanders for electronic correspondence, as reported on 27 July 2026.

Stations doing the digital entry. The 2025-2029 plan describes internet connectivity as poor in most police facilities, and schedules it for the six regional headquarters in 2025 and provincial divisional headquarters in 2027 and 2028.

Not found. Whether the 2025 survey of case management was done, or any other step taken to prepare the planned system. No count of stations, and no budget for the system.

SOM.short: Police used paper-based systems in April 2024, when a donor-funded case system was tendered for Mogadishu only; no source found says whether police now use one.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The International Development Law Organization (IDLO) procures the planned case management system with the Office of the Attorney General, which is to receive the source code on completion, and the vendor reports to IDLO (April 2024). The money is from the United States Department of State, under its two-year Somalia Justice Support Programme.

Records made digitally. IDLO stated on 19 April 2024 that the police use paper-based systems, and that the planned system would be the first electronic case management system for Somalia's federal justice institutions.

How the record is made. On the same date IDLO said the police and the Custodial Corps had never made a serious attempt to develop an electronic case management system.

Last twelve months. IDLO invited bids on 19 April 2024, due 3 June 2024, for a system to be developed over 15 months.

Stations doing the digital entry. The tender's criminal investigation module would let investigators create a complaint when it is received at a police station or call centre; its first phase covers only the Criminal Investigation Department in Mogadishu, and nothing was built in April 2024. In Puntland, a member state with its own police, computer stations for nine regional investigation offices, linked to a server in Garowe, were still to be installed in 2021, on equipment given by the European Union's mission.

Not found. No source found says whether the police enter reports or cases in any system built since the 2024 tender, and no station is named as doing so. A plan naming a station record system and anything dated in the last twelve months are not held.

SSD.short: A case system shared by courts, justice ministry and police ran in Juba only in 2021; no source found says how many stations use it.
SSD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNDP supported the setup in Juba of a unified case management system for the courts, the justice ministry and the South Sudan National Police Service, its rule of law report on 2021 states.

Records made digitally. UNDP reports that 10,836 cases, 2,508 of them brought by female claimants, were recorded in 2021 through the system, which it names the Case Monitoring Information Management System, set up for the judiciary, the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs and the police service.

How the record is made. The police service uses a paper-based system for handling crime reporting, with crime files misplaced or lost from police shelves, the abstract of a thesis listed on 7 June 2026 states.

Last twelve months. The thesis listed on 7 June 2026 describes a web application for crime reports that its researcher built and tested for Jubek State; the application is the researcher's own.

Stations doing the digital entry. UNDP's report on 2021 places the case management system in Juba only.

Not found. No count of police stations using the Juba system has been found, nor how many of its cases the police entered or whether the file passes digitally to the court. Nothing on the system is dated after 2021, and the thesis gives no year of its own.

STP.short: A police crime-statistics system was being put in place in 2024; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

SWZ.short: Police trainers were trained in 2025 to enter cases in a justice ministry system; no source found says whether any station enters cases.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Integrated Electronic Case Management System, which Eswatini calls IECMS, is the Ministry of Justice's programme, with a Technical Working Group supporting its training sessions and Synergy International Systems supporting implementation, Independent News reported in August 2025.

Records made digitally. Royal Eswatini Police Service officers were trained on entering new cases into the system and were walked through all the components of a docket at the ministry's training of trainers in August 2025.

How the record is made. At the Mbabane and Manzini One Stop Centres the police record by hand in occurrence books, and police, prosecution and social welfare keep separate paper registers, UNICEF's evaluators stated in 2025.

Last twelve months. The training of police trainers on the system was reported on 20 August 2025.

Stations doing the digital entry. At the Manzini One Stop Centre the police complete paper forms that go to headquarters every 2 to 3 months and are not kept on site, UNICEF's evaluators stated in 2025.

Not found. No station, region or start date has been found for police entry of cases in the IECMS, and the paper recording is described at two One Stop Centres only, not at stations nationally. A plan, the finance and whether the police case file passes digitally to the court are not held.

SYC.short: Police stations are all connected to a national case system, by a 2025 vendor account; no source found says how many enter their own records.
SYC.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The vendor Winsoft, in an account published on 6 January 2025, says the Seychelles Police Department wanted the case app and brought in Transmedia, a British Claris partner, to build it, and that the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime funded and supported the project.

Records made digitally. The app manages cases from start to finish and is the repository of every case recorded, by Winsoft's account of January 2025. Development began with the intake form for incident reports, the record of a single crime; digitising the Occurrence Book itself, the daily record of incidents, was listed as an enhancement to come.

How the record is made. The app runs on desktop computers or iPads as a central resource holding every case, and officers search crimes from other districts (January 2025).

Last twelve months. Winsoft's account of 6 January 2025 says the department has continued to evolve its use of the app since deployment.

Stations doing the digital entry. The detective commander of Mont Fleuri station is quoted by Winsoft, in January 2025, saying all police stations are connected. The same account says the database is bedding in at headquarters in Victoria.

Not found. The number of police stations and the share of them entering their own records: the one figure is a station commander's statement that all are connected, with no year. No plan is stated, and nothing is dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

TCD.short: A police data centre was inaugurated in 2025; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

TGO.short: Police said in April 2026 all police and gendarmerie stations have the regional police information tool; no source found says whether any enters reports in it.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. SIPAO, the West African police information system, is an ECOWAS programme implemented by INTERPOL with European Union funding, and was handed to ECOWAS and the national authorities on 8 April 2025, after that funding ended.

Records made digitally. A police divisional commissioner said on 14 April 2026 that the country's commissariats and gendarmerie brigades have SIPAO as a tool.

How the record is made. The tool in the stations is that of the regional programme, SIPAO, on the commissioner's account of 14 April 2026.

Last twelve months. The police stated on 14 April 2026 that every station has the tool, a year after the programme's handover of 8 April 2025.

Stations doing the digital entry. All commissariats and gendarmerie brigades in Togo have the SIPAO tool, the police said on 14 April 2026.

Not found. No source found states whether any station enters reports or cases in the tool, which records, or how, and the police give no count of stations. No plan or source of finance has been found.

TUN.short: Twenty-one model National Guard and National Security centres were under construction in 2025; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
TUN.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

TZA.short: A digital case file system was installed and central stations in 23 regions connected by April 2024; no source found says whether stations enter cases.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Minister for Home Affairs told Parliament in May 2024 that the ministry had installed the digital case file management information system itself, in carrying out the Criminal Justice Commission's recommendations. The ministry's 2024/25 budget carried TZS 40.5 billion for strengthening the ICT system, installing the biometric system and buying police radios.

Records made digitally. The case file. The minister said in May 2024 that the ministry has installed a digital case file management information system, to be connected with the criminal justice institutions.

How the record is made. By April 2024 the regional Central Police Stations were connected over the national broadband backbone and linked to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Last twelve months. In May 2024 the minister said police stations in other regions were still being connected to the system.

Stations doing the digital entry. The minister said that by April 2024 the Central Police Stations in 23 regions had been connected.

Not found. Whether a station enters the case file when the case is opened, how many stations there are in all, and whether the link to the prosecutor carries the case file. No plan or funding source for the system, and nothing dated after May 2024.

UGA.short: Digital case files were piloted in ten Kampala divisions in 2017, with upcountry stations outside in 2021; no source found reports use since.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Uganda Police Force's ICT Directorate developed the Crime Records Management System itself, and the force resolved in October 2022 to embark on the Electronic Policing Information System, ePIS. A UNODC consultancy notice of 2023 gives the ePIS programme four interventions: business process reform, automation of case management, enabling infrastructure and digital skilling.

Records made digitally. The case file. The force said in December 2017 that its crime records system processes and tracks the progress of case files. A journal article of June 2024 says ePIS is to manage all cases registered and investigated by the police from inception to conclusion.

How the record is made. The UNODC notice of 2023 calls the force's collection, processing and sharing of data largely manual. The Independent reported in 2021 that stations had one records officer for case files and detectives kept the files of their own cases.

Last twelve months. In June 2024 ePIS was in its design phase.

Stations doing the digital entry. In December 2017 the crime records system was being piloted in ten divisions of Kampala Metropolitan. The Independent reported in 2021 that it had been upgraded and tested in Kampala, with tests in upcountry stations to follow. The justice sector's bulletin of May 2024 lists lack of internet connectivity at upcountry police stations among the obstacles.

Not found. Whether any station outside Kampala Metropolitan enters cases digitally, how many stations the Kampala pilot covered and whether it still runs. No costing, period or funding source for ePIS, and nothing dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

ZAF.short: Case dockets were captured digitally at 998 of 1,157 police stations in May 2021, 86.3% of all police stations; no source found reports the rural share.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The South African Police Service runs the case docket system as its own. Its Strategic Plan 2025 to 2030, tabled on 4 April 2025, lists the enhancement of case docket management, with full functionality in 2027/28. The 2025/26 plan funds its information systems from Programme 1 of Vote 28.

Records made digitally. When a complaint is taken at a station and the elements of a crime exist, a case docket is opened and captured on what the police call the Crime Administration System and the Investigate Case Docket Management System, by the Acting Minister's reply to a question of 31 December 2025.

How the record is made. The docket is captured at the station's Community Service Centre, signed off on the system by the Shift Commander and verified on it at station, provincial and national level, with a physical docket kept beside it. In May 2021 the docket system depended on the station's network link.

Last twelve months. On 11 April 2025 the Police Minister announced a partnership with the private sector to digitise case dockets and upgrade five police stations.

Stations doing the digital entry. The police told Parliament's police committee on 4 May 2021 that the docket system was in 998 police stations with 159 still to be covered, 86.3% of all police stations. The 159 registered cases on the old system, which fed the same database. In 2023/24, 789 of 1,160 stations sent complainants text messages about a docket through the system.

Not found. No count of stations registering dockets on the system later than May 2021, and no rural share. Whether the first report of an occurrence is recorded digitally, and whether the docket passes digitally to the prosecutor or the court.

ZMB.short: Stations recorded on paper in 2024; network equipment for 40 arrived by February 2026, and no source found says whether any yet records digitally.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Zambia Police Strategic Plan 2023-2026 gives guidelines for an e-record management system for the service's electronic records, by a University of Zambia study. The service's Technical Services Directorate, the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security and the SMART Zambia Institute build and run the police's electronic systems.

Records made digitally. In 2024 the occurrence books, crime register books and docket movement books were kept on paper at headquarters and across the service. Headquarters had a Police Information Management System, a database of police records including crime reports and case files, officials told the study between November 2024 and January 2025. UNDP said in November 2021 that an Electronic Occurrence Book had been rolled out to the Victim Support Unit.

How the record is made. Statements are recorded and dockets opened by hand, so complainants and witnesses attend a station in person, informants told the study between November 2024 and January 2025.

Last twelve months. The SMART Zambia Institute received routers, switches, access points and firewalls for 40 police stations, to connect them to a centralised digital system, as reported on 3 February 2026.

Stations doing the digital entry. In 2024 the occurrence book, crime register and docket were digitised nowhere in the service, and rollout from headquarters to divisions and stations was planned.

Not found. No fact shows a station entering a report or a case digitally, and who enters the records held in the headquarters database is not stated. The centralised system the 40 stations are to join is not yet in place, with no pilot, station count or source of finance given for it.

ZWE.short: An electronic docket system was announced in December 2025 as coming soon; no source found says whether any station yet records digitally.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Home Affairs minister said on 17 January 2024 that computerising police operations, under what he called the ZRP Integrated Information System, is part of the ministry's ICT strategy approved by Cabinet in 2022, and that the police had finished a needs assessment and were looking for a partner. In December 2021 the Information minister said government would bear all costs of digitising rural stations.

Records made digitally. The officer commanding Harare Province said, in remarks reported on 9 December 2025, that the police would soon move to an electronic system for processing all dockets.

How the record is made. The force's Horizon 2025 strategic plan, as reported on 16 December 2021, decries the manual management of information, which it says makes information hard to retrieve and leads to its loss and destruction.

BFA.short: In June 2026 a workshop with business, universities and civil society reviewed the draft AI roadmap; no source found says whether their comments were published.
BFA.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. On 17 June 2026 the Ministry of Digital Transition held a national validation workshop on its draft national artificial intelligence roadmap for 2026 to 2030, where government, the private sector, universities, civil society organisations and technical partners reviewed the draft. The ministry had drafted it with the private sector, universities, research centres, civil society and the diaspora. SSD.short: A workshop on the data protection bill was held with civil society, reported in 2026; no source found says whether what was said was published.
SSD.summary:

The regulator, the National Communication Authority, and Digital Rights Frontlines, a civil society group, convened a two-day workshop on the Data Protection Bill 2025, reported on 5 May 2026. More than 30 people took part, among them members of parliament and civil society groups. A ministry workshop in Juba on 8 to 10 September 2026 prepared for the same bill. About 50 people attended, among them civil society groups and telecom operators. In October 2025 the chair of the Assembly's Information Committee said its work on the cybercrime bill included public consultations and workshops.

Required consultation and standing body. The South Sudan Internet Governance Forum is a national forum of government and people outside it, with a Multistakeholder Advisory Group. Its 2026 meeting was held in Juba, reported on 4 July 2026. The National Constitutional Review Commission is consulting the public on the permanent constitution, reported in August 2026.

Not found. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy has been found from the last three years. Nor have the comments received, or a written answer to them.

STP.short: The national cybersecurity strategy was put out for public comment in 2025; no source found says whether anything said in reply was published.
STP.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. In September 2025 AGER, under the STP Digital project, put the National Cybersecurity Strategy of São Tomé and Príncipe 2024-2028 out for public consultation, together with the action plan annexed to it. It invited contributions by telephone and by email within 30 days of publication. The notice of the consultation is on AGER's website.

Required consultation and standing body. AGER convened the first Fórum de Governança da Internet de São Tomé e Príncipe on 28 to 30 July 2026, the country's internet governance forum, known as FGI STP. Government, the private sector, academia, civil society and the technical community took part in it. The forum was not a consultation on a named law or policy.

SWZ.short: In 2025 the communications regulator consulted on retiring 2G and 3G and published its answers to comments; no rule requiring consultation is known.
SWZ.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Eswatini Communications Commission, ESCCOM, put its proposed decision on retiring 2G and 3G networks out for public consultation on 9 November 2024, and its final decision of 17 June 2025 summarises the comments stakeholders sent, sets out its response to them and extends the timelines by two years. It also invited written comments from all interested stakeholders and the public on a proposed broadcasting licence fee schedule, with a deadline of 11 August 2025. The Ministry of ICT's Department of Research, Science, Technology and Innovation held a two-day validation session in February 2026 on the draft review of the National STI Policy and the combined 4IR and 5IR Strategy, which covers artificial intelligence, automation and data governance. The department's director said the draft was brought back to those consulted to refine, and ESEPARC, an economic policy research centre, presented. The Ministry also held a validation workshop at Ezulwini, reported on 22 July 2026, on the draft National Data Governance Policy (2027-2031). It brought together government ministries, regulators, the private sector, civil society, academia and development partners.

Required consultation and standing body. The long title of the Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act 2022 names a National Cybersecurity Advisory Council.

Not found. No source from the last three years says a consultation on a digital law or policy was held because a law, decree or published procedure required it.

SYC.short: In 2023 and 2024 the financial regulator consulted on a virtual asset law and published a response; no rule requiring it is known.
SYC.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. On 20 December 2023 the Financial Services Authority, for the Ministry of Finance, launched a public consultation on the proposed Virtual Asset Service Providers framework. It invited written responses and held a live session on 9 January 2024, in person and online, attended by about 50 to 60 people, with further sessions for Securities Act licensees, corporate service providers and virtual asset providers already operating. The Ministry and the Authority published a consultation response dated 7 March 2024 summarising the consultation, which drew about 15 detailed written responses. A member of the drafting team says the National Digital and AI Strategy 2026-2031 followed consultations with the private sector, academia and civil society, closing with a national validation workshop in mid-2026.

Required consultation and standing body. The National AML/CFT Committee approved and launched that consultation. The Cabinet approved the holding of a Digital Economic Transformation Forum with members from several sectors, on record in September 2026.

Not found. No source from the last three years says a consultation on a digital law or policy was held because a law, decree or published procedure required it.

TCD.short: In 2024 the media regulator held a public hearing on web radio and television rules that its law requires; no standing body's view is known.
TCD.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The media regulator HAMA held a day of public consultation at the Cefod on 22 November 2024. It put its draft specifications for web radio and web television to the managers of private media. The telecommunications ministry, with ECA and GIZ, held consultations in N'Djamena on 13 to 15 May 2026 for the National Data Governance Strategy. The private sector, academia, civil society and telecom operators were listed among the participants. A three-day workshop opened on 18 May 2026 with technology incubators and security specialists, to feed the drafting. On 7 October 2026 the ministry held a national validation workshop on the draft strategy, with academics, civil society and the private sector invited. The Minister asked the academic and civil society representatives to say frankly what they think.

Required consultation and standing body. HAMA's head of legal affairs said the November 2024 hearing was required by article 43 of the audiovisual communication law. That article has HAMA set such specifications after a public hearing. Civil society and other interested parties give their views at it.

Not found. No standing body with members from outside government has been found giving its view on a named digital law or policy. No report of the November 2024 hearing has been found either.

TGO.short: In January 2025 the Ministry of Commerce held workshops on e-commerce rules with outside groups; nothing found shows published results or a required consultation.

Consultation and what was published of it. The Ministry of Commerce held a two-phase national stakeholder workshop on strengthening the e-commerce regulatory framework, in Kara on 21 January 2025 and in Lomé on 24 January 2025. Businesses, consumer associations, regulators and financial service operators took part in it. The ministry's page on the workshops is the only record of it held. On 19 December 2025 a ministry workshop on the draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy brought in the private sector and civil society and gathered their contributions.

Required consultation and standing body. No standing body with members from outside government has been found. The nearest held fact is the Forum National sur la Gouvernance de l'Internet au Togo, a national internet governance forum run by Internet Society Togo and held each year since 2010. Its 12th edition was on 19 June 2026, and the data protection authority sat on a panel at it.

Not found. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them has been found from the last three years.

TUN.short: In 2025 and 2026 the telecommunications regulator put fibre-sharing rules out for public comment; no source found says whether it published what it was told.
TUN.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Instance Nationale des Télécommunications, the telecommunications regulator, ran a first public consultation from 26 September to 26 November 2025 on the conditions for sharing fibre-optic access infrastructure. It opened a second from 6 March to 2 April 2026 on the rules for that sharing, which any contributor could answer by email or post. The E-Government Unit of the Presidency of the Government drew up the 2023-2025 open government action plan, whose commitments cover open data and the digitalisation of administrative services, through three regional workshops in Gafsa, Kairouan and Kef. Over 320 proposals were collected through a digital participation portal, workshops, email and public structures, and the Tunisian Civil Forum for OGP took part, as a results report published on 4 August 2026 states.

Required consultation and standing body. Government decree 2018-328 of 29 March 2018 requires public consultation on public policies and draft texts, with a published consultation report.

Not found. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years has been found.

TZA.short: In 2026 regulators and academic institutions gave views on a draft data governance strategy at a workshop; no source found says whether they were published.
TZA.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. On 12 March 2026 the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, working with the Government of Tanzania, convened a national validation workshop in Dodoma on the draft Tanzania Electronic Data Governance Strategy, known as TZeDGS. Regulatory authorities, academic institutions and sectoral agencies took part in the workshop and gave their views on the draft, and what they said informed refinements to the strategy. The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology closed the workshop. On 20 October 2026 Parliament's Standing Committee on Infrastructure invited the public to give views on ratifying the Malabo Convention, in person or in writing.

Required consultation and standing body. The Africa Internet Governance Forum 2025 was held in Dar es Salaam, with the Government of Tanzania as host. National consultations on the East African Community's Regional AI Strategy were held in Tanzania on 12 February 2026.

Not found. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years has been found.

It announced a multi-stakeholder committee on licensing for resellers. On 4 June 2025 the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance held a validation workshop on draft guidelines for ICT infrastructure in buildings, roads and transport. Private telecom companies and professional bodies took part, after stakeholder consultations in 2024/25.

Required consultation and standing body. The nearest fact is the committee UCC announced in October 2026, a multi-stakeholder committee on licensing for resellers. ZAF.short: Parliament, the communications regulator and the Treasury put digital bills and draft rules out for public comment in 2026; no source says what they heard.

The communications regulator, ICASA, published draft amendments to its radio spectrum regulations on 15 May 2026 and held public hearings on 19 and 20 August for those who had sent written comments. The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies put its draft national artificial intelligence policy out for public comment on 10 April 2026 and later withdrew it. The National Treasury and the Reserve Bank asked for written comments by 30 September 2026 on a draft crypto asset manual, and said comments on the draft capital flow regulations published on 17 April were being considered. The universal service agency opened a public consultation on the 2010 determination on universal access, reported on 10 October 2026. The Bureau of Standards invited comment on draft AI standards until 10 November 2026. Home Affairs took written comments on draft digital identity regulations until 6 June 2026.

ICASA gave notice on 4 September 2026 of an inquiry under section 4B of the ICASA Act into the affordability of telecommunications services, inviting written answers to a questionnaire and public comment on a discussion document. A gazette of 30 September 2026 withdrew that notice and carried a new draft notice inviting comment on a questionnaire and a discussion document.

Not found. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them has been found from the last three years.

On 29 August 2025 it signed a memorandum in Bujumbura with the Office congolais de contrôle, its counterpart in the Democratic Republic of Congo, on cooperation in standardisation, quality control and certification. It publishes an annual work programme of standards projects; issue 341, updated on 16 April 2026, covers April 2026 to March 2027. None of the three sources names a standard on information technology or data.

CMR.short: Cameroon's standards agency, ANOR, was listed as developing and certifying standards in 2026; no source found says whether any covers information technology or data.
CMR.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Cameroon's standards body is ANOR, the Agence des Normes et de la Qualité, which the international standards organisation's member page describes as responsible for developing and certifying standards in Cameroon, as at 16 October 2026. That page is the one held statement of the body's role. It names no national standard on information technology or data, and it gives no law or decree that set the body up.

Certification. The same member page gives the body a certifying role in general terms and names no certification against a standard on information technology or data. The nearest held fact is the ISO 27001 certification of ST DIGITAL, a private pan-African data centre operator, reported on 3 March 2026. It is a private company's certificate, and no public body in Cameroon is recorded as certified.

COD.short: The Office congolais de contrôle, set up in 1974, is the national standards and certification body; no national standard on information technology or data known.

ISO's member page for the office, dated 2026, says it was created by Ordinance No. 74-013 of 1974, so it rests on an act of the state and not on a private initiative. The same page names no national standard on information technology or data that the office has issued or adopted, and says nothing of the content of its catalogue.

Certification. ISO's member page gives certification as one of the office's three functions, beside metrology and standardisation. It does not say what the office certifies, names no certification against a standard on information technology or data, and names no public body, ministry or agency that the office has certified. It gives no figure for the organisations that hold its certificates.

COG.short: The national standards body was created by law in 2015; no source found says whether it has issued a standard on information technology or data.
COG.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Congo's standards body is the Agence Congolaise de Normalisation et de la Qualité, known as ACONOQ. The international standards organisation's member page says that Law No. 19-2015 of 29 October 2015 created it as the national standardization body, and that it manages the national standards register. The page names no standard on information technology or data that the agency has issued, and gives no catalogue of national standards or count of them.

Certification. The same member page describes an agency that manages the national standards register. It records no certification offered or granted by the agency against a standard on information technology or data, and names no organisation the agency has certified, whether in government or outside it.

Cabo Verde's standards body is the Instituto de Gestão da Qualidade e da Propriedade Intelectual, which publishes the list of Cabo Verdean standards, updated in March 2024. The list runs from NCV 001:2015 to NCV 025:2023. Of its 25 national standards, 21 are on agricultural, fisheries and food products and four on tourism; it holds none on information technology, information security, software or data. The list does not state the law that set the institute up.

Certification. The catalogue of March 2024 is the nearest text held. It lists standards and no certification scheme. Certificates held by a port company, a data centre and the state's digital agency against international standards are listed below, and none names the institute or a certifier accredited in the country.

Not found. No source found names a national standard on information technology or data.

DJI.short: Djibouti's standards agency, created by law in 2021, set up its first two technical committees in 2025; neither covers information technology or data.
DJI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Djibouti's standards body is the Agence Djiboutienne des Normes et de la Qualité, created by a law of 7 January 2021 as a public industrial and commercial body attached to the commerce ministry and named the national reference body for drawing up standards. A decree of 4 May 2022 organises it. The international standards organisation's member record lists it as the national standards body, put into operation in 2022. The Council of Ministers of 13 January 2026 examined its 2026 budget of 134.9 million Djibouti francs, up from 112.1 million in 2025, and recorded that in 2025 it made two technical committees operational, for agri-food products and for electrical and household appliances. No standard on information technology or data is named.

Certification. The 2022 decree charges the agency with certifying conformity to standards and accrediting the bodies that assess it. It names no scheme for information technology or data.

DZA.short: Algeria's standards institute holds a national standard on ordering text in information technology, due for revision in 2026; no source found reports certification against such standards.
DZA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Algeria's standards body is the Algerian Institute of Standardisation, created by executive decree 98-69 of 21 February 1998 as a public industrial and commercial establishment under the industry ministry, charged with drawing up, publishing and disseminating Algerian standards. Its draft national standardisation programme for 2026, published in February 2026, lists the revision of an existing national standard, NA 13037, against the 2025 edition of the international standard on comparing and ordering character strings in information technology.

Certification. The 1998 decree also charges the institute with adopting conformity marks and authorising their use. Nothing in it, or in the draft programme for 2026, names certification against a standard on information technology or data, or an organisation certified against one.

EGY.short: Egypt's standards organisation issued a national standard on exchanging electricity metering data in 2025; no source found reports certification against such standards.
EGY.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Egyptian Organization for Standardization and Quality states that it is the sole official body for preparing and issuing Egyptian standards, set up by Presidential Decree 2 of 1957 and given its present name by Presidential Decree 83 of 2005. ISO's member page says a 1979 Presidential Decree reorganised it as the only official authority for standardization, quality control and metrology. Its register lists Egyptian Standard 7982-1/2025, endorsed on 1 October 2025, which adopts the international standard on the exchange of electricity metering data and is classed under information technology. The standard is not obligatory. A ministerial decision of 2022 lets an international or foreign standard stand where no Egyptian one exists.

Certification. The register entry for the 2025 standard is the nearest text held, and it names no certifier and no organisation certified against the standard.

Not found. No source found says the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country offers certification against a national standard on information technology or data.

ERI.short: Eritrea's standards institution, set up in 1995, has published 446 national standards; no source found says whether any covers information technology or data.
ERI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Eritrea's standards body is the Eritrean Standards Institution, established by Proclamation No. 75 of 1995 as an autonomous body with legal personality. The proclamation makes it the sole national organ for standardisation, quality assurance and metrology, and gives it the power to prepare compulsory Eritrean Standards. The international standards organisation's member record gives 446 national standards published, and calls the institution the sole standardisation body in the country. The proclamation names no standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 1995 proclamation covers quality assurance as well as standardisation and measurement. The record held names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the institution has certified against any standard.

ETH.short: Ethiopia approved mandatory national cybersecurity standards in April 2026; no source found says whether anyone can be certified against them.

The approval is the most recent dated fact held on the country's standards, and it names the board as the approving body.

Certification. The nearest held fact is the approval in April 2026 of mandatory cybersecurity standards and guidelines by the Ethiopian Standards Board. The announcement describes the standards and who drafted them. It names no organisation that has been certified against them and no certifier that offers certification.

Not found. Nothing found says the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country offers certification against a national standard on information technology or data.

GAB.short: Gabon's standards agency was created by decree in 2014; no source found says whether it has issued any standard on information technology or data.

The international standards organisation's member directory lists the agency. The decree makes it the country's national body for standardization, and its standards are published as Gabonese standards. Neither page names a standard on information technology or data.

KEN.short: Kenya's standards bureau was set up by statute and began operating in 1974; no source found reports a national standard on information technology or data.
KEN.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Kenya's standards body is the Kenya Bureau of Standards, which was established by the Standards Act, Chapter 496, and started operations in July 1974. A 2026 release says it provides standards development, metrology, conformity assessment, training and certification. In August 2026 it was led by a director general and overseen by a National Standards Council. The ICT Authority's Government Data Centre Standard, approved in January 2020, names the bureau as the source of information on valid national and international standards and says it took part in developing the authority's standards under a memorandum of understanding. None of these sources names a national standard on information technology or data that the bureau has issued.

Certification. The 2026 release lists certification among the bureau's services, and names no scheme for information technology or data.

Not found. No source found names a national standard on information technology or data.

LBR.short: Liberia established its standards authority by an Act published in 2022; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
LBR.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Liberia's standards body is the Liberia Standards Authority. An Act to amend the Executive Law and establish the authority was published by the commerce ministry on 5 August 2022. Its preamble cites the quality infrastructure of the Economic Community of West African States and the country's obligations under the World Trade Organization's agreement on technical barriers to trade. Only the preamble of the Act is held, and it names no national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The Act's preamble is the only text held on the authority. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the authority has certified. The country's national quality policy is listed below.

LBY.short: Libya's standards centre, created by a 1990 law, adopted new standards in 2026; none is known to cover information technology or data.
LBY.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Libya's standards body is the National Centre for Standardization and Metrology, created by Law 5 of 1990, issued on 15 May 1990. The law charges the centre with quality control and with preparing, adopting and supervising standards, and makes the standards it adopts binding nationwide. On 3 February 2026 the centre's supreme committee, meeting at the planning ministry, adopted its plan for 2026 and a number of Libyan standards. The report of the meeting names none of them as a standard on information technology or data. ISO's member page lists the centre as Libya's national standards body, a public organization established in 1990, which issues and approves standards.

Certification. The 1990 law gives the centre quality control as well as standard-setting. Neither it nor the report of the 2026 meeting names certification against a standard on information technology or data.

Not found. No source found names a national standard on information technology or data.

LSO.short: Lesotho's standards institution became operational in 2020; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
LSO.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Lesotho's standards body is the Lesotho Standards Institution. The trade and industry minister said on 16 September 2020 that the institution, created by an Act published in 2014, was now operational as the country's national standards body, with a mandate to develop and publish national standards. The minister's address is the only source found on the institution, and it names no national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The minister's address of 2020 sets out the institution's mandate to develop and publish standards. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the institution has certified. The communications regulator's quality-of-service rules of 2023 are listed below.

MAR.short: Morocco's standards body, IMANOR, has existed since 2010; no source found reports its standards on information technology and any certification against them.
MAR.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Morocco's national standards body is IMANOR, the Moroccan Institute for Standardisation, which ISO's member page lists under its own heading as Institut Marocain de Normalisation. The same page says IMANOR was created in 2010 to replace SNIMA, the earlier body, and that it produces Moroccan standards. Nothing found names a Moroccan standard on information technology or data, or says which of its standards cover that field.

Nothing found says IMANOR or a certifier accredited in Morocco offers certification against a standard on information technology or data, or that any organisation, public or private, has been certified against one.

Standards body and its standards. Madagascar's standards body is the Bureau des Normes de Madagascar, which was created by decree 98-944 of 4 November 1998 and is now governed by decree 2014-1570 of 30 September 2014. A United Nations Development Programme assessment published in December 2025 describes it as the national standards body and a correspondent member of the international standards organisation, and says public information shows no specific programme on standards for artificial intelligence or data governance. Neither source names a national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The bureau's own description of its activities is the nearest text held. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the bureau has certified.

MLI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Mali's standards body is the Agence Malienne de Normalisation et de Promotion de la Qualité, created by an ordinance of 19 March 2012 as a public administrative body with legal personality and financial autonomy, charged with implementing national policy on standardisation and quality promotion. The international standards organisation records it as Mali's national standards body and a full member. Its board, meeting on 29 January 2026, adopted a 2026 budget of 243.3 million CFA francs, against 318.4 million in 2025. None of the three names a national standard on information technology or data.

MOZ.short: Mozambique's standards institute certifies quality management under a 2022 decree; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
MOZ.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Mozambique's standards body is the Instituto Nacional de Normalização e Qualidade, which the ISO member page says was established on 24 March 1993 as the central body coordinating standardisation and quality nationally. Decree 8/2022 of 14 March 2022 approves the regulation on standardisation and conformity assessment and gives the institute the job of coordinating standardisation and implementing Mozambican technical standards. On 7 May 2026 the economy ministry and the institute announced that a certificate of conformity becomes mandatory from 1 June 2026 for listed imports, among them rice, fortified foods, used vehicles, tyres and construction steel. Neither names a standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 2022 decree also charges the institute with certifying management systems, products, services and people. On 16 March 2026 it awarded a quality management certificate to the finance area of the National Institute of Health; no certificate against a standard on information technology or data is named.
