MRT.short: Mauritania set up a standards office and a standardisation council by decree in 2023; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
MRT.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Mauritania's standards body is the Office National de Normalisation et de Métrologie, which Decree 2023-113 of 7 September 2023 says was instituted by a decree of 9 May 2023. The same decree creates a national council for standardisation and quality promotion, an advisory body under the industry minister, under a 2010 law on standardisation and quality promotion, and gives the office its secretariat. The decree was published in the official journal of 15 October 2023. It names no national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. Decree 2023-113 also gives the office the secretariat of the accreditation cell it creates, the Mauritanian accreditation committee listed below. It names no body accredited to certify, and no certification against a standard on information technology or data.

MUS.short: Mauritius's standards bureau certifies against the national information security standard; six public bodies held its certificates at the end of 2025.
MUS.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Mauritius Standards Bureau became a corporate body under the Mauritius Standards Bureau Act 1993, in effect from 16 July 1993, with the object of preparing and revising Mauritian Standards. The national standard on information security management is MS ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the designation under which the bureau's certification register lists it.

Certification. The bureau certifies organisations itself. Its certification unit ran the national information security certification scheme in 2021/2022, under regulations of 2008, and kept eight organisations certified; the scheme is accredited by the national accreditation service. A telecoms company says the bureau first certified its data centre in 2013. The bureau's register at 31 December 2025 lists ten certificates, all marked as accredited. Six are held by public bodies: the Passport and Immigration Office, the national computer emergency response team, the Mauritius Revenue Authority, the central information systems division of the technology ministry, the police information technology unit and the National Sanctions Secretariat.

Not found. All four questions are answered.

MWI.short: Malawi's standards bureau, established by a 2012 Act, is accredited to certify quality management; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
MWI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Malawi Bureau of Standards is established by the Malawi Bureau of Standards Act, No. 14 of 2012, assented to on 12 July 2012, as a body corporate under a Malawi Standards Board, with the object of preparing and issuing standards. The Act was published on 27 July 2012. ISO's member page lists the bureau as the national standards body responsible for preparing and publishing Malawi standards in 2026. The text of it held names no standard on information technology or data.

Certification. A certificate of the Southern African Development Community's accreditation service, dated 14 December 2025, accredits the bureau to certify quality management systems and describes it as established by the Act. The accreditation, listed below, covers quality management; the certificate names no national standard on information technology or data, and no accreditation to certify against one.

NAM.short: Namibia's standards institution had published 235 standards by 2025; none on information technology or data is known.
NAM.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Namibian Standards Institution is established by the Standards Act, 2005, signed on 23 December 2005, as the national institution for the promotion, issue and maintenance of standards, under a Namibian Standards Council. Its chief executive said in October 2025 that it had published 235 standards since it was set up in 2008, that the national stock is 275, and that a national standardisation strategy targets 1,267 within three years. A notice of 15 June 2026 announced four new Namibian Standards, on chilled seafood, dates, laundry processes and the energy performance of refrigerating appliances. ISO's member page lists the institution as Namibia's national standards body. No standard on information technology or data is named.

Certification. The Standards Act is the nearest text held, and it names no certification against a standard on information technology or data.

NGA.short: Nigeria's standards organisation was set up by an Act of 1971 to prepare standards; no source found says whether any covers information technology or data.
NGA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Nigeria's standards body is the Standards Organisation of Nigeria, established by an Enabling Act of 1971 to prepare standards, as the international standards organisation's member page for it states. That page is the one source found on the body's standing, and it dates the body's founding rather than any later work. It names no national standard on information technology or data, and neither does any other source found.

It records no certification against a standard on information technology or data, and no source found says that an organisation in Nigeria can be certified against one.

RWA.short: Rwanda's standards board has published more than 4,130 standards, as reported in 2025; none on information technology or data is known.
RWA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Rwanda Standards Board is established by Law 50/2013 of 28 June 2013, with legal personality and the mission to establish and publish national standards, which the law defines as voluntary. The international standards organisation said in October 2025 that the board has developed and published more than 4,130 standards, covering food, engineering, services, water, chemistry and consumer products. The Official Gazette of 20 November 2025 carries the board's notice publishing a list of national standards; the passages held do not show the list. A Korean grant of 8 million dollars for 2024 to 2028 supports the use of digital tools in the board's work. No standard on information technology or data is named.

Certification. On 6 March 2026 the board signed mutual recognition arrangements with the standards bodies of Congo and Zimbabwe. No certification against a standard on information technology or data is named.

The catalogue lists a 2019 standard on the digital repository and a 2016 standard on an application protocol for open systems interconnection, a 2015 standard on managing metadata for records and a 2020 standard on the messages financial cards exchange, and a 2018 information technology standard on the yield of printer toner cartridges.

General Notice No. 79 of 2025, under the Standards and Quality Act, 2023, designated 19 new Eswatini National Standards in August 2025. Tunisia's standards body is the Institut National de la Normalisation et de la Propriété Industrielle, which ISO's member registry describes in October 2026 as a public institution under the Ministry of Industry, in charge of standardisation and of product and quality systems certification. Standards body and its standards. Tanzania's standards body is the Tanzania Bureau of Standards, which the international standards organisation's member page says was established by the Standards Act of 1975 and operational from 6 April 1976. It published its list of new and revised compulsory Tanzania Standards as of October 2025, enforceable under the Standards Act, which the list cites as chapter 130 of the laws in its revised edition of 2023. The entries held on that list are on batteries, conductors, fasteners, wire and similar goods. In October 2026 the Director General of the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority said the bureau has newly introduced a Tanzania Standard on accessibility of communications and ICT products and services for persons with disabilities. In February 2025 the bureau circulated drafts for comment, including adoptions of ISO/IEC 23894, 27032, 27035, 27036 and 27043.

Inclusion counted. UNDP says 38,026 IDPs were enrolled in the national ID in Baidoa, of over 500,000 IDPs there.

Not found. Nothing further is asked of this indicator.

SSD.short: Refugees or displaced people could use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID in 2026; how many do is not counted.
SSD.summary:
Registration and documents. The World Bank ID4D diagnostic says nearly 90% of South Sudan's population lacks government-recognised identification, with women, internally displaced people, returnees and refugees disproportionately excluded. The World Bank project paper says targeting and registration of beneficiaries of the SNSOP cash transfers, which expects 7,000 refugee households, has started using an MIS linked to a biometric registration tool and payment application. The World Bank project paper states 448,243 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered in South Sudan as of March 2024, in over 21 locations.

Digital services. A GSMA, REACH and UNHCR survey of 2,135 households in four refugee-hosting locations found about 78% of respondents (refugee and host community together) had SIM cards registered in their own name, though focus groups revealed barriers to registration in certain locations.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID.

STP.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

SWZ.short: Refugees or displaced people could use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID in 2026; how many do is not counted.
SWZ.summary:
Registration and documents. Eswatini hosts 5 058 registered refugees and asylum seekers, and the Ministry of Home Affairs dispatched 70 refugee status permits and 77 machine-readable Convention Travel Documents in April-June 2026. UNHCR's regional report says Eswatini has incorporated refugees and asylum-seekers into national registration systems. 3 facts are held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined. In March 2025 the central bank's Deputy Governor said the bank and the Commissioner for Refugees had prepared a know-your-customer information pack for asylum seekers and refugees, and recommended that every refugee get a permit or registration document giving entry to the civil registry and a personal identification number, not yet in place.

Digital services. The Ministry of Home Affairs says refugee status permits let holders obtain personal identification numbers, national identity cards and access to government and financial services.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID.

SYC.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

TCD.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2025; their access to digital services is not on record.
TCD.summary:
Registration and documents. The World Bank states that, with other actors, 25,000 secure identity documents have been issued to refugees to date, against a target of 80,000. More than 4,000 refugees in N'Djamena had received NNIR identity documents as of 1 May 2025, against a pilot target of 7,000, per Biometric Update citing UNHCR. UNHCR, with ANATS and CNARR, launched at the Abeche guichet unique an operation to enrol Sudanese refugees biometrically into the national database.

Digital services. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

TGO.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2025; their access to digital services is not on record.
TGO.summary:
Registration and documents. CNAR states that after four registration operations between 2023 and 2025, 41,773 Burkinabe officially obtained refugee status in Togo. CNAR states a decentralised operation from 22 May to 16 July 2025 produced and distributed 10,972 refugee identity cards in the Savanes region, produced by the DGDN. The African Development Bank approved a $1 million grant, run by UNHCR with the Togolese authorities over twelve months, that will support the registration and documentation of 5,000 new arrivals in the Savanes region.

Digital services. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

TUN.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

TZA.short: A 2026 source says refugees or displaced people are not registered or are barred from digital services.
TZA.summary:
Registration and documents. GSMA research cited by Biometric Update says refugee women in Tanzania are more likely than men to rely on relatives or citizens to register SIM cards in third-party names because of identity documentation requirements. GSMA states that in Tanzania national identity requirements mean refugee women often rely on local citizens or intermediaries to register SIMs. 2 facts are held on the subject: no news story or official notice read for this study says more about it, the documents the earlier cell cited were not read, and the systems themselves were not examined.

Digital services. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says: is registration or digital inclusion under way.

UGA.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
UGA.summary:
Registration and documents. UNHCR says that by 31 March 2026, 22,474 individuals and 7,746 births were registered through mobile and continuous registration in Uganda. UNHCR says it coordinates the Protection Sector, scaling registration and documentation through mobile and continuous registration, with 30,220 new arrivals registered in Q1 2026. The Office of the Prime Minister says its Department of Refugees receives and documents refugees and issues refugee identity cards, household attestation forms, asylum seeker certificates and conventional travel documents. NIRA says OPM and UNHCR are carrying out a nationwide verification exercise of all registered refugees and asylum seekers.

Digital services. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

ZAF.short: Home Affairs planned a biometric online registration system for asylum seekers in 2026; no source found says whether any are documented.
ZAF.summary:
Registration and documents. In October 2026 Minister Leon Schreiber said Home Affairs is building a biometric online platform for asylum applications, due to work by 10 November 2026. The Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration said the phased system will register intention to apply and book appointments. Each applicant is to get a receipt with personal particulars, biometrics, a reference number and an appointment. Biometric and identity data are to be collected to verify applicants and stop duplicate registrations.

Digital services. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. The nearest held fact: Home Affairs plans a digital asylum registration and appointment system by 10 November 2026.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or asylum seekers are registered and documented with a number stated.

ZMB.short: Registration or a digital service for refugees or displaced people was under way in 2025; documents issued are not on record.
ZMB.summary:
Registration and documents. The Home Affairs Minister announced that applications for refugee travel documents can now be made online through the ZamPortal, integrated into the Government Service Bus. Zambia's Ministry of Home Affairs is launching the Zambia Refugee and Host Communities Project, funded with $30 million by the World Bank with UNHCR support, under which biometric national registration cards will be issued to refugees and former refugees.

Digital services. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Inclusion counted. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. The nearest held fact: the one given above.

Not found. No source found since October 2023 says: are they registered and documented.

ZWE.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
ZWE.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

AGO.short: Angola signed agreements in 2026 for Mozambique and Namibia to use its satellite; no shared link or facility is known to be in service.
AGO.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Angola and Mozambique signed a memorandum in June 2026 under which Mozambique's state telecommunications operator and state broadcaster would carry their signals over Angola's ANGOSAT-2 satellite, with a commercial agreement still to be made final. Angola's space programme office signed a commercial pilot agreement with Telecom Namibia, reported in August 2026, to test the satellite as backhaul for the Namibian network. On land, a company secured a US$31 million loan in November 2023 to pay for a data centre in Luanda and three fibre routes, one of them from Luanda through Lusaka to Dar es Salaam.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The pilot with Telecom Namibia is a test of the satellite on a working network, and the memorandum with Mozambique awaits its commercial agreement.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

BDI.short: Burundi's government adopted a memorandum in 2024 for a fibre link with the DRC; no source found says whether building has started.
BDI.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Burundi's Council of Ministers analysed and adopted a memorandum of understanding on 8 May 2024 for the DRC-Burundi fibre-optic interconnection project. The government communique, reported by the Burundian press agency ABP, describes the project as a joint initiative of the two countries. The memorandum covers a cross-border fibre-optic link between Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the Council of Ministers adopted it at its meeting of 8 May 2024.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The nearest held fact is the same memorandum adopted on 8 May 2024 for the DRC-Burundi fibre-optic interconnection project. It is an agreement to build the link, as reported by ABP on 15 May 2024, and not a link in use.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

BEN.short: A Lagos-Accra fibre route through Benin was announced tested in May 2025; no source found says whether building began or it is in use.
BEN.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. CSquared, Phase3 and SBIN announced on 6 May 2025 a new terrestrial fibre route from Lagos to Accra, running through Ghana, Togo and Benin. The three companies are the parties named to the route. They describe it as configured, activated and tested, and the 6 May 2025 announcement is the latest word held on the route.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The same announcement says the date on which the route will be ready for service has not yet been announced, so the route stands tested and awaiting a service date, as that announcement states. The announcement reports no traffic carried across a border, no capacity sold and no user from another country.

Not found. Nothing found says building has started on a shared link in the last three years, or that a shared link is in service.

BFA.short: A company's fibre cable from Morocco to Niger through Burkina Faso was completed in 2022; no source found reports traffic carried for another country.
BFA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A telecommunications company based in Morocco began investing about US$100 million in 2020 in a terrestrial fibre cable linking Morocco, Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. The cable is the company's own, built to join its subsidiaries in the four countries to its home network, and the investment ran from 2020 to 2022.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The 5,700 km cable is recorded as completed in 2022. It runs from Morocco to Niger through Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso, and lets the company's subsidiary in landlocked Burkina Faso reach international bandwidth over the parent's network. Burkina Faso has no coast, and the cable gives that subsidiary a route over land to the capacity its parent holds.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

BWA.short: A fibre route from the Botswana border to Bulawayo went live in July 2026; no source found reports traffic carried for another country.
BWA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Namibia's MTC and Botswana's BoFiNet signed a memorandum of understanding in Gaborone, reported on 18 February 2026. It provides for cooperation on cross-border fibre interconnection, internet transit and wholesale capacity, and for the development of the corridor between Buitepos, on the Namibian border, and Ngoma. The memorandum is between the two companies, and names the corridor as work to be developed.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A fibre route into Zimbabwe from the Botswana border was live and carrying traffic on 3 July 2026. The two companies behind it describe the section from Plumtree to Bulawayo as the first active route of its network into Zimbabwe and as linking Zimbabwe to Botswana.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

CAF.short: Fibre links to Cameroon and Congo have been in service since February 2023; no source found says how much traffic they carry.
CAF.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The six central African states are developing the Central African Backbone to join their national fibre networks, with about $273 million from member states and partners, as reported in August 2026. The government received grants from the African Development Bank and the European Union for its part of the project. A regional prospectus lists the country among eleven in a USD 9 million project for six new data centres, one of them here, which is still being defined.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The national fibre backbone was inaugurated on 6 February 2023: 935 km of fibre on land and under rivers, joined to Cameroon at Gamboula and to Congo at Bomassa. The project closed in September 2023 with both cross-border links installed. The authorities judged in May 2026 that reaching the sea cables through the networks of coastal neighbours had markedly improved speeds.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire uses a pan-African satellite organisation's capacity, its broadcaster since 2023; no cross-border fibre link is known.
CIV.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The pan-African satellite organisation RASCOM counts Côte d'Ivoire among the countries that use its services, as its director general said on 31 July 2026. The organisation serves the continent as a whole, and Côte d'Ivoire is one of the countries he named.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. RASCOM's director general said on 31 July 2026 that the organisation's services are already in use in Côte d'Ivoire. His example was the national broadcaster, RTI, which used RASCOM satellite capacity during the Africa Cup of Nations in 2023. The user he names is Ivorian. He names no other country's operator using the same capacity, and gives no figure for what is carried.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

CMR.short: A fibre link to the Central African Republic has been in service since February 2023; a route to Chad was suspended in February 2026.
CMR.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Cameroon's and Chad's ministers ended a four-day technical mission on 16 May 2025 that set the completion of the Nana-Mbéré fibre section, towards the Chadian border, for the following fourteen days, with targets running to July 2025. On the Chadian side, the memorandum between two operators for the route from N'Djamena to the Cameroon border was suspended by Chad's regulator, as reported on 9 February 2026, and Chad's government asked the operators to revise it before work could start.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The Central African Republic's fibre backbone was inaugurated on 6 February 2023 with 935 km of fibre installed and working. It joins the Central African Republic to Cameroon at Gamboula, and to Congo, as one part of the Central African Backbone project that the African Development Bank and the European Union paid for.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

COD.short: A fibre route from Goma to Mombasa went live in February 2026 and carries traffic for wholesale customers who are not named.
COD.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Tanzania's foreign minister reaffirmed on 5 September 2026 that Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are pursuing a fibre cable across Lake Tanganyika, from Kigoma to Kalemie, and agreed with the Congolese ambassador to speed it up. The digital ministers of the Central African Republic and the DRC agreed on 8 October 2026 on the need for a fibre link between them to reach the Moanda cable landing. Burundi's Council of Ministers adopted on 8 May 2024 the memorandum for a fibre interconnection with the DRC.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A company activated a 2,000 km fibre route from Mombasa to Goma in February 2026, through Nairobi, Kampala and Kigali, giving the east of the country a direct path to the sea cables on the Kenyan coast. The company said on 9 February 2026 that the route was already carrying traffic for its first wholesale customers, with partner companies in Uganda and Kenya. It said again on 9 September 2026 that the route was live and carrying traffic.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

COG.short: A fibre link to the Central African Republic has been in service since February 2023; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
COG.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The Central African Backbone project was still at work in January 2026 extending Congo's fibre backbone to secondary towns and to neighbouring countries, as an analyst's brief of that month describes it.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The Central African Republic inaugurated its fibre backbone on 6 February 2023, and with it the interconnection with the Republic of Congo at Bomassa, in the presence of a representative of the Congolese telecommunications ministry. The 935 km of fibre were installed and working, and the African Development Bank said the component completed those of Cameroon and Congo. Cables have also been laid across the Congo river to join Brazzaville to Kinshasa, as the January 2026 brief records.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

COM.short: Nothing found names a digital link or facility Comoros shares with another African country, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a digital link or facility the country shares with another African country, or says it has none.

CPV.short: A 2024 loan pays for a branch to a submarine cable reaching South Africa; no source found says building has started.
CPV.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The European Investment Bank signed a EUR 37 million framework loan to Cabo Verde on 2 September 2024. It pays for a branch joining the national network to a new submarine cable from Europe to South Africa. It also pays for an upgrade of the national transmission network and of Cabo Verde Telecom's information systems. The bank's notes put the project's total cost at EUR 80 million. They name the cable as Equiano.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The bank's record of the loan, as accessed in June 2026, lists it as active and shows nothing yet disbursed. The record gives no date for the branch to be built or brought into service.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

DJI.short: A sea cable has joined Djibouti to Somalia and Kenya since 2021; a land corridor to Ethiopia and Sudan was agreed in February 2026.
DJI.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The heads of Djibouti Telecom, Ethio telecom and Sudatel signed in Djibouti on 4 February 2026 the agreement for Horizon, a terrestrial fibre corridor of nearly 2,800 km and 144 fibre pairs joining Djibouti, Addis Ababa and Port Sudan. It turned a memorandum of December 2024 into a binding agreement. The three operators presented the project to prospective carriers in Addis Ababa on 7 September 2026, ahead of deployment and commercial launch.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The DARE1 submarine cable links Djibouti City with Bosaso and Mogadishu in Somalia and Mombasa in Kenya, with 36 terabits a second over three fibre pairs, and has been operational since 2021. Djibouti Telecom announced in 2025 that the cable would be extended south from Mombasa.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

DZA.short: Algeria and Niger opened a 100-gigabit fibre link at Assamaka in October 2026; no source found reports capacity sold or users from Niger.
DZA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Algérie Télécom and Niger Télécom signed a convention in Niamey on 8 September 2026. Under it the Algerian operator gives fibre transmission equipment to set up a link from Agadez to Assamaka, on the Algerian border, with a first capacity of 100 gigabits a second, and the Nigerien operator took delivery of the equipment. On 5 October 2026 Niger's communications ministry reported its minister and an Algerian technical delegation in Agadez to launch the works of the fibre interconnection. In June 2026 Algeria and Tunisia agreed to upgrade the existing terrestrial link between them.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The two countries' ministers launched the operation of the trans-Saharan fibre link at Assamaka on 6 October 2026, joining In-Guezzam in Algeria to the Arlit and Agadez region of Niger at 100 gigabits a second from the start, to carry data traffic between the two countries. Niger's ministry called the link operational the same day, and the national press agency reported the launch.

Not found. No source found reports capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

EGY.short: A fibre cable to Sudan has been in service since 2004; no source found reports traffic carried across it in the last three years.
EGY.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Telecom Egypt and Sudatel signed a cooperation agreement in April 2021. It covers international traffic over the fibre that joins the two countries. The two operators also planned to link Sudatel's landing station at Port Sudan to Telecom Egypt's landing stations on the Red Sea.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Egypt's telecommunications minister opened a 400 km fibre-optic cable to Sudan in October 2004. The Egyptian Telecommunications Company built it in one year for US$4 million, to carry telephone and internet traffic between the two countries. Its president said the cable would serve millions of Sudanese and give Sudan a route to the world through Egypt. The 2021 agreement with Sudatel describes the same fibre as connecting Egypt and Sudan.

Not found. No source found reports the link carrying another country's traffic in the last three years. That would be published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user in the other country.

ERI.short: Eritrea had no international fibre connection in April 2026.
ERI.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A World Bank overview of 2021 found that the planned regional cable along the coast and the regional data projects carried no commitment to serve Asmara.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Eritrea still had no international fibre connection in April 2026, as a commentary on African telecommunications published that month records. The World Bank's regional overview had said in June 2021 that the submarine cable planned along the coast of the Horn of Africa, and the regional data infrastructure projects planned beside it, lacked any commitment to serve the whole region, Asmara included. No agreement with a neighbour, no works and no link in service are recorded for the country in the five years between the two.

Not found.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's operator began deploying a fibre corridor to Djibouti and Sudan in August 2026; it is not yet in service.
ETH.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Ethio telecom, Djibouti Telecom and Sudatel signed a tripartite agreement in Djibouti on 4 February 2026 for Horizon, a terrestrial fibre corridor from Djibouti's cable landing stations across Ethiopia to Sudan's, building on a memorandum signed in Addis Ababa on 3 December 2024. Ethio telecom had moved from planning to deployment by 20 August 2026, with the design settled and materials bought and delivered to site.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The three operators presented Horizon to large cloud companies, carriers and suppliers in Addis Ababa on 7 September 2026, in a phase before commercial launch, to gather interest before the corridor is deployed and opened. The corridor had no announced buyer of capacity and no date for service three days later.

Not found. No source found says a shared link or facility is in service.

GAB.short: Gabon's fibre backbone was joined to Equatorial Guinea's in November 2025; no source found reports traffic carried across the border.
GAB.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Gabon and Equatorial Guinea signed an agreement on joining their fibre networks at Mongomo on 10 November 2025, between the two ministers for the digital economy. The agreement and the inauguration of the link fell on the same day.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The two ministers inaugurated the interconnection of the national fibre backbones on 10 November 2025, at Meyo-Kyé on the Gabonese side and Ebebeyin on the Equatoguinean. Gabon's backbone company reports that tests confirmed traffic exchanged across the border. An earlier phase of the Central African Backbone programme paid, from 2012, for a backbone from Libreville through Franceville to the Congolese border, on a World Bank loan of US$58 million.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

GHA.short: A fibre route from Accra to Lagos through Togo and Benin runs in service as of 2025; no traffic carried across the border is reported.
GHA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. CSquared, Phase3 and SBIN announced on 6 May 2025 a new terrestrial fibre route from Lagos to Accra through Ghana, Togo and Benin. The announcement describes the route as configured, activated and tested, and gives no date yet for it to be ready for service. The route is a new one, separate from the infrastructure the same company already runs between the two cities.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. CSquared said on 11 August 2025 that its existing infrastructure runs from Accra to Lagos. It said that this is now integrated with a new route from Abidjan to Monrovia, which ties the Accra to Lagos fibre to a link between Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia in one West African backbone.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

GIN.short: Guinea agreed in 2024 and 2025 with Sierra Leone and Mali to join fibre networks; no source found reports a link in service.
GIN.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Guinea and Sierra Leone signed an agreement in November 2024 to join their national internet backbone networks, as Sierra Leone's regulator records. Guinea's backbone company and its Sierra Leonean counterpart then signed an interconnection agreement in Conakry, reported on 23 June 2025, to link the two fibre networks at Pamelap on the border. In June 2024 Guinea's backbone company and Mali's SMTD agreed, with ministry facilitation, to interconnect the two countries' fibre networks.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The interconnection agreement sets a first capacity of 42.5 gigabits a second at Pamelap and plans 100 gigabits a second by 2026. Those are the terms of the agreement between the two backbone companies. Sierra Leone's regulator, writing in November 2025, described the agreement of the year before and did not describe a link carrying traffic.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

GMB.short: Gambia's national operator held a backup link through a Senegalese operator in 2026; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
GMB.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Gamtel, the national operator, lists on its company profile a backup link with the Senegalese operator Free. The link, named Cross Gambia (CG2), has a capacity of 28 gigabits a second. The profile carries no date of its own. It was captured on 21 September 2026.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Gamtel says that when the ACE submarine cable fails, its traffic is rerouted automatically over the link with Free. Its main international capacity is 25 gigabits a second on ACE, through four separate gateways. That capacity is bought from the Portuguese and French operators. The company gives the link through Senegal as the basis of its 99.9 per cent redundancy.

Not found. No source found reports the link carrying another country's traffic in the last three years. That would be published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user in the other country.

GNB.short: A shared submarine cable was agreed in April 2023 and unfunded in June 2024; nothing newer is known, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not found. No shared digital link or facility agreed, being built or in service in the last three years is held, and no source from those years says the country has none. The Amilcar Cabral submarine cable was agreed in April 2023 and was still unfunded in June 2024.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea's fibre backbone was joined to Gabon's in November 2025; no source found reports traffic carried across the border.
GNQ.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Equatorial Guinea and Gabon signed an agreement on joining their fibre networks at Mongomo on 10 November 2025, between the two ministers for the digital economy. The agreement and the inauguration of the link fell on the same day.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The two ministers inaugurated the physical and logical interconnection of the national fibre backbones on 10 November 2025, at Ebebeyin on the Equatoguinean side and Meyo-Kyé on the Gabonese. Gabon's backbone company reports that tests confirmed a stable exchange of traffic between Bitam and Ebebeyin, the two border towns, and between Libreville and Bata, the two countries' main coastal cities. The inauguration was held on the day the two governments signed their agreement.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

KEN.short: Kenya has had fibre links to Uganda and Tanzania since 2025, and a route to eastern Congo live since February 2026.
KEN.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Kenya's and Tanzania's governments launched a cross-border project at the Lunga Lunga and Horohoro border on 20 July 2025, to join Kenya's national fibre backbone and its submarine cable landings to Tanzania's network. Kenya's ICT Authority and Tanzania's state telecommunications company carry it out.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A company completed a fibre network from Mombasa to Kampala in May 2025, and Tanzania's state telecommunications company and Kenya's ICT Authority put a terrestrial fibre link from Dar es Salaam to Mombasa into operation in July 2025. A 2,000 km route from Mombasa to Goma, through Nairobi, Kampala and Kigali, was activated in February 2026, and its owner said it was already carrying traffic for its first wholesale customers.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

LBR.short: Orange Liberia's new fibre link connects through Côte d'Ivoire and was reported in service in May 2025; no traffic from another country is known.
LBR.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Orange Liberia says it has completed a new fibre link from Monrovia to Lugato, reported in May 2025. The operator says the link joins Liberia to six other undersea cables by way of Côte d'Ivoire. The route is Liberia's connection to the cable systems of its neighbour, and it is built rather than planned, so no work is still pending on it.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The same Monrovia-to-Lugato link is in service. Orange Liberia's chairman says it carried all of Liberia's international traffic during the outage on the Africa Coast to Europe cable in 2025. The traffic he names is Liberia's own, sent out through Côte d'Ivoire. He names no other country's operator on the link, and gives no figure for capacity sold across the border.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

LBY.short: A Mediterranean sea cable joining Libya to Morocco, Tunisia and Egypt was inaugurated in May 2025; no source found reports traffic between them.
LBY.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A Libyan company signed a contract in November 2023 to connect Libya to the Medusa submarine cable, a system that the same account says links Libya with Morocco, Tunisia and Egypt among others. A project official said in October 2026 that Libya's fibre link to the Chadian border, already built to the Egyptian border, should be finished by the end of 2026.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Libya's state telecommunications holding company inaugurated the Medusa submarine cable at Misrata on 10 May 2025. The system is 8,700 km long and joins Libya to other Mediterranean countries, Morocco, Tunisia and Egypt among them. The inauguration at Misrata is the Libyan landing; the account of it gives no figure for traffic between Libya and the three African countries, and names no operator in any of them that uses the Libyan landing.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

LSO.short: South Africa's state wholesaler said in 2019 that its network reached Lesotho; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
LSO.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. South Africa's state wholesaler Broadband Infraco said in July 2019 that its regional network reached the borders of all six land neighbours. Lesotho is one of those six countries. The company was then upgrading its route to Botswana and adding redundancy to it. It said it expected to take a leading role in a planned regional fibre project, the SADC superhighway.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Broadband Infraco said in July 2019 that it provided connectivity to all six neighbouring countries, Lesotho included. Its chief executive said the company acted as the gateway to international capacity for South Africa's landlocked neighbours. Lesotho, surrounded by South Africa, is one of them.

Not found. No source found reports the link carrying another country's traffic in the last three years. That would be published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user in the other country.

MAR.short: A company's fibre cable from Morocco to Niger was completed in 2022; no source found reports traffic carried for the countries along it.
MAR.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A Moroccan telecommunications company's terrestrial fibre cable runs from Morocco to Niger through Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso. It is 5,700 km long and belongs to the company, which has subsidiaries in each of the four countries, and which invested about one billion dirhams in it between 2020 and 2022.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The cable is recorded as completed in 2022. Morocco is the end of it that reaches the sea, and the four countries along it are those where the company's subsidiaries trade. The record of the investment names the route and its length and gives the year the work ended. It gives no figure for the traffic the cable carries into Morocco from the south, and names no operator outside the company's own group that uses it.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

MDG.short: A cable owner plans landings in Madagascar by 2028; no agreement or link shared with another African country is known, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not found. No shared link or facility agreed or being built in the last three years, or in service, is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has none.

MLI.short: Mali and Senegal inaugurated a backbone interconnection in October 2026, and a Morocco-to-Niger cable was completed in 2022; no source found reports traffic carried.
MLI.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. In June 2024 Mali's SMTD and Guinea's SOGEB agreed to interconnect the two countries' fibre networks. A telecommunications company based in Morocco began investing about US$100 million in 2020 in a terrestrial fibre cable linking Morocco, Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. The cable is the company's own, and the investment ran from 2020 to 2022.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. On 5 October 2026 SENUM SA of Senegal and SMTD-SA of Mali inaugurated the interconnection of their national fibre-optic backbones at the Kidira-Diboli border bridge, described by a speaker as the putting into service of the infrastructure. The 5,700 km Morocco-to-Niger cable is recorded as completed in 2022 and lets the company's subsidiary in landlocked Mali reach international bandwidth over the parent's network. Afribone Mali says its international links run over fibre via Dakar and Abidjan to the submarine cables ACE and MainOne.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

MOZ.short: A fibre link between Mozambique and Zambia was commissioned in February 2026; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
MOZ.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A development fund and a telecommunications group announced in May 2023 a partnership to build a terrestrial fibre network of some US$320 million, linking landlocked countries to the sea cables on Africa's east and west coasts, and named Mozambique among the twelve countries it would cover.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Zambia and Mozambique commissioned a cross-border fibre interconnector between Chanida and Cassacatiza, at a ceremony reported on 23 February 2026 at which Zambia's technology minister and Mozambique's communications minister both spoke. The interconnector joins Zambia's national backbone to Mozambique's network and, through it, to the submarine cables that land on the Mozambican coast. For Zambia, which has no coast, it is a route to the sea; for Mozambique it is a link that carries a neighbour's traffic to its landings.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

MRT.short: A company's fibre cable from Morocco to Niger through Mauritania was completed in 2022; no source found reports traffic carried for another country.
MRT.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A telecommunications company based in Morocco began investing about US$100 million in 2020 in a terrestrial fibre cable linking Morocco, Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. The cable is the company's own, built to join its subsidiaries in the four countries to its home network, and the investment ran from 2020 to 2022.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The 5,700 km cable is recorded as completed in 2022. It runs from Morocco to Niger through Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso, and lets the company's subsidiary in Mauritania reach international bandwidth over the parent's network. Mauritania is one of the four countries the cable serves, and the company has a subsidiary there as it has in the other three.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

MUS.short: A submarine cable has joined Mauritius to Madagascar and South Africa since 2021; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
MUS.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The METISS cable was built by a consortium of six Indian Ocean operators, among them CEB and Emtel of Mauritius. Its members paid the cost of about EUR 50 million themselves. It was laid from March 2020 and reached each landing in June 2020. Its entry into service then waited on landing agreements in South Africa and on training for the operating teams.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. METISS entered service on 5 March 2021, a 3,200 km cable joining Mauritius, Réunion and Madagascar to a landing near Durban in South Africa. The consortium said its first links to Africa were already used by its operators' customers. It measured transit times to South Africa below 50 milliseconds.

Not found. No source found reports the link carrying another country's traffic in the last three years. That would be published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user in the other country.

MWI.short: Malawi's TNM ran its internet over fibre links to Zambia and Mozambique in 2024; no source found reports traffic carried for those countries.
MWI.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Africa50 and Bayobab (MTN Group) partnered on 15 May 2023 to develop Project East2West, a US$320 million to US$325 million terrestrial fibre network joining landlocked countries to the subsea cables on the east and west coasts. Malawi is among the countries the document names as covered, and it reports no start of construction.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. TNM, a Malawian mobile operator, says its internet runs over cross-border fibre links to Zambia, through Mchinji and Chipata, and to Mozambique, through Muloza and Mulanje. The operator restored or acquired both links in May 2024, after sea cable cuts disrupted its service, and the report does not say whether either link carries traffic for a user in Zambia or Mozambique.

Not found. No source found reports a link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

NAM.short: Namibia signed agreements with Angola in June 2026 on a sea cable and a satellite; neither is known to be in service.
NAM.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Telecom Namibia signed a master service agreement with Angola Telecom and a cable company on 12 June 2026 to join the Southern African Regional Submarine System to the Equiano cable at its Swakopmund landing station. Telecom Namibia hosts the landing and provides Angola Telecom with one terabit a second on Equiano. The agreement builds on a memorandum and commercial terms signed in April 2026. Telecom Namibia also signed a pilot commercial agreement with Angola's space programme office that week, for a trial of the Angosat-2 satellite on its working network.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The satellite pilot is a trial, with a full commercial launch to follow it. It came after talks that began in June 2025 and a proof of concept reported in October 2025.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

NER.short: A company's fibre cable from Morocco reached Niger in 2022; Niger's own fibre to five borders was built by November 2025.
NER.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Niger's minister took provisional delivery on 14 November 2025 of the country's part of the trans-Saharan fibre backbone: 1,031 km on five routes to the Algerian, Chadian, Nigerian, Beninese and Burkinabe borders, built with African Development Bank money. Niger and Chad signed a memorandum on joining the two sides on 19 June 2025. The project's steering committee adopted its work programme for 2026 and 2027 on 13 March 2026.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A Moroccan telecommunications company's 5,700 km terrestrial cable from Morocco to Niger, through Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso, is recorded as completed in 2022, and joins the company's subsidiary in landlocked Niger to international bandwidth. The link to Algeria was declared operational at Assamaka on 6 October 2026, after 30 September 2026.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

NGA.short: A fibre route from Lagos to Dakar was activated in May 2025; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
NGA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A Nigerian fibre company and Equatorial Guinea's minister for transport and telecommunications signed an agreement in Malabo in February 2026 for a direct submarine fibre cable between Nigeria and Equatorial Guinea, with a commercial data centre. It is an agreement of principles that follows a state visit of August 2024, and its specifications, cost and timetable were not disclosed. CSquared, Phase3 and SBIN also announced on 6 May 2025 a terrestrial fibre route from Lagos to Accra through Benin, Togo and Ghana, with no date yet for it to be ready for service.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A Nigerian fibre company and a Senegalese operator activated a 3,500 km terrestrial fibre route from Lagos to Dakar, reported on 9 May 2025. The route runs through Benin, Togo and Ghana. Lagos and Dakar are its two ends. Commercial availability and service packages were still to be announced at that date, and no figure for traffic on the route has been published.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

RWA.short: Rwanda and three neighbours resolved in 2026 to study a shared satellite; no link agreed or in service is known, so no stage is set.
RWA.summary: Not found. No shared link or facility agreed or being built in the last three years, or in service, is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has none.

SDN.short: Sudan's operator signed a binding agreement in February 2026 for a fibre corridor to Ethiopia and Djibouti; no source found reports building in Sudan.
SDN.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Sudatel signed a tripartite agreement with Djibouti Telecom and Ethio telecom on 4 February 2026 for Horizon, a terrestrial fibre corridor from Djibouti's cable landing stations through Ethiopia to Sudan's, following a memorandum of December 2024. The corridor is planned at about 2,800 km with 144 fibre pairs, joining Djibouti, Addis Ababa and Port Sudan. Sudan's state news agency reported the agreement the same day.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The three operators presented Horizon to large cloud companies and carriers in Addis Ababa on 7 September 2026, in a phase before deployment and commercial launch. The corridor had no announced buyer of capacity and no date for service three days later.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

SEN.short: A fibre route from Dakar to Lagos was activated in May 2025; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
SEN.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A Senegalese operator and a Nigerian fibre company built a terrestrial fibre route of 3,500 km between Dakar and Lagos, crossing Ghana, Togo and Benin. It is a route agreed and built between two companies, and no government is named as a party to it.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The two companies activated the route, as reported on 9 May 2025. Commercial availability and service packages were still to be announced at that date. Dakar and Lagos are its two ends, and Senegal is named at one of them. No figure for traffic on it has been published, and no operator from the countries it crosses is named as a customer.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone and Guinea agreed in 2024 and 2025 to join their fibre networks at the border; no source found reports a link in service.
SLE.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Sierra Leone and Guinea signed an agreement in November 2024 to join their national internet backbone networks, as Sierra Leone's regulator records. Guinea's backbone company and its Sierra Leonean counterpart then signed an interconnection agreement in Conakry, reported on 23 June 2025, to link the two fibre networks at Pamelap on the border.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The interconnection agreement sets a first capacity of 42.5 gigabits a second at Pamelap and plans 100 gigabits a second by 2026. Those are the terms of the agreement between the two backbone companies. The regulator, writing in November 2025, described the agreement of the year before and did not describe a link carrying traffic.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

SOM.short: A sea cable has joined Somalia to Djibouti and Kenya since 2021; no source found reports traffic carried between them.
SOM.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Somalia signed a grant of SDR 59.5 million with the World Bank's fund for the poorest countries on 21 June 2023, to pay for cross-border terrestrial links and backbone in Somalia and Somaliland, under a regional project shared with South Sudan and two regional bodies. The project had prepared the ground for fibre by 30 June 2026, with deployment in Somaliland expected to begin in the second half of the year.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The DARE1 submarine cable has been operational since 2021. It joins Bosaso and Mogadishu in Somalia to Djibouti City and to Mombasa in Kenya. Somalia has two landings on it, one on the northern coast and one at the capital.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

SSD.short: South Sudan invited bids in September 2026 for a fibre route towards Kenya; nothing shared is known to be in service.
SSD.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. South Sudan's ministry invited international bids, reported on 14 September 2026, for about 397 km of terrestrial fibre from Juba to Nadapal, towards the Kenyan border, paid for by a World Bank grant under a regional project. The same project counts the first memorandum on cross-border digital connectivity between Kenya and South Sudan as signed, in its report of June 2026. South Sudan also gave a company a fifteen-year licence in October 2025 to build and run national and cross-border fibre networks.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The Juba to Nadapal route is at the stage of procurement, with bids closing on 26 October 2026. The works it would pay for have not been let.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

STP.short: A sea cable joining São Tomé and Príncipe to Côte d'Ivoire has been in service since 2013; no source found reports traffic carried.
STP.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. São Tomé and Príncipe joined the consortium of the Africa Coast to Europe cable in 2010, through a construction and maintenance agreement signed by its telecommunications company. The cable arrived in the country in November 2011, on a World Bank grant that took effect that July.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The cable was commercially launched in February 2013, after tests across the sixteen countries it connects. The segment from Côte d'Ivoire to São Tomé and Príncipe was among those in service in its first phase, and the landing station in São Tomé had been inaugurated in October 2012. The cable links Europe with the west and southern African coast, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea among its other landings.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

SWZ.short: Eswatini's access fund set up a route to Maputo over a power line's fibre, reported in 2023; no source found reports a link in service.
SWZ.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Eswatini's universal access fund and the national backbone operator set up an alternative route to the east, joining the national backbone to Maputo, in Mozambique, over the fibre strung on a regional power transmission line. The fund bought the equipment needed to connect to that fibre. Its account of the work was published on 3 October 2023.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The fund's account of the Maputo route describes it as an alternative route for the national backbone, running east. Eswatini has no coast, and all its international traffic leaves through a neighbour. The fund reports the equipment bought and the route set up. It gives no date on which traffic began to run over it, no capacity, and no figure for what the route carries.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

SYC.short: Submarine cables have joined Seychelles to Kenya, Djibouti and Tanzania, the newest since 2022; no source found reports traffic carried across them.
SYC.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Seychelles Cable Systems, owned by the government and two operators, signed a contract in 2018 for a branch of the PEACE cable to reach the islands. Laying of the system was completed in October 2022. The company paid for the PEACE branch itself; the African Development Bank and the European Investment Bank had helped finance SEAS.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Operators in Seychelles could carry traffic over PEACE from 16 November 2022. The 15,000 km cable connects Pakistan, Seychelles, Kenya, Djibouti and France. The older SEAS cable connects Seychelles and Tanzania and was the country's first international cable; in May 2023 one operator still relied on it for its international traffic.

Not found. No source found reports the link carrying another country's traffic in the last three years. That would be published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user in the other country.

TCD.short: Chad's part of a trans-Saharan fibre backbone was 60 per cent built in February 2026; no shared link is known to be in service.
TCD.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Chad's part of the trans-Saharan fibre backbone, which is to join it to Niger and through Niger to the Mediterranean, was 60 per cent complete in February 2026. Works began in 2023 with €29 million from the European Union, stood at 32 per cent in March 2025, well behind a ten-month schedule, and were found slowed, with one site vandalised, at an inspection in January 2026. A Libyan project official said in October 2026 that Libya's fibre link to the Chadian border should be finished by the end of 2026, with the connection to Chad under way with Chadian authorities and operators.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The fibre route from N'Djamena to the Cameroon border had not been started in February 2026. The memorandum between two operators for it, signed in April 2025, was suspended by Chad's regulator over clauses touching sovereignty, and the government asked the operators on 9 February 2026 to reopen talks.

Not found. No source found says a shared link or facility is in service.

TGO.short: Togo's Equiano landing station carried Ghanaian operators' traffic in 2024; no source found reports the Lagos-Accra route's service date.
TGO.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. CSquared, Phase3 and SBIN announced on 6 May 2025 a new terrestrial fibre route from Lagos to Accra through Ghana, Togo and Benin. The announcement describes the route as configured, activated and tested, and gives no date yet for it to be ready for service. It adds a path between Nigeria and Ghana that crosses Togo, announced jointly by CSquared with Phase3 and SBIN.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. CSquared's chief executive said in March 2024 that the company had connected its cross-border circuits from Togo into Ghana and Benin. He said it had provided capacity to MTN Ghana and Vodafone Ghana through the Equiano landing station in Lomé, according to the March 2024 report in Capacity.

Not found. Nothing found gives the date the Lagos to Accra route is ready for service, or figures for capacity sold or traffic carried across Togo's borders.

TUN.short: Tunisia and Algeria agreed in June 2026 to upgrade their existing terrestrial link; no source found says whether any building has started.
TUN.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Delegations of the Algeria-Tunisia Joint Technical Commission agreed on 6 June 2026 to upgrade the existing terrestrial link between Algeria and Tunisia, as reported by Ecofin in June 2026. The agreement concerns a link that is already in place between the two countries, and it is the one shared digital link between Tunisia and another African country that the evidence names.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Nothing found gives capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user on the Algerian side, for any year. The nearest held fact is the June 2026 agreement between the Algeria-Tunisia Joint Technical Commission delegations to upgrade the existing terrestrial link between the two countries.

Not found. No source found says building has started in the last three years.

TZA.short: A fibre link from Dar es Salaam to Mombasa has been in service since July 2025, with Kenyan companies using it; no source reports volumes.
TZA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Tanzania's and Kenya's ministers launched a cross-border project at the Horohoro and Lunga Lunga border on 20 July 2025, to join Tanzania's network to Kenya's national fibre backbone and submarine cable landings. Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo agreed to speed up a fibre cable across Lake Tanganyika, from Kigoma to Kalemie, as reported on 5 September 2026.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Tanzania's state telecommunications company and Kenya's ICT Authority put a terrestrial fibre link from Dar es Salaam to Mombasa into operation in July 2025. Tanzania and Kenya launched a redundancy route of the national fibre network at the Horohoro border post on 20 July 2025. The state telecommunications company says it runs at 1.6 Tbps, and several Kenyan companies have started using it.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

UGA.short: A fibre network from Kampala to Mombasa was completed in May 2025; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
UGA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A development fund and a telecommunications group announced in May 2023 a partnership to build a terrestrial fibre network of some USD 320 million, linking landlocked countries to the sea cables on Africa's coasts, and named Uganda among the countries it would cover.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A subsidiary of that telecommunications group completed a fibre network linking Mombasa, in Kenya, to Kampala in May 2025. Uganda has no coast, and the network is a route to the Kenyan port owned by a single company from end to end. A second account gives the same month and the same two cities. Neither gives the network's capacity, a figure for traffic, or the name of a Ugandan operator that buys capacity on it.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

ZAF.short: A cable to Mauritius has run since 2021 and a fibre route to Kenya since 2023; no source found reports traffic carried across them.
ZAF.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. Google said in May 2024 that the land section of its Umoja fibre route had been built, working with a pan-African carrier. The route runs from Kenya through Uganda, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia and Zimbabwe to South Africa. Its crossing of the Indian Ocean to Australia had still to be laid.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The METISS submarine cable entered service on 5 March 2021, joining Mauritius, Réunion and Madagascar to a landing near Durban. Liquid Dataport launched a land-only fibre route from Mombasa to Johannesburg in May 2023. It crosses Uganda, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The state wholesaler Broadband Infraco said in July 2019 that its network reached all six land neighbours. It said its point of presence at Beitbridge carried Zimbabwe's broadband traffic to data centres in Johannesburg.

Not found. No source found reports the link carrying another country's traffic in the last three years. That would be published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a named user in the other country.

ZMB.short: A fibre link between Zambia and Mozambique was commissioned in February 2026; no source found reports traffic carried across it.
ZMB.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A development fund and a telecommunications group announced in May 2023 a partnership to build a terrestrial fibre network of some US$320 million, linking landlocked countries to the sea cables on Africa's east and west coasts, and listed Zambia among the countries it would cover.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. Zambia and Mozambique commissioned a cross-border fibre interconnector between Chanida and Cassacatiza, reported on 23 February 2026. It joins Zambia's national backbone to Mozambique's submarine cable network, and so gives Zambia, which has no coast, a route to the sea. A World Bank project document had said in January 2025 that cross-border infrastructure between countries was missing in Zambia and that this held back digital trade.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

ZWE.short: A fibre route from the Botswana border to Bulawayo went live in July 2026; an extension to Zambia is being built.
ZWE.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A Zimbabwean company and a regional fibre company signed a partnership agreement in June 2025 to invest together in long-distance fibre on a corridor joining Botswana, Zimbabwe and Zambia. The second phase, from Bulawayo to Livingstone in Zambia, was being built in July 2026 and was due to be lit in September 2026.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The first phase, from Plumtree on the Botswana border to Bulawayo, was live and carrying traffic on 3 July 2026, with 800 gigabits a second of equipped capacity. The companies call it the first active route of the regional company's network into Zimbabwe, linking the country to Botswana. A newspaper column of September 2026 describes the same link as active, and reports another operator expanding capacity on the crossings to Zambia, Botswana and South Africa.

Not found. No source found reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

AGO.short: Angola ratified the African Union's cyber security and data protection convention in 2020; no national law giving effect to it is known.
AGO.summary:
African digital law signed and ratified. The African Union's register of its Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection, known as the Malabo Convention, dated 2 February 2026 records Angola as having ratified it on 21 February 2020 and deposited the instrument on 11 May 2020. The register counts 21 signatures and 20 instruments deposited among the Union's 55 member states, and the convention has been in force since 8 June 2023. Angola's Resolution 33/19 of 9 July 2019 is the national instrument on the convention.

Taken into national law and applied across a border. No national law, decree or regulation passed to give effect to a shared African legal text is recorded for Angola, and nor is a licence or signature recognised, a request between authorities answered or a ruling under one. The African Union's register lists the dates each state signed, ratified and deposited, and says nothing of national law.

A regional data governance workshop was held in Senegal in May 2026. Senegal is one of ten members of the West African Backbone Network and hosted its ministers' meeting in Dakar on 8 October 2026.
